(2) External sandhi is decomposed with ^. (3) Prose sections are subdivided by a.
b, c, etc.
***************************************************************** = Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstraṃ = (Book 1: Concerning the Subject of Training)
(Chapter 1: Enumeration of Sections and Books) Oṃ. Homage to Śukra and Bṛhaspati.

Having for the most part compiled all the treatises on statecraft (*artha-śāstra*) concerning the acquisition and protection of the earth that were previously established by former teachers, this single treatise on statecraft has been composed.
This is the enumeration of the topics and the sections thereof.
The exposition of knowledge, the exposition of the elders,
and the conquest of the senses.
The recruitment of ministers; the recruitment of counselors and domestic chaplains;
and the testing of ministers' integrity or lack thereof through secret trials.
The employment of secret agents;

the protection of the factions of those who should be won over and those who should not be won over within one's own territory; and the winning over of the factions of those who should be won over and those who should not be won over in the territory of an enemy.
KAZ01.1.03c: The section on counsel, the dispatch of envoys, and the protection of the prince.
The conduct of one under restraint,
the behavior toward one under restraint, and the king’s secret agent.
The end of the night's duties and self-protection— this is the first section concerning discipline.
The settlement of the countryside, the filling of gaps in the territory,
and the construction of fortresses.
The establishment of fortresses, the work of the storekeeper and the accumulation of stores,
and the dispatching of revenue by the collector-general.
In the section on dice (akṣapaṭala), the jurisdiction of the comptroller (gāṇanikya) consists of:
the recovery of revenue embezzled by officials,
and the examination of expenditures.
The administration of the government, the examination of gems to be entered into the treasury, and the management of mines and manufactories.
In the gambling hall,
the Superintendent of Gold shall oversee the operations of the goldsmiths in the market street, as well as the Superintendent of the Granary.
The Superintendent of Commerce, the Superintendent of Forest Produce, and the Superintendent of Armaments.
Weights, measures, and coinage; the measurement of space and time; and the superintendent of tolls.
The superintendent of textiles,
the superintendent of agriculture,
and the superintendent of liquor.
The superintendent of slaughterhouses,
the superintendent of courtesans,
and the superintendent of boats.
The superintendent of cattle, the superintendent of horses, and the superintendent of elephants.
The superintendent of chariots, the superintendent of infantry, and the conduct of the commander-in-chief.
The Superintendent of Minting,
the Superintendent of Pasture Lands,
and the Conduct of the Collector-General.
Spies disguised as householders, merchants, and ascetics, and the appointment of the city prefect— this concludes the second book, titled "The Activity of the Superintendent."
The establishment of legal procedure,
the recording of the points of dispute,
and matters concerning marriage.
Partition of inheritance, building sites, and non-performance of agreements.
Recovery of debts,
deposits,
and the rules concerning slaves and laborers.
Joint undertakings,
rescission of sale and purchase,
and the non-repayment of what has been given; KAZ01.1.05b.
Sale without ownership, the relationship between property and its owner, and violence.
Harshness of speech, harshness of punishment, gambling, and betting.
The miscellaneous [section]— thus ends the third book, the Dharma-sthīya.
The protection of artisans and laborers,
the protection of merchants,
and the counteraction of calamities.

Protection of those who live by secret means; the exposure of spies disguised as students by means of perfected agents; and the apprehension of those suspected of performing acts of a suspicious nature.
The examination of sudden deaths, the investigation of speech and actions, and the protection of all administrative offices.
The ransom for the injury of a single limb; the rules for punishment consisting of both simple and diverse forms; and the violation of a maiden.
Penalties for transgressions—thus ends the fourth book, "The Purification of Thorns."
Punitive measures,
replenishment of the treasury,
and the maintenance of dependents.
The conduct of dependents, customary practices, and the consolidation of the kingdom.
"Uniqueness of sovereignty"—thus ends the fifth section, the "Practice of Yoga."
The endowments of the constituent elements,
and tranquility and exertion— this is the source of the circle of states, the sixth book.
The enumeration of the six measures of policy,
the determination of decline, stability, and growth,
and the conduct of seeking refuge.
Devotion to the qualities of those who are equal, inferior, or superior;
making peace with the inferior;
and remaining in a state of neutrality after declaring war.
Making peace and remaining stationary,
waging war and marching, making peace and marching—
Marching in concert;
consideration regarding the seizure of the enemy to be attacked and the neutral power;
and the causes of decline, greed, and disaffection among the constituent elements of the state.
Deliberation with the confederates;
marching after forming an alliance; treaties concluded with stipulations, without stipulations, or involving a withdrawal.
The dual policy consisting of peace and war, the conduct toward an enemy to be attacked, and the specific types of allies worthy of support— these are the topics.
Treaties for the sake of allies, gold, land, and works;
consideration regarding the rear-attacker;
and the replenishment of deficient power.
Causes for siege after engaging in conflict with a powerful king;
the conduct of one who has submitted by force; the conduct of one who has been brought under subjection by force.
The act of reconciliation, the release from meditative absorption, and conduct in the middle way.
The conduct of the neutral king and the conduct of the circle of kings— thus concludes the seventh book, "The Sixfold Policy."
The section on the calamities of the constituent elements; the consideration of the calamities of the king and the kingdom; and the section on the calamities of men.
The section on oppression, the section on obstructions,
and the section on attachment to the treasury.
The section on the calamities of friends—thus ends the eighth book concerning calamities.
Knowledge of power, place, time, strength, and weakness; the times for marching; and the times for mobilizing the army.
The qualities of the armor,
the function of counter-force,
and consideration of subsequent hostility.
Remedies for internal and external uprisings of the constituent elements—KAZ 1.1.11b:
consideration of loss, expenditure, and gain;
and external and internal calamities.

Those [women] who are associated with wicked men or enemies, or who are involved in matters of gain, loss, and doubt— their successes arising from various strategic means— constitute the ninth book, titled "The Operation of an Attack."
The encampment of the army, the marching of the army,
and protection against the calamities of the forces and the time of attack.
The varieties of treacherous warfare,
the encouragement of one's own army, and the deployment of one's own forces against those of the enemy.
The battlefields; the maneuvers of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants;
and the division of the army's front into the wings, the flanks, and the center.
The classification of the strong and the weak forces;
the combat of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants;
and the formation of arrays in the staff, snake, circle, and detached configurations.
The deployment of counter-arrays—thus ends the tenth book, concerning military affairs.
The means of sowing dissension and silent punishments— thus ends the eleventh book, "The Conduct of Corporations."
The duties of an envoy, war by means of counsel, the slaying of army commanders, and inciting the circle of states.
The employment of weapons, fire, and poison; the destruction of supplies, reinforcements, and outposts;
and the application of strategic deception.
Punishment, overreaching, and single victory— this is the twelfth book, "Concerning the Stronger," consisting of twelve chapters.
Sowing dissension, the strategic subjugation by means of stratagem,
the employment of secret agents,
and the act of siege.
Assault and the pacification of what has been acquired— these constitute the thirteenth book, "The Means of Capturing a Fortress."
The employment of means to destroy the enemy's forces,
deception, and countermeasures against injuries to one's own forces— this is the fourteenth book, "Secret Means" (Aupanishadika).
KAZ01.1.17: The methods of exposition (tantra-yukti)—thus concludes the fifteenth book, "The Methods of Exposition."
KAZ01.1.18: The exposition of the treatise consists of fifteen books, one hundred and eighty sections, one hundred and fifty chapters, and six thousand verses.
This treatise, composed by Kauṭilya, is easy to grasp and understand, its words determined according to their true meaning,
and it is free from the prolixity of redundant explanations.
(i) Establishing (the necessity of) philosophy:
KAZ01.2.01 / Philosophy, the three Vedas, commerce and agriculture, and the science of government— these are the branches of knowledge.
The three Vedas, commerce, and the science of government—so say the followers of Manu.
For Ānvīkṣikī is indeed a specific branch of the Trayī.
"Commerce and the science of government," say the followers of Bṛhaspati.
"For the triple Veda is merely a means of concealment for those who know the ways of the world."
"The science of government (daṇḍanīti) is the sole science," say the followers of Uśanas.
For it is upon this that all undertakings of knowledge depend.
"There are only four branches of learning," says Kauṭilya.
KAZ01.2.09: That by means of which one may know dharma and artha—that is the "science-ness" (vidyātva) of the sciences.
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Lokāyata constitute Ānvīkṣikī.

By investigating through these means of reasoning the nature of virtue and vice in the triple science (trayī), profit and loss in commerce (vārttā), and right policy and wrong policy in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), as well as strength and weakness, it benefits the world; it stabilizes the intellect during times of adversity and prosperity, and it produces proficiency in wisdom, speech, and action.

Anvīkṣikī is eternally considered the lamp of all sciences, the means for all actions, and the foundation of all duties. KAZ01.2.12ab/ pradīpaḥ sarva-vidyānām upāyaḥ sarva-karmaṇām / KAZ01.2.12cd/ āśrayaḥ sarva-dharmāṇāṃ śaśvad ānvīkṣikī matā //E Establishing (the necessity of) [Anvīkṣikī]
In the Vedic lore, the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajus Vedas are the three; these three constitute the Trayī.
The Atharvaveda and the Itihāsaveda are also Vedas.
The auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) are phonetics (śikṣā), ritual liturgy (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chanda-viciti), and astronomy (jyotiṣa).
This dharma of the three Vedas is beneficial for the four castes and the four stages of life by means of establishing them in their respective duties.
KAZ01.3.05: The specific duty of a Brāhmaṇa consists of studying, teaching, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
For a Kṣatriya, the duties are study, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, living by the sword, and the protection of beings.
For the Vaiśya, there are study, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.
For a Śūdra, the duties are service to the twice-born, the occupations of trade and agriculture, and the work of artisans and performers.

For the householder, livelihood through his own duty, marriage with those of equal status but not from the same ancestral lineage (*ṛṣi*), approaching one's wife during her season, honoring gods, ancestors, and guests, generosity toward dependents, and eating only what remains [after these obligations] constitute his specific dharma.

For a religious student (brahmacārin), there shall be the private recitation of the Veda, the tending of the sacred fires, the ritual bathing, and the vow of living on alms; his livelihood may last until the end of his life with his teacher, or, in the absence of the teacher, with the teacher’s son or a fellow student.

For the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), there is lifelong celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair and animal skins, performing the fire-sacrifice and ritual ablutions, honoring the deities, ancestors, and guests, and subsisting on forest-grown food.

For the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), there is the conquest of the senses, non-undertaking of worldly activities, possessionlessness, renunciation of attachments, the vow of begging for alms, dwelling in various places and in the forest, and both external and internal purity.
For all [castes], non-violence, truthfulness, purity, lack of envy, kindness, and forbearance are common duties.
One's own duty leads to heaven and to infinity.
If he were to transgress this, the world would perish through the confusion of social orders.
Therefore, a king should not cause living beings to deviate from their own duty (*svadharma*);
for by adhering to their own duty, they rejoice both in this world and after death.
When the boundaries of the noble are firmly established, when the system of castes and stages of life is maintained,
and when the world is protected by the three Vedas, it prospers and does not decline.
Economics, and (iv) the Science of Politics) KAZ01.4.01/ Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade constitute the science of livelihood (vārtā).
The benefit derived from the granting of grain, cattle, gold, base metals, and labor is termed *aupakārikī*.
By means of that [policy], he brings both his own side and the side of the enemy under his control through treasury and army.
KAZ01.4.03: Punishment is the means for securing the acquisition and preservation of the results of the sciences of logic, the three Vedas, and economics.
The policy regarding that punishment is "daṇḍanīti" (the science of government).
Its purpose is to acquire what has not been acquired, to protect what has been acquired, to increase what has been protected, and to bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
The course of worldly existence depends upon that [speech].
"Therefore, one who desires the maintenance of worldly life should always have the rod of punishment uplifted."
"For there is no such means of bringing beings under control as the rod," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
For one who inflicts severe punishment on living beings becomes a source of terror to them.
One who employs mild punishment is treated with contempt.
One who inflicts punishment according to what is deserved is honored.
For punishment, when well-understood and properly administered, unites the subjects with virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
KAZ01.4.12: A king who governs poorly, whether through lust, anger, or contempt, provokes even forest-dwellers and wandering mendicants; how much more so, then, householders?
But when not led [by a ruler], it brings forth the law of the fish.
For the stronger swallows the weak in the absence of one who wields the rod of punishment.
Protected by him, he becomes powerful.

The world, consisting of the four castes and four stages of life, being protected by the king through the power of punishment, remains devoted to its own duties and actions, following its respective paths.
(Section 2: Association with Elders)
Therefore, the three branches of knowledge have their root in the power of punishment.
Punishment rooted in discipline brings about the security and well-being of living beings.
Discipline is both acquired and innate.
For action disciplines one who possesses substance, not one who lacks substance.
Knowledge disciplines only that intellect which is intent upon the truth through service, hearing, grasping, retention, comprehension, reasoning, and refutation; it does not discipline any other.
But regarding the sciences, discipline and regulation are determined by the authority of their respective teachers.
Having performed the rite of tonsure (caula), he should apply himself to writing and arithmetic.

Having completed his initiation, he shall learn the three Vedas and the science of inquiry (Ānvīkṣikī) from learned men; the science of livelihood (Vārttā) from the superintendents; and the science of government (Daṇḍanīti) from both theorists and practitioners.
And celibacy [must be maintained] from the sixteenth year.
Therefore, for him there is the gift of cows and the taking of a wife.
And constant association with those advanced in learning must be maintained for the sake of increasing discipline,
because discipline has its root in that.
During the first part of the day, he should devote himself to training in the arts of elephants, horses, chariots, and weaponry;
during the latter part, he should listen to the Itihāsas (ancient histories).
Itihāsa consists of ancient history, narratives, illustrative stories, the treatises on dharma, and the treatises on artha.
During the remainder of the day and night, he should practice the learning of new material and the review of what has already been learned,
as well as frequent listening to that which has not yet been mastered.
For from hearing, wisdom arises; from wisdom, yoga; and from yoga, self-possession—such is the efficacy of the sciences.
For a king disciplined by learning, devoted to the discipline of his subjects, and intent on the welfare of all beings, enjoys the earth without rival.
(Section 3: Control over the Senses, Part i)
Mastery over the senses, which is the cause of learning and discipline, must be achieved by renouncing lust, anger, greed, pride, intoxication, and arrogance.
KAZ01.6.02: Mastery over the senses consists in the absence of improper engagement of the sense organs—the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose—with respect to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell;
or it is the practice of the treatises.
For this entire treatise consists of the conquest of the senses.
A king who acts contrary to that, even if he possesses mastery over his senses and rules over the four quarters of the earth, perishes immediately.
Just as the Bhoja named Dāṇḍakya, out of lust, perished along with his kinsmen and kingdom for having lusted after a Brahmin maiden, as did Karāla of Videha.
Out of anger, Janamejaya was violent toward the Brahmins,
and Tālajaṅgha toward the Bhṛgus.
Out of greed, Aila extorted wealth from the four social orders,
as did Ajabindu of Sauvīra;
out of pride, Rāvaṇa refused to restore another's wife.
Duryodhana [was deprived] of his kingdom and his share.
From pride arose Dambhodbhava, who held all beings in contempt,
as did Arjuna of the Haihaya clan.
Out of arrogance, Vātāpi attacked Agastya,
and the host of Vṛṣṇis attacked Dvaipāyana.
These and many other kings, having relied upon the six-fold circle of enemies and failing to conquer their senses, perished along with their kinsmen and their realms.
Having cast off the sixfold circle of enemies, the son of Jamadagni, who had conquered his senses,
and Ambarīṣa Nābhāga both enjoyed the earth for a long time.
(The Life of a Sage-like King)
Therefore, by abandoning the sixfold group of enemies, one should achieve mastery over the senses;
through association with the elderly, one should acquire wisdom; and through spies, one should obtain the eye of insight.
The accomplishment of security through exertion,
the establishment of one's own duty through the supervision of affairs,
and discipline through the instruction of knowledge;
Popularity among the people is the livelihood resulting from the acquisition of wealth.

Thus, having his senses under control, he should avoid women belonging to others, as well as the taking of property and acts of violence; he should also avoid sleep, greed, falsehood, ostentatious dress, association with harmful things, and any conduct associated with unrighteousness or useless pursuits.
One should enjoy pleasure without contradicting virtue and material interest;
one should not be devoid of happiness.
Or, one may pursue the three goals of life equally, as they are mutually interconnected.
For when any one among virtue, wealth, and pleasure is pursued to excess, it afflicts both itself and the other two.
Kautilya maintains that wealth alone is the primary objective.
For both virtue and pleasure have their root in wealth.
He should appoint teachers or ministers as guardians who would restrain him from dangerous situations;
or, when he is negligent in private, they should strike him with the goad of the shadow-dial.
KAZ01.7.09ab: Kingship is to be accomplished with the aid of others; a wheel does not turn by itself.
KAZ01.7.09cd: Therefore, he should appoint ministers and listen to their counsel.
(The Appointment of Ministers)
“Bhāradvāja maintains that one should appoint fellow students as ministers, because their integrity and capability have been observed.”
"For they become trustworthy to him," so it is said.
"No," said Viśālākṣa.
“Because they played together, they treat him with contempt.”
For he should appoint as ministers those whose secret nature is similar to his own, because they share common character and susceptibility to the same calamities.
"For they do not offend him out of fear that he knows their vital spots."
"This fault is common to all," say the followers of Parāśara.
“Even with regard to those [offenses], one should follow up on what has been done and what has not been done out of fear of those who know one's vital points.”
To as many people as the lord of men reveals his secret,
he becomes subject to them through that very act, even if he is otherwise unwilling.
"Those who assist him in times of calamity when his life is in danger, he should appoint as ministers,
because their devotion has been proven."
"No," said Piśuna.
“‘Devotion’ is this; it is not a quality of the intellect.”

"Those who, when appointed to tasks involving specific numerical requirements, perform the assigned work exactly as instructed or even with excellence— those one should appoint as ministers, because their competence has been proven."
"No," says Kauṇapadanta.
“Indeed, these are devoid of other qualities of a minister.”
He should appoint as ministers those who have served his father and grandfather, because their proven loyalty has been witnessed.
For they do not abandon him even when he behaves improperly, because of their shared kinship.
And this is observed even among non-human beings.
"For cows, having bypassed a herd of cattle that does not share their kinship, remain only with those who do share it."
"No," said Vātavyādhi.
For they, having seized everything belonging to him, conduct themselves like masters.
Therefore, one who knows the principles of policy should appoint new ministers.
"But those who are new [to the office], considering the wielder of the rod to be Yama himself, do not commit offenses."
"No," said Bāhudantīputra.
“An expert in the scriptures who has not witnessed the performance of such acts should feel despondency regarding those rituals.”
"Therefore, one should appoint as ministers those endowed with noble birth, wisdom, purity, heroism, and loyalty, because of the preeminence of these qualities."
Kautilya says that all this is logical.
For it is from the capacity for the task that the capacity of the person is inferred.
And their capacity— having divided the wealth of the ministers, as well as the place, time, and task—
all these may be appointed as mere ministers (*amātyas*), but not as counselors (*mantrins*).
KAZ01.9.01: A person from the countryside who is of noble birth, self-controlled, trained in the arts, keen-sighted, wise, retentive,

capable, eloquent, bold, resourceful, endowed with energy and power, enduring of hardships, pure, friendly, firm in devotion, possessed of good character, strength, health, and courage, free from arrogance and fickleness, and beloved by his enemies.
Being non-doing is the excellence of a minister.
Therefore, those deficient by one-quarter and one-half [of these qualities] are the middling and the lowest, respectively.
He should verify their native country and lineage through reliable sources; he should examine their craft from those of equal learning, as well as their insight into the scriptures;
and he should observe their wisdom, reliability, and skillfulness in the commencement of works.
In the context of conversation, one should observe eloquence, boldness, and quick-wittedness;
from those with whom he lives, the possession of good character, strength, health, and courage, as well as lack of arrogance and fickleness;
and through direct observation, his being beloved and free from enmity.
For the conduct of a king is indeed perceptible, imperceptible, and inferable.
What is seen by oneself is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That which is taught by another is indirect (parokṣa).
In the case of actions, the fact that something has not been done can be inferred from what has already been performed.

However, because actions occur simultaneously, are manifold, and are situated in various places, he should have them carried out by his ministers behind his back so that there may be no lapse regarding place or time.

Thus ends the duties of the minister. (KAZ 1.9.9) He should appoint as domestic priest one born of a highly distinguished family and character, thoroughly trained in the Veda with its auxiliary branches, in the science of portents, in divination, and in the science of government; and he should be one who can counteract both divine and human calamities through the rituals of the Atharvaveda and through strategic means.
A pupil should follow that teacher as a son follows his father, and a servant his master.

The Kṣatriya power, nourished by the Brāhmaṇa, consecrated by the counsel of ministers, and sharpened by weapons following the guidance of the Śāstras, conquers the unconquered forever. (KAZ 1.9.11ab-11cd) (Ascertainment of the integrity or lack of integrity of a minister through secret tests)
KAZ01.10.01: Having appointed ministers to general administrative offices, the king, accompanied by his counselor and domestic priest, should test them through secret trials (*upadhā*).
KAZ01.10.02: The king shall dismiss a domestic priest who, being appointed to officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice or to teach them, is unable to endure his duties.
KAZ01.10.03. He, together with his confederates, should first administer an oath and then instigate each minister individually, saying: "This king is unrighteous;

it would be well if we were to install another who is righteous—one of his own lineage, a rival prince, a kinsman, a single-leader, a neighboring king, a forest chieftain, or one born of noble descent.
This is pleasing to all of us."
Or how is it for you? Thus he spoke.
If he refuses, he is pure.
This is the test of integrity regarding religious duty (*dharma-upadhā*).

KAZ01.10.05 / A commander-in-chief who has been dismissed due to the failure of his policy should, through secret agents, instigate each of the king's ministers with an alluring offer for the purpose of destroying the king, saying:
"This is pleasing to everyone; what do you think?"
In the case of refusal, he is pure;
such is the test by means of wealth.

KAZ01.10.07: A female wandering ascetic who has gained confidence and received honors within the harem should secretly instigate each high official, saying: "The queen desires you; she has devised a means for our meeting, and there will be great wealth for you."
"In the event of refusal, he is pure.
Thus ends the test by means of desire.
KAZ01.10.09: On the pretext of a banquet, one minister should invite all the ministers.
On account of that agitation, the king should restrain them.
And there, a *kāpaṭika* (disguised spy) previously imprisoned should secretly instigate each one of their ministers with wealth and honors, saying: "This king has set himself on an evil course;
it would be well to kill him and install another in his place.
This is pleasing to everyone."
Or how is it for you? thus [he asked].
In the case of refusal, he is pure;
thus ends the examination by means of fear.

Among them, those proven pure by the test of dharma should be appointed to duties concerning the judiciary and the removal of thorns; those proven pure by the test of wealth to the offices of the Collector-General, the Treasurer, and the management of stores;
and those proven pure by the test of pleasure to the protection of the inner and outer pleasure-grounds.
Those proven pure by the test of fear should be employed by the king in matters of immediate importance.
KAZ01.10.14: He should appoint as ministers those who have been proven pure through all tests of integrity.
In all cases, he should employ those who are impure in mines, in the production of raw materials, in elephant forests, and in manual labor.

The teachers are settled in their view that one should appoint ministers to their respective duties according to their purity, once they have been thoroughly tested through the three aims of life and the presence of fear.
But a lord should never make himself or his queen a target for the sake of the purity of his ministers; this is the view of Kauṭilya.
One should not attempt to corrupt one who is already incorruptible, just as one would not try to poison water with poison;
for it may happen that no remedy can be found for one who has been corrupted.
And a corrupted intellect, once produced by the fourfold tests (*upadhā*),
shall not turn back until it has reached its ultimate conclusion, for it remains fixed in the fortitude of those possessed of true character.
Therefore, having established an external agency for the fourfold business,
the king should investigate the integrity or lack thereof among his ministers through means of secret agents.
(The Appointment of Persons in Secret Service)

KAZ01.11.01: Having purified his circle of ministers through tests of integrity (*upadhā*), he should recruit secret agents (*gūḍhapuruṣa*): namely, those disguised as fraudulent students (*kāpaṭika*), wandering mendicants (*udāsthita*), householders (*gṛhapati*), merchants (*vaidehaka*), and ascetics (*tāpasa*), as well as spies (*sattrin*), poisoners (*tīkṣṇarasada*), and female mendicants (*bhikṣukī*).
A student who knows the vital secrets of others and is bold is a *kāpaṭika*.
Having encouraged him with wealth and honor, the minister should say: "Taking both the king and me as your authority, whatever you perceive to be improper in anyone, report it immediately."
One who has returned from the life of renunciation, being endowed with wisdom and purity, is an Udāsthita.
On land designated for agricultural work, he should have the labor performed by means of abundant gold and resident workers.
And from the proceeds of their work, he shall provide food, clothing, and lodging for all those who have renounced the world.
And he should instigate those who desire a livelihood, saying: "In this very disguise, you must carry out the king's business and present yourselves at the time for food and wages."
And all renunciants should thus instigate their respective groups.
A cultivator who has lost his livelihood, yet is endowed with wisdom and purity, is one disguised as a householder.
On land designated for agricultural work—hear now that this is the same as what was stated previously.
A merchant whose livelihood has failed, but who is endowed with wisdom and integrity, is one disguised as a *vaidehaka*.
On land designated for the business of merchants—thus it is the same as the previous case.
A shaven-headed man or one with matted hair, desiring a livelihood, acting under the guise of an ascetic; this is the thirteenth [type].
In the vicinity of the city, he should openly consume vegetables or a handful of barley once every month or two while appearing as one with many shaven-headed and matted-haired disciples;
but in secret, he should take his desired food.
And the merchants and apprentices should honor him with offerings of kindled fires.
And his disciples should report of him: "This man is a perfected one (siddha) who brings prosperity."

And for those who have approached with hopes of prosperity, one should, by means of the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyā*) and the designations of disciples, prescribe the results according to their birth: a small gain, a fire, fear of thieves, the death of a traitor, a gift of satisfaction, or knowledge of events in foreign lands.
"Today or tomorrow this will happen;
or the king will do this."
His secret agents and spies should bring this about for him.
One should proclaim the royal fortune of those endowed with courage, wisdom, and the power of speech, and one should speak of their alliance with ministers.
And the minister shall supervise them with regard to both their livelihood and their duties.
Those who are angry for a specific cause he should pacify with wealth and honors;
those who are angry without cause, as well as those who act against the king's interests, he should subdue silently with punishment.
When honored by the king with wealth and respect, they shall ensure the integrity of those who live off the king;
these are proclaimed as the five types of secret agents.
(The appointment of wandering spies and rules for secret servants.)

And those kinsmen of ours who must necessarily be supported, being secret agents (*sattriṇaḥ*), shall study the science of bodily marks (*lakṣaṇam*), the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyām*), the science of sorcery (*jambhakavidyām*), the art of illusion (*māyāgatam*), the duties of the religious orders (*āśramadharmam*), the science of omens (*nimittam*), the science of internal wheels (*antaracakram*),
and the science of social intercourse (*saṃsargavidyām*).
Those who, being heroes in the countryside, having renounced their own lives, would fight against an elephant or a wild beast for the sake of wealth, are the *tīkṣṇas* (the fierce ones).
Those who are devoid of affection for their kinsmen, cruel, and lazy are the "rasada" (poison-givers).
A wandering female ascetic (parivrājikā), desirous of livelihood, poor, a widow, and bold—a Brāhmaṇī who has received honors in the inner apartments—should frequent the families of high ministers.
By this, the cases of shaven-headed Śūdra women are explained.

Thus are the movements. (KAZ 1.12.6) The king should employ them within his own territory among the ministers, the domestic priest, the commander-in-chief, the crown prince, the door-keeper, the master of the harem, the administrator, the collector-general, the treasurer, the commissioners, the leaders, the city magistrate, the judicial officer, the superintendent of manufactories, the members of the council of ministers, the heads of departments, the chief of the army, the governor of the fort, the guardian of the frontiers, and the forest-dwellers.
One should employ spies by means of credible reports regarding country, dress, craft, language, lineage, and occupation, through both devotion and the application of capability.
Spies disguised as attendants carrying the royal parasol, water-vessel, fan, sandals, seat, carriage, or mount shall ascertain their external movements.
The secret agents should cause him to be implicated in the sacrificial sessions.
Chefs, cooks, bath-attendants, masseurs, bed-spreaders, barbers, decorators, toilet-attendants, water-bearers, and those who serve food;

as well as those disguised as hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the deaf, the mentally dull, and the blind; and actors, dancers, singers, instrumentalists, storytellers, bards, and women—these shall know the internal movement [of the enemy].
The mendicant nuns should go to him at the conclusion of their assemblies.
The students of the various guilds shall carry out the movement of spies by means of secret signs and scripts.
Nor should those officials know one another's positions.

To prevent the entry of female mendicants, those stationed at the gate shall form a chain of transmission; or else, women disguised as mothers, fathers, artisans, actors, or female slaves may carry out the intelligence by means of songs, recitations, instrumental music, musical instruments, secret signs, or written messages.
Or, one may effect a secret exit by means of a long illness, insanity, fire, or the discharge of poison.
When three [words] form a single sentence, there is mutual expectancy.
If they repeatedly commit such offenses, the punishment shall be silence and prohibition.

And the secret agents (apasarpas) mentioned in the section on the removal of thorns (kaṇṭaka-śodhana), having been paid their wages, should reside among the enemies without mingling with them for the purpose of espionage.
These are those who receive wages from both sides.
One should employ those whose sons and wives have been taken hostage as double-agents;
one should recognize them as being sent by the enemy, and their integrity should be verified by those of similar character.
In this manner, one should station spies among the enemy, the ally, and the intermediate state; likewise among the neutral power, and among their eighteen constituent elements.
Moving within the inner apartments of those [palaces] shall be hunchbacks, dwarfs, eunuchs,
women skilled in the arts, the mute, and various tribes of Mlecchas.
In the forts, there shall be guilds of merchants; at the edge of the fort, perfected ascetics; in the countryside, farmers and retired officials; and at the edge of the countryside, cattle-herders.
In the forest, forest-dwellers such as ascetics (*śramaṇa*) and forest-tribesmen (*āṭavika*) should be employed;
they serve as a rapid succession of spies for the purpose of knowing the activities of the enemy.
These [spies] must be understood by the enemy as being of the same kind, through the employment of similar agents;
these include the wandering spies (*cāra-saṃcārin*), the established secret agents (*saṃsthā*), and those designated as non-secret (*agūḍha*).
KAZ01.12.25ab: Having identified those who are susceptible to subversion through the agents of the subversion department by means of motives for action, KAZ01.12.25cd:
he should station them at the frontiers in order to gain knowledge of the enemy’s secret agents.
(On keeping watch over the seducible and non-seducible parties within one’s own territory)
Having employed secret agents among the high ministers, he should employ secret agents among the citizens and country folk.
Secret agents, acting as rivals, should provoke disputes among people gathered in sacred places, assemblies, guilds, or public crowds.
“Moreover, it is heard that this king is endowed with all virtues,
yet no virtue of his is seen who oppresses the citizens and country-folk with punishments and taxes.”
In that case, he should restrain those who might offer praise as well as the person being praised.
“Overcome by the law of the fish (*mātsya-nyāya*), the subjects made Manu Vaivasvata their king.”
They assigned him a sixth part of the grain, a tenth part of the merchandise, and a share of the gold as his portion.
Supported by that [revenue], kings bring about the acquisition and preservation of the welfare of their subjects.
Those who do not pay fines take away their wealth and bring about the lack of security and well-being for the subjects.
Therefore, even the forest-dwellers set aside a sixth part of the gleaned grain, saying: "This is his portion, he who protects us."
This is the station of Indra and Yama; kings here have their wrath and favor manifest before one's eyes.
Even divine punishment touches those who treat them with contempt.
Therefore, kings must not be disregarded.
In this manner, he should prohibit petty offenses.
And they should find out what people are saying.
And those who subsist on his grain, cattle, and gold assist him in times of calamity or prosperity;
they turn back an enraged kinsman or the kingdom [from hostility].
When they are repelling an enemy or forest-dwellers,
spies disguised as shaven-headed ascetics or matted-haired hermits shall ascertain whether those [enemies] are satisfied or dissatisfied.
He should further honor those who are satisfied with wealth and marks of respect.
But those who are dissatisfied, he should appease by means of gifts and conciliation for the sake of their satisfaction.
Or he should cause them to be divided from one another, and from their neighbors, forest tribes, members of their own family, and those who have been deposed.
Even so, if he remains unsatisfied, the king should cause him to incur the enmity of the people by granting him authority over the collection of fines and taxes.
He should subdue those who have become disaffected either by secret punishment or by inciting a revolt among the people.
He should cause those whose sons and wives are under guard to reside in mines or at manufactories, out of fear that they might provide a foothold for enemies.
But those who are angry, greedy, frightened, or arrogant among the enemy are the ones susceptible to being won over.
Among them, spies appearing as fortune-tellers, soothsayers, astrologers, and secret agents should ascertain their mutual connections or their links with enemies and forest tribes.
One should honor those who are satisfied with wealth and honors;
one should win over those who are dissatisfied through conciliation, gifts, sowing dissension, and force.

Thus, being discerning regarding those who may be subverted and those who may not within his own domain, he should protect both the principal and the minor officials from the intrigues of others. (On winning over those susceptible to persuasion and those who are not in the enemy’s territory)

The acquisition of friends from among those who are capable of action and those who are incapable of action has been explained regarding one's own territory; it shall now be discussed regarding the territory of another.
One who has been deceived after promising wealth; one who has been insulted when performing equal work in either craft or service; or one whose favorite has been superseded.
One who has been summoned and defeated, one distressed by exile,
and one who has incurred expenses without achieving his purpose.
One who is obstructed from his own duty or from his inheritance, one who has fallen from honor and office, or one who has been excluded by his kinsmen;
One who has forcibly violated a woman,
one who has been subjected to torture, and one who has been punished for the words of another.

One who has been restrained from improper conduct, one whose entire property has been confiscated, one afflicted by imprisonment, and one whose kinsmen have been exiled— this is the group of the enraged.
One who has been self-inflicted injury, one who has been treated with hostility, or one notorious for evil deeds;
One who is alarmed by the imposition of equal punishment,
one whose territory has been seized,
and one who has been brought into subjection by force.
He presides over all administrative offices,
has acquired wealth rapidly, and seeks the favor of those born into that same lineage.
"Hated by the king and hating the king"— this is the group of the fearful.
One who is impoverished, one whose property has been seized by another, and a miser.
One who is addicted to vice and one whose conduct is reckless— this is the group of the greedy.
Self-important,
desiring honor,
and unable to endure the worship of his enemies.
Humble, sharp, and impetuous.
"Unsatisfied with enjoyments"—this is the section on pride.
Among them, by means of spies disguised as shaven-headed ascetics or those with matted hair, one should instigate to treason that person who is devoted to a particular faction.

“Just as a mad elephant blinded by rut, when mounted by another in rut, crushes everything it encounters, so too this blind king, who lacks the eye of the treatises, has risen up for the slaughter of the people of the city and the countryside;
it is possible to thwart him by inciting a rival elephant against him.”
"Let indignation be aroused!"—thus he should instigate the faction of the angry.

“Just as a snake, when crouched down, discharges its venom toward whatever it perceives as a threat, so too this king, suspecting that some fault has arisen in you, will soon discharge the venom of his anger upon you;
therefore, depart elsewhere. Thus he should instigate the faction of those who are afraid.

“Just as the cow of those who keep packs of dogs is milked for the dogs and not for Brahmins, so too this king is milked by those deficient in courage, wisdom, and the power of speech, and not by those endowed with his own virtues; that king is one who recognizes the excellence of individuals.”
In that case, he should instigate the group of hunters with the words, "Let us go there."

“Just as a water-trough belonging to the Caṇḍālas is for the use of the Caṇḍālas alone and not for others, even so this base king is for the use of the base alone and not for noble men such as yourself; that king is one who knows the distinctions between men.”
In that case, he should win over the group of proud men by saying, "Let us go there."
Having agreed to "so be it," he should, according to his ability, employ those who have entered into a compact through a formal agreement, along with secret agents, in their respective tasks.
One should win over those who are susceptible to influence in enemy territories through conciliation and gifts,
and win over those who are not susceptible through sowing dissension and the use of force, while pointing out the faults of the enemy.
(The Topic of Counsel)
Having secured the support of his own party and that of others, he should consider the commencement of his undertakings.
All undertakings should be preceded by counsel.
KAZ01.15.03: The location for those [councils] should be enclosed, such that it is not audible to outsiders and cannot even be seen by birds.
KAZ01.15.04: For it is heard that secret counsel has been betrayed by parrots and mainas, and even by dogs and other animals.
Therefore, one who is not appointed should not approach the recitation of the mantras.
One who divulges secret counsel shall be executed.
For the disclosure of counsel among envoys, ministers, and masters occurs through their gestures and facial expressions.
KAZ01.15.08: A gesture is a change in behavior.
The apprehension of form is *ākāra*.
Its concealment consists in guarding it through appointed officials until the time for the performance of its purpose arrives.
For among them, negligence, intoxication, sleep, or incoherent talk, as well as an excess of passion and the like,
or a secret or disparaged person, will betray their counsel.
Therefore, one should protect the secret counsel.
“Indeed, the disclosure of secret counsel causes the loss of security for the king as well as for those officials appointed by him.”
"Therefore, one should deliberate on secret matters alone," so says Bhāradvāja.
“Indeed, ministers also have their own ministers, and they too have others.”
This very succession of ministers causes the secret counsel to be divulged.
"Therefore, others should not know any action he intends to perform;
rather, they should only know it once it has been commenced, or indeed once it is completed."
“There is no success in counsel for one person alone,” said Viśālākṣa.
“Indeed, the conduct of a king is based on what is perceptible, what is imperceptible, and what is to be inferred.”

Knowledge of what has not yet been perceived, the strengthening of the certainty regarding what has been perceived, the resolution of doubt concerning a twofold matter, and the perception of the remainder of that which was seen in one part—
this is to be accomplished by the minister.
Therefore, one should deliberate on counsel together with those who are advanced in wisdom.
“One should not despise anyone; one should listen to the opinion of everyone. A wise man should employ even the words of a child if they are meaningful.
This is the knowledge of counsel.
"This is not the protection of the mantra," say the followers of Parāśara.

KAZ01.15.24: “Regarding whatever task he intends to undertake, he should question his ministers with a simulated version of it: ‘This task was thus; or, if it were to be so, how should it be carried out?’”
He should do whatever they may say.
"In this way, there is both the attainment of counsel and its concealment."
"No," said Piśuna.
"For ministers, when questioned about a matter that is remote—whether it has occurred or not—either speak with disregard or reveal [the truth]."
That is a fault.
Therefore, regarding those specific tasks for which particular individuals are intended, he should deliberate with them.
"For by deliberating with them, one indeed attains success in counsel as well as security."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
For this would lead to an infinite regress.
He should deliberate with three or four ministers.
For one deliberating with only a single person regarding difficult matters of state would not arrive at a certain decision.
And with only a single minister, he moves about as he pleases, without restraint.
When consulting with two [ministers], one is held back by them when they are united, but destroyed when they are divided.
That occurs with difficulty only after three or four [days].
But if it is accompanied by a great offense, it becomes [a case for] a heavy penalty.
Beyond that, the determination of the enemy's purpose is understood only with difficulty,
or else their counsel must be guarded.
However, depending on the requirements of place, time, and the matter at hand, one person may deliberate with two, or two with one, according to their respective capabilities.
(Alternative views approved) KAZ01.15.42:

The means of undertaking actions, the excellence of personnel and resources, the division of place and time, the counteraction of setbacks, and the accomplishment of the task—these are the five constituent elements of counsel.
He should question them one by one and also collectively.
And by means of these reasons, one should discern the distinctions in their intellects.
Having achieved his objective, he should not let the proper time pass by.
One should not deliberate for too long,
nor with the partisans of those whom one intends to harm.
“The king should appoint twelve ministers from the council of counselors,” so say the followers of Manu.
"Sixteen," say the followers of Bṛhaspati.
"Twenty," say the followers of Auśanasa.
"According to their capacity," says Kauṭilya.
For they would deliberate upon both his own side and the enemy's side.
They shall carry out the commencement of works not yet begun, the execution of those already commenced, the completion of specific tasks already executed, and the fulfillment of assigned duties.
He should observe the performance of duties together with those who are nearby.
With those who are not nearby, he should deliberate by means of sending written messages.
For Indra’s council of ministers consists of a thousand ṛṣis.
That is his eye.
Therefore, they call this two-eyed one "the thousand-eyed."
In an urgent matter, he shall summon his ministers and the council of ministers and speak to them.
In that case, he should do what the majority says, or what will ensure the accomplishment of the task.
And for one who acts thus:
"His secrets others shall not know, but he shall know the vulnerabilities of his enemy; he should conceal his own exposed parts as a tortoise hides its limbs. (KAZ 1.15.60)

For just as one who is not learned in the Vedas does not deserve to eat at the *śrāddha* ceremony of the virtuous, so too one who has not heard the meaning of the treatises does not deserve to hear the secret counsel. (Rules for the Envoy)
KAZ01.16.01: The employment of envoys involves the use of subversive counsel.
One who is endowed with the qualities of a minister is a plenipotentiary envoy.
One who is deficient in the qualities of a quarter [of the required merit] has limited wealth.
A messenger carrying a royal edict is punished with half that reduction in merit.
He should set out with his chariots, vehicles, men, and equipment well-prepared.
The instruction is as follows: "The opponent should be addressed in this manner; he will say this; to that, this shall be the reply."
Thinking, "In this way I must outwit him," he should go along reciting [the mantra].
And he should maintain contact with the forest-guardians, the boundary-guards, and the chiefs of cities and districts.
He should examine the positions for the array of troops, the ground for battle, the ground for receiving reinforcements, and the ground for retreat, both for himself and for the enemy.
He should ascertain the dimensions of the fort and the kingdom, as well as their essential resources, means of subsistence, defensive works, and vulnerabilities.
Having been granted permission, he may enter the presence of the sovereign.
And he should deliver the royal edict exactly as stated,
even when a threat to life is perceived.

One should observe the favor shown toward another’s speech, face, and gaze; the honoring of one's words; inquiries about what is desired; association with conversations regarding one's virtues; being granted a seat nearby; receiving hospitable treatment; being remembered among those who are dear; and the extension of trust—these are the signs of one who is pleased. The opposite of these indicates one who is displeased.
He should say to him: "Kings indeed have envoys as their mouths, as do you and others."
Therefore, even when weapons are raised, envoys should speak exactly as they have been instructed.
Even among them, the outcasts (anta-avasāyins) are not to be killed, how much less so the Brahmins?
This is the statement of another.
"This is the duty of an envoy."
He should dwell there without permission, honoring [his host] but not becoming arrogant.
One should not consider oneself superior in strength toward others.
One should endure unpleasant speech.
One should avoid women and intoxicants.
He should sleep alone.
For it is observed that the knowledge of the internal state of those who are asleep or intoxicated [is possible].

He should carry out the instigation of the faction of those who can be won over toward the faction of those who cannot; he should employ secret agents among the faction of those who cannot be won over; and he should ascertain the loyalty or disloyalty of the subjects toward their master, as well as any vulnerabilities, by means of spies disguised as ascetics or merchants, through the disciples of those two, or through spies disguised as physicians or heretics, or those who are double-agents.

If they cannot be spoken with directly, one should obtain information regarding their movements through the chatter of beggars, drunkards, the insane, or those who are asleep, or by means of signs at sacred sites, temples, paintings, or inscriptions.
Once he has gained access to him, he should employ subversive intrigue.
And when questioned by another, he should not disclose the extent of his own constituent elements.
He should say, "Your Honor knows everything," or he should say that which brings about the accomplishment of the task.
If his undertaking fails and he is being obstructed, he should deliberate: "Does [the enemy] see some impending calamity for my lord, or does he wish to counteract his own calamity?
Or does he wish to incite a rear-attack, an ally, internal rebellion, or a forest-dweller?"
Desiring to cause a rift between a friend and his ally;
or desiring to counteract an attack from another, internal unrest, or a forest-dwelling tribal chief; or desiring to frustrate the successful timing of my master’s expedition.

Desiring to collect grain, merchandise, and forest produce; wishing to undertake the construction of fortifications or the mobilization of troops; awaiting the proper place and time for the exercise of his own forces; or due to the enemy's contempt or negligence.
"Or perhaps he obstructs me because he desires association and continued connection."
Having ascertained [the situation], he should either remain or depart.
Or he may consider the desired purpose.
If, after speaking an undesirable command, one departs even without being dismissed due to fear of imprisonment or death,
he shall be restrained otherwise.
Sending out missions, guarding the peace treaty, demonstrating majesty, gathering allies, sowing dissension, creating rifts among friends, and the secret dispatching of punitive forces.
The abduction of kinsmen and jewels, knowledge of spies, valor, the release from confinement, and the employment of envoys constitute the duties of a messenger and the basis of his application.
He should have this carried out by his own envoys and guard the enemy’s envoys with counter-envoys and secret agents,
as well as with guards who are both visible and invisible.
A king who is protected protects his kingdom from those close to him and from enemies; first, however, he must protect it from his wives and sons.
We shall discuss the protection of wives in the section on the management of the harem.
But the protection of the son [is as follows].
“From birth onwards, one should protect the princes.”
For princes who devour their progenitor share the nature of crabs.
"Bharadvāja maintains that when their father is devoid of affection, a secret punishment is best."
“Cruelty, the slaughter of the innocent, and the destruction of the seed of the kṣatriyas,” says Viśālākṣa.
“Therefore, confinement in a single location is better.”
"This is a danger from snakes," say the followers of Parāśara.
“Indeed, the prince, realizing that ‘my father imprisons me out of fear of my prowess,’ would place him alone upon his lap.”
Therefore, residence in a fort protected by a frontier-guard is better.”
"This is a danger from the butcher," said Piśuna.
"For having understood that very cause for his reformation, he should become a friend to the superintendent of the prisons."
Therefore, it is better to reside in a fort belonging to a neighboring king than in one that has been drawn away from its own territory.
"This is the place for the calf," said Kauṇapadanta.
"For a neighboring king might milk his father, just as one milks a cow by means of its calf."
Therefore, dwelling among one's maternal relatives is better."
"This is the place for the banner," [thinking thus], he suffers from wind-disease (vāta-vyādhi).
“In that case, by means of this banner, his maternal kinsmen shall beg for alms just like Aditi-Kauśika.”
Therefore, one should let him indulge in the pleasures of village life.
"For sons who are restrained by happiness do not plot against their father."
"This is living death," says Kauṭilya.
Like wood eaten by woodworms, a royal family with undisciplined sons will break as soon as it is attacked.
Therefore, when the queen has reached her fertile season, the officiating priests shall offer a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
When a woman has conceived, the pediatrician shall attend to her during the maintenance of the fetus and at the time of birth.
The domestic priest shall perform the sacramental rites for the son of a woman who has given birth.
Those who are experts in that matter should discipline anyone capable [of such conduct].
KAZ01.17.28: “One of the secret agents should entice him with hunting, gambling, wine, and women, saying: ‘Seize the kingdom by attacking your father.’”
"Another secret agent should dissuade him," so say the Āmbhīyas.
Kautilya maintains that awakening those who are not yet enlightened is fraught with great danger.
For a new substance absorbs whatever kind of material it is smeared with.
Thus, this person of immature intellect understands whatever is said to him as if it were the instruction of a sacred scripture.
Therefore, one should instruct him in what is consistent with dharma and what is beneficial, and not in what is contrary to dharma or detrimental.
But secret agents, declaring "We are yours," should protect him.

If a man, out of the arrogance of youth, sets his mind upon the wives of others, they should terrify him at night in deserted houses by means of women disguised as noble ladies who are actually foul-smelling and impure.
Those who desire liquor they should cause to become intoxicated by means of a decoction.
They should cause those who are fond of gambling to be harassed by spies disguised as fraudulent gamblers.
They should frighten one who desires to go hunting by means of spies disguised as forest-robbers.

They should instill a spirit of aggression toward the father and, having gained his assent by saying "so be it," cause dissension, saying: "The king is not to be petitioned; if he fails, there is death;
if he succeeds, there is a fall into hell."
There will be lamentation, and the people will be struck down as if by a single clod of earth.”
They should report his disaffection.
One should imprison a beloved only son.
A man with many sons should be sent to a frontier region or another territory where there is no danger of pregnancy, trade goods, or riots.
One who is endowed with self-mastery should be established in the command of the army or in the position of crown prince.
The intelligent, the one of acquirable intellect, and the evil-minded—these are the specific types of sons.
An intelligent person, when being instructed, both understands and practices the principles of dharma and artha.
One who perceives [the truth] but does not practice it possesses a mind that must be drawn out.
One who is constantly prone to ruin and who hates both virtue and wealth is a man of evil intellect.
If he has an only son, he should strive for the birth of another son.
Or he may procreate sons through an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
But a king who is aged or afflicted by disease shall cause seed to be sown in his field by one among the following: a maternal relative, a kinsman, or a neighboring chief endowed with good qualities.
And he should not install an undisciplined son as the sole heir to the kingdom.
When many are united under one head, that father may be as beneficial as a son;
except in times of calamity, sovereignty belongs to the eldest, who is thus honored.

Either the kingdom shall belong to the family, for a family confederacy is difficult to conquer; or, free from the affliction of royal calamities, it shall dwell eternally upon the earth. (The Conduct of a Prince in Disfavor)

(Conduct toward a prince in disfavour) KAZ01.18.01: A disciplined prince, even when subjected to difficult circumstances or appointed to an unworthy task, should obey his father, except in cases that endanger life, provoke the subjects, or constitute a mortal sin.
When appointed to a meritorious task, he should request a person to act as his supervisor.
And, supervised by a man, he should carry out the specific instructions with particular care.
And he should present to his father the fruit of his labor, which is worthy of praise, as well as the gains obtained as gifts.
Even so, if he remains unsatisfied and shows affection for another son or for his wives, one should take leave of him to go to the forest.

Or, if a neighboring king is of righteous conduct, virtuous, truthful, and non-deceptive, one who grants favors and honors those who seek refuge, he should take shelter with him out of fear of imprisonment or death.

Established there, and endowed with treasury and army, he should form alliances with heroic men and princesses, establish connections with forest tribes (aṭavīs), and win over factions of traitors (kṛtyapakṣa).
A solitary traveler may earn his livelihood through the processing of gold, the coloring of gems, and the manufacture of goods from gold and silver, as well as through mining operations.

Having secretly infiltrated the property of a heretical community (*pāṣaṇḍa-saṃgha*) that is not to be used by those learned in the Vedas, or the property of a deity, or the property of a wealthy widow, and having deceived caravans, vehicles, and vessels through the application of *madana* poison, one should seize it.
Or he may employ a stratagem directed against the enemy's village.
Or he should act by winning over his mother’s attendants.

KAZ01.18.12 / Or, having disappeared under the guise of an artisan, a craftsman, an actor, a physician, a professional storyteller, or a heretic, and entering through vulnerabilities accompanied by a companion in that same disguise, he should strike the king with a weapon or poison and say: "I am that prince;
this kingdom is to be enjoyed by us together."
"One person alone does not deserve to eat;
those who wish to support me, I shall serve with double the food and wages."
Thus ends the conduct regarding one who has been displaced from his position.
As for the displaced prince, secret agents posing as the sons of a chief minister should win him over and bring him back,
or his mother, having been won over, should do so.
Secret agents should kill those who have abandoned [the cause] by means of weapons and poison.
Having enticed him who has not left [the household] with women of similar character by means of drinking or hunting, they should seize him at night and bring him back.
And one who has presented himself [as a claimant] with the words "the kingdom is mine after me," the king should conciliate;
then, if he remains loyal, he should keep him confined, but if he has sons, he should banish him.
(Rules for the King)
When the king rises, his servants rise after him.
When one is negligent, others become negligent after him.
And his merits consume his actions.
Moreover, one is deceived by enemies;
therefore, one should exert oneself for one's own advancement.
One should divide the day and the night into eight parts by means of water-clocks (nālikās), or by measuring the length of the shadow.
A shadow of three puruṣas, one puruṣa, four aṅgulas, and no shadow at midday—these are the four preceding eighth parts of the day.
By these, the western [forts] have been explained.
Therein, during the first eighth part of the day, he should hear reports on the arrangements for security as well as income and expenditure.
In the second [court], he shall examine the affairs of the citizens and the people of the countryside.
On the third day, he should partake of bathing and food,
and he should also engage in the private study of the Veda.
In the fourth year, he should accept gold and appoint superintendents.

In the fifth [period], he should deliberate with the council of ministers by means of sending written messages, and he should ascertain those matters concerning spies and secrets that require to be brought to his attention.
In the sixth watch, he should engage in private recreation or hold counsel.
In the seventh [chapter], he shall inspect the elephants, horses, chariots, and armed troops.
In the eighth [section], one who is a friend of the commander-in-chief should consider valor.
When the day has begun, he should perform the twilight devotions.
In the first part of the night, he should inspect the secret agents.
In the second watch, he should perform his bath and meal,
as well as his private Vedic study.
At the third sound of the trumpet, having retired to bed, he should sleep during the fourth and fifth watches.
In the sixth watch, having been awakened by the sound of musical instruments, he should contemplate the sacred scriptures and the duties to be performed.
In the seventh month, he should attend to counsel and dispatch secret agents.

In the eighth [month], he should receive the benedictions from the officiating priests, the teacher, and the domestic chaplain, and he should visit the physicians, the superintendents of the kitchen, and the astrologers.
Having circumambulated a healthy cow and a bull, he should proceed to the place of worship.
Or, dividing the portions of night and day according to what is favorable to his own strength, he should attend to his duties.
When he has gone to the audience hall, he should ensure that those seeking redress of their affairs do not crowd at the entrance.
For a king is difficult to see clearly when those close to him cause him to mistake what ought to be done for what ought not to be done.
By that means, he may fall into the provocation of his own subjects or come under the power of the enemy.

Therefore, he shall examine the affairs of temples, hermitages, heretics, Vedic scholars, cattle, and holy places, as well as those of children, the elderly, the sick, the distressed, the helpless, and women, in their proper order,
or according to the gravity of the matter or the urgency of the situation.
He should hear all urgent business and not let it pass by;
for that which has been delayed becomes difficult to accomplish or even impossible to achieve.
Having gone to the fire-sanctuary, he should attend to the affairs of physicians and ascetics.
Accompanied by his domestic priest and preceptor, he should rise and offer salutations; however,
he should have the affairs of ascetics conducted by those learned in the three Vedas,
and likewise those of masters of illusion and yoga, but not personally, for fear of provoking their wrath.
For the king, exertion is his vow; the performance of duties is his sacrifice;
equanimity in conduct is his sacrificial fee, and his consecration is his initiation.
The happiness of the subjects is the happiness of the king, and the welfare of the subjects is the welfare of the king.
What is dear to the king is not necessarily beneficial; rather, that which is dear and beneficial to the subjects [is what he should pursue].
Therefore, the king, ever industrious, should practice the administration of affairs.
Industry is the root of prosperity, while its opposite is the root of misfortune.
In the absence of exertion, the destruction of both what has been acquired and what is yet to come is certain.
Through exertion, one attains the fruit and gains the perfection of wealth.
*Regulations for the Royal Residence* (KAZ01.19.36ab–cd)
In a location praised according to the rules of architecture, he should cause a harem to be constructed, provided with walls, moats, and gates, and surrounded by many courtyards.
In accordance with the regulations for a treasury, there shall be a residence in the center;

or a house of delusion with secret passages through the walls, or a residence in its midst; or an underground chamber with a door concealed by a wooden image of a deity near a shrine, containing many secret tunnels for passage.
Above that, he should have a palace constructed, with concealed walls and stairs, or a residential chamber with hollow pillars providing secret entrances and exits,
equipped with mechanical floors and drop-traps for the purpose of countering an attack or in times of emergency.
Or he may make a different arrangement from this,
out of fear of his fellow students.
The inner apartment, circumambulated three times from right to left by a human fire, is not burned by any other fire;
nor does any other fire blaze there,
provided it has been smeared with lightning-ash mixed with clay and water from a water-jar.
Serpents or poisons have no power over one who is protected by *jīvantī*, white *muṣkaka* flowers, *vandākā*, and the spreading vine of an *aśvattha* tree grown on an *akṣīva* plant.
The release of peacocks, mongooses, and spotted deer devours snakes.
A parrot, a maina, or a peacock cries out when there is suspicion of snake venom.
The curlew becomes intoxicated near poison;
the jīvañjīvaka bird faints; the intoxicated cuckoo dies.
The eyes of the cakora bird lose their luster.
In this manner, one should provide protection against fire, poison, and snakes.

KAZ01.20.10: Behind [the palace], according to the division of the enclosures (kakṣyā), there shall be the women's quarters, the place for confinement and medical treatment, and the location for trees and water.
Outside [the palace] is the enclosure for the maidens and the princes.
To the east are the grounds for ornaments, the grounds for counsel, the assembly hall, and the office of the superintendent of princes.
In the inner courtyards, the army of the harem attendants (antarvaṃśika) should remain stationed.
Having entered the inner apartments, he may see the queen who has been cleared of suspicion by an elderly woman.
For hidden in the queen's chamber, the brother killed Bhadrasena; and the son, lying within his mother's bed, killed the king of Karūṣa.
Having mixed parched grain with honey with poison, he [assassinated] the King of Kāśī;
with a sandalwood slipper smeared with poison, the King of Vairantya; and with the gem from his girdle, the King of Sauvīra.
Having concealed a weapon within her braid, the queen struck Vidūratha with a mirror.
Therefore, one should avoid these bases of attachment.
He shall prohibit contact with shaven-headed ascetics, those with matted hair, and impostors, as well as with female slaves from outside the household.
And these women shall not be seen by their kinsmen, except in cases of miscarriage, illness, or childbirth.

Those who live by their appearance shall, having bathed and rubbed themselves with fragrant powders so that their bodies are clean, and having changed their clothes and ornaments, look upon [the king].

Men aged eighty or women aged fifty who possess the physical characteristics of parents, as well as senior attendants, eunuchs, and domestic servants, shall ascertain the state of purity and impurity among the women of the harem and shall ensure that they remain devoted to the welfare of their master.
Everyone shall dwell in their own territory and shall not wander in the territory of another.
No one from within [the kingdom] shall enter into association with anyone from outside.
And all goods shall be inspected, with their imports and exports duly recorded.
KAZ01.20.23cd: He should either go out or enter [the palace] with his status marked by a seal.
[Section E: Concerning the Protection of the King’s Own Person] KAZ01.21.01: Having risen from his bed, he is surrounded by groups of women and by archers.

In the second enclosure were chamberlains wearing robes and turbans, along with eunuchs and personal attendants; in the third, hunchbacks, dwarfs, and Kirātas; and in the fourth, ministers, relatives, and doorkeepers armed with spears.

He should employ as his personal attendants people who are hereditary, related by kinship, well-trained, loyal, and of proven service; he should not employ those from other lands who have not yet rendered their services, nor even those from his own land who have been brought over after having committed offenses.
The army of the inner-council (antarvaṃśika) shall protect the king and the harem.
In a guarded place, the superintendent of the kitchen shall have all work performed with an abundance of tasteful food.
The king should consume it in that very same manner, having first offered an oblation to Agni and to the birds.
In the case of fire infused with poison, there is a blueness of the flame and smoke, a bursting sound,
and the death of birds.
The steam of cooked food has the luster of a peacock’s neck; when it has quickly become spoiled, it exhibits coldness, discoloration, and a watery yet non-moist appearance.
In condiments, there is rapid drying, and the destruction of smell, touch, and taste through the presence of scum, dark discoloration, and layers of foam.
In liquids, one observes shadows that are either deficient or excessive, as well as the appearance of layers of foam, hair-like lines, and vertical streaks.
In the midst of juice there is a blue streak;
in milk, a copper-colored one; and in liquor and water, a black one.
From curd comes the dark-colored [mushroom],
from honey the white-colored; and among moist substances, there is rapid wilting, a state of over-cooking, and a bluish-black coloration from boiling.
In the case of dry [substances], there is rapid decay and discoloration;
in the case of hard [substances], there is softening, and in the case of soft [substances], there is hardening;
furthermore, there is the killing of small creatures in their vicinity.
For bedspreads and coverlets: a darkening of the surface, and the shedding of threads, hair, and down;
for objects made of metal or gems: a coating of mud or soot, and the destruction of their luster, color, weight, brilliance, and texture—these are the signs of that which is poisoned.
But for one who administers poison, there is a dry and darkened complexion of the face, obstruction of speech, perspiration, excessive yawning,
trembling, stumbling, evasion of speech, agitation, and instability in one's own duties.
Therefore, those skilled in the science of snake-venoms (jāṅgulī) and physicians should remain close to him.
Having taken medicine from the physician’s pharmacy that has been proven pure by taste, and having tasted it himself along with the cook and the grinder, he shall present it to the king.
Drinking water and beverages are explained by the same rules as medicinal drinks.
Barbers and attendants, with hands holding garments purified by bathing, should attend to him after taking the necessary equipment from the hand of the *antarvaṃśika*.
Bathers, masseurs, bed-spreaders, washermen, garland-makers, and female slaves whose work is slavery should perform these tasks, as they are known for their cleanliness;
or artisans may do so under the supervision of those women.
Having fixed their gaze upon themselves, they should offer garments and garlands;
and they should apply baths, ointments, fragrant powders, perfumes, and bathing substances to their own chests and arms.
By this, that which has come from another is explained.
Performers shall provide entertainment, with the exception of playing with weapons, fire, or poison.
Their musical instruments, as well as the ornaments for horses, chariots, and elephants, should remain inside.
He should mount a vehicle or a carriage attended by trustworthy men,
and a boat attended by a trustworthy boatman.
Nor should one approach a boat that is tied to another or one that is under the power of the force of the wind.
The army should be stationed at the edge of the water.
One should plunge into water that is free from fish and crocodiles.
He should go to a park that is cleared of wild beasts and crocodiles.
Accompanied by hunters and packs of dogs, he should go to a deer-park to familiarize himself with moving targets, having dispelled the fear of thieves, wild beasts, and enemies.
Surrounded by trusted swordsmen, he should see a perfected ascetic and, together with his council of ministers, a messenger from a neighboring vassal.
25. Fully armored and mounted on either a horse or an elephant, he should observe the fully armored army.

During the departure and the march, he should travel along the royal highway, which is guarded on both sides by those bearing weapons and staffs, and from which weapons, mendicants with hands bearing marks, and the deformed have been cleared;
he should not enter a place crowded with people.
He shall attend processions, assemblies, festivals, and drinking parties, accompanied by the officer in charge of the ten-member unit (daśavargika).
Just as a king presides over others through his officers of yoga, so should the self-possessed ruler protect himself from the injuries caused by others. (Eighth Book:
The Activity of the Heads of Departments)
