(Chapter 1, Section 19: Settlement of the Countryside) KAZ02.01.01:

He shall settle a district that was previously inhabited or one that was not previously inhabited, either by inducing people from foreign lands to migrate there or by causing those from his own territory who are overcrowded to emigrate.

He should establish villages consisting mostly of Śūdras and cultivators, with a minimum of one hundred families and a maximum of five hundred families, having boundaries of one or two *krośas* in extent, and providing mutual protection for one another.
At the boundaries of the borders, one should establish water-channels, rocks, forests, mounds, caves, embankments, *śamī* trees, *śālmalī* trees, and milky trees.
KAZ02.01.04: Among eight hundred villages there shall be a *sthānīya*, among four hundred villages a *droṇamukha*,
and among two hundred villages a *kārvaṭika*.
He should establish a collection by means of a group of ten villages.
At the frontiers, he should establish frontier-guard forts at the gates of the inhabited territory, commanded by frontier-guards.
The gaps between them shall be guarded by trappers, Śabaras, Pulindas, Caṇḍālas, and forest-dwellers.

KAZ02.01.07a: To officiating priests, teachers, domestic chaplains, and those learned in the Vedas, he shall grant lands as religious endowments (*brahmadeya*), which are exempt from fines and taxes, and which have capable heirs.

KAZ02.01.07b: To superintendents, accountants, and others, as well as to cowherds, station masters, troop commanders, physicians, horse trainers, and couriers, he shall grant lands excluding those subject to sale or mortgage.
KAZ02.01.08: To those who pay taxes, he should assign cultivated fields that are held by a single individual.
KAZ02.01.09 / Those [pledges] which have not been formally executed shall not be recoverable from the debtors.
He should confiscate the lands from those who do not cultivate them and bestow them upon others.
Or village laborers and merchants may cultivate [the land].
Or, those who do not cultivate it shall pay the lost amount.
And he should favor these [offenders] with grain, cattle, and gold.
They should grant those [privileges] with ease.
KAZ02.01.15: He should grant favors and exemptions to those who increase the treasury, and avoid those who cause harm to the treasury.
For a king with depleted treasury devours his own citizens and country-folk.
He shall grant an exemption either at the time of settlement or according to the circumstances as they arise.
He should favor those who have fulfilled their obligations, just as a father favors his children.
He should establish mines, manufactories, stores of goods, elephant forests, cattle pens, and trade routes, as well as ports for water and land transport.
He should construct a dam that either brings in water along with it or holds back the water.
Or, he should provide assistance with land, roads, trees, and equipment to others who are building,
as well as to sacred sites and groves.
KAZ02.01.22: If one deserts a collective irrigation work (setubandha), the laborers and oxen shall perform the work [in his stead].
And he shall be entitled to a share in the expenses of the undertaking,
yet he shall not receive a share of the profits.
KAZ02.01.24: Regarding fish, water-fowl, monkeys, and forest produce, the king shall obtain ownership over them at the dams.
KAZ02.01.25/ If a slave, a pledged servant, or a kinsman fails to report [a crime], the king shall compel them to undergo punishment.
The king shall support the young, the old, those addicted to vice, and the helpless; likewise, he shall support a woman who has not borne children, as well as the sons of one who has borne.
The village elders shall manage the property of minors and the property of the gods until they reach legal majority.

KAZ02.01.28: For one who is capable but fails to maintain his children, wife, parents, brothers who have not attained legal majority, sisters, or widowed daughters, a fine of twelve paṇas shall be imposed, except in the case of those who are outcastes (patita) or in the case of the mother.
For one who goes forth into the religious life without having provided for his son and wife, the punishment is the first amercement; the same applies to one who causes a woman to go forth.
When his physical strength has failed, he may renounce the world after taking leave of the judges of dharma.
Otherwise, it would be restricted.

No one other than a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) shall adopt the life of a wandering mendicant; no group other than one of common birth shall form a corporation; and no association other than one based on a common undertaking shall settle within his territory.
And in those places there shall be no pleasure groves or halls intended for monasteries.
Actors, dancers, singers, instrumentalists, storytellers, and bards shall not cause any obstruction to their work.
Because the villages lack other sources of support and because the men are devoted to their fields, there is an increase in the treasury, labor services, raw materials, grain, and liquids.
The king should abandon a territory seized by a foreign army or forest tribes, or one afflicted by disease and famine; he should also prohibit wasteful expenditures and frivolous diversions.
He should protect agriculture from the hardships caused by forced labor, military service, and taxes.

He should clear the cattle-pastures from thieves, wild beasts, poisoners, and predators, as well as from diseases; and he should purify the trade routes when they are being harassed by favorites of the king, royal officers, thieves, and frontier guards, or when they are being depleted by herds of livestock.
In this manner, the king shall protect existing irrigation works for the purification of water and resources, as well as mines;
he shall maintain those already established and initiate new ones.
(Disposal of Non-Agricultural Land)
KAZ02.2.01: On land unfit for cultivation, he shall grant pasture-lands (*vivīta*) to cattle.
And he shall grant to ascetics forest-tracts for the Veda and Soma-sacrifices, where both stationary and moving beings have been granted safety, and which extend beyond the range of cattle's lowing.

KAZ02.2.03: To the extent necessary, the king should cause a deer-park to be constructed for his pleasure, provided with a single entrance, protected by a moat, containing sweet fruit-bearing shrubs and clusters, consisting of thornless trees, possessing shallow water-reservoirs, inhabited by tame four-footed animals, where predators have their claws and fangs broken, and which is accessible to deer, wild boars, elephants, and female elephants.
KAZ02.2.04: On the frontier, he should establish another deer-preserve that is open to all guests, or he may establish it according to the nature of the terrain.
He shall establish forests for each of the commodities specified as forest produce,
as well as forest tracts for the processing of those commodities and wilderness areas that serve as refuges for the forest-produce industries.
KAZ02.2.06: At the frontier, he should establish an elephant forest protected by a wilderness guard.

The Superintendent of Elephant Forests shall protect the elephant forests—whether mountainous, non-extractable, excellent, or marshy—with guards who know the boundaries and the points of entry and exit;
he shall cause those who kill elephants to be put to death.
For one who brings a pair of teeth from an animal that has died naturally, the profit shall be four paṇas plus a quarter.

KAZ02.2.10: Forest guards, elephant trainers, foot-fetterers, border-watchmen, forest-rangers, and laborers, disguised as friends and masked by the scent of elephant urine and dung, shall move about with five or seven female elephant-keepers, under the pretext of [observing] the sleeping places, standing spots, paths, dung-heaps, riverbanks, and bathing sites of the elephants.
They should know it as being encompassed by the elephant lineage.

They shall ascertain by means of records the elephant that moves in a herd, that moves alone, that has strayed from its herd, the leader of the herd, the rogue elephant, the intoxicated one, the young, and the one released from bondage.
Based on the measurements of elephants in the army, they should capture wild elephants that possess auspicious physical marks and behavior.
For a king, victory depends primarily upon the elephant.
For elephants, possessing bodies of immense size and performing life-ending deeds, are indeed capable of crushing enemy armies, fortified encampments, and military camps.
Those born in Kaliṅga and Aṅga are the best; those born in the eastern regions of Cedi and Karūṣa, as well as the Dāśārṇas and those from the western borders, are considered mediocre among elephants.
Those from Saurāṣṭra and the Pañcanada region are recorded as the lowest of them all.
KAZ02.2.16cd: Through all these activities, the vigor, speed, and energy of everyone increase.

[Section on the Construction of Forts] KAZ02.3.01: At the edge of the inhabited territory in the four directions, he should cause a fort to be built for defensive purposes against both human and divine threats.
An island or a piece of land surrounded by water is a watery terrain;
a rocky slope or a cave is a mountainous terrain; and a salt-flat or a barren waste devoid of water is a desert terrain.
A marshy place, a thicket of reeds, or a forest fastness.
Among these, a fortress consisting of rivers and mountains is a place for protecting the inhabited territory;
a desert or forest fortress is a place for forest tribes, or a retreat in times of calamity.

KAZ02.3.03: In the midst of the territory, he should establish a capital city (*sthānīya*) as a center for the collection of revenues, on a site approved by the rules of architecture, at the confluence of rivers, on the bank of a lake that never dries up, or beside a marsh or a reservoir; it should be circular, oblong, or square according to the requirements of the site, with water flowing clockwise around it, serving as a place for the distribution of merchandise, and provided with both land routes and waterways.

He should cause three moats to be made around it, separated by intervals of one *daṇḍa*, with widths of fourteen, twelve, and ten *daṇḍas* respectively; they should be as deep as one-quarter or one-half of their width, and their depth should be one-third of their width at the base.
They may have square foundations, be lined with stone, or have their sides bound with stone bricks;
they should be near water, filled with incoming water, provided with overflow channels, and contain lotuses and crocodiles.

One should cause an embankment (*vapra*) to be constructed from the ditch (*parikhā*), set back four *daṇḍas* and rising six *daṇḍas* high; its width should be twice that [height], and it should be built above ground level, with a surface like a platform, or shaped like the belly of a jar, and trampled by elephants and cattle; it should be covered with thorny shrubs, poisonous creepers, and spreading vines.
Or one may fill a gap in the site or the royal palace with the remaining soil.

On top of the rampart, he shall cause a brick wall to be constructed with a height double its width; it should be made of odd or even numbers of cubits, starting from twelve cubits up to twenty-four cubits.
It should provide space for the movement of chariots, have a base like a palm tree, and its summit should be covered with small drums and lion-heads.
Or he should have a stone fortress constructed using large slabs of rock, but never one made of wood.
For the fire, once established, dwells within it.
One should cause a watchtower (aṭṭālaka) to be built, square with its width, with a staircase whose projection is equal to its height, and situated at intervals of thirty daṇḍas.
Between two watchtowers, one should cause a gateway (pratolī) to be constructed, featuring two stories with upper chambers (saharmya-dvitālā), and having a length one and a half times its width.

In the middle of the watchtowers and main streets, one should cause an "Indrakosa" (a defensive turret) to be constructed, supported by three archers, consisting of a mass of planks with concealed apertures and a closing lid.
In the intervals, one should cause a divine path to be made, two hastas in width and four times that length along its sides.

He should cause the patrol routes to be established at intervals of one *daṇḍa* or two *daṇḍas*, and in areas where it is impossible to station guards, he should provide for running patrols and exit gates.

KAZ02.3.15: One should cause a concealed path to be constructed, hidden by means of a breaking-joint outside the knee, a stake, a trench, a pit, a trap, a precipice, thorns, a winding path, a snake’s back, palm leaves, a horn, a watchtower, a dog’s fang, a bolt, a jumping-off place, wooden sandals, a frying pan, or water-drinking troughs.

Having constructed a wall with a *meṇḍhaka* (a projecting buttress) on both sides at one and a half *daṇḍas*, he should establish a gate with an interval of six *tulās* between the *pratolīs* (gate-towers), measuring from five *daṇḍas* up to eight *daṇḍas* increasing by one each time; it should be square, with its width exceeding its length by one-sixth or one-eighth.
The height of the floor shall be from fifteen cubits, increasing by one cubit up to eighteen cubits.
The circumference of the pillar is six times its width; it is buried twice as deep as its height above ground,
and the capital (cūlikā) is one-fourth of its height.
Five parts of the ground at the front shall be occupied by the hall, the water-tank, and the boundary-house.
Two tenieth-parts shall be for the two *pratimañcas*,
and the space between them shall be for the *āṇī-harmya*.
At half the height of the total elevation, there shall be a pillar-base.
A half-plot of land shall be for an upper apartment, or with an interval of one-third; its sides shall be constructed with brickwork.
On the left is a staircase with steps facing clockwise, and on the other side is a staircase hidden within the wall.
The top of the archway shall be two cubits high.
Two door-panels, each consisting of three parts and five sections, [are joined together].
Two [types of] crossbars.
The *indrakīla* is one *aratni*.
The gate for the axle-pins shall be five cubits wide.
There are four elephant-enclosures.
The *hastinakha* (elephant-nail) type of rampart is half the height of the *niveśa* (the main defensive wall).
A bridge with a level surface, made of earth, or situated on dry land, is easy to dismantle.

Having established the gateway (mukha) level with the rampart wall, one should cause a gate-tower (gopura) to be constructed with a front resembling a lizard's mouth (godhāmukha), occupying one-third of its width.
Having constructed a pond within the enclosure wall, there shall be a gate for the lotus-pool;
the princesses' quarters shall consist of four halls with an interval of one and a half [parts] and be provided with a screen-wall; the gatehouse shall be a two-storied structure with a flat roof.
Or one may establish it according to the nature of the ground and the materials.
He should cause irrigation channels for carrying goods to be constructed with a length exceeding one-third [of the width].

In those [fortifications], stone-hammers, pickaxes, axes, and shafts should be prepared; likewise, musuṇḍhīs, mallets, staffs, discus-engines, and *śataghnīs* should be made. Iron spikes and bamboo poles with piercing tips should also be fashioned.
KAZ02.3.35cd: [The construction of] camel-necks and fire-connections, as well as the procedure prescribed in the section on base metals (kupya-kalpa).
[End of the layout of the fortified city.
KAZ02.4.01: Three royal roads running eastward and three running northward constitute the division of the site.
It shall have twelve gates, provided with a water-channel and covered passages.
The carriage roads shall have a width of four daṇḍas between them.

Royal highways, roads leading to granaries, crossroads, fortifications, pasture lands, and paths for cattle-pens; as well as roads for processions, military arrays, cemeteries, and village streets—these shall be eight *daṇḍas* in width.
A path for embankments and forests shall be four daṇḍas wide; a path for elephants and fields shall be two daṇḍas wide;
and a path for chariots shall be five aratnis wide.
There are four paths for large animals,
and two paths for small animals and humans.
In a site abounding in heroes, the royal residence shall be established, providing a livelihood for the four social orders.

In the ninth division to the north of the heart of the site (vāstu-hṛdaya), one should cause the inner apartments (antaḥpura) to be constructed according to the prescribed rules, facing either east or north.
In its north-eastern quarter, the teachers, domestic chaplains, sacrificial priests, water-supply stations, and ministers shall reside;
in the south-eastern quarter, the kitchen, elephant stables, and the granary shall be located.
Beyond that, those who deal in perfumes, garlands, and liquids, barbers, and craftsmen, as well as Kṣatriyas, shall reside in the eastern quarter.
The southeastern quarter shall contain the storehouse for goods, the gambling hall, and the workshops;
the southwestern quarter shall contain the warehouse for forest produce and the armory.

Beyond that, the superintendents of the city, grain, commerce, and manufactories, as well as the commanders of the army, along with vendors of cooked food, liquor, and meat, courtesans, musicians, and Vaiśyas, shall occupy the southern quarter.
The southwestern portion shall contain the stables for donkeys and camels, as well as the workshop; the northwestern portion shall contain the sheds for vehicles and chariots.
Beyond that, artisans who produce wool, thread, bamboo, leather, armor, weapons, and shields, as well as Śūdras, shall inhabit the western direction.
The northwestern portion shall be the warehouse for merchandise and medicines; the northeastern portion shall be the treasury and the stable for cattle and horses.
Beyond that, the city deities, the royal deities, metal-workers, jewelers, and Brāhmaṇas shall dwell in the northern direction.
In the vacant spaces between houses and along the rows of buildings, guilds, market-stalls, and corporations shall reside.

One should cause the apartments for Aparājita, Ajita, Apratihata, Jayanta, and Vaijayanta, as well as the houses for Śiva, Vaiśravaṇa, the Aśvins, Śrī, and Madirā, to be constructed in the center of the city.
Or, he should install the deities of the site according to their respective locations.
The gates are dedicated to Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and the Commander-in-Chief (Saināpatya).
Outside the moat, at a distance of one hundred bows, shrines, sacred sites, groves, and embankments should be constructed,
and the deities of the directions should be established according to their respective quarters.
The northern or eastern part of the cemetery is for those of the higher castes; to the south of the cemetery is for those of the lower castes.
In case of its violation, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
Heretics and Caṇḍālas shall dwell at the edge of the cremation ground.
KAZ02.4.24: He shall establish the boundaries of the households according to the extent of their fields and the nature of their agricultural activities.
In those [villages], they may, with permission, establish flower and fruit gardens as well as stores of grain and merchandise.
A site for a well shall consist of a fenced enclosure containing ten families.

KAZ02.4.27: He should cause to be prepared stores of all kinds of oils, grains, alkalis, salts, perfumes, medicines, dried vegetables, fodder, dried meat, grass, wood, metals, skins, charcoal, sinews, poisons, horns, bamboo, bark, heartwood, timber, weapons, armor, and heaps of stones, which are capable of withstanding use for many years.
One should purify the old with the new.
He should station the elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry forces under the command of many chiefs.
For when there are many leaders, they do not succumb to the instigations of an enemy due to their mutual fear of one another.
By this, the fortifications of frontier-guard forts are explained.
And one should not allow outsiders who cause injury to the city or the kingdom to remain;
one should expel them from the inhabited territory or make them pay all taxes.
(The Superintendent of Stories: The Work of Store-Keeping)

KAZ02.5.01. The Superintendent of the Treasury shall cause the treasury-house, the warehouse for merchandise, the granary, the storehouse for forest produce, the armory, and the prison to be constructed.
Having caused a square pond to be excavated that is not subject to water-soaking, and having piled broad stones on both sides and at the base,

one should cause an underground chamber (*bhūmigṛha*) to be constructed; it should have a framework of strong timber, be level with the ground, consist of three stories, possess various arrangements, have a floor-levelled by a paved surface (*kuṭṭima*), a single entrance, and a staircase equipped with a mechanical device.
Above that, he should cause a treasury house— or a palace— to be constructed, enclosed by a rampart on both sides with a gateway, built of brick, and surrounded by a convoy of transport wagons.
At the border of the kingdom, he should cause a permanent storehouse to be established for the sake of emergencies by those who have renounced all worldly attachments.

A storehouse for merchandise and a granary shall consist of four halls with a single door, constructed with baked bricks, having multiple floors and locations, with open spaces between the pillars on both sides.

A treasury shall consist of many long halls with walls enclosed by corridors, containing stores of raw materials within; that same structure, when provided with an underground chamber, serves as an armory.

He should cause a prison to be built with separate quarters for men and women, well-guarded courtyards, and secure cells for the confinement of those awaiting trial, as well as separate administrative offices for the high officials.

He should cause all the quarters to be provided with halls for latrines, water-drinking, excrement disposal, and bathing; with protection against fire and poison; with cats, mongooses, and guards; and with the worship of their respective tutelary deities.
In the storehouse, one should install a water-receptacle with an opening of one aratni that allows rainwater to enter.
Supervised by the officer in charge of manufactured goods, he shall receive old or new gems, valuable items, worthless items, or base metals.

In that regard, for the substitution of precious gems, the highest fine shall be imposed on both the perpetrator and the instigator; for the substitution of high-value goods, the middle fine; and for the substitution of low-value goods or base metals, the fine shall be equal to the value of those items.
He should accept gold that has been purified by a goldsmith.
If it is impure, he shall have it cut off.
The first amercement shall be the penalty for the one who brings it forward.
He shall accept grain that is pure, full, and fresh.
In the case of the opposite, the fine shall be double the value.
By this, the treatment of merchandise, forest produce, and weapons is explained.

KAZ02.5.16: In all administrative departments, for officials—whether appointed or retired—who embezzle funds, the punishments shall be the first, middle, or highest amercement, or death, respectively, for thefts ranging from one *paṇa* up to four *paṇas*.
For one entrusted with the treasury who misappropriates the treasury, the punishment is death.
For those who assist in that [theft], the fines shall be half [of the prescribed amounts].
Reprimand is for an offense that was not previously known.
For the violent assault of thieves, the punishment is execution by various tortures.
Therefore, the superintendent, presided over by trustworthy persons, shall attend to the stores.

He should know both external and internal revenue even after a hundred years, so that when questioned, he may not falter regarding expenditures, remaining balances, and accumulations. The establishment of revenue by the administration.
The Collector-General shall inspect the fort, the countryside, mines, irrigation works, forests, herds, and trade routes.

KAZ02.6.02: Toll, fines, weights and measures, the city superintendent, the superintendent of minting, the superintendent of seals, liquor, slaughterhouses, thread, oil, ghee, salt, the state goldsmith, the market stalls, courtesans, gambling, building sites, the guilds of artisans and craftsmen, the superintendent of gods, and the revenues from gates and the outskirts constitute the fort.

The cultivated land, the sharecropper’s portion, the tribute, the tax, the merchant, the river-guardian, the ferry, the boats, the port, the toll-road, the cord, and the police-cord constitute the kingdom.
Gold, silver, diamonds, gems, pearls, coral, conch shells, metals, salt, land, stone, liquids, and minerals constitute mines.
Flower gardens, fruit orchards, groves, rice fields, and root plantations constitute a *setu* (an irrigation embankment).
The forest consists of the possession of forests containing domestic animals, wild game, timber, and elephants.
Cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, donkeys, camels, horses, and mules constitute the herd.
The merchant's route consists of both land routes and water routes.
Thus ends the section on the body of income.
The price, the share, the premium, the duty, the fixed fee, the minting charge, and the penalty constitute the sources of revenue.
The worship of gods and ancestors, the giving of gifts,
the recitation of benedictions,
and the inner apartments.
The kitchen, the messenger-office, and the storehouse.
The armory,
the warehouse for merchandise, and the warehouse for forest produce.
Labor service,
forced labor,
and the maintenance of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants;
The cow-pens, the enclosures for domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, and snakes,
and the enclosures for wood and grass— these constitute the body of expenditure.

The king’s regnal year, month, fortnight, and day constitute the elapsed time; of the rainy, winter, and summer seasons, the third and seventh fortnights are deficient by one day, while the remaining ones are full; and the intercalary month is distinct—this is the reckoning of time.
The tasks to be performed, those already accomplished, the remainder, income and expenditure, and the net balance.
The establishment [of the office], its operation, the maintenance of the personnel, the collection [of revenue], the total sum of all income, and the net surplus—this is what is to be done.

What has been deposited in the treasury, royal gifts, and city expenditures; what has been entered [into the records], what pertains to the previous year, what is released by edict, and what is ordered by a verbal command—these are not to be set aside (apātanīya).

This is the application of the methods for accomplishing tasks. What remains of fines, what is to be recovered, what was forcibly withheld, and what was misappropriated—this is the remainder, consisting of the worthless and the slightly valuable.
Current revenue, arrears, and revenue from other sources constitute the income.
That which continues from the day is the current one.
A year-old [grain] that has been stored for a full year, or that which has been transferred from another region, is considered stale.

Property lost and forgotten, fines from officials, property from those who have deserted, tributes, gifts, property seized during riots, the estate of one who dies without heirs, and treasure-troves found by others belong to the state.
The expenditure and revenue shall consist of the cost of dispersal, expenses for the sick, the commencement of new works, and the balance of unfinished projects.

In the sale of commodities, the increase in price is the *upajā*; the difference in measures and weights is the *vyājī*; and the increase in price due to competition among buyers is the *vārddha-vṛddhi*—this constitutes revenue.
The constant revenue is that which produces constant income; the occasional revenue is that which produces occasional income; and expenditure is likewise of these two kinds.
That which follows the day is constant.
Profit is that which is gained in a fortnight, a month, or a year.
The expenditure arising from those two is of two kinds: that which results in constant production and that which results in the production of profit.
KAZ02.6.27: The *nīvī* is the net revenue derived from the surplus after subtracting expenditures from the total receipts;
it is both what has been received and what is being carried forward.
In this manner, the wise official should manage the collection of revenue and demonstrate the increase in income;
he should likewise reduce expenditure and bring about its reversal [into profit].
[The Topic of Accounts in the Records and Audit Office]
The Superintendent of Dice shall cause the gaming hall to be constructed facing either the east or the north, with separate seating areas and a place for the register books.

In that regard, there shall be a record of the number, activity, and total revenue of the administrative offices; the quantity of commodities used, the increase, decrease, expenditure, effort, fees, application of interest, locations, wages, and laborers employed for various works; and the prices, quality, measures, weights, balances, and containers for gems, raw materials, forest produce, and base metals.

The establishment of the legal procedures, customs, and conduct for regions, villages, castes, families, and guilds; and the acquisition of favors, land allotments, tax exemptions, food provisions, and wages for those dependent upon the king.

He shall cause the records in the bound volumes to include the king’s queens and sons, the acquisition of jewels and land, the receipt of instructions and measures for remedying portents, and the treaties, hostilities, gifts, and confiscations involving friends and enemies.

KAZ02.7.03: Thereafter, he shall provide, by means of a formal record (*nibandha*), the tasks to be performed, the completed work, the remainder, income and expenditure, the net balance (*nīvī*), the reports submitted (*upasthāna*), the current operations (*pracāra*), established customs (*caritra*), and the administrative structure (*saṃsthāna*) for all departments.

KAZ02.7.04: For superior, middling, and inferior tasks, he shall appoint supervisors (*adhyakṣa*) of corresponding status; however, for those related to revenue collection (*sāmudayika*), he shall appoint those who are experienced and capable.
That which, having been harmed, would cause the king no regret.
The co-conspirators, sureties, those living off his labor, sons, brothers, wives, daughters, and servants shall bear the burden of the interruption of his work.
Three hundred and fifty-four days and nights constitute a working year (karma-saṃvatsara).
He shall pay that [amount] by the end of the month of Āṣāḍha, whether it be deficient or full.
One should have an intercalary month established by the court officials.
And he should supervise the movements of his spies.
For a minister who does not investigate the movements, conduct, and established conditions [of the people] causes the revenue to be lost through ignorance;
through laziness, because he cannot endure the exertion required for effort;
and through negligence, because he is addicted to the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.
Out of fear for reproach, unrighteousness, or misfortune;
out of desire, the intention to favor those who seek his service;
and out of anger, the intention to cause harm.
[One acts] out of pride through reliance on learning, wealth, a beloved, or [powerful] patrons; and out of greed through deception regarding weights, measures, logic, mathematics, or other [matters].
"Among those [offenses], the fine shall be one more than the preceding amount, proportional to the extent of the injury to property," so say the followers of Manu.
“Everywhere it is eightfold,” so say the followers of Parāśara.
"The [revenue] is tenfold," say the followers of Bṛhaspati.
"A twentyfold [fine]"—this is the view of the followers of Auśanasa.
"According to the offense," says Kauṭilya.
The accounts of revenue and expenditure shall be submitted by the Āṣāḍhī full moon day.
When those who have arrived with oceanic books, merchandise, and capital arrive, he shall cause them to be confined in one place and prohibit them from conversing with one another.
Having heard the totals for income, expenditure, and the net balance (nīvī), he shall cause the net balance to be brought forward.

Whatever surplus of income may arise from the difference between the highest estimate and the actual receipt, or whatever expense the superintendent may cause to be omitted, he shall cause that to be paid to him eightfold.
In the opposite case, it should apply to that very same person.
For those who do not arrive at the appointed time, or who fail to bring their books, merchandise, or capital, the fine shall be ten times the amount due.
And when a laborer has arrived for work and the supervisor does not engage him, the former fine for violence shall be imposed.
In the case of the opposite, the fine for the artisan shall be double.
The high ministers, being unanimous and free from discordant counsel, shall cause it to be proclaimed throughout the countryside.
One who acts separately from them or speaks falsely shall pay the highest fine.
If the form [of the debt] has not been settled within a day, he should wait for a month.
After one month, he shall pay a fine of two hundred panas plus an additional pana for each subsequent month.
If only a small remainder of the written accounts and the balance (nīvī) remains, one should wait for five nights.

Thereafter, he should supervise the treasury and the collection of daily revenue through the application of legal procedures, judicial inquiries, customs, established rules, accounting, settlement, estimation, and the employment of spies;
and he should reconcile the accounts by day, five nights, fortnight, month, four-month period, and year.

And he should reconcile this with the witnesses regarding the place, time, and circumstances; the origin and subsequent course of the transaction; the amount; and the giver, the one who caused it to be given, the recorder, and the receiver.

One should reconcile the expenditure with the following: the place, time, and occasion of the outlay; the source of income; the reason for the expenditure; the nature of what is to be given; the quantity; the person who issued the order; the person who made the withdrawal; the person who executed the act; and the person who received it.
One should bring in the merchandise (nīvī) by verifying the place, time, and destination; the face, form, characteristics, and quantity; and the deposit, the container, and the guardians.

KAZ02.7.34: For an accountant who, for the sake of the king’s interest, fails to check or obstructs an order, or who otherwise records the income, expenditure, or net balance in the ledger, the fine shall be double the amount involved.
For one who writes down a legal matter (vastuka) out of order, skipping over parts, in reverse order, unintelligibly, or with repetitions, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
For one who tears at the waist-knot, the fine is double.
For one who eats [the meat], the fine is eightfold.
For one who destroys [the property], the penalty is five times its value as a fine, and he must make restitution.
In the case of false testimony, the punishment shall be that for theft.
If the claim is made after the time limit has passed, or if it arises from something forgotten, the fine shall be double.
He should tolerate a minor offense, be satisfied even with a small increase in revenue,
and honor a superintendent who provides great assistance with rewards.
(The Recovery of Revenue Misappropriated by State Employees)
All undertakings are preceded by the treasury.
Therefore, one should first examine the treasury.

KAZ02.8.03: Prosperity from trade, favor toward the people's customs, suppression of thieves, prohibition of improper acts, abundance of crops, a great variety of merchandise, exemption from calamities, reduction of exemptions, and the receipt of gold as tribute—these constitute the increase of the treasury.
Obstruction, employment, transaction, concealment, causing loss, consumption, exchange, and embezzlement—these constitute the depletion of the treasury.
KAZ02.8.05: The non-accomplishment of successes, or their failure to emerge, or their failure to enter [the enemy's territory], constitutes an obstruction.
In that case, the fine shall be ten times the value.
The application of treasury funds for the purpose of generating interest constitutes *prayoga*.
The legal proceeding concerning trade in commodities is the judicial process.
In that case, the fine shall be double the value of the profit.
To make a completed time-period unattained, or to make an unattained one attained, is *avastāra* (concealment).
In that case, the fine shall be five times the amount [of the debt].
"Parihāpaṇa" refers to the case where one causes the established revenue to fall short or increases the expenditure.
In that case, the fine shall be four times the lesser amount.
KAZ02.8.14: "Upabhoga" (enjoyment) consists of the personal or by others' use of the king's property.

In that regard, for the consumption of gems, the penalty is death; for the consumption of valuable goods, the middle amercement; and for the consumption of inferior or base metals, the fine shall be equal to the value of the object plus an additional amount.
KAZ02.8.16: The exchange of royal goods for the goods of another is *parivartana*.
That has been explained by [the discussion on] enjoyment.
If he does not enter revenue that has been realized,
does not pay expenses that have been recorded,
or denies a deposit (nīvī) that has been received, this constitutes embezzlement.
In that case, the fine shall be twelvefold.
There are forty methods for seizing them.
That which was previously established is later set aside; that which was later established is earlier set aside;
the probandum is not established.
The unachievable was made achieved; the achieved was made unachieved;
the unachieved was made achieved.
That which was accomplished with little effort was made much; that which was accomplished with great effort was made little;
what was accomplished as one thing was made another.
What was established by one person but altered by another;
what was not to be given but was given, or what was to be given but was not given.
Given at the wrong time, given at the right time, little given but made much.
Much was given, but little was done; one thing was given, but another was done; it was given from one source, but performed elsewhere.
What was entered as not entered, what was made [as such], what was not entered as entered,
and base metal (kupya) entered without its price being paid;
The price paid has not been entered [into the records]:
either a consolidation has been made into a dispersal, or a dispersal has been made into a consolidation. (KAZ02.8.21d)
When a high-priced item is exchanged for a low-priced one, or a low-priced item for a high-priced one—
the price has been inflated. (KAZ 02.8.21e)
Or he has been demoted,
or a year has been made inconsistent with its months, or a month has been made inconsistent with its days.
Irregularity in the junctions, irregularity in the openings,
and irregularity in the craftsmanship—
Irregularity in the exchange, irregularity in the total amount,
and irregularity in the quality.
Inequality in the offering of water (argha),
inequality in measurement (māna),
and inequality in weighing (māpana).
"Discrepancy in the vessel"—these are the means of embezzlement.
In this regard, one should interrogate each individually the person who deposited the goods, the binder, the receiver, the giver, the one who caused it to be given, the counselor, and the attendant.
And for false testimony regarding these matters, the punishment shall be equal to that prescribed for perjury.
And he should cause a proclamation to be made throughout the public thoroughfares: "Let those who have been harmed by this perpetrator come forward."
If he reports it, the king shall cause him to pay compensation according to the extent of the damage.
And when there are multiple charges and the defendant denies them all, if he is once declared defeated by the opponent, he shall be liable for the whole.
In cases of inequality, he should apply the interrogation in every instance.
And in the case of a large embezzlement of wealth, even one who has succeeded with only a small portion shall share in the whole.
A spy who has successfully carried out his mission after having received his reward shall receive a sixth part [of the prize];
one who acts as a hired agent shall receive a twelfth part.
If, despite great effort, the yield is small, he shall receive a share of what has been produced.
If the work is not completed, he shall receive corporal punishment or a fine of gold,
and he is not to be granted any favor.
Upon the settlement of the case, he should either deposit the dispute [in the treasury] or cause himself to be removed [from the jurisdiction].
However, an informant who instigates a defendant shall incur the penalty of death.
(Inspection of the Work of Officers)
All superintendents, endowed with the qualities of a minister, should be appointed to their respective tasks according to their capacity.
And he should constantly cause the examination of these men regarding their duties,
because the minds of human beings are unstable.
For humans, when appointed to tasks, behave like horses and act perversely.
Therefore, one should ascertain among these the doer, the instrument, the place, the time, the purpose, the expenditure, and the profit.
They shall carry out their duties according to the instructions, neither acting in concert nor in opposition.
United they may enjoy [the spoils],
but divided they will bring about destruction.
And they should not undertake any enterprise without having informed their master,
except in cases of countering emergencies.
And for any negligence on their part in these matters, he shall impose a fine equal to twice the daily wage and expenses.
And whoever among them performs the task as instructed, or even with distinction, shall receive status and honor.
"If there is little income but great expenditure, he consumes [the treasury]."
"In the opposite case, as [stated] in KAZ02.9.11, he does not consume [the revenue], provided that there is neither increase nor decrease"—so say the teachers.
Kautilya maintains that he should be discovered only by means of a secret agent.
He who causes the revenue to fall short consumes the king's wealth.
If he causes [the work] to be abandoned through ignorance and other such reasons, then the king shall make him pay for it according to the quality of the work.
He who causes the revenue to increase twofold devours the countryside.
If he brings [goods] for the sake of the king, he should be restrained in the case of a minor offense, but in the case of a major one, he should be punished according to the nature of the offense.
He who brings revenue into expenditure consumes the labor of the men.
KAZ02.9.18: He shall be punished according to the offense for stealing the value of the workday's materials or the wages of the laborers.
Therefore, whoever is appointed to a particular office shall report to him the true state of that business, as well as its income and expenditure, both in detail and in summary.
He shall also prohibit those who misappropriate the principal, those who act only for the immediate moment, and the miserly.
He who unjustly consumes the wealth inherited from his father and grandfather is a "root-destroyer" (*mūlahara*).
He who eats whatever is produced at that very moment is one who lives for the present.
He who accumulates wealth by oppressing his servants and himself is a miser (*kadarya*).
If he possesses allies, he is not to be seized;
in the opposite case, he is to be extorted.
KAZ02.9.25: When a miser, situated amidst a great accumulation of wealth, hoards it, buries it, or causes it to flow out— hoarding it in his own house,
burying it among the citizens and country folk,

or causing it to flow out into another territory— an agent (sattrin) shall ascertain the circle of his ministers, friends, servants, and kinsmen, as well as the sources from which his wealth comes and the ways in which it goes.
And whoever should carry out travel for him in a foreign territory, having gained access to that person, he should discover the secret counsel.
Once he has been well identified, the king should have him killed under the pretext of an enemy's command.
Therefore, his superintendents—accompanied by accountants, scribes, examiners of goods, receivers of the nīvis, and assistant superintendents—should carry out their duties.
The superintendents of the northern division shall be the riders of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Their pupils, who are disciplined in their craft and purity, shall serve as spies for the accountants and other officials.
One should establish an office that has many chiefs and is not permanent.

For just as honey or poison resting on the surface of the tongue cannot be tasted without being consumed, so too the king’s revenue, even if it be very small, cannot be enjoyed by the revenue officer without being experienced. Just as fish moving within the water cannot be known while they are drinking that water, so it is with the king's affairs.
Likewise, those who are appointed to the execution of duties cannot be known when they are taking wealth [for themselves].
It may be possible to know the path of birds flying in the sky; but it is not possible to know the path of those secret agents who move about in disguise.
One should cause those who have accumulated wealth to leak it away and divert them from their tasks,
so that they do not consume the state’s revenue or, having consumed it, exhaust it.
However, those who do not consume the revenues but increase them through lawful means should be retained.

KAZ02.9.36cd: "Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of the king, they should perform their duties with constant authority. [End of section] (On Edicts) KAZ02.10.01: "In the matter of edicts, they say 'the edict'."
For kings have policy as their primary concern, since peace and war are rooted in it.

Therefore, a scribe should be endowed with the qualities of a minister, conversant with all conventions, swift in composition, possessing graceful handwriting, and capable of both writing and reading.

KAZ02.10.04: Having heard the king’s message with an undistracted mind, he should compose a letter of certain meaning; for a sovereign, it should include the customary mention of his country, dominion, lineage, and name, whereas for one who is not a sovereign, it should include only the customary mention of his country and name.

Having considered birth, family, station, age, learning, success in action, character, as well as place and time, and the connection by marriage, one should compose a document for a given matter that is appropriate to the person concerned.
The excellence of a document consists of: sequence of meaning, logical connection, completeness, sweetness, dignity, and clarity.
In that regard, the sequence of meaning (*artha-krama*) consists of first applying oneself to the primary objective according to the proper successive procedure.
The connection is that the formulation of the subsequent [point] continues until the conclusion, without obstructing the subject matter already introduced.

Completeness consists in the absence of deficiency or excess in the meaning, the words, and the syllables; the thorough description of the matter through reasons, examples, and illustrations; and the quality of tireless phrasing.
Mādhurya (sweetness) is the expression of words whose meanings are beautiful and easily understood.
KAZ02.10.11: Nobility (*audārya*) consists in the employment of words that are not vulgar.
KAZ02.10.12: The use of well-known words constitutes clarity.
KAZ02.10.13: The phonemes beginning with the letter *a* are sixty-three in number.
A word (pada) is a collection of phonemes (varṇa).
And that [word] is of four kinds: nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles.
In that context, "nāman" (name) indeed denotes a sentient being (*sattva*).
A verb, which expresses action, has no specific gender.
KAZ02.10.18: The particles beginning with *pra* are *upasargas* (prefixes) when they qualify an action (*kriyā*).
KAZ02.10.19: And the words beginning with "avyaya" (indeclinables) are called *nipātas* (particles).
KAZ02.10.20: A collection of words constitutes a sentence when there is a completion of the sense.
KAZ02.10.21: A section (varga) should be composed with a minimum of one word and a maximum of three words, provided that this does not conflict with the meaning of the subsequent section.
The word "iti" is used for the purpose of concluding the letter, and [the phrase] "vācikam asya" (this is its oral message) is also used.
Censure, praise, inquiry, as well as narration, and then a request;
refusal, reproach, prohibition, and then an exhortation;
conciliation, assistance, as well as threats and entreaty.
In these thirteen [categories], all matters concerning written documents proceed.
Among them, speaking of the defects of one's lineage, physical body, or actions is "censure" (*nindā*).
KAZ02.10.26: A statement of quality is a praise of these very [qualities].
"How is this so?"—this is the question.
"Thus" refers to the narrative.
"Give!"—this is the request for a favor.
“I will not give it,” is a refusal.
“‘This is unbecoming of you’—this is the censure.”
"‘Do not do it’—this is a prohibition."
KAZ02.10.33: "Let this be done"—this is an injunction (*codanā*).
KAZ02.10.34: “He who I am, you are he;
that which is my wealth, yours is it”—this is conciliation by means of identification (*upagraha*).
Assistance in times of calamity is *abhyupapatti*.
KAZ02.10.36: Threatening with the display of future misfortune when one is already at fault is intimidation.
KAZ02.10.37: Conciliation is threefold: [applied] when a purpose has been accomplished, when there has been a transgression, and when there is misfortune to men and so forth.

The *prajñāpana*, *ājñā*, *paridāna*, and *lekha*; likewise the *parihāra* and *nisṛṣṭi* letters; the *prāvṛttika*, the *pratilekha*, and the *sarvatraga*—these indeed are the royal edicts (*śāsana*).
"By this [person], it has been thus represented; he says this: 'If that is the truth, let that be granted.'"
KAZ02.10.39cd: This various instruction for conveying messages near the king has thus been taught.
KAZ02.10.40ab: Wherein the master’s command regarding punishment and favor is contained, KAZ02.10.40cd:
especially concerning his servants—that is the defining characteristic of a royal edict.
Wherever worship characterized by qualities appropriate to the recipient is observed,
those two— whether in the form of a pledge (*ādhi*) or a formal entrustment (*paridāna*)— constitute forms of conciliation (*upagraha*).
[This applies] toward specific castes, among others, and likewise toward various villages and regions.

KAZ 2.10.42cd: A favor granted by the command of the king, one who knows this should determine it to be a *parihāra* (exemption). KAZ 2.10.43ab: Authorization (*nisṛṣṭi*), entrustment (*sthāpanā*), and likewise the execution of a task or the delivery of a message; KAZ 2.10.43cd: This constitutes a verbal or written order, or it may also be an authorization (*naisṛṣṭika*).
Regarding royal commands, they determine that activity (*pravṛtti*) is of two kinds: that which is connected with destiny (*daiva*), and that which arises from human agency (*mānuṣī*).
Having examined the document according to its true nature and having responded to it accordingly, [one should act].
A written reply (pratilekha) should be made in accordance with the king’s word.
Wherever the king has commanded the lords and officials regarding protection and assistance for the sake of travelers,
that is to be known as the "all-pervading" (sarvatraga) [order], applicable on the road and everywhere throughout the region.
KAZ02.10.47: The means [of policy] are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force.
In that regard, conciliation (*sāman*) is of five kinds: the proclamation of virtues,
the narration of relationships, the demonstration of mutual assistance, [the pointing out of common interests, and the praise of one's own power].
The demonstration of the future and the comparison with oneself.

KAZ02.10.49: In this context, the apprehension of qualities regarding lineage, body, actions, nature, learning, wealth, and so forth; their praise, eulogy, and the proclamation of their virtues [constitute commendation].
The narration of kinship, marriage, maternal relations, paternal relations, family, heart-felt affection, friendship, and lineage constitutes the discourse on connections.
KAZ02.10.51: Proclaiming the mutual assistance between one's own side and the enemy's side is "demonstrating mutual benefit."
KAZ02.10.52: “If this is done by you, this will happen for both of us”—this is the generation of hope, which is the demonstration of future results.
KAZ02.10.53: “He who I am, you are he;
whatever property is mine, let that be employed by you for your own affairs”—this is the surrender of one’s self. Thus [ends the section].
KAZ02.10.54: A bribe is the offering of wealth as a favor.
Sowing suspicion and intimidation constitute the method of sowing dissension.
Punishment consists of execution, torture, and the confiscation of property. Thus [it is said].
Lack of elegance, contradiction, tautology, incorrect word, and redundancy are the defects of a written document.
In that regard, black-leafed poison (kālapattraka) is unpleasant, toxic, lacks color and texture, and is unattractive.
KAZ02.10.59: Contradiction (vyāghāta) is the impossibility of the latter following from the former.
A second utterance of that which has already been stated without distinction is called "repetition" (punarukta).
KAZ02.10.61: The incorrect application of gender, number, tense, and grammatical case is ungrammatical speech (apaśabda).
In the case of a non-group, there is the formation of a group, the operation of non-subtraction, the reversal of the multiplier, and the confluence [of these]. Thus it is said.
Having examined all the treatises and having observed their practical application,
Kauṭilya has composed this rule for royal edicts for the benefit of the lord of men.
(Evaluation of Precious Articles to be Received into the Treasury)

The Superintendent of the Treasury, presided over by experts in the valuation of those materials, shall receive whatever is to be entered into the treasury—whether gems, valuable goods, inferior goods, or base metals.
Tāmraparṇika, Pāṇḍyakavāṭaka, Pāśikya, Kauleya, Caurṇeya, Māhendra, Kārdamika, Srautasīya, Hrādīya, and Haimavata are the varieties of pearl.
Oyster shells, conch shells, and miscellaneous sources are the origins [of pearls].
The *masūraka*, *tripuṭaka*, *kūrmaka*, *ardhacandraka*, *kañcukita*, *yamaka*, *kartaka*, *kharaka*, *siktaka*, *kāmaṇḍaluka*, *śyāva*, *nīla*, and *durviddha* are considered inferior.
That which is thick, round, oval, lustrous, white, heavy, glossy, and pierced by the [proper] region is praiseworthy.
The types of staffs (*yaṣṭi*) are: the *śīrṣaka*, the *upaśīrṣaka*, the *prakāṇḍaka*, the *avaghāṭaka*, and that which is attached to a central gem (*tarala-pratibaddha*).
Eight thousand yaṣṭis constitute the Indrachchandas.
KAZ02.11.08: Half of that is the *vijayacchanda*.
Sixty-four [pearls] constitute the *ardhahāra* (half-necklace).
The bundle of rays consists of fifty-four [rays].
Thirty-two form a *guccha*.
The garland of constellations consists of twenty-seven.
Twenty-four [guñjās] constitute one half-guccha.
Twenty [māṣakas] make one māṇavaka.
KAZ02.11.15: Half of that is the *ardhamāṇavaka* coin.
These very same [beads], when placed in the center of a *maṇi*, become those *māṇavaka* beads.
A single-strand necklace with one central pendant is called a *śuddha-hāra*.
The remaining [cases] are likewise.
The *ardhamāṇavaka* has its center at the jewel.
It has three planks with a plank-ledge, or it has five planks.
KAZ02.11.21: The single-string necklace (ekāvalī) is pure.
That same staff has a jewel set in its middle.
A jeweled necklace variegated with gold and gems.
A counterfeit coin containing gold, gems, or pearls [is a form of fraud].
The stairway consists of intervals of gold and thread.
Or it may have a jeweled center or jeweled steps.
By this, the various types of arrangements for the head, hands, feet, waist, and the network of hair are explained.
Kaz02.11.28: Gems are those from Koṭa, Māleyaka, and beyond the sea.
The *saugandhika*, the *padmarāga*, the *anavadyarāga*, the *pārijātapuṣpaka*, and the *bālasūryaka*.

Vaiḍūrya [gems] are of the color of the blue lotus, the śirīṣa flower, the color of water, the color of bamboo, the color of a parrot’s wing, the color of the Puṣya asterism, cow’s urine, or cow dung.
The Indranīla, the Nīlāvalīya, the Kalāyapuṣpaka, the Mahānīla, the Jambvābha, the Jīmūtaprabha, the Nandaka, and the Sravannmadhya.
The pure crystal (śuddhasphaṭika), the one with the color of a *mūlāṭa* flower, the cold-rain (*śītavr̥ṣṭi*), and the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*)—
these are the gems.

KAZ02.11.33/ Hexagonal, quadrangular, or circular; intensely colored, well-proportioned, clear, glossy, heavy, radiant, with internal luster, and emitting a pervasive glow—these are the qualities of a gem.
KAZ02.11.34/ Faintly colored, lacking luster, containing grit, having flower-like flaws, fractured, poorly perforated, and covered with scratches—these are the defects.

The *antara-jāti* (intermediate species) are: *vimalaka*, *sasyaka*, *añjanamūlaka*, *pittaka*, *sulabhaka*, *lohita-akṣa*, *mṛgāśmaka*, *jyotī-rasaka*, *māleyaka*, *ahicchatraka*, *kūrpa*, *pratikūrpa*, *sugandhi-kūrpa*, *kṣīravaka*, *śukti-cūrṇaka*, *śilā-pravālaka*, *pulaka*, and *śukla-pulaka*.
The remaining glass-gems are [of the same quality].
The Sabhārāṣṭraka, Tajjamārāṣṭraka, Kāstīrarāṣṭraka, Śrīkaṭanaka, Maṇimantaka, and Indravānaka are the diamonds.
Mines, streams, and miscellaneous sources are the origins [of revenue].

The colors of diamonds (*vajra*) are as follows: the color of a cat’s eye, the color of a *śirīṣa* flower, the color of cow’s urine, the color of cow dung, pure crystal, the color of *mūlāṭī*, or any other color resembling that of precious gems.
A diamond is praised when it is large, heavy, resistant to blows, has even edges, scratches vessels, leaves a whorl-mark like a lathe-turning, and is lustrous.
A house with a missing corner, lacking sides, or having its sides distorted is inauspicious.
Coral is of three kinds: *āla*, *kandaka*, and *vaivarṇika*;
and the red *padmarāga* (ruby) is valued except for that which is *karaṭa* or *garbhiṇikā*.
Sandalwood is of three kinds: white, red, and earth-scented.
Kālatāmra has the head of a cow and the smell of fish.
Hari-candana is the color of a parrot’s wing, has the fragrance of mango, and is produced from grass.
And there is also tārnasa.
Grāmeruka is red or dark red, and has the smell of goat's urine.
The *daivasabheya* is red, has the fragrance of a lotus, and is used for recitation (*jāpaka*).
Jongaka is red or dark red, glossy, and has the appearance of a peacock's neck.
Māleyaka is pale red.
Kucandana is rough, and its agaru is black, red, or reddish-black.
Kālaparvataka is blackish-red or of flawless color.
A treasury-house with mountain-like structures, or one that is black and variegated in color.
That which has cold water is like the luster of a lotus, or it is dark and glossy.
The *nāgaparvataka* stone is rough and has the color of moss.
Śākala and Kapila. Thus [ends the section].

Light, unctuous, non-sticky, smeared with the oiliness of ghee, pleasant in scent, spreading along the skin, not excessive, not fading, heat-tolerant, absorbing burning sensations, and pleasant to the touch—
these are the qualities of sandalwood.
Agallochum (aguru) from Joṅgaka is black, or variegated with black, or marked with circular spots.
The *doṅgaka* is dark-colored.
That which comes from across the sea is of variegated appearance and has the fragrance of uśīra or the fragrance of navamālikā. Thus it is said.

Heavy, unctuous, possessing a delicate fragrance, portable, fire-resistant, emitting smoke that does not spread excessively, and capable of withstanding friction—these are the qualities of agallochum (aguru).
Kaz02.11.61: Tailaparṇika is from Aśokagrāma; it has the color of meat and the fragrance of a lotus.
Jongaka is red-yellow, has the fragrance of a blue lotus, or the smell of cow urine.
Grāmeruka is unctuous and has the smell of cow urine.
It has golden walls, is red and yellow in color, and possesses the fragrance of a citron.
It has the fragrance of full-blown lotuses, or the scent of fresh butter.
Bhadraśrī from Pāralauhityaka, of the Jātī caste.
The *āntaravatya* variety has the color of *uśīra*.
Both [types] smell like kuṣṭha. Thus [it is said].
Kāleyaka, produced in Svarṇabhūmi, is glossy and yellowish.
KAZ02.11.70: That which comes from the northern mountains is reddish-yellow; these are the heartwoods (sāra). KAZ02.11.71:
It withstands being pounded, boiled, and smoked, does not lose its color, and is suitable for various applications.
And their qualities are like those of sandalwood and aloe-wood.
Kāntanāvaka, praiyaka, and uttaraparvataka are types of skins.
Kāntanāvaka is like the luster of a peacock's neck.
The *praiyaka* is variegated with blue, yellow, white lines, and spots.
Both of these shall be eight finger-breadths in length.
A *bisī* and a *mahābisī* [are the taxes] in a district of twelve villages.
The *duhilitikā* is of indistinct form, or it is variegated like a lotus fiber (*bisī*).
The *mahābisī* is coarse, predominantly white, and possesses large fibers.
Both [ends] shall be twelve finger-breadths in length.
Śyāmikā, kālikā, kadalī, candrottarā, and śākulā are those born from the ascent (ārohajāḥ).
A tawny cow, variegated with spots, or a dark-colored one.
The *kālikā* is brownish-black or the color of a dove.
Both of these are eight finger-breadths in length.
The *paruṣā* lute has a girth like that of a plantain tree and is as long as an arm.
That same [constellation] is called Candra-citrā and Candra-uttarā.
A *śākulā* [shield] made of three parts of plantain, variegated with circles and spots, or variegated with artificial bosses like a deer skin—thus it is described.
Sāmūra, cīnasī, and sāmūlī are the varieties belonging to the Bāhlava region.
Sāmūra leather is thirty-six finger-breadths in length and has the color of collyrium.
Cīnasī is reddish-black or pale black.
The *sāmūlī* is the color of burnt cow-dung. Thus [it is said].
Kaz02.11.92: *Sānti*, *nalatūla*, *vṛttapṛcchā*, and *caudra* are [types of] honey.
The black variety is produced by sowing.
Nalatūlā is [a woman] who has the color of nalatūla.
A tawny cow with a rounded tail.
Thus end the varieties of skins.
Among skins, that which is soft, glossy, and thick-furred is the best. (KAZ 2.11.96)
Woolen cloth is of four kinds: pure, pure-red, half-red, and variegated;
it may also be embroidered, woven with patterns, made by joining pieces, or woven with broken threads.

KAZ02.11.98: Woolen blankets (*kambala*), *kaucapaka*, *kulamitikā*, *saumitikā*, horse-blankets (*turagāstaraṇa*), *varṇaka*, *talicchaka*, *vāravāṇa*, *paristoma*, and *samantabhadraka* are varieties of sheep’s wool.
KAZ02.11.99: That which is glossy, as if moist, fine, and soft is the best.
The *bhiṅgisī* made of eight joined pieces, black in color, used for rain protection and as a screen, is of Nepalese origin.
The *sampuṭikā*, the *caturaśrikā*, the *lambarā*, the *kaṭavānaka*, the *prāvaraka*, and the *sattalikā*—these are garments made of deer hair.
Vāṅgaka silk is white, smooth, and glossy.
The Pauṇḍraka stone is dark and as lustrous as a gem.
The *sauvarṇakuḍyaka* (gold-walled) [carpet] is sun-colored, with a weave smooth as a gem and water-like, featuring square-patterned weaving and mixed-patterned weaving.
Of these, there are those consisting of one *aṃśuka*, and those of one and a half, two, three, or four *aṃśukas*.
By this, the linen cloth from Kāśī and that from Pauṇḍra are explained.
The *māgadhikā*, *pauṇḍrikā*, and *sauvarṇakuḍyakā* are varieties of leaf-cotton (*pattra-ūrṇā*).
The *nāga*, *likuca*, *bakula*, and *vaṭa* trees are the sources [of these materials].
The yellow *nāgavṛkṣikā* [is used].
The *laikucī* is the color of cow-smoke.
White *bākulī* [is used].
The remaining ones have the color of fresh butter.
Among those, the one with walls made of gold is the best.
By this [rule], silk cloth and Chinese pattas produced in the land of China are explained.
Cotton cloth from Mādhura, Āparāntaka, Kaliṅga, Kāśī, Vaṅga, Vatsa, and Mahiṣaka is the best. Thus.
KAZ02.11.116/ Henceforth, one should know the measurement, price, characteristics, origin, appearance, storage, and the method of manufacture for other precious gems.
KAZ02.11.117/ One should understand their species, form, provenance, and whether they are new or old works.
The restoration of old [mines and factories], secret operations, and tools;
the utilization according to place and time, and the countermeasures against harmful creatures. (KAZ02.11.118–119)

The Superintendent of Mines shall be an expert in the treatises on metallurgy and mineral ores, as well as in the processing of liquids (alchemical preparations) and the coloring of gems; or he may be one who associates with such experts.

Equipped with the necessary tools for the specific tasks of his office, he shall inspect a mine—whether previously exploited or not—to determine its characteristics through the presence of dross, crucibles, charcoal, and ashes, and to ascertain whether it contains subterranean deposits of liquid minerals or ores of exceptional color and weight.
One should examine it for its pungent odor and taste.

KAZ02.12.02: In mountains with well-known locations, within caves, caverns, valleys, dwellings, or hidden pits, there are internal flowing liquids—juices that possess the colors of the ripe fruit of the *jambu*, mango, and palmyra; of turmeric, *guḍa* (molasses), *haritāla* (yellow orpiment), realgar, honey, vermilion, white lotus, parrot, or peacock feathers; which are bounded by water and medicinal plants of similar color, and which are viscous, clear, and heavy—these are *kāñcanikā* (gold-bearing ores).
Those who pierce more than one hundred [leaves] of copper or silver—[the metal] which, when cast into water, spreads like oil and clings to the mud at the bottom—are [worthy of a reward].
One should know that rock-lac, which resembles it and possesses a pungent smell and taste, is a counterfeit.

KAZ02.12.05: Those ores of the earth’s crust that are yellow, coppery, or reddish-yellow; which, when broken, show blue streaks or have the color of mung beans, black gram, or *kṛsara*; which are variegated with spots like drops of curd; which, when broken, possess the flawless colors of turmeric, myrobalan, lotus petals, water-moss, liver, or spleen;
which bear markings of *cuñcu*, sand, lines, dots, or svastikas; and which are well-rounded and radiant—these do not [lose their luster] when heated.
Gold ores that emit much foam and smoke are to be broken up; they serve as additives for the transmutation of copper and silver.

[Gold] having the color of conch-shell, camphor, crystal, fresh butter, a dove, a pigeon, the *vimalaka* gem, or a peacock’s neck; having the color of *sasyaka*, *gomedaka*, molasses, or raw sugar; having the color of the flowers of *kovidāra*, lotus, *pāṭalī*, *kālaya*, linen, or flax; containing lead, containing collyrium, smelling of raw flesh, or appearing broken; being white-tinged, black, black-tinged, or white; or all of them variegated with lines and spots.
Silver ores, when being smelted, are soft; they do not burst apart, and they produce much foam and smoke.
KAZ02.12.07: When there is an increase in the weight of all minerals, there is an increase in the quality of the substance.

If those [medicines] are impure or contain undigested matter, they may be treated with sharp urine and alkaline substances; then, bound together with pills made from the dung of the *rājavṛkṣa*, *vaṭa*, *pīlu*, cow, buffalo, donkey, and camel, or mixed with their bile and bezoars, or smeared with them, they flow out pure when applied as an antidote or an ointment.
A mixture of barley, black gram, sesame, *palāśa*, and *pīlu* ashes, or cow’s milk and goat’s milk, with the addition of plantain and *vajra-kanda*, acts as a softener [of metals].
Honey, madhuka, goat’s milk, oil, ghee, molasses, yeast, and kandalī—
though it may be split into a hundred thousand pieces, it becomes soft after just three drenchings with these.
The application of cow-teeth and horns is for the purpose of softening and fixing [the soil].
A heavy, oily, and soft mineral-bearing stratum or a patch of ground that is brownish-yellow, green, pale red, or crimson is copper ore.

The lead ore (sīsadhātu) is that which resembles the color of a pigeon's eye or is streaked with white lines; it smells like raw flesh (visra). It is called "crow-releaser" (kākamocaka) because crows release it when they touch it.
The tin ore is saline and variegated, or has the color of a baked clod of earth.
Kharumba, which is pale red or the color of a *sinduvāra* flower, is a sharp mineral (*tīkṣṇadhātu*).
Alternatively, the vaikṛntaka mineral has the color of a crow’s egg, a snake’s hood, or a leaf.
Transparent, glossy, radiant, resonant, cool, intense, and lightly colored—such is the mineral of precious gems.
One should employ that which originates from minerals at the conclusion of the birth-rites and similar ceremonies.
He should establish a monopoly on the trade of manufactured goods and impose a penalty on those who manufacture, purchase, or sell them elsewhere.
One who steals from a mine shall be made to pay eight times the value, except in the case of precious gems.
One should compel a thief and one who lives on unpermitted goods to perform labor while bound, as well as one who has benefited from a fine.
A mine that involves heavy expenditure should be given away either as a share or for a purchase price; one that involves little expense, however, he should work himself.
The Superintendent of Metals shall cause the manufacture of copper, lead, tin, vaikṛntaka, kārakūṭa, vṛtta, kaṃsa, tāla, and iron, as well as their various works,
and the trade in metal vessels.

The Superintendent of Minting shall cause silver coins to be struck from copper weighing four parts, alloyed with one *māṣaka* seed-measure of any one of the following: *tīkṣṇa*, tin, lead, or antimony—namely, the *paṇa*, the half-*paṇa*, the quarter-*paṇa*, and the eighth-part coin.
Copper coins shall be made for a livelihood consisting of a quarter [of the value], namely the *māṣaka*, the half-*māṣaka*, and the *kākaṇī*.
"A half-kākaṇī."
The superintendent of coinage shall establish the currency for trade and that which is to be entered into the treasury.
An eight-per-cent premium on the value,
a five-per-cent brokerage,
and an eighth-part inspection fee.
A fine of one hundred [paṇas] and an additional penalty of twenty-five paṇas shall be imposed, except upon the maker, the buyer, the seller, and the examiner.
The Superintendent of Mines shall cause the working of conch-shells, diamonds, gems, pearls, corals, and salt-works to be carried out, as well as their sale and trade.

The Superintendent of Salt shall collect at the proper time the portion of salt produced from boiling, as well as the purchase price; and from its sale, he shall collect the value, the toll, and the premium.
Imported salt shall pay a sixth part as duty.
The sale of land whose share has been assigned involves a five percent premium, as well as a *rūpa* and a *rūpika* fee.

The purchaser shall pay the toll and a compensatory fine (*vaidharaṇa*) proportionate to the loss of the king's merchandise; otherwise, the purchaser shall pay a fine of six hundred *paṇas* and a penalty.
One who sells salt without authorization shall pay the highest fine,
as shall one who lives by selling it without permission, except for forest hermits (*vānaprastha*).
Vedic scholars, ascetics, and laborers shall take rice and salt as their wages.
Other than this, the category of salt and alkaline substances shall pay a toll.

In this manner, [the superintendent shall fix] the price, the share, the premium, the toll, the penalty for delay, the customs duty, the compensation for loss, the fine, the form [of coin], and the minting fee.
From mines, one should collect twelve kinds of minerals and commodities;
in this manner, one should establish control over the price of all commodities.
The treasury has its source in the mines; from the treasury the army is produced;
and by means of the treasury and the army, the earth—adorned with the treasury—is acquired.

The Superintendent of Gold shall cause a workshop for the various crafts of gold and silver to be constructed, consisting of four halls connected together, with a single door and equipped with a lathe-hall.
In the center of the marketplace, he shall station a goldsmith who is skilled in his craft, of noble birth, and trustworthy.

Jāmbūnada, śātakumbha, hāṭaka, vaiṇava, that which comes from horn or oyster shell, jātarūpa, that which is infused with mercury (rasaviddha), and that which is produced in mines—these are the varieties of gold.
That which is the color of a flower-stamen, soft, glossy, without a seam, and lustrous is the best;
that which is reddish-yellow is middling; and that which is red is inferior.
For the finest [articles], pale-white and white are considered unblemished.
Therefore, that which is not yet purified should be refined with lead four times its weight.
When it is being split by means of lead, one should blow upon it with dry layers of cloth.
When it begins to crack due to dryness, one should pour oil and cow-dung over it.
Lead extracted from a mine, when processed by means of lead-bearing ore, should be made into cooking-plates and pounded upon anvils,
or it should be infused into a paste of plantain and *vajrakanda* roots.
Silver [is of four kinds]: *tuttha-udgata*, *gauḍika*, *kāmbuka*, and *cākravālika*.
White, glossy, and soft is the best.
In the opposite case, bursting [the seed] is also defective.
One should purify it with one-fourth part of lead.
With its crest uplifted, it is clear, radiant, the color of curd, and pure.
For pure gold, one *hāridra* is the measure for the color. For gold that is yellowish, it is one *suvarṇa*.
Thenceforth, there are sixteen varieties [of coins], starting from the *śulba-kākaṇī* and extending downward as far as the four boundaries.
Having first rubbed the gold on the touchstone, one should afterwards rub the test-piece (varṇikā) upon it.

One should recognize as fraudulent a document that has been rubbed on a surface of even color and free from depressions or elevations, or one that has been smoothed over, licked with the fingernail, or dusted with red ochre.
Gold touched by the tip of a hand smeared with *jāti-hiṅguluka* or *puṣpaka-sīsa*, both processed with cow’s urine, turns white.
That which has filaments, is glossy, soft, lustrous, and possesses a brilliant streak on the touchstone is the best.
The touchstone from Kaliṅga or the stone from the Tāpī river, having the color of a mung bean, is the best for testing gold.
One who is impartial in passion and intent on both selling and buying [is fit for the office].
Elephant-hide that is greenish and possesses a natural dye is suitable for sale.
One that is firm, rough, of uneven color, and lacking luster is beneficial for purchase.
A cut that is glossy, even-colored, smooth, soft, and lustrous is the best.
The *tāpa* (heat) is excellent when it is uniform both externally and internally, having the color of a lotus filament or the color of a *kuraṇḍaka* flower.
One who is dark-brown or blue-black is one who has not attained [his goal].
We shall explain the standards for weights and measures in the section concerning the Superintendent of Weights and Measures.
By that instruction, one should give and receive silver and gold.
No one who is not appointed shall enter the gambling hall.
One who approaches [a woman] in this manner shall be punished with the death penalty.
Or, if he is employed with silver and gold of the same quality, he shall be defeated by that very [standard].

Goldsmiths, lapidaries, carvers of ivory, and workers in gold, silver, and copper, as well as blowers, assistants, and sweepers, shall enter and exit with their hands and private parts covered by searched garments.
And all their equipment and unfinished projects shall remain right there.
The gold received and the interest accrued shall be paid into the midst of the court proceedings.
In the evening and in the morning, he shall deposit what has been inspected, marked with the seals of both the maker and the employer.
The throwing-net, the cord, and small implements—these are the tools for these tasks.
Kṣepaṇa consists of the application of glass and similar substances.
The subsidiary activities include weaving thread and so forth.
Solid, hollow, and those provided with spots and so forth are termed "minor" (kṣudraka).
One should apply five parts of gold for the work of glass, and ten parts for the measurement of the pungent substance.
Silver mixed with one-quarter part of copper, or gold mixed with one-quarter part of silver, is refined coinage;
therefore, one should protect it from adulteration.
In the manufacture of spotted glass, there are three parts for the decorative ornaments and two for the main body;
or alternatively, four parts for the main body and three for the decorative ornaments.
The artisan working in metal should combine the raw materials for his work with an equal amount of gold.
Silverware, whether solid or hollow, should be coated with half as much gold.

The Superintendent of the Granary shall oversee the receipts of grain from the fields (*sītā*), the countryside (*rāṣṭra*), purchases, exchanges, loans for consumption, loans for seed, grain collected as a levy, and other miscellaneous expenses and revenues.
Grain of various qualities brought in by the Superintendent of Agriculture constitutes the *sītā* (field-produce).
