(Superintendent of Commerce)

The Superintendent of Commerce shall know the difference in value between superior and inferior goods among the various kinds of merchandise produced on land or in water that arrive by land or water routes, as well as their quality— whether they are desirable or undesirable—
and likewise the times for their distribution, consolidation, purchase, sale, and application.
And whatever commodity may be abundant, having brought it together into a single mass, one should fix its price.
Or, when the price has been reached, he may cause another price to be set.
He shall establish a single-channel system of trade for royal merchandise produced within his own territory, and a multi-channel system for that produced in foreign territories.
And he should cause both to be sold by favoring the subjects.
And he should prevent even a large profit if it is harmful to the subjects.
He should not cause a delay in time or congestion and disorder for goods that are constantly in demand.
Alternatively, merchants may sell royal merchandise through various channels at a fixed price.
And they shall pay a fine of confiscation proportionate to the severity of the cutting.
The toll on measures is one-sixteenth part; on weights and balances, it is one-twentieth part; and on commodities counted by number, it is one-eleventh part.
He should cause merchandise produced in foreign lands to be imported by means of a favor.
And one should not grant tax exemptions that are sustainable for the future to those who transport wool, skins, or other goods.
And newcomers shall not be subjected to legal suits regarding property,
except for those who assist the members of the court.
The supervisors of the merchandise shall place the value of the goods in a wooden chest with a single opening and a single lid.
And at the eighth part of the day, they shall report to the Superintendent of Commerce: "This has been sold;
this is the remainder."
And they shall deliver the weights, measures, and balances.
Thus it has been explained regarding one's own territory.

But regarding foreign territories: having ascertained the market value and the cost price of both the goods to be exported and the goods to be imported in exchange, he should calculate the profit after deducting the expenses for customs duties, road-tolls, ferry-fees, guard-station charges, port-dues, freight, and the king's share.
If there is no profit from the sale, he should look for gain by exporting the goods or by bringing back merchandise in exchange for local products.
Thereafter, he should conduct land transactions by way of a secure road with a strong escort.
And he should maintain contact with the forest-guardians, the border-protectors, and the chiefs of cities and districts for the purpose of showing them favor.
In times of calamity, he should rescue his essential property or himself.
Or, having obtained land for himself, he should conduct the transaction purified by the payment of all dues.

On a water route, he should ascertain the freight rates for vehicles, the food and provisions for the journey, the prices of commodities and their equivalents, the duration of the voyage, the means of countering dangers, and the customs of the merchant ports.
Having understood the commercial practices on river routes according to established custom,
he should proceed where there is profit and avoid that which yields no gain.
The Superintendent of Forest Produce shall cause forest produce to be collected by the guardians of the timber forests.
And he should employ those engaged in the work of timber forests and the production of forest products.
One should fix a fine for the loss of timber from the forest and establish a penalty for its removal, except in times of distress.

The superintendent of the armory shall establish workshops for the manufacture of all types of implements both inside and outside the city; these workshops, which employ artisans in various branches of work, shall be maintained for the purpose of providing a livelihood and for the protection of the city.

The Superintendent of the Armory shall have weapons, armor, and equipment— whether for battle, for fortification, or for attacking enemy cities— manufactured by artisans and craftsmen skilled in those respective crafts, according to the specifications of the work, the time required, the wages, and the completion of the product;
and he shall store them in their proper locations.

Puppet-figures, divine scepters, pig-shaped weapons, clubs, staffs, elephant-goads, palm-leaf fans, mallets, maces, *spṛktalā* (striking-pieces), spades, *āsphāṭima* (crushing machines), *utpāṭima* (uprooting machines), *udghāṭima* (opening machines), *śataghni* (centicide engines), tridents, and discuses— these are mobile mechanical devices.

Spears, darts, lances, *hāṭaka*, *bhiṇḍipāla* javelins, pikes, *tomara* clubs, *varāhakarna* hooks, *kaṇaya* barbed missiles, *karpaṇa* slings, *trāsika* weapons, and others of similar type are known as *hula-mukha* (blunt-tipped) weapons.
*Tāla*, *cāpa*, *dārava*, and *śārṅga* are synonyms for *kārmuka*, *kodaṇḍa*, and *drūṇa*; they denote bows.

Swords with blades shaped like a curved scimitar, a circle, or a straight staff are *khaḍgas*.

The axe, the hatchet, the shield, the pickaxe, the spade, the saw, and the tools for cutting reeds are similar to razors.
Machines, goṣpaṇas, muṣṭis, stones, rocanīs, and dṛṣads are stone weapons.

chests made of leather, "elephant-ear" shields, *tālamūla* shields, *dhamanī* armor, *kākapāṭa* shields, *kiṭikā* shields, and *apratihatabalāhakānta* shields are types of defensive coverings (*āvaraṇa*).

The practice of sorcery and the practice based on secret doctrines.

Twenty *taulikās* constitute one *bhāra*.
Ten *dharaṇas* constitute one *pala*.
One hundred palas of that [gold] constitute the āyamānī.
The scale used for legal transactions and for the women's quarters shall weigh at least five palas.
Of these, the lowest weight for a *pala* is half a *dharaṇa*;
the lowest for superior metal is two *palas*;
and the minimum length of the handles is six finger-breadths.
In the case of the two preceding [categories], the surcharge (*prayāma*) shall be five *palas*, with the exception of meat, metals, salt, and gems.
A wooden balance eight cubits long, provided with foot-rests, equipped with counter-weights, and supported by a peacock-foot base.
Twenty-five palas of wood are required for the preparation of one prastha of rice.
This is the rule for determining the relative magnitude of much and little.
Thus, the rules concerning scales and weights have been explained.
Now, for grain and beans, one hundred and two palas make a *droṇa* as the standard measure (*āyamāna*);
one hundred and eighty-seven palas and half a pala is the commercial measure (*vyāvahārika*);
and one hundred and seventy-five palas is the measure for containers (*bhājanīya*).
One hundred and sixty-two palas and half a pala is the portion to be used by the women of the inner apartments.
Among these, the āḍhaka, prastha, and kuḍuba are each one-fourth less [in size] than the preceding.
Sixteen droṇas make one khārī.
A kumbha consists of twenty droṇas.
A load for ten jars is a *vāha*.
One should have a measuring rod made of dry, solid wood, equal in thickness, with a tip consisting of one-fourth of its width, or with the tip inside the body of the rod.
In the case of spirituous liquor, flowers, fruits, chaff, charcoal, and lime, the interest shall be double the principal amount.
The price of a *droṇa* is one *paṇa* and a quarter; that of an *āḍhaka* is less than a quarter [of a *paṇa*]; six *māṣakas* for a *prastha*;
and one *māṣaka* for a *kuḍuba*.
The value of liquids and other such substances shall be calculated at double their measured quantity.
The fine for counterfeiting a standard weight is twenty paṇas.
The value of a balance is one-third [of the standard].
He shall cause the examination of imported goods to be conducted every four months.
For one who has not been pierced [by the arrow], the fine for the offense is twenty-seven paṇas and one-quarter.
Every day, they shall pay one *kākaṇī* as a stamping fee (*prātivedhanika*) to the Superintendent of Weights and Measures (*pautavādhyakṣa*).
The heated surcharge (tapta-vyājī) on clarified butter is one-thirty-second part;
on oil, it is one-sixty-fourth part.
The loss of liquid substances through evaporation during measurement is one-fiftieth part.
One should have measures made for one-fourth, one-half, one-eighth, and one-sixteenth of a *kuḍuba*.
Eighty-four kudubas are considered to be one vāraka of clarified butter.
Sixty-four palas of oil and one-quarter of a ghaṭikā for each of these two.
KAZ02.20.01: The Superintendent of Measurements shall be knowledgeable regarding the measurement of space and time.
Eight ultimate atoms (paramāṇu) constitute a particle from a chariot wheel (rathacakravipruṭ).
Eight of those [yūkās] are one *likṣā*.
Eight of those [yavas] make one yūka.
Those eight [aṅgulas] constitute one *yavamadhyam*.
Eight yavamadhyas make one angula.
The middle finger of a man of medium size, or the middle joint of that finger, is one *aṅgula*.
The bow-grip is four finger-breadths wide.
The grip of the bow is eight finger-breadths long.
Twelve finger-breadths make a span (vitasti), as does the shadow of a man's height.
Fourteen aṅgulas make a śama, a śala, a parīraya, and a pada.
Two vitastis make one aratni, which is the prājāpatya hasta.
He shall supervise the measurement of weights, balances, and pasture lands, along with the handling of bows.
A *kuṣku* or a *kaṃsa* consists of a *dhanurmuṣṭi*.
A carpenter’s *kiṣku* consisting of forty-two *aṅgulas* is the standard measure for army encampments, fortresses, and royal residences.
The measuring rod for forest timber from reservoirs shall be fifty-four finger-breadths long.
A fathom (vyāma) consists of eighty-four finger-breadths; this is the measure for ropes and the standard human depth for excavations.
A staff of four aratnis, a bow, a nālikā, and a pauruṣa constitute the gārhapatya measure.
A bow measuring eight hundred aṅgulas is the standard for the measurement of roads and ramparts, as well as for the height of men and the dimensions of fire-altars.
A staff weighing six kaṃsas is the measure for the property of a Brahmin and for hospitality.
Ten daṇḍas make one rajju.
A boundary is defined by two ropes.
A *nivartana* consists of three ropes on one side.
The upper arm is two daṇḍas longer.
Two thousand bow-lengths constitute a *goruta*.
Four *go-rutas* constitute one *yojana*.
Thus ends the measurement of distance.
KAZ02.20.28: From this point forward is the measurement of time.

KAZ02.20.29–30: A *tuṭa*, a *lava*, a *nimeṣa*, a *kāṣṭhā*, a *kalā*, a *nālikā*, a *muhūrta*, the forenoon and afternoon, day, night, a fortnight (*pakṣa*), a month, a season (*ṛtu*), a solstice (*ayana*), a year, and a *yuga*—these are the divisions of time. Two *tuṭas* make one *lava*.
Two *lava*s constitute one *nimeṣa*.
Five *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *kalā*.
Forty kalās constitute one nālikā.
Four gold māṣakas, four fingers in length, constitute a nālikā, which is either the hole of a water-jar or a measure of one āḍhaka of water.
A muhūrta consists of two nālikās.
In the months of Caitra and Āśvayuja, both day and night consist of fifteen muhūrtas.
Thereafter, for three muhūrtas, one [of the two] increases and [the other] decreases by six months.
In a shadow of eight puruṣas, the reduction is one-eighteenth; in a shadow of six puruṣas, it is one-fourteenth;
in a shadow of three puruṣas, it is one-eighth.
In a cord of two puruṣas, there are six parts; in one puruṣa, four parts;
and in one of eight aṅgulas, thirteen parts.
In a [shadow] four finger-breadths long, there are three eighths;
this is midday when no shadow is cast.
When the day has turned, one should understand the remainder in this same manner.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, at midday, the shadow disappears.
From this point forward, for the six months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, the shadow increases by two aṅgulas; for the six months beginning with Māgha, it decreases by two aṅgulas.
Fifteen days and nights constitute a *pakṣa* (fortnight).
The Śukla (White) [Soma sacrifice] is characterized by the swelling of the Soma.
The *bahula* [measure] is that which cuts off the *soma*.
A month consists of two fortnights.
Thirty days and nights constitute a working month.
A solar day is one and a half [tithis].
A lunar month is less by half [a day].
Twenty-seven [solar days] constitute a lunar (nākṣatra) month.
Thirty-two *bala*s make one *māsa*.
Thirty-five [māṣas] for a horse-load.
There are forty elephant-vehicles.
Two months constitute a season (*ṛtu*).
Śrāvaṇa and Prauṣṭhapada constitute the rainy season (varṣā).
The months of Āśvayuja and Kārttika constitute the autumn season.
Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa constitute the winter season (hemanta).
Māgha and Phālguna constitute the season of Śiśira (dew).
Caitra and Vaiśākha constitute the spring season.
Jyeṣṭhāmūlīya and Āṣāḍha constitute the summer season (grīṣma).
The northern solstice begins with the winter season.
The southern solstice begins with the rainy season.
A year consists of two solstices (ayanas).
A cycle of five years is a *yuga*. Thus [it is said].
During a season, the sun takes away one-sixtieth part of the day;
likewise, the moon causes the loss of one day and [adds] one [day].
In this manner, after two and a half years, they produce an intercalary month:
the first at the end of the summer season, and the last at the end of five years.
KAZ02.21.01: The Superintendent of Customs shall establish the customs house and its flagstaff facing either the east or the north, in the vicinity of the main gate.

KAZ02.21.02–03: Four or five customs officers shall record the merchants arriving with their caravans—specifying who they are, where they are from, what goods they carry, and where a seal or mark of identification has been applied.
For those without such seals, a fine equal to twice the duty to be paid shall be imposed.
For those who forge seals, the fine shall be eight times the amount of the customs duty.
For those whose seals have been broken, there shall be a fine, and they shall be placed in the position of a *ghaṭikā-sthāna*.
In the case of altering the royal seal or changing the name [of the ship], one shall cause the vessel to pay a fine of one and a quarter paṇas.
KAZ02.21.07: When the merchandise has arrived at the foot of the flagstaff, the merchants shall state its quantity and price: "Who will buy this merchandise for such a quantity and at such a price?"
What has been kept for three years in deposit shall be given to the claimants.
In the case of competition among buyers, the increase in price along with the tax shall go to the treasury.
If, out of fear of customs duties, one declares a lower quantity or value for merchandise, the king shall confiscate the excess amount.
Or he may pay eight times the amount of the toll.

KAZ02.21.12–13: He shall apply the same [penalty] to one who lowers the price of merchandise already displayed by using inferior imitation goods, or who conceals high-value goods with low-value goods.
Or, if out of fear of a buyer he increases the price above the actual value of the merchandise, the king shall confiscate the increase in price, or impose double the amount as a fine.
That same amount, multiplied eightfold, is the penalty for a superintendent who conceals it.
Therefore, the sale of commodities shall be conducted by weight, measure, or count; whereas for light goods and those subject to favor, an estimate shall be made.
For those who have passed beyond the base of the flagstaff without having paid the toll, the fine shall be eight times the amount of the toll.
Travelers and those on wrong paths shall know this.

Goods used for marriage, for following a bride (anvāyana), for expedients (aupāyika), or as incidental requirements for sacrificial rites— such as vessels used in specific ceremonies like divine worship, the tonsure ceremony (caula), initiation (upanayana), the gift of a cow (godāna), vows, and consecration (dīkṣā)— shall pass free of toll.
For one who speaks falsely, the punishment for theft shall apply.

For a merchant who exports goods for which duty has not been paid when duty has already been paid, or who steals a package of merchandise by breaking it open with a single seal, the punishment shall be that same amount [of duty] and a fine equal to its value.
If one steals cow-dung or straw from a customs station by making it appear as if it were a standard measure, the punishment shall be the highest amercement.

For one who exports any of the following—weapons, armor, mail, iron, chariots, gems, grain, or livestock—without having first obtained permission, the punishment shall be as publicly proclaimed and the merchandise shall be confiscated.
If any one of them is brought [into the city], his goods may be sold outside the city without the imposition of customs duty.
The frontier guard shall collect one-quarter of a paṇa as a road-toll for a vehicle carrying merchandise,
one paṇa for a single-hoofed animal,
half a paṇa for large cattle, and one-quarter of a paṇa for small animals.
A fine of one māṣa for carrying a load on the shoulder.
And he shall provide compensation for what has been lost or stolen.
The superintendent shall send a foreign caravan to the official after having provided him with identification and a seal, following an inspection of their valuable and non-valuable goods.
Or, one disguised as a merchant may send a report to the king regarding the size of the caravan.
In that region, the king shall inform the Superintendent of Tolls of the size of the caravan for the purpose of proclaiming his omniscience.
Then the superintendent, having approached the caravan, should say: "This is the merchant's goods—both valuable and inferior—and they must not be concealed;
such is the power of the king."
For one who conceals inferior goods, the fine shall be eight times the customs duty; for superior goods, the entire amount shall be confiscated.
He should confiscate merchandise that causes distress to the kingdom and that which is unprofitable; however,
he should exempt from duty goods that are of great utility and seeds that are difficult to obtain.
Hospitality is both external and internal.
Customs duties shall be levied on both exports and imports.
For goods to be imported, one-fifth of their value shall be paid as duty.
He shall take a sixth part of flowers, fruits, vegetables, roots, tubers, climbing plants, seeds, dried fish, and meat.

Regarding conch shells, diamonds, gems, pearls, corals, and necklaces, he shall have them manufactured by persons born of those respective trades, based on the specifications of the work, the time required, the wages, and the final yield.
For linen, silk, products of worms (silk), woven cloth, armor, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, vermilion, and metallic ores;

for sandalwood, aloe-wood, pungent substances, fermenting agents, and inferior items; for skins, ivory, rugs, coverlets, products derived from insects, and the wool of goats and sheep—the tax shall be one-tenth or one-fifteenth.

For garments, quadrupeds, bipeds, thread, cotton, perfumes, medicinal herbs, wood, bamboo, bark, skins, clay, and eggs, as well as for grain, oils, alkalis, salt, liquor, cooked food, and similar items, the tax shall be one-twentieth or one-twenty-fifth.

KAZO 2.22.08: He shall establish as a door-fee (dvārādeya), a toll (śulka), a five-part share (pañcabhāga), or a favor-based levy (ānugrāhika), according to the specific benefit provided to the locality.
KAZO 2.22.09: And the sale of commodities is restricted to their respective places of origin.
KAZO 2.22.10: For taking mineral ores or merchandise from mines, the fine is six hundred panas.
KAZO 2.22.11: For taking flowers or fruits from flower or fruit orchards, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas.
KAZO 2.22.12: For taking vegetables, roots, or tubers from vegetable gardens, the fine shall be forty-five paṇas.
For taking all the crops from fields, the fine is fifty-three paṇas.
The fine for the loss of cultivated land shall be one paṇa or one and a half paṇas.
Therefore, based on the region, caste, and custom,
he shall fix the white tax (*śukla*) and the penalty (*atyaya*) for goods, distinguishing between those that are new and those that are old, according to their potential for harm.
The Superintendent of Thread shall have the trade of thread, armor, cloth, and rope carried out by men born of that craft.

And one should have wool, bark-fiber, cotton, tūla-cotton, hemp, and linen woven by widows, deformed women, virgins, female ascetics, those serving as substitutes for fines, courtesans, mothers of prostitutes, old royal slave-girls, and temple slave-girls whose service has ceased.
Having ascertained whether the thread is fine, thick, or of medium thickness, as well as its quantity— whether it is much or little— one should determine the wages.
Having determined the measurements according to the sūtras, one should treat these women with massages using oil, *āmalaka* fruit, and unguents.
On the lunar days (tithis), they should be made to perform their work by means of gifts of food and other provisions.
In the case of a reduction in the length of the thread, there shall be a corresponding reduction in wages, according to the quality of the material.

He should cause work to be performed by artisans according to the nature of the task, the standard of quality, the time required, the wages, and the completion of the product, and he should maintain regular contact with them.
Employing the various crafts of weaving linen, silk, wool, hair-cloth, and cotton thread, he should win them over with gifts of perfumes, garlands, and other such gratifications;
he should also produce various types of garments, bedspreads, and coverlets.
And he should have armor-work executed by artisans and craftsmen born of that same trade.

KAZ02.23.11: Those women who do not leave their homes while their husbands are away—whether they be widows, those with physical defects, or unmarried girls—who support themselves, shall be followed by female slaves and made to perform work under supervision. KAZ02.23.12: Or, for those who come of their own accord to the thread-manufactory at dawn, he shall cause the exchange of raw materials for wages to take place.
The lamp serves merely for the purpose of examining the thread.
If a woman shows her face or engages in conversation for some other purpose, the first amercement shall be imposed;
likewise for failing to pay wages at the stipulated time, or for not paying wages for work that has been performed.
If she, having received her wages, does not perform the work, he shall cause her thumb to be pinched with a pair of tongs;
the same applies to those who have consumed, stolen, or deserted their duties.
And regarding wages, punishment for laborers shall be imposed according to their offense.
He should personally supervise the rope-twisters and the armor-makers.
And he shall cause the equipment, such as leather thongs and the like, to be manufactured.
The Superintendent of Agriculture shall cause ropes made of fibers from creepers, leather thongs,
or straps made of cane to be prepared for the harnessing and binding of vehicles and draft animals.

The Superintendent of Agriculture, being an expert in the science of agriculture, geometry, arboriculture, and medicine— or accompanied by those who possess such knowledge— shall collect at the proper time the seeds of all kinds of grain, flowers, fruits, vegetables, tubers, roots, climbing plants, flax, and cotton.
On his own land that has been ploughed by many pairs of oxen, he shall have the seeds sown by slaves, laborers, or those who discharge their fines through work.

He should ensure that their ploughing equipment, implements, and oxen remain free from damage, as well as their tools handled by artisans such as smiths, cutters, distillers, rope-makers, snake-catchers, and others.
KAZ02.24.04: When their actions result in failure, the punishment consists in the forfeiture of those fruits.

The annual rainfall measure for arid regions (*jāṅgala*) is sixteen *droṇas*; for marshy regions (*ānūpa*) where sowing is done according to local conditions, it is one and a half times that; and for the Aśmaka country, it is twelve and a half *droṇas*.
The [revenue] of the Avantis is twenty-three [crores];
that of the Aparāntas and the Haimanyas is immeasurable;
and that of the Kulyāvāpas is according to the time.
One-third of the year consists of the first and last months, while two-thirds consist of the middle months; this constitutes the form of the "Golden Age" (suṣamā).
Its perception is derived from Jupiter’s stationing, its movement, and its entry into pregnancy; from the rising, setting, and courses of Venus; and from the natural and abnormal states of the Sun.
From the Sun comes the perfection of seeds;
from Jupiter, the clustering of crops;
and from Venus, rain. Thus it is said.
Three seven-day clouds, eighty drizzling mist-clouds,
and sixty heat-clouds— this is established as the standard for rain.
Where it rains while the wind and the influence of the sun are divided,
and where three types of dried cow-dung are produced, there the arrival of crops is certain.
Then, he should sow crops in land that has either abundant water or limited water.
Śāli, vrīhi, kodrava, sesame, priyaṅgu, udāraka, and varaka are the crops to be sown first.
Mudga, māṣa, and śaimbya are sown in the middle.
Safflower, lentils, horse gram, barley, *godhūma*, peas, linseed, and mustard seeds are sown subsequently.
Or, the sowing of seeds may be according to the influence of the seasons.
Those who cultivate land beyond the area allotted for sowing shall pay half of the produce;
or those who subsist on their own labor may pay a fourth or a fifth part of the yield.
They shall give the share as desired, provided it is not yet finalized,
except in cases of distress.
From their own irrigation works, they shall pay a fifth part of the water-revenue for water turned by hand, a fourth part for water turned by shoulder-labour,
and a third part for water turned by water-wheels or streams.
The fourth is the opening of rivers, lakes, ponds, and wells.
One should establish paddy crops, winter crops, or summer crops according to the measurement of labor and water.
Rice and the like are the best;
sugar-cane is middling; and sugarcane juice is the lowest.
For sugarcanes involve much hardship and entail great expenditure.
The overflow of froth is for vine-fruits;
drainage channels are the limit for long pepper, grapes, and sugarcane;
and wells are the limit for leafy vegetables and roots.
The *haraṇī* plant is the limit for the *haritaka* group;
the *pālī* plant is the limit for the *lava* group, including fragrant medicinal plants such as *uśīra*, *hrībera*, *piṇḍāluka*, and so forth.
And he should plant in their respective lands both cultivated plants and wild herbs suited to marshy ground.
For grain seeds, there shall be soaking in frost, exposure to smoke, and drying for up to seven nights;
or for three or five nights in the case of sheathed grains (kośīdhānya).
For bulbous roots (kāṇḍabīja), a paste made from honey, ghee, and the fat of a boar mixed with dung shall be applied to the cut surface.

For tubers, an application of honey and clarified butter; for plants with seeds in their wood, a coating of dung; for trees, burning the pits around them with cow-bones and dung at the proper time, and likewise providing for their *dauhṛda* (pregnant longings).
Once they have grown and the fish are no longer raw or pungent, one should feed them with the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant.
One should collect the inner fibers of cotton and the sloughed skin of a snake;
snakes do not remain where this smoke abides.
KAZ02.24.27: At the first sowing of all seeds, however, one should sow the first handful drenched with gold-water and recite this mantra: "Homage ever to Prajāpati, to Kaśyapa, and to the God;
may the Goddess Sītā prosper for me in seeds and in wealth."
KAZ02.24.28: One shall provide food to eunuchs, gardeners, cowherds, slaves, and laborers according to the rations assigned to each person, and shall also give them one pāda and one paṇa per month.
Food and wages for artisans shall be given in accordance with the work performed.

They may gather fallen flowers and fruits for the sake of rites for the gods, and rice and barley for the sake of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice; likewise, those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and ascetics (*tapasvin*), as well as those who live by gleaning (*uñchavṛtti*), may take from the base of the grain heaps.
And as each crop and so forth comes into being at the proper time, he should have it brought in; a wise man should not leave even a single stalk of straw remaining in the field.
One should not construct parapets or watchtowers on the walls that are too closely packed together, nor should their tops be hollowed out.
One should construct enclosures for the threshing floor situated at the perimeter of the circle;
the attendants at the threshing floor should be provided with water and must not keep fire.

The Superintendent of Liquor shall cause the trade in liquor and fermenting agents (kiṇva) to be conducted—whether in the fort, the countryside, or the camp—by those who deal in the production and sale of such liquor and agents; this may be through a single outlet or multiple outlets, according to the requirements of purchase and sale.
He shall impose a fine of six hundred panas as a penalty, except in the case of the maker, the buyer, and the seller.
Within the village, there shall be no carrying out of liquor nor its mixing with other substances,
for fear of negligence among those engaged in ritual acts,
and for fear of the transgression of boundaries by the Aryas.
And because of the fear of the energetic [officers], the spies [are kept secret].
If the quantity is marked as small—whether a fourth part, half a *kuḍuba*, one *kuḍuba*, half a *prastha*, or one *prastha*—those whose purity is known may carry it out.
Or they may drink in taverns, provided they do not wander about.

KAZ02.25.06: For the purpose of identifying goods that have been stolen from deposits, sealed trusts, or loans, or those that have come into his possession through undesirable means, he should, upon finding ownerless base metals or gold,
cause the depositor to be apprehended under a pretext,
as well as anyone who has incurred excessive expenditure or expenditure beyond their means.
And one shall not give spirituous liquor that is either overpriced or intended for immediate consumption, except in the case of spoiled liquor.
He shall cause her to be sold elsewhere.
Or he may pay wages to the slaves and laborers.
Or he may provide fodder for draft animals or engage in the breeding of pigs.

He should cause taverns to be constructed with many courtyards, containing separate quarters for beds and seats, designated drinking areas provided with perfumes, garlands, and water, and made pleasant according to the seasons.
Those stationed there shall ascertain the secret, inherent, and incidental expenditures,
as well as those that are adventitious.
They shall know that from the ornaments, clothing, and gold of buyers who are intoxicated or asleep, [the thieves] may take these items.
In the event of its loss, the merchants shall pay both that amount and an equivalent fine.

But merchants, within the private chambers, shall ascertain the state of mind of both newcomers and residents who appear to be noble, while they are intoxicated or asleep, by means of their own female slaves of beautiful form.
Of *medaka*, *prasannā*, *āsava*, *ariṣṭa*, *maireya*, and *madhu*.
One droṇa of water, half an āḍhaka of rice, and three prasthas of fermenting agent (kiṇva) constitute the preparation for *medaka*.

Twelve āḍhakas of flour, five prasthas of fermenting agent (kiṇva), combined with areca nut, cinnamon bark, and fruit, constitute the ingredients for the *jāti* variety; this is the preparation for *prasannā*.
KAZ02.25.19: One tulā of wood-apple (*kapittha*) and five *tulas* of inspissated juice (*phāṇita*) with one *prastha* of honey constitute a preparation for fermented liquor (*āsava*).
One who exceeds by one-quarter is the eldest; one who is deficient by one-quarter is the youngest.
The fatal signs (ariṣṭas) of various diseases are to be determined by the authority of physicians.

Maireya is a liquor distilled from a decoction of *meṣaśṛṅgī* bark, with molasses added as a secondary fermenting agent, and mixed with a seasoning of long pepper, black pepper, or the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
Or, for all [these] combined with jaggery, there is a preparation consisting of the three fruits (triphalā).
The juice of the grape is honey.
Its native country is explained as Kāpiśāyana and Hārahraka.

A *kiṇvabandha* (fermenting agent) consists of one *droṇa* of raw or cooked *māṣa* beans, with three parts more rice added, combined with one *karṣa* portion each of *moraṭa* and other such ingredients.
A mixture of five karṣas each of pāṭhā, lodhra, tejovatī, elā, vāluka, madhuka, madhurasā, priyaṅgu, dāruharidrā, marica, and pippalī constitutes the preparation for *medaka* and *prasannā*.
Sugar-candy mixed with a decoction of madhuka is a purifier of the complexion.
The ingredients for the āsava consist of one karṣa each of coca, citraka, vilaṅga, and gajapippalī; and two karṣas each of kramuka, madhuka, mustā, and lodhra.
And their seed-fund shall consist of a tenth part [of the profits].
The preparation of *prasannā* is from white wine.

Mango liquor (*sahakārasurā*) is either superior in flavor (*rasottarā*) or superior in its fermenting base (*bījottarā*), or it may be a "great liquor" (*mahāsurā*) prepared from a collection of ingredients (*sambhārikī*).

KAZ02.25.33: A handful of powdered burnt brick-dust and sugar, saturated with a decoction of *moraṭā*, *palāśa*, *pattūra*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *karañja*, and milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*), combined with half its weight of a paste of *lodhra*, *citraka*, *vilaṅga*, *pāṭhā*, *mustā*, *kaliṅga*, barley, *dāruharidrā*, blue lotus (*indīvara*), *śatapuṣpā*, *apāmārga*, *saptaparṇa*, *nimba*, and *āsphota*, and applied with the nails tucked inside, clarifies turbid water fit for a king.
In this case, an increase of juice amounting to five palas of inspissated sugarcane juice (phāṇita) should be added.
Householders shall be permitted to prepare white liquor for ritual purposes,
*vāriṣṭa* for medicinal purposes, or any other [type of liquor].
During festivals, social gatherings, and processions, a surcharge of one-fourth (catur-aha) must be paid for the sale of spirituous liquor.
Among those [offenders], for those who have not obtained permission, he shall impose a daily fine up to the point of forced labor.
Women and children shall carry out the search for fermented liquor and yeast.
Those who trade in goods not belonging to the king shall pay a five percent tax (*pañcaka-śatam śulkam*),
as shall those dealing in *surā*, *medaka*, *ariṣṭa*, honey-wine, fruit-wine, sour gruel, and *śīdhu*.
Having ascertained the daily sale and the commission on measures and gold,
he shall likewise fix the *vaidharaṇa* and follow established custom.
(Superintendent of Animal Slaughter)

The Superintendent of Slaughter-Houses shall impose the highest fine for the binding, killing, or injuring of wild animals, domestic animals, birds, and fish that have been granted protection or that dwell in protected forests; however, he shall impose a middle fine for such acts committed within the protected forest tracts belonging to householders.
For the binding, killing, or injuring of fish or birds that have not yet begun to breed, one shall impose a fine of twenty-six-and-a-quarter paṇas;
for wild animals and domestic livestock, the fine shall be double.
He should take a sixth part of those who practice violence against unclaimed [animals],
or more than a tenth part of fish and birds, or a toll or more for deer and cattle.
In the sanctuaries where no harm is done to living beings, one should release a sixth part of the birds and wild animals while they are still alive.

Fish shaped like sea-monsters, elephants, horses, men, bulls, or donkeys, as well as those found in lakes or irrigation channels, must not be caught. Furthermore, birds such as the *krauñca*, *utkrośaka*, *dātyūha*, swan (*haṃsa*), ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), *jīvanjīvaka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *cakora*, intoxicated cuckoo, peacock, parrot, *madana*, and *śārikā*,
along with other auspicious birds and wild animals, must be protected from injury and harassment.
In the case of violating the rules of protection, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
They shall sell the boneless flesh of wild animals and domestic beasts that has been killed immediately.
They shall pay the penalty for the destruction of bone-bearing animals.
If the balance is deficient, the fine shall be eight times the deficiency.
Among these, the calf, the bull, and the milch cow are not to be killed.
The fine for one who strikes, or causes another to strike, so as to inflict injury, is fifty *paṇas*.
They shall not sell what is emaciated, boneless of head or feet, foul-smelling, or dead of its own accord.
Otherwise, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
Cruel beasts, wild animals, and predators, as well as fish, shall not be harmed while roaming in areas where they are granted safety;
however, elsewhere, except in designated protected zones, they shall be subject to killing or capture.

The Superintendent of Courtesans shall cause a girl from a family of courtesans, or even one not from such a family, who is endowed with beauty, youth, and artistic skill, to be made a courtesan for a fee of one thousand [paṇas], and a secondary courtesan (pratigaṇikā) for half that amount.
If the daughter or sister of one who has fled or died should maintain the household, or if the mother should establish another courtesan in her place; KAZ02.27.02.
In their absence, the king shall take them.

KAZ02.27.04: By means of an increase in good fortune and ornaments, or by a thousand [pieces of gold], he should cause the bridegroom to ascend the canopy, the water-pitcher, the fan, the palanquin, the throne, or the chariot—whether it be the lowest, the middle, or the highest rank—for the sake of distinction.
In the event of a loss of good fortune, one should perform the *mātṛkā* rite.
The ransom for a courtesan is twenty-four thousand [paṇas],
and that for the son of a courtesan is twelve thousand.
From the age of eight years onward, one shall perform the work of a *kuśīlava* for the king.
A courtesan’s slave girl who has ceased her service shall perform labor in the storehouse or in the kitchen.
A woman who, having been detained, does not enter [the house], shall pay one pāda- and a half paṇa as monthly wages.
He shall record the enjoyment, inheritance, income, expenditure, and future prospects of the courtesan, and he shall prevent excessive spending.
KAZ02.27.11: For depositing jewelry with anyone other than a mother's hand, the fine is four paṇas and one-quarter.
For a woman who disposes of her husband's property by means of sale or mortgage, the fine is fifty-four paṇas; for cutting off a finger or similar limb, the fine is one paṇa and a half.
In the case of an act of violence against an unwilling maiden, the highest amercement shall be the punishment; if she was willing, the first amercement for violence shall be the punishment.
For one who imprisons a courtesan against her will, drives her away, or disfigures her by inflicting wounds or tearing her skin, the fine is one thousand panas.
Or, the fine may be increased according to the specific location, up to twice the amount of the ransom.
For one who causes the death of a courtesan who has attained her full rights, the fine shall be three times the ransom.
In the case of killing a mother, a daughter, or a female slave who has been purchased for her beauty, the highest amercement shall be the punishment.
In all cases, for the first offense, the fine is the first [level];
for the second, it is double;
for the third, it is triple.
In the fourth [year], he may act according to his desire.
If a courtesan does not go to a man by the king's command, she shall receive a thousand lashes with a whip, or a fine of five thousand [paṇas].
If a woman, having taken her maintenance, shows hostility, the fine shall be double the amount of that maintenance.
In the case of misappropriation of the profits from a lodging-house, he shall pay eight times the profit, except in cases of illness or defects in the person [of the guest].
For a woman who kills a man, there shall be immersion in water after being exposed to the heat of a funeral pyre.
For one who misappropriates the maintenance, the property, or the earnings of a courtesan, the fine shall be eightfold.
The courtesan shall report her earnings, her future prospects, and the man [with whom she has consorted].

By this same rule, actors, dancers, singers, instrumentalists, storytellers, bards, acrobats, jugglers, and wandering performers who deal with women, as well as their women and those living by secret means, are explained.
For these, one should pay five *paṇas* as a fee for the performance, provided the musical instruments are brought from elsewhere.
Those who live by their beauty shall pay double the value of their enjoyment for one month.

KAZ02.27.28: One who causes courtesans, slave-girls, or those who subsist on the stage to learn the arts of singing, instrumental music, recitation, dancing, acting, calligraphy, painting, the lute, the flute, the drum, reading the minds of others, the preparation of perfumes and garlands, massage, shampooing, and the erotic arts, shall receive a livelihood from the royal circle.
They should appoint the sons of courtesans and the leading performers among those who subsist on the stage, as well as all the musicians and dancers.
Women who are acquainted with their names and dialects should be employed among those [enemies] who are not their own kin,
along with their relatives and vehicles, for the purpose of spying, assassination, and creating negligence.

The Superintendent of Ships shall inspect the operations of sea-voyages, river-mouth crossings, and river traffic, as well as the crossing points at divine lakes, reservoirs, and rivers, in the various administrative centers and other locations.
Villages situated on the banks at that time shall pay the fixed amount.
Fishermen shall pay one-sixth as a fee for the hire of boats.
Merchants shall pay the portion of customs duty corresponding to the port,
and those traveling by royal ships shall pay the fare for the voyage.
Those who collect conch shells and pearls shall pay the hire for the boat,
or they may cross using their own boats.
And the superintendent of these is explained by the [rules for the] superintendent of mines.
The Superintendent of Ships shall maintain the regulations for the merchant port as established by the Superintendent of Ports.
He should support ships struck by adverse winds, just as a father supports his children.
Goods that have been carried by water shall be made free of customs duty, or subject to half-duty.
And these women, as specified, he shall dispatch during the times for voyages to market towns.
He should demand a toll from boats that are well-yoked and traveling along the river-banks.
One should destroy those who are injurious, those who cross into the territory of an enemy, and those who obstruct the conduct of trade in market towns.
Large boats, equipped with a helmsman, a navigator, a steersman, a handler of the ropes, and a bailing person, should be employed on great rivers that are navigable during the winter and summer;
smaller boats should be used on small streams that overflow during the rainy season.
Furthermore, these crossing-points should be fortified against those who act with hostility toward the king, out of fear of being intercepted while crossing.
For one who crosses at an improper time or at an improper place, the first amercement for violence shall be imposed.
KAZ02.28.16: For those who do not allow others to cross at the proper time or at a suitable ferry, the penalty for the offense of obstructing the crossing is twenty-seven paṇas less one-quarter.
There shall be no penalty for fishermen, carriers of eight loads of grass, those with flowers, fruits, gardens, groves, and cowherds;
nor for those who follow along with messengers carrying provisions, nor for those crossing on their own boats while transporting military equipment,
nor for those ferrying seeds, food, goods, and utensils from villages situated in marshy regions.
Brahmins, renunciants, children, the elderly, the sick, messengers carrying official orders, and pregnant women shall cross by means of the seals of the superintendent of ships.
Those from foreign territories who have already been granted entry, or those traveling in caravans of a specified size, may enter.

One who is carrying away another’s wife, daughter, or wealth; or one who is suspected of stealing property; one who is agitated; one whose goods have been confiscated; one concealing a heavy load on his head with a large cloth; one who has recently assumed the marks of an ascetic or is a non-ascetic pretending to be one; one who appears diseased though not so; one whose appearance betrays fear; or one who carries concealed valuables, documents, weapons, or incendiary materials.
One should cause a person with poison in his hand, a long-distance traveler, or one without a seal to be apprehended.
Small livestock and a human carrying a load shall pay one *māṣaka*; a head-load or a body-load, as well as a cow or a horse, shall pay two;
and a camel or a buffalo shall pay four.
Five for a light carriage, six for a *goliṅga*,
seven for a cart.
The load of merchandise is one quarter.
By this, the case of the load of merchandise is explained.
The ferry fare on great rivers is double that amount.
Villages situated along riverbanks or marshlands shall provide the prescribed food and wages.
At the frontiers, ferrymen shall collect tolls, transit fees, and road taxes;
they shall also seize the goods of anyone departing with unsealed merchandise, as well as those crossing at excessive loads, at improper times, or at places other than designated ferries.
If a ship is wrecked due to a lack of personnel or equipment, or because it was not properly maintained, the superintendent of ships shall make good whatever is lost or destroyed.
Between the full moon days of Āṣāḍhī and Kārttikī, which have passed seven days,
the superintendent of cattle shall provide a report on the herd and ensure that the daily milk yield is regularly brought in.

The Superintendent of Cattle shall supervise the wages and perquisites, the principal tax and the additional tax, the animals lost or abandoned, those included in the share [of the king], the total number of cattle in the pens, those that are missing or destroyed, and the production of milk and ghee.
Cowherds, milk-vendors, milkers, churners, and hunters shall each protect one hundred cows, provided they are paid with gold.
"For if they were filled with milk and ghee, they would kill the calves"—
thus is the rule regarding the payment of wages.
One person shall tend a hundred head of cattle consisting of equally divided groups of old cows, milch cows, pregnant cows, four-year-old heifers, and young heifers.
One should pay eight *vārakas* of clarified butter, one *paṇa* for the tail, and the branded hide as an annual tax; such is the system of taxes and counter-taxes.

For those that are diseased, deformed, incapable of being milked by others, difficult to milk, or those that kill their calves, they shall maintain a hundred head as a common herd and provide a share according to the species;
thus ends the section on "broken" and "abandoned" cattle.
Those who have entered [the forest] out of fear of enemy armies or forest-dwellers shall pay a tenth part of their livestock as a fee for protection;
this is the rule regarding those who have entered [the forest] for a share.
Calves, yearlings, domestic animals fit for taming, draft oxen, bulls, and prime bulls;
yoke-bearing oxen, cart-drawing oxen, breeding buffaloes, and buffaloes that carry loads on their backs or shoulders;
female calves, heifers, those that calve every year, those that conceive, milch cows, those that have not yet calved, and barren cows and buffaloes.
Their offspring, born at intervals of one or two months, are calves and heifers.
One should brand those born one month or two months old.
One should mark goods that have been stored for one month or two months.
One should register the brand, the mark, the color, and the distance between the horns as the identifying characteristics of the offspring; such is the procedure for the management of the herd.
Lost is that which has been stolen by thieves, entered another herd, or has become hidden.

That which is exhausted by mud, uneven terrain, disease, old age, water, or lack of food; that which is struck down by trees, riverbanks, timber, or rocks; and that which is destroyed by the elements, wild beasts, snakes, crocodiles, or forest fires—such [cattle] they may recover through negligence.
One should know that such is the excellence of form.
One who kills on his own, one who causes another to kill, one who steals, and one who causes another to steal, shall be put to death.
One who exchanges the cattle of others using the royal seal shall pay the first amercement for the value of the animal.
Having recovered stolen goods from thieves belonging to his own country, he shall take the merchandise at its appraised value.
One who liberates those from a foreign land shall receive half [of the reward].
Cowherds shall provide medical care for calves, the elderly, and those afflicted by disease.
Driven away by hunters and packs of dogs, they should graze [the cattle] in a forest divided according to the seasons, where there is no fear of harm from predatory beasts.
To frighten away snakes and wild beasts, and for the purpose of knowing the movements of cattle, they should tie bells and musical instruments to timid animals.
They should cause the troops to descend into water that has evenly distributed fords and is free from mud and crocodiles, and they should protect them there.
They shall report a person seized by thieves, wild beasts, snakes, or crocodiles, or one overcome by disease or old age;
otherwise, they shall share the value of the person's appearance.
In the case of one who has died by violence, the branded hide of a cow or buffalo,
the ear-mark of goats or sheep,
and the tail and branded hide of horses, donkeys, or camels [shall be taken].
And they should collect the skins of young animals, bladders, bile, tendons, teeth, hooves, horns, and bones.
They shall sell meat, whether fresh or dried.
They shall give the whey to dogs and pigs.
They shall collect fodder for the army's provisions.
Kilāṭa is for the purpose of moistening the oil-cake used for scenting.
A seller of livestock shall pay a one-quarter fine in the form of a penalty fee.
During the rainy season, autumn, and winter, they should milk [the cows] twice a day; during the cool season, spring, and summer, once a day.
For one who milks [the cow] at the second time, the punishment is the cutting off of the thumb.
For one who lets the time for milking pass by, the punishment is the forfeiture of the fruit [of that labor].
By this, the times for the application of nose-strings, training, yoking, and the taming of horses are explained.
From a drona of cow's milk, one prastha of ghee is obtained;
for buffaloes, it is five parts more;
for goats and sheep, it is two parts more.
Or, the *mantha* (the mixed drink) may serve as the standard for all.
For indeed, an increase in milk and ghee results from the excellence of the land, grass, and water.
For one who causes a herd-bull to fall by means of another bull, the first amercement shall be imposed;
for one who causes it to be killed, the highest amercement.
The protection of the ten [villages] shall be ensured by the suppression of caste distinctions.
The division of the directions for the settlement shall be determined by the grazing grounds of cattle, the strength of the surrounding terrain, or the capacity to protect the cattle.
One should cause the wool of goats and sheep to be shorn every six months.
By this, the herds of horses, donkeys, camels, and boars are explained.
For oxen that have undergone nose-strings and possess the gait of a horse or a noble steed, half a *bhāra* of barley grain and double that amount of fodder;
one *tulā* of oil-cake for the snout,
and ten *āḍhakas* of broken rice and husks.
Five palas of salt for the mouth,
one kuḍuba of oil as nasal drops, one prastha as a drink, and one tulā of meat.
One āḍhaka of curd, one droṇa of barley or a measure of boiled mung beans,
one droṇa of milk or half an āḍhaka of liquor, one prastha of oil, ten palas of alkali, and one pala of ginger.
and a drinking vessel.
For mules, cattle, and donkeys, the fine is one-quarter less;
for buffaloes and camels, it is double.
Laborers, oxen, and milch cows intended for watering shall be assigned in accordance with the requirements of the work and the yield of their labor.
All have the right to use grass and water as they please.
Thus the circle of cattle (go-maṇḍala) has been explained.
For donkeys and horses, he should form herds of five with one bull; for goats and sheep, herds of ten with one bull; and for cows, buffaloes, and camels, herds of one hundred with four bulls.
(Superintendent of Horses)

The Superintendent of Horses shall cause a record to be kept of the total number of horses— whether acquired as merchandise, received from the treasury, obtained by purchase, born in the stables, received as assistance, pledged for a sum, or held on loan— according to their breed, age, color, marks, herd, and source.
And he should report those who have deformed limbs or are afflicted by disease as being undesirable.
And having taken from the treasury and the granary, the horse-keeper should calculate his monthly profit.

KAZ02.30.04: One should establish a stable for horses, measuring twice the width of the length of a horse, with four doors and a central courtyard, provided with neck-rings, equipped with seats and wooden platforms at the main entrances, and filled with monkeys, peacocks, spotted deer, mongooses, chakoras, parrots, and sarikas.

For the horse, he should establish a stall facing either east or north, equipped with a smooth, non-quadrangular wooden plank for bedding, provided with a manger, and furnished with separate places for the voiding of urine and excrement.
Or he may determine the division of the directions according to the layout of the hall.
Mares, stallions, and colts [should be kept] in secluded places.
When a mare has given birth, a *prastha* of clarified butter is her drink for three nights.
From this point forward, for ten nights, one prastha of groats (saktu) with an intake of unctuous medicinal substances is prescribed.
Then there shall be grain-particles, fodder, and seasonal food.
After ten nights, the diet for a colt until it reaches six months consists of one-fourth part ghee, one kuḍuba of parched grain flour, and one prastha of milk.
Thereafter, for one month, the price increases by half; a *prastha* of barley [is the rate] until the third year, and a *droṇa* until the fourth year.
From this point forward, one who is four or five years old is capable of work and has reached full stature.
The face of the best horse is thirty-two aṅgulas; the length from the mouth to the chest is five faces,
and the lower leg is twenty aṅgulas.
The height is four times the length of the shank.
In the case of the middle and lowest classes, [the fine] shall be at least three finger-breadths less.
The circumference is one hundred finger-breadths.
In the case of the middle and lowest grades, the fine shall be at least one-fifth of the value.

For a superior horse, there shall be two *droṇas* of rice, paddy, barley, or millet, either half-dried or half-cooked, or a measure of boiled green gram or black gram; one *prastha* of oil, five *palas* of salt,
fifty *palas* of meat, and one *āḍhaka* of broth— or double that amount of curd— for the purpose of moistening the food balls.
The after-drink consists of five palas of alkali with one prastha of liquor, or double that amount of milk.

For those exhausted by long journeys and heavy loads, one *prastha* of oil for eating, one *kuḍuba* for an oily enema (*anuvāsana*), and one *kuḍuba* for nasal therapy (*nasya-karman*) shall be provided.
Half a *bhāra* of fodder and twice that amount of grass shall be given; or alternatively, they may be provided with a six-cubit circumference of bedding or a bundle of straw.
This [fine] is one-quarter less for those of middle and lower status.
A charioteer equal to the best is excellent, and one who is like a bull is mediocre.
And the middle equal is inferior.
For mares and Pāraśava women, the fine shall be one-quarter less.
Half of this amount shall be for the young colts.
Thus ends the section on the application of methods.
The supervisor, the cook, the thread-holder, and the physician shall each receive a share of the taste.
Those who have been worn out by war, disease, old age, or labor shall subsist on alms.
Bulls unfit for battle should be employed with mares for the sake of the citizens and country folk.
Among those suitable for training, the best are the Kambojas, Saindhavas, Āraṭṭas, and Vanāyujas;
the middling are the Bāhlīkas, Pāpeyakas, Sauvīrakas, and Taitalas;
the rest are inferior.
According to whether they are fierce, mild, or dull, he should employ them in tasks requiring armor or in riding duties.
The four-cornered armor of the ritual horse is called the *sāmnāhya*.
The *valgana*, *nīcairgata*, *laṅghana*, *ghoraṇa*, and *nāra-uṣṭra* are the mounts for riding (*aupavāhya*).
In that regard, the *aupaveṇuka*, the *vardhamānaka*, the *yamaka*, the *ālīḍhapluta*, the *pṛthagastrikacālī*, and the *valgana* are [the types of leaping].
That same [wind], when it has reached the head and ears and flows downwards,
is the sixteenfold path.

The *prakīrṇaka* (scattered), *prakīrṇottara* (scattered-advanced), *niṣaṇṇa* (seated), *pārśvānuvṛtta* (following the side), *ūrmmimārga* (wave-path), *śarabhakrīḍita* (sporting like a śarabha), *śarabhapluta* (leaping like a śarabha), *tritāla* (three-beat), *bāhyānuvṛtta* (following the exterior), *pañcapāṇi* (five-hand), *siṃhāyata* (extended like a lion), *svādhūta* (shaken), *kliṣṭa* (distressed), *śliṅgita* (embraced), *bṛṃhita* (roared), and *puṣpābhikīrṇa* (strewn with flowers)— these constitute the paths of movement at a low level.
The monkey-leap, the frog-leap, the snake-leap, the one-footed leap, the cuckoo-movement, the chest-borne, and the crane-walk are the modes of leaping.
The *kāṅka*, *vārikāṅka*, *māyūra*, *ardhamāyūra*, *nākula*, *ardhanākula*, *vārāha*, and *ardhavārāha* are the types of *dhoraṇa*.
The remedy for the disease known as *nāra-uṣṭra* is as follows.
The distance for chariot horses is six, nine, or twelve yojanas; the distance for back-carrying horses is five, seven and a half, or ten yojanas.
Vikrama, Bhadra-aśva, and Bhāra-vāhya are the types of roads.
Valour, leaping, the approach to the vicinity, the rush, the speed, and the streams [of movement].
The masters of training shall assign them their binding equipment and implements, and the charioteers shall provide the war-chariots and the ornaments for the horses.
The veterinarians shall provide remedies for the emaciation or obesity of horses' bodies and prescribe a diet divided according to the seasons.

The holders of the training ropes, the horse-keepers, the fodder-suppliers, the preparers of food, the guards of the stables, the barbers, and the snake-charmers shall attend to the horses by means of their respective duties.
And in case of their failure to perform their work, he shall impose the forfeiture of their daily wages.
For one who drives a carriage obstructing a *nīrājana* procession, or one obstructed by a physician, the fine is twelve *paṇas*.
If a disease increases due to attachment to medical treatments or remedies, the fine shall be double the cost of the counter-measures.
If a reversal occurs due to that offense, the fine shall be the value of the document.
By this, the rules for herds of cattle, as well as those of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, goats, and sheep, are explained.
One should cause horses to bathe twice a day and provide them with perfumes and garlands;
on the junctions of the dark fortnights, sacrifices to the spirits (bhūtas) should be performed, and during the bright fortnights, the recitation of auspicious prayers (svastivācana).

On the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja, one devoted to rites of pacification should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) at the beginning of a military expedition, at its conclusion, or during an illness. (Superintendent of Elephants)

The Superintendent of Elephants shall attend to the protection of the elephant forests; the maintenance of the stables, enclosures, and bedding for male elephants, female elephants, and calves that are trained for work; the regulations regarding the quantity of fodder; the assignment of labor; the equipment for tethering; the war-accoutrements; the ornaments; and the staff consisting of physicians, trainers, and attendants.

He should cause a stable to be constructed facing either east or north, with a height and width twice the length of an elephant, with an additional space for female elephants, provided with a neck-protrusion (pragrīva), and equipped with a stall for young females.

He should establish a stable for the elephants that is four-sided with the length of an elephant, provided with smooth hitching posts and wooden planks for bedding, and equipped with a place for the discharge of urine and excrement.

In a fort, the beds for the *sāmnāhya* (war-horses) and *aupavāhya* (state-bred horses) should be level with the ground and provided with half-supports; outside the fort, this applies to the *damya* (young horses) and *vyāla* (wild or vicious horses).
The first and seventh-eighth parts of the day are the times for bathing; after that is the time for religious observances.
The forenoon is the time for physical exercise;
the afternoon is the time for providing water for drinking.
Two parts of the night are for sleep; one part is for retiring to bed and rising.
In summer, the time for collection [of revenue] is the period of the heat.
One who is twenty years old is to be accepted.
A bull, a buffalo, a monkey, one that is ill, a pregnant cow, and a female elephant are not to be seized.
KAZ02.31.11: Seven *aratnis* in height, nine in length, and ten in circumference according to measurement— such a person is the best at forty years of age,
the middling at thirty years,
and the lowest at twenty-five years.
For those two, the rule for distribution is one-quarter less.
In an aratni [measure], there is one droṇa of straw, half an āḍhaka of oil,
and three prasthas of clarified butter.
Ten palas of salt,
fifty palas of meat, and one āḍhaka of broth— or double that amount of curd— for the purpose of moistening the balls of food.
Ten palas of alkali with one āḍhaka of wine, or twice that amount of milk, as a drink;
one prastha of oil for anointing the limbs,
and one-eighth part for anointing the head and as an eye-salve.
Two and a quarter bhāras of grain,
two and a half bhāras of dried grass, and an indefinite amount of fodder for the draft animals.
One who is eight *aratnis* tall and eats as much as one seven *aratnis* tall is called *atyarāla*.
The remainder is as follows: six *aratnis* and five *aratnis*, according to the cubit.
A cowherd who grazes cattle on fodder should be seized for the purpose of recreation.

The varieties of beauty (śobhā) are: *saṃjātalohitā* (reddened), *praticchannā* (covered), *samliptapakṣā* (with smeared flanks), *samakakṣyā* (even-sided), *vyatikīrṇamāṃsā* (with flesh scattered), *samatalatalā* (with a level surface), and *jātadroṇikā* (having formed hollows).

One should cause the *bhadraka* elephant to perform strenuous exercise according to its physical beauty, while the *manda* elephant should perform it mildly; likewise, the *mṛga* and the *saṃkīrṇaliṅga* elephants should be exercised according to their respective natures or according to the season.

(Activities of Elephants) KAZ02.32.01: There are four categories of elephant labor: the one to be tamed (*damya*), the one for war (*sāmnāhya*), the one for riding (*aupavāhya*), and the wild (*vyāla*).

In that regard, the animal to be tamed (*damya*) is of five kinds: one situated on a mound (*skandhagata*), one situated on a pillar (*stambhagata*), one situated in water (*vārigata*), one situated in a pit (*avapātagata*), and one situated in a herd (*yūthagata*).
Its secondary activity is the work of a butcher.

The equipment for war (*sāmnāhya*) consists of seven operational paths: the stationing of troops, the withdrawal of forces, the marching of armies, the slaughter and pursuit of the enemy, elephant warfare, the elephant treasury, and the conduct of battle.
Its subordinate duties are the work of the inner enclosures, the work of the neck-ropes, and the work of the herds.

The riding elephant is of eight kinds: the one trained for riding, the one used for carrying, the one with a steady gait, the one ridden with a staff, the one ridden with a goad, the one ridden purely for pleasure, and the one employed on long journeys.
Its subordinate branches are autumnal labor, inferior labor, and the labor of men and camels.

The elephant that follows the same path as a rogue elephant, the suspicious one, the confined one, the one in distress, the rutting one, the one certain of its rutting state, and the one certain of the cause of its rutting.
Its secondary function is the act of guarding the single [fortress] after having extended [the defenses].
One who fails in his duty, a rogue, one who is pure, one who is well-vowed, one who is erratic, and one corrupted by all vices; these are the types [of witnesses].
Their equipment for captivity shall be equal in measure to that of the soldiers stationed in the ranks.
The equipment for tethering consists of the hitching post, the neck-rope, the breast-band, the halter, the girth-strap, and the upper-tether, among others.
The equipment consists of hooks, bamboo poles, mechanical devices, and so forth.
The Vaijayantī, the kṣura-pramāla, the āstaraṇa, the kutha, and so forth constitute the ornaments.
Armor, javelins, quivers for arrows, siege engines, and so forth constitute the equipment for battle.

KAZ02.32.16: The group of attendants (*aupasthāyika*) consists of the physician, the groom, the rider, the elephant-driver, the elephant-keeper, the attendant, the cook, the fodder-supplier, the foot-fetterer, the stable-guard, the bedding-provider, and others.
KAZ02.32.17: The physician, the stable-guard, the attendant, and the cook shall take one *prastha* of cooked rice, one *prasṛti* of oil, and two *palas* each of alkali and salt;
they may also take ten *palas* of meat.
Except for physicians.
Physicians shall provide medical treatment for those afflicted by travel, disease, labor, intoxication, or old age.

KAZ02.32.19: Impurity of the station, failure to take fodder, lying down on dry ground, striking when not one's turn, being mounted by another, traveling at the wrong time, and causing the animals to descend at a place that is neither a ford nor a suitable spot, or entering a thicket of trees—these are the grounds for punishment.
He should deduct that from their food and wages.
Three lustration ceremonies (nīrājanā) should be performed at the junctions of the four-month periods and the seasons;
sacrifices for the spirits (bhūta) should be offered by the army commanders at the junctions of the dark fortnights, and at the junctions of the bright fortnights.
Having subtracted twice the circumference of the root of the tusk, one should calculate [the length]:
for those born in rivers, after two and a half years; for those dwelling in mountains, after five years.
(Superintendent of Chariots)
(The Superintendent of Foot-Soldiers) (The Duties of the Commander of the Army):
KAZ02.33.01 / The duties of the superintendent of chariots have been explained by [the rules for] the superintendent of cavalry.
He should cause the chariot craftsmen to work.
A chariot with a twelve-fathom interval between its shafts is for ten men.
Therefore, there are seven chariots, starting from those separated by one interval and ending with those separated by six intervals.
He should cause to be constructed chariots for the king, pleasure chariots, battle chariots, transport chariots, those for attacking enemy cities, and those for training.
He shall know the preparation of arrows, missiles, weapons, armor, and equipment, as well as the training of charioteers, chariot-warriors, and infantrymen in their duties;

and he shall provide food and wages for those who are hired until the completion of their tasks, ensure the protection and maintenance of those who are not hired, and administer honors and rewards according to merit.
By this, the superintendent of infantry is explained.

He should ascertain the relative strength and weakness of his hereditary, hired, guild, allied, enemy, and forest-dweller forces; he should also determine their training for fighting in low ground, on level ground, in the open, in ambushes, in trenches, in the air, by day, or by night, as well as their fitness or unfitness for specific military operations.

Therefore, the commander-in-chief, trained in all the sciences of weapons for war and renowned for his skill in the maneuvers of elephants, horses, and chariots, shall know how to supervise the execution of the fourfold army.

He should examine his own territory, the time for war, the enemy force, the breaking of the unbroken, the reconciliation of the divided, the breaking of the compact, the slaughter of the broken, the destruction of the fort, and the time for marching.
One devoted to the discipline of the troops should establish signals for the battle arrays by means of musical instruments, standards, and banners,
regarding the halting, marching, and striking of the army.
The Superintendent of Minting shall issue a coin for one *māṣaka*.
Only those bearing a seal shall be permitted to enter or exit the inhabited territory.
A person from the countryside who does not possess a seal shall pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
In the case of a counterfeit seal, the first amercement shall be the punishment; if it belongs to another territory, the highest amercement shall be imposed.
The superintendent of pasture lands shall examine the seal.
And he should establish pasture lands for grazing between the villages.
He should clear out low-lying forest areas from the dangers of thieves and wild beasts.
In waterless regions, he should establish wells, embankments, reservoirs, and springs,
as well as groves for flowers and fruits.
Hunters and leaders of dog-herds shall roam through the forests.

In the event of an attack by thieves or enemies, those who cannot be captured should raise the sound of conch shells and drums while perched upon mountains or trees, or else they should do so on swift mounts.
And he should cause the king's movements through enemy territory and forest regions to be signaled by house pigeons carrying sealed tokens, or by a succession of smoke and fire signals.

He shall cause [the superintendent] to manage the livelihood derived from timber and elephant forests, the maintenance of roads, the protection against thieves, the escorting of caravans, the guarding of cattle, and commercial transactions. (The Duties of the Administrator)
(Secret agents disguised as householders, merchants,
and ascetics)
The Collector-General, having divided the population into four classes according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior, shall record the following:

the head of the village, those exempt from taxes, those serving in the armed forces, and the assessments for grain, cattle, gold, forest produce, labor, and taxes—specifying that "this is the amount of this.
He shall thus establish a formal register.
Appointed by him, the village headman (gopa) shall look after a group of five villages or ten villages.

The head of the village shall determine the boundaries by counting the cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, gardens, groves, enclosures, forests, building sites, sacred trees, temples, embankments, cemeteries, almshouses, water-stations, holy places,
pasture lands, and roads; and by that same boundary, he shall calculate the number of taxable and non-taxable holdings among the fields.
Among them, there are these many members of the four castes;
there are these many cultivators, cowherds, merchants, artisans, laborers, and slaves;
and there are these many bipeds and quadrupeds.
And this [revenue] arises from them in the form of gold, labor, tolls, and fines.
He shall know the number of women and men in the households, as well as the extent of the labor, conduct, livelihoods, and expenditures of the young and the old.
And in this manner, the district officer (sthānika) shall supervise one-fourth of the inhabited territory.
In the stations of the *gopas* and *sthānikas*, the *pradeṣṭṛs* shall carry out the administration of affairs and the collection of taxes.

And those persons disguised as householders (gṛhapatika-vyañjana), appointed by the Collector-General and stationed in various villages, shall ascertain the total number of fields, houses, and families in those villages: fields by their measurement and produce; houses by their enjoyment and exemptions; and families by their caste and occupation.
They should know their personal expenditures, income, and outgoings.

They should ascertain the reasons for the departure and return of those who have set out on journeys, as well as the reasons for their absence from home or their return to it, and they should monitor the movements of women and men who are undesirable.

In this manner, those disguised as merchants from Videha shall know the quantity and the price of the royal commodities produced in their own territory, such as those from mines, irrigation works, forests, manufactories, and fields.

They shall ascertain the quantity of goods produced in foreign lands— whether arriving by water or land routes, and whether they are valuable, of poor quality, or common— as well as the measures for duties, road-tolls, transit fees, guard-station charges, ferry-dues, shares, and the size of warehouses for merchandise.
In this manner, spies disguised as ascetics, directed by the Collector-General, shall ascertain the integrity or lack thereof among cultivators, cowherds, merchants, and superintendents.

And spies disguised as old thieves, along with their disciples, shall ascertain the entry points, locations, movements, and purposes of thieves, enemies, and brave men in sacred shrines, crossroads, deserted places, water reservoirs, rivers, watering holes, holy fords, temples, hermitages, forests, mountains, and dense groves.
The Collector-General, having thus risen to his duties, shall consider the welfare of the countryside;
and the various administrative departments, as well as other agencies of their own origin, shall likewise deliberate upon it.
(Rules for the City-Superintendent)
The city superintendent shall look after the city in the same manner as the collector-general.
A cowherd [shall tend] ten families, twenty families, or forty families.
There, he should ascertain the number of men and women by their caste, lineage, names, and occupations, as well as the income and expenditure for the area up to the frontier.
In this manner, the local official shall supervise one-fourth of the fort.

The officers in charge of the guest-house for the righteous shall provide lodging to heretics and travelers after reporting them; they may also provide lodging to ascetics and Vedic scholars who are personally known to them.
Artisans and craftsmen shall cause their own people to reside in their respective workshops, and merchants likewise shall do so for one another in their respective workshops.
They shall report anyone who sells merchandise at an improper place or time, as well as anyone who fails to provide the required animal-stamp.
Liquor-sellers, sellers of cooked meat, rice-cookers, and those who live by their appearance shall be allowed to reside only after being thoroughly vetted.
They shall report anyone who commits excessive expenditure and anyone who performs acts that endanger the state.

A physician who causes a wound to be treated in secret, as well as the owner of the house who administers unwholesome food or drink, shall be released from liability upon reporting the matter to the village headman (*gopa*) and the district officer (*sthānika*);
otherwise, they shall be equally culpable.
He shall report when [the messenger] has departed and when he has returned; otherwise, he shall incur the penalty for the night's offense.
On nights of security, one should pay three paṇas.

Travelers and wayfarers, both outside and inside the city, should apprehend anyone who has a wound, carries undesirable implements, has discarded his belongings, is agitated, sleeps excessively, is exhausted from travel, or is a stranger— especially in temples, sacred sites, forests, and cremation grounds.
In this manner, they shall conduct searches within the interior of the city among vacant dwellings, workshops, taverns, rice-sellers, meat-sellers, gambling-houses, hermitages, and residences.
And in the summer, he shall take measures for the protection against fire.
During the two middle quarters of the day, the fine for fire-accidents shall be one-eighth of the total.
Or they may perform the placing [of the vessel] on the fire outside [the hearth].
A fine of one-quarter [of a paṇa] shall be imposed for failing to provide five water-jars, a large water-vessel, a ladder, an axe, a winnowing-basket, a hook, a hair-seizer, and a leather-bag.
One should have those thatched with grass and mats removed.
Those who live by fire should be settled in one place.
At night, they shall stay at the main gates of their own houses, remaining within the house of the owner and not wandering about.
In the streets, thousands of water-jars should be stationed at crossroads, gates, and royal precincts.
If the owner of a house does not run toward it when it is on fire, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for the tenant, it is six paṇas.
If fires are ignited through negligence, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas.
A arsonist shall be put to death by fire.
In the case of throwing dust onto a carriage road, the fine shall be one-eighth of a paṇa; in the case of obstructing it with mud or water, the fine shall be one-quarter of a paṇa.
On the royal highway, the fine is double.
In marketplaces, water-stations, temples, and royal property, the fines for defecation start at one paṇa and increase progressively;
for urination, the fines are half of those amounts.
Those who act for the purpose of medicine, disease, or fear shall not be punished.
KAZ02.36.30: For the disposal of the corpses of cats, dogs, mongooses, snakes, and human beings within the city, the fine is three paṇas;
