for the corpses of donkeys, camels, mules, and horses, it is six paṇas; and for the corpses of human beings, it is fifty paṇas.
In the case of a deviation from the path, or when a corpse is carried out by a route other than the designated gate for corpses, the first amercement shall be imposed.
The gatekeepers shall number two hundred.
For depositing or burning anything other than in a cemetery, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
The watch-drums shall sound with a mournful and discordant tone at both ends of the night-watch.

KAZ02.36.35: When the sound of musical instruments is heard in the vicinity of the king’s palace, the punishment for striking with dice shall be one and a quarter paṇas during the first and last watches of the night; double that during the middle watch; and four times that at the end of the night.
One should interrogate a person who has been apprehended in a suspicious place, with suspicious signs, or with a prior criminal record.
For entering the royal precincts or climbing onto the city ramparts, the middle amercement shall be the punishment.

Those carrying a woman who has recently given birth, a physician, a corpse, a lamp, a vehicle, a city watchman, musical instruments, or those attending a spectacle, as well as those with a fire for a specific purpose, shall not be stopped even if they bear official seals.
During the nights of patrol, mendicants who are disguised or dressed in contrary attire, as well as men with clubs or weapons in their hands, shall be punished according to their offense.
For guards who fail to stop those who should be stopped, or who stop those who should not be stopped, the fine shall be double the amount for each moment of negligence.

For those who commit adultery with a female slave, the first amercement shall be the punishment; for one who is not a slave, the middle amercement; and for one who has been taken into the harem, the highest amercement.
Killing a woman of good family [is a minor offense].
If a city official fails to report a nocturnal offense involving either a conscious or unconscious perpetrator, he shall be punished with a fine corresponding to the gravity of the offense,
as well as for any instance of negligence.

KAZ02.36.43: He must constantly supervise the protection of water reservoirs, roads, bridges, covered paths, embankments, and ramparts; and he must ensure the protection of those who are lost, forgotten, or have run away.
And in the prison, there shall be the release of children, the elderly, the sick, and the helpless on their birth-star days, on full-moon days, and on the new-moon days.
Those whose occupation is trade, or who are bound by a contract, shall pay a fine as compensation for any offense.
Every day or every five nights, he should release those held in prison,
either by means of labor, corporal punishment, or the granting of gold.
Upon the acquisition of a new territory, upon the consecration of a crown prince,
or upon the birth of a son, the release of prisoners is ordained.

(Kaz03.1.01) Judicial Officers: Three ministers each shall preside over judicial matters concerning legal disputes in the districts, at the boundaries, in the collection centers, at the granaries, and in the provincial headquarters.
They shall prohibit legal transactions conducted in secret places, inside houses, at night, in forests, under pretexts, or in private.
For the one who commits [the offense] and for the one who causes it to be committed, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
For each of the listeners, the punishment shall be half of that [prescribed for the speaker].
But in the case of trustworthy persons, there shall be the forfeiture of their property.
If they take out an excessive loan under false pretenses, or if they remain hidden while acting as unaccountable agents, they shall be brought to justice.

Transactions concerning inheritance, deposits, trusts, and marriages, as well as those conducted within the inner apartments by women who have not left the house, by those who are ill, and by those whose minds are not deranged, shall be valid.

Transactions involving violence, secret entry, quarrels, marriage, or royal commissions, as well as those conducted by people active during the first watch of the night, shall be valid even if performed at night.
Among caravans, herds, hermitages, hunters, and wandering minstrels, those who dwell in the forest shall achieve success through their forest-based activities.
And among those who live by secret means, those who act through fraudulent stratagems shall be successful.
And in the case of a mutual compact, those made in secret shall be valid.
Otherwise, they would not be established;
nor would they be valid when performed by those who have a protector,
such as by a son who has a father.
By a father who has sons, by a brother who is without kin, or by a younger brother whose share has not been divided;
By a woman whose husband is living and who has sons, by a female slave and a person held in trust,
and by those whose legal capacity has not yet been reached or has already passed.
Nor with those who have been accused, those who have renounced the world, those with missing limbs, or those afflicted by calamity,
except for those whose legal cases have been formally dismissed.
In that case as well, legal transactions entered into by one who is angry, distressed, intoxicated, insane, or under duress shall not be valid.
KAZ03.1.14: For the perpetrator, the instigator, and the listener, the punishments shall be distinct as previously stated.

KAZ03.1.15: However, within their respective categories, regions, and times, all legal transactions (*vyavahāra*) performed by their own agents, provided they are complete in procedure, conducted in a pure location, and have their form, characteristics, quantity, and quality verified, shall be valid.
KAZ03.1.16: Furthermore, among these, a subsequent transaction is to be trusted, except in cases involving a formal decree (*ādeśa*) or a pledge (*ādhi*).
Thus ends the establishment of the legal procedure (vyavahāra-sthāpanā).

Having recorded the year, season, month, fortnight, day, the judicial method (karaṇa), the court (adhikaraṇa), the debt, the place, village, caste, lineage, name, and occupation of both the plaintiff and the defendant, as well as their respective capacities and circumstances at the time the transaction was made, one shall record the questions of the plaintiff and the defendant. (Kautalya Arthaśāstra 3.1.17)
One should arrange them according to the sequence of their meaning.
And he should look after those who have settled.
He abandons the established argument and shifts to another argument;
he does not reconcile what was stated previously with the subsequent meaning; and having seized an unseizable statement of the opponent, he persists in it.
When told, "Having made a promise, point out the location," he does not point it out;
or he points out a low-lying place or a non-place; or he substitutes a different location for the one that was pointed out.
When the place has been reached, he denies the matter by saying "it was not so";
he does not wish for the witnesses to be examined; and in a place where conversation is improper, he converses secretly with the witnesses.
Thus end the reasons stated by the opponent.
When the punishment has been pronounced by another, the fine shall be five times the amount.
KAZ03.1.21: The fine for one who speaks for himself is ten times his stake.
The maintenance of the personnel shall be one-eighth [of the revenue].
Traveling provisions for food shall be provided according to the specific rank of the guest.
The person under restraint shall pay both of those.
One who is being prosecuted shall not counter-prosecute,
except in cases of quarrels, acts of violence, or collective disputes involving groups.
And when one has been formally accused, there is no further accusation against that same charge.
If the plaintiff, having been answered by the defendant, does not respond on that very same day, he shall be considered defeated.
For it is the accuser who has determined that his purpose is accomplished, not the accused.
If he does not respond, [the fine shall be] for three nights or seven nights.
From this point forward, one shall impose a fine ranging from a minimum of three paṇas to a maximum of twelve paṇas.

KAZ03.1.31: After three fortnights, if the defendant does not respond, the judge shall impose the fine for a defeated party and cause whatever property the defendant possesses to be handed over to the plaintiff, with the exception of those items necessary for his livelihood.
One should apply that very same [tactic] to an assailant who is rushing forward.
When the time for the assailant's departure coincides with the time for the defendant's departure, it is called *parāuktabhāva*.
The testimony of a witness who is deceased or afflicted by calamity is unreliable.
The accuser, having paid a fine, shall perform the labor.
Or he may, at his pleasure, cause the pledge to be brought into [the creditor's] possession.
Or he may cause the work to be executed by one protected by Rakshoghna mantras,
except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa.
Because he protects the conduct of this world consisting of the four castes and stages of life,
the king is the promoter of dharma when all dharmas are perishing.
Law (*dharma*), legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), custom (*caritra*), and royal edict (*rāja-śāsana*) constitute the four feet of a lawsuit; each subsequent one overrides the preceding.
In that regard, dharma is established in truth, while legal procedure rests upon witnesses; customary law resides in the consensus of men, whereas the king’s command is the edict.
KAZ03.1.41ab: For a king who protects his subjects according to dharma, his own duty leads to heaven.
KAZ03.1.41cd: But for one who fails to protect them or who inflicts unjust punishment, it leads to the opposite result.
For punishment alone protects both this world and the next,
when it is applied equally by the king toward his son and his enemy alike, according to the gravity of the offense.
For by instructing according to dharma, by judicial procedure, by established custom,
and by the fourth means, logic, he shall conquer the earth bounded by the four oceans.
If a legal procedure prescribed by the Dharmaśāstra or a rule of customary law should conflict with a specific matter, one should decide the matter according to the Dharma.
If a scriptural text should conflict with established law (dharma) by some logical reasoning,
then that reasoning shall be the authority in that case, for in such a situation the literal reading is set aside.
A self-accusation regarding one's own or another's position is a proof when its fault has been observed;
likewise, straightforward questioning, logical reasoning, and an oath are means for establishing the truth of a matter.
When there is a contradiction between the plaintiff's and defendant's statements, when the witness provides a valid reason for their testimony,
or when the matter is established through the agency of a spy, defeat must be decreed.
(Concerning marriage)
(i) Law of Marriage; (ii) Rules concerning Women’s Property; (iii) Concerning Supersession (of a Wife).
KAZ03.2.01: Legal proceedings concerning a remarriage take precedence over those concerning the first marriage.
KAZ03.2.02: Bestowing a daughter after having adorned her constitutes the Brāhma form of marriage.
The Prājāpatya rite consists of the practice of dharma together [with the wife].
The Ārṣa form [of marriage] consists in the taking of a pair of cattle.
The Daiva form [of marriage] consists of giving [the bride] to a priest within the sacrificial altar.
The Gāndharva form arises from mutual agreement.
The Āsura form [of marriage] arises from the taking of a bride-price.
The Rākṣasa [form of marriage] arises from taking [the girl] by force.
The Paiśāca form [of marriage] arises from taking [a girl] while she is asleep or intoxicated.
The first four [sons] are righteous when authorized by their father; the remaining ones are authorized by both mother and father.
For those two are the sharers of the bride-price for the daughter; in the absence of one, the other may take it.
The woman shall take the second dowry.
For all [of these], the bestowal by way of affection is not prohibited.
Thus concludes the law concerning marriage. Property given to a woman shall be her maintenance or her dowry.
The maintenance fee shall be fixed at no more than two thousand [paṇas] per person; there is no restriction on the number of persons to be supported.

In the case of maintaining one's own self, children, or daughters-in-law, and in the absence of provisions for travel, it is not a fault for the wife to consume [the property]; nor is it a fault for the husband to do so when countering an assailant, disease, famine, or danger, or for performing religious duties;
or when the couple, having united, have procreated offspring together.
And if it has been enjoyed for three years in marriages that are righteous, one should not question it.
If the property was enjoyed under the Gāndharva or Āsura forms of marriage, both the principal and interest shall be made to be paid;
if it was enjoyed under the Rākṣasa or Paiśāca forms, he shall make restitution for theft.
If the husband dies, she who desires to follow the dharma may, at that very moment, set aside her ornaments and receive the remainder of the nuptial fee (śulka).
Or, having received it, if she is found to be obtaining it again, she shall be made to pay both [the principal and the interest] along with the interest.
But she who desires to maintain a family may receive what was given by her father-in-law or husband at the time of her marriage.
For we shall explain the time for settling [the army] in the context of a long-term expedition.
Or, a woman who has married against the natural order of her father-in-law may lose what was given to her by her father-in-law or her husband.
KAZ03.2.24: If she has been touched by the hand of a kinsman, her kinsmen shall restore her to him exactly as she was taken.
The husband who has lawfully obtained a wife shall protect her property.
A woman who acquires her husband's property shall forfeit it.
One who desires merit should eat at those times.
A woman who has already borne children, upon remarrying, shall forfeit her woman’s property.
But that woman's property the sons shall take.
Or, if she is obtaining [wealth] for the sake of maintaining her son, she may increase it for the sake of the son.
KAZ03.2.31: Among sons born of many wives, one should establish the women's property according to what was given by each respective father.
Even if she obtains property that may be used at her own will, a woman should place it in the custody of her sons.
A childless woman, preserving the husband’s bed and remaining near her elders, shall enjoy the woman’s property until the end of her life.
For a woman’s property is intended for use in times of distress.
After that, it shall go to the heir.

KAZ03.2.36: When the husband is alive, the sons and daughters of a deceased woman shall divide the woman’s property; if she dies without sons, her daughters [shall divide it]; in their absence, the husband [shall take it].
The nuptial fee, the subsequent gift, or any other property given by kinsmen shall be taken by the kinsmen.
Thus ends the section on the property of women (strīdhana-kalpa).
One should wait for eight years for a woman who does not bear children, one who has no sons, or one who is barren; for ten years for a woman who bears only female offspring.
Twelve [days] for one who has given birth to a daughter.
Then, one desiring a son may take a second wife.
In the event of his transgression, he shall pay the nuptial fee, the woman’s property, and half the amount for supersession,
as well as a fine of up to twenty-four paṇas.

Having given the nuptial fee (*śulka*), the woman’s property (*strīdhana*), and for one who has no such property, an equivalent amount as compensation for taking a second wife (*ādhivedanika*), as well as a suitable maintenance, he may take many wives.
For women exist for the sake of sons.
KAZ03.2.43: And when these women are gathered at a sacred ford (tīrtha), he should first approach her who was married first, or one who has sons living, according to the order of their marriage.
KAZ03.2.44: For concealing or approaching a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), the fine is ninety-six paṇas.
One should not approach a woman who has sons, one who desires religious merit, a barren woman, a woman who hates her husband, or one who has ceased menstruating, unless she is willing.
Furthermore, a man who does not desire it should not approach a woman afflicted with leprosy or one who is insane.
But a woman, for the sake of obtaining a son, may approach such a man.
A husband who has committed an offense against the king, one who has set out for a low state or a foreign land,
one who seeks to take his own life, one who is fallen, or even one who is impotent, shall be abandoned.
(vi) Maintenance,
(vii) Cruelty, (viii) Disaffection.
(ix) Misconduct: Prohibition of favors and transactions.
KAZ03.3.01: A woman who has reached twelve years of age becomes capable of conducting legal affairs.
A man who is sixteen years old.
KAZ03.3.02: From this point forward, in the case of refusal to obey, the fine for a woman is twelve paṇas; for a man, it is double that amount.
Thus ends the section on service (śuśrūṣā).
Regarding maintenance (bharmaṇyā) for an indefinite period, one should provide food and clothing, or more than that, according to the specific means of the individual, with special consideration.
If the time specified has elapsed, he shall calculate that same amount and pay it along with interest.
And also in the case of failing to pay the marriage-fee, the wife’s property, or the compensation for supersession.

KAZ03.3.06: When she has entered the family of her father-in-law or when she is separated from him, the husband is not to be prosecuted. This concerns maintenance. KAZ03.3.07: "Lost," "destroyed," "deficient in limb," "fatherless," or "motherless"—by such descriptions, she is to be subjected to disciplinary measures.
Or, with one of bamboo, a leaf, or a rope, there shall be three strikes on the back.
In the event of its violation, the fines shall be half those prescribed for verbal abuse and physical assault.
The same applies to a woman who has become notorious for her faults toward her husband.
KAZ03.3.11: Due to jealousy, the penalty for [illicit conduct] in public pleasure gardens and at the gates is as previously specified.
Thus ends the section on harshness.

(KAZ 3.3.12) A woman who hates her husband shall not adorn herself for seven menstrual periods; having set aside her ornaments at that very time, she shall lie down with another man while her husband is sleeping.
(KAZ 3.3.13) Or, the husband, hating his wife, shall lie down with one of the following: a female mendicant, a creditor, or a relative from her family.
KAZ03.3.14: In cases where there is visible evidence of sexual intercourse, theft, or association with a spy of equal caste, one who speaks falsely shall pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
A wife who is hostile to her husband cannot be released by him if he is unwilling; nor can a husband be released by his wife.
Liberation [from conflict] occurs through mutual hatred.
If a man seeks release from the mistreatment of his wife, he shall give her back whatever was taken from her according to the original agreement.
Or, if a woman desires release from the maltreatment of her husband, one shall not restore to her what was taken [from her] according to the original agreement.
KAZ03.3.19: There shall be no release for those who have entered into marriages according to the [proper] dharmas; this is the rule regarding enmity.
KAZ03.3.20: A woman who is forbidden [from doing so] shall pay a fine of three paṇas for engaging in play with pride or intoxication.
KAZ03.3.21: For going to see women or for recreation during the day, the fine is six paṇas; for going to see men or for recreation, the fine is twelve paṇas.
At night, it is double.
If she goes out while her husband is asleep or intoxicated, or if she fails to open the door for him, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
If he departs at night, the fine is double.

KAZ03.3.25: When a man and a woman engage in physical gestures for the purpose of sexual intercourse, or hold private and indecent conversation, the fine for the woman shall be twenty-four paṇas, and for the man, double that amount.
In cases of seizing by the hair, the waist-knot, the teeth, or the nails, the first amercement shall be imposed;
for a man, it shall be double.
In the case of conversation at a suspicious place or at a gambling den, the punishment shall be flogging with a whip.
A Caṇḍāla who enters the midst of women in a village shall be made to pay five *śiphās* every fortnight.
Or he may pay a fine of one paṇa for each blow.
Thus ends the section on transgressions. (KAZ 3.3.30) When a man and a woman, both of whom are prohibited [from such association], assist one another with minor articles, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for major articles, the fine is twenty-four paṇas.
For stealing gold or fine gold, the fine for a woman is fifty-four paṇas;
for a man, it is double that amount.
KAZ03.3.31: The same half-penalties apply for those two [types of women] when they are unapproachable, as well as in cases of transactions with prohibited men.
Thus is the prohibition.
By the king’s disapproval, by transgression, and by her own departure,
a woman loses ownership over women, wealth, and the nuptial fee (KAZ 3.3.32).
For a woman who has run away from her husband’s family— whether for a short absence from home or a long absence from home— the fine is six paṇas.
Except in the case of an offense.
If she is forbidden [from doing so], the fine is twelve paṇas.
For one who has gone beyond the house of a neighbor, the fine is six paṇas.
For providing shelter, alms, or merchandise to neighbors, mendicants, or merchants, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
For those who violate prohibitions, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
For a woman who has entered another's house, the fine is twenty-four paṇas.
For providing shelter to another's wife, the punishment shall be one hundred panas,
except in cases of distress.
In the case of an elephant or ignorance [of the animal], there is no fault.

KAZ03.4.09: “In the event of mistreatment by her husband, it is not an offense for her to go to any one of the following who is without a male guardian: her husband’s kinsmen, those in a state of comfort, the village headman, a person to whom she has been entrusted as a deposit, or the kinsmen of a female mendicant,” so say the Teachers.
Or, she may go to the kinsmen of her own family who have male guardians. KAZ03.4.10.
For how could there be deception on the part of virtuous people?
"This is easy to understand," says Kauṭilya.
Going to the family of a kinsman for the sake of a deceased relative, illness, misfortune, or pregnancy is not prohibited at all.
For one who prevents such a cause from occurring, the fine is twelve paṇas.
In that case as well, a woman who conceals her property shall lose it;
or, kinsmen who conceal it shall forfeit the remainder of the nuptial fee (śulka).
Thus ends the section on elopement.
(KAZ 03.4.16) For a woman who has eloped from her husband's family and gone to another village, the fine shall be twelve paṇas, and she shall forfeit the jewelry provided for her maintenance.

KAZ03.4.17: Or, when setting out together with a man who is to be approached for sexual intercourse, the fine is twenty-four paṇas and there is a forfeiture of all rights; except in the case of providing maintenance or going on a pilgrimage.
In the case of a man who is equal or superior [to the woman], the first amercement shall be the punishment;
if he is inferior, the middle amercement.
A relative is not subject to punishment.
In cases of prohibition, the fines shall be half of those prescribed.

KAZ03.4.21: One should recognize as adultery (saṃgrahaṇa) the act of approaching a secluded spot on a road, or following someone along a path when that person has been suspected or forbidden from engaging in sexual intercourse for such purposes.

KAZ03.4.22: For performers on the *tāla* instrument, wandering minstrels, fishermen, hunters, cowherds, vintners, and others who have sent their wives along, following the path with them is not an offense.
KAZ03.4.23: Or, when [intercourse] is forbidden, those same half-penalties apply to the man who leads her away or to the woman who goes with him.
Thus concludes the section on following the advice of the physician.

(KAZ 03.4.24) The wives of Shudras, Vaishyas, Kshatriyas, and Brahmins who have gone abroad for a short duration shall wait for one year if they have not borne children; if they have borne children, they shall wait for more than one year.
If it is provided for, the period shall be doubled.
Those who are not provided for shall maintain them in a state of comfort; however, kinsmen may do so for at most four or eight years.
Then, having taken back what was given, they should release them.
One should wait for ten years for a Brāhmaṇa who is studying the Veda if he has not yet fathered offspring, and for twelve years if he has;
one should wait for a royal official until the end of his life.
And one born from a woman of the same caste shall not incur censure.
Or, in the event of the ruin of the family estate, she may obtain what she desires from those living in comfort when released;
or, having fallen into distress, she may do so for the sake of her livelihood.
KAZ03.4.31: A maiden married according to the *dharma* form of marriage, having not informed her husband, shall wait for seven *tīrtha*s (lunar stations) if he has gone abroad and is unheard of;
she shall wait for one year if he is heard from.
Having announced that he has gone abroad and is not heard from, one should wait for him at five *tīrtha*s;
if he is still heard from, one should wait for ten.
If the bride-price has been paid in part, she shall wait for three *tīrtha*s if the groom is not heard from;
if he is heard from, she shall wait for seven *tīrtha*s.
A woman for whom the bride-price has been paid may wait five years if she is not heard from,
and ten years if she is heard from.
Thereafter, released by those established in dharma, she may live as she pleases.
For the obstruction of a sacred ford (tīrtha) is the destruction of Dharma, says Kauṭilya.
Thus ends the brief discussion on temporary absence.

The wife of one who has gone on a long journey, of one who has renounced the world, or of one who is deceased, shall wait for seven *tīrtha*s; if she has given birth [to a son], she shall wait for a year.
After that, she should go to her husband's uterine brother.
Among many [brothers], the one who is nearest, righteous, capable of supporting [the family], and either the youngest or without a wife [should be appointed].
In the absence of that [uterine brother], a non-uterine sapiṇḍa, or a kulya who is a near relative, [shall take the property].
For these, this very sequence applies.

KAZ03.4.42ab: Having bypassed these heirs in the matter of discovering [a secret lover] or in the act of adultery, KAZ03.4.42cd: the paramour, the woman, the giver, and the discoverer shall all incur the penalty for adultery.
(Partition of inheritance)
(Order of inheritance) Sons who have a father living, and whose mother is still alive, have no independent authority over the property.
After them, the division of the paternal estate among the father's property shall take place according to the fathers.
What has been acquired by oneself is not subject to partition, except for those things derived from paternal property.
KAZ03.5.04: Sons or grandsons up to the fourth generation of those who have entered [the family] while the paternal property was undivided are entitled to a share.
For that long, the bodily mass remains unbroken.
KAZ03.5.06: Those whose ancestral offerings have been discontinued shall all divide [the property] equally.
Those who have not inherited paternal property, or those who have already divided their paternal property, may divide it again while living together.
And from whichever [share] he may rise [to take his place], he shall receive two shares.
The uterine brothers of a man who dies without a son, or those who lived together with him, or his unmarried daughters shall take his property.
KAZ03.5.10: The inheritance of one who has sons belongs to the sons, or to the daughters born of marriages according to the most righteous rites.
In his absence, the father, if he is living, [shall take charge].
In the absence of the father, the brothers and the sons of the brothers [shall take the inheritance].
Even many brothers who have no father, as well as the sons of brothers, shall take one share from the father's estate.
KAZ03.5.14: Among uterine brothers who have more than one father, the division of inheritance is according to their respective fathers.
KAZ03.5.15: Among sons of a father’s brothers, while the elder exists, they do not depend on the latter; and while the eldest exists, the younger does not take possession of the property.
In the partition of property while the father is still living, he shall not favor one son over another.
And one should not divide a single thing without a reason.
In the absence of the father's property, the elder brothers shall provide for the younger ones,
except in the case of those who lead a life of misconduct.
The partition [of inheritance] belongs to those who have attained legal capacity.
For those who have not yet attained legal capacity, their guardians shall deposit the cleared amount of what is due with maternal relatives or village elders until they reach legal age,
or in the case of one who has gone abroad.
Those who have settled should provide housing for those who have not yet settled, at a rate equal to their own,
and they should also provide dowries for unmarried girls.
KAZ03.5.22: There shall be an equal division of both debts and inheritances.
"Even water-vessels should be divided among those who possess nothing," so say the teachers.
"This is a fallacy," says Kauṭilya.
The division of an existing object pertains to that which exists, not to that which does not exist.
Having restated that "this much is the common property" and "this much is the share of each," he should cause the division to be made in the presence of witnesses.
KAZ03.5.27: They shall divide again property that was improperly partitioned, stolen from one another, lost, or produced without being recognized.
The king shall take property that has no heir, with the exception of what is required for the maintenance of the widow and the funeral rites of the deceased, excepting the property of a Śrotriya.
He should bestow that upon those learned in the three Vedas.
One who is outcasted, one born of an outcasted man, a eunuch, and those who are mentally deficient, insane, blind, or afflicted with leprosy, are entitled to no share.
If there is a wife, their offspring who does not belong to that same class shall take the share.
The others, excluding those who have fallen from their caste (patitas), shall receive food and clothing.
And when the procreative capacity of those who have already taken wives has failed,
their kinsmen may produce sons for them; one should allot shares to these [adopted] sons.
KAZ03.6.01 / Regarding those who have sons by only one wife, the additional share for the eldest is as follows: goats for Brāhmaṇas,
horses for Kṣatriyas,
and cows for Vaiśyas.
For Śūdras, the age limit is ten years.
Those who are one-eyed or lame shall receive a middle share;
those of different castes shall receive the smallest share.
In the absence of quadrupeds, the eldest shall take one-tenth share of the ten types of goods, excluding gems.
For he becomes one whose bonds of *svadhā* have been released.
Thus is the division according to Auśanasa.

From the father’s estate, the carriage and ornaments constitute the share of the eldest; the bed, the seat, and the used bronze vessels constitute the share of the middle son; and black grain, iron, the household utensils, and the ox-cart constitute the share of the youngest.
KAZ03.6.07: Of the remaining goods, there shall be an equal division, whether among many items or a single item.
Sisters are not heirs; they are entitled to a share of their mother's personal property, consisting of used bronze vessels and ornaments.
A son who is deficient in human qualities shall receive one-third of the eldest's share; one who behaves improperly, or who has ceased performing his religious duties, shall receive one-fourth.
If one acts according to desire, everything shall be lost.
By this, the middle and the lowest [fines] are explained.
Of these two, the one endowed with human qualities shall receive half of the eldest’s share.

KAZ03.6.13: Among sons born of different wives, however, seniority is determined by the order of birth, whether they have been consecrated or not, whether they are virgins or have lost their virginity, and even in the absence of such distinctions; this applies to sons of one wife or to twins. KAZ03.6.14: For Sūtas, Māgadhas, Vrātyas, and Rathakāras, the division of property is according to their respective status.
The remaining [officers] shall subsist upon him.
They have no authority over one another and share equally in all things.
Among the sons of the four castes, the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife shall take four shares;
the son of a Kṣatriya wife, three shares; and the son of a Vaiśya wife, two shares.
One [share] for the son of a Śūdra woman.
By this, the division of inheritance among the sons of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, who have sons belonging to three or two castes respectively, is explained.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa born of a woman of the next lower caste shall receive an equal share.
For a *kṣatriya* or a *vaiśya*, the share shall be half or an equal portion, provided they are endowed with human qualities.
KAZ03.6.21: The only son of both a similar and a dissimilar [mother] shall take the entire estate and maintain the relatives.
But among Brāhmaṇas, the *pāraśava* son shall receive one-third share, while two shares shall go to a *sapiṇḍa*, a *kulya*, or a close relative,
for the purpose of offering the *svadhā*.
In his absence, the father, the teacher, or a resident pupil [shall perform the duties].
Or, being authorized, he may procreate a son on his field; this is the "field-born" (kṣetraja) son.
To him, the maternal relative or a member of the same lineage shall assign that wealth.
(Classification of Sons)
"Seed sown in the field of another belongs to the owner of the field," so say the teachers.
"Another [view] holds that 'the mother is merely a skin-bag; the offspring belongs to him whose seed it is.'"
Kautilya maintains that both [the treasury and the army] must be currently available.
A son born of one's own self, when the sacramental rites have been performed, is an *aurasa* (legitimate) son.
A son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) is equal to him.
A son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) by one appointed—whether he be of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or of a different lineage (*anyagotra*)—is the *kṣetraja* son.

KAZ03.7.07: If there is no other son for the biological father, that very son becomes one who has two fathers and two lineages, and he becomes the recipient of the funeral offerings (*svadhā*) and the inheritance from both.
One born secretly in the house of kinsmen, possessing the same status as they, is called a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born).
One who has been abandoned by his kinsmen and cast off becomes the son of the one who performs his sacraments.
The son born of a maiden is the *kānīna*.
The son of a woman married while pregnant is called *sahoḍha*.
The son of a woman who has been remarried is a *paunarbhava*.
A son born of his own accord is an heir to both his father and his paternal kinsmen.
A son born of another belongs to the one who performs the sacraments alone, not to his biological relatives.
One who possesses the same status as that [son] is one released by his mother and father with water and given away.
He is one who has come of his own accord, or through his kinsmen, having entered into the state of being a son.
An adopted son is one who has been authorized for the status of a son.

"An adopted son is one who has been purchased. (KAZ 3.7.18) However, when a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) is born, sons of the same caste (*savarṇa*) shall receive a third share, while those of a different caste (*asavarṇa*) shall be entitled only to food and clothing. (KAZ 3.7.19)
KAZ03.7.20: For a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, sons born of women one degree lower are of the same caste (savarṇa); those born of women two degrees lower are of a different caste (asavarṇa).
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother is born an Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra mother is born a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother, an Ugra is born.
A Śūdra alone [is the attendant] of a Vaiśya.
And among these, those born of women of the same caste from men who have not performed their vows are called *vrātyas*.
Thus end the sons born in the direct order of castes (anuloma).
From a Śūdra [with women of the three higher castes] are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaidehaka are born.
From a Kṣatriya [father] and a Śūdra mother is born a Sūta.
But the *paurāṇika* Sūta and Māgadha are different; they are distinguished from the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya.
These [groups], being born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) due to the transgression of their own duties (*svadharma*), come into existence through the king.
From an Ugra and a Niṣāda woman is born a Kukkuṭa; in the reverse case, a Pulkasa.
From an Ambaṣṭha man and a Vaidehikā woman is born a Vaiṇa; in the reverse case, a Kuśīlava.
From an Ugra father and a Kṣattṛ mother is born a Śvapāka.
These and others are the intermediate regions (antarālas).
By his occupation, a Vaiśya is a chariot-maker (rathakāra).
Their marriage is within their own caste (svayoni), involving a union between the preceding and the succeeding classes, and characterized by both adherence to and deviation from established conduct.
Or they may follow the same laws as Śūdras, except for the Caṇḍālas.
A king who conducts himself solely in this manner attains heaven; otherwise, he goes to hell.
The division of all intermediate spaces shall be equal.
Whatever law is customary for a region, a caste, a corporation, or even a village,
one should determine the rules for the distribution of inheritance according to that very same law.
(Immovable Property)
KAZ03.8.01: Disputes concerning dwellings are to be settled based on the testimony of the neighbors.
A house, a field, a garden, an embankment, a tank, or a reservoir constitutes immovable property (*vāstu*).
A bridge with iron clamps and wedges is [the best] for a house.
He shall cause a house to be built according to the dimensions of the bridge.
Or, having moved away from another's wall by two *aratnis* or three *padās*, he should cause a boundary-mark (*deśabandha*) to be made.
One shall not discharge refuse, sweepings, or water from a well anywhere other than in a place suitable for a house, except for the case of a maternity well until ten days have passed.
In the event of its violation, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
By this, the [procedures for] striking firewood and the paths for rinsing water used in auspicious rites are explained.
He should cause a watercourse or a spring-fed waterfall to be constructed, extending three paces or one and a half cubits beyond the edge and sloping steeply downward.
In the event of its violation, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas.
One should cause a single-stone footpath, or a space for four carts measuring one cubit, to be made at the site of the fire-altar, the site of the water-channel, or the site of the grinding-mill.
In case of its violation, the fine shall be twenty-four paṇas.
Between two buildings made of all types of materials, or between two thatched huts, the intervening space shall be one *kiṣku* or three *padas*.
Between those two, there shall be a projection (nīpra) of four finger-breadths, or they may be set flush together.

One should cause a door-post opening of one *kiṣku* in width to be made in the middle for the purpose of repairing broken or cracked parts, ensuring it does not interfere with the passage of the bolt.
One should construct a small or high window for the purpose of light.
When that [house] is finished, one should roof it.
Or, acting together, the householders may have whatever they desire done,
or they may prevent what is undesirable.
And above the bamboo lattice-work, one should have a partition constructed, either concealed by mats or consisting of a solid wall, out of fear of damage from rain.
For its violation, the first amercement shall be imposed;
likewise for causing obstruction through a door or a window facing the opposite direction,
except in the case of the royal highway or the main street.
In cases of obstruction outside the boundary or the restriction of enjoyment, [the offense applies] regarding excavations, steps, drains, ladders, and refuse-removal areas.
For one who damages another's wall with water, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for damage caused by urine or excrement, it is double.
If the watercourse is opened while it is raining,
there shall be a fine of twelve paṇas otherwise.

And for one who resides in a prohibited manner, or for one who evicts a tenant, there shall be punishment except in cases of verbal or physical assault, theft, violence, adultery, or wrongful enjoyment of property.
One who departs of his own accord shall pay the remainder of the annual rent.
For one who does not provide assistance in a common dwelling,
or who obstructs the use of a common property within a house, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
For one who destroys it, the fine is double that amount.
For storehouses, courtyards, latrines, fire-places, and threshing-floors,
as well as for all open spaces, common use is prescribed.
Kinsmen, neighboring chieftains, and creditors shall, in that order, have the right to purchase the lands they have acquired.
KAZ03.9.02: Beyond those, others are the outsiders.
In the case of forty neighboring households, they shall announce the house at its front entrance;

in the case of fields, gardens, embankments, tanks, reservoirs, or boundaries among the elders of the neighboring villages, they shall announce it according to the usage of the boundary markers: "Who is the purchaser for this price?"
The purchaser shall have the right to purchase [the property] if it has been proclaimed three times and no objection has been raised.
If the price is increased out of competition, that increase in price, together with the tax, shall go to the treasury.
One who objects to a sale shall pay the toll.
In the case of denying ownership when there is no owner to contest it, the fine is twenty-four paṇas.
After seven nights, if he does not come forward, he may sell [the property] at a public outcry.
In the case of violating a prohibition regarding a building site, the fine shall be two hundred paṇas;
in other cases, the fine shall be twenty-four paṇas.
Thus ends the section on the sale of land.

Regarding disputes over boundaries between two villages, the neighboring villagers—either those from five or ten villages—shall determine the boundary by means of natural landmarks or artificial marks.

KAZ03.9.11: Farmers, cowherds, and elders, or those who have long enjoyed the land, or outsiders well-acquainted with the boundaries—whether many or a single person—having been designated, shall lead the way to the boundary markers while disguised in altered dress.

KAZ03.9.12: If the boundary markers specified are not found, the fine shall be one thousand panas. KAZ03.9.13: The same penalty shall be imposed on those who mislead regarding the boundary, as well as on those who destroy the boundary markers.
Or, in the case of a boundary where the landmarks and the enjoyment of the land have perished, the king shall divide it according to what is beneficial to each party.
Thus ends the dispute concerning boundaries.
Regarding disputes over fields, the elders of the neighboring villages shall settle them.
In the event of a division among them, they should withdraw from whichever side has many members who are pure or approved, or they should take the middle position.
Property declared by both [the owner and the finder] shall be taken by the king,
as shall property whose owner has disappeared.
Or he may divide [the property] according to the benefit [each person has provided].
In the case of taking land by force, the punishment for theft shall be imposed.
In the case of taking an instrument, having calculated the labor expended and the means of livelihood, he shall grant a bond.
Thus ends the dispute concerning fields.
(KAZ 3.9.21) For the removal of boundary markers, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
In the case of breaking a boundary marker, the fine is twenty-four paṇas.
By this, disputes concerning penance groves, pasture lands, high roads, cremation grounds, temples, sacrificial sites, and sacred places are explained.
Thus ends the establishment of boundaries.
All disputes whatsoever depend upon the testimony of the neighbors.
Among pasture lands, dry fields, irrigated fields, groves, threshing floors, houses, vehicles, and storehouses, each preceding one shall tolerate the encroachment of the following one.
KAZ03.9.26: Land areas are those excluding sites for Brahmins, Soma-plantations, forests, places of divine worship, and sacred spots.

In cases of damage caused to another's field by the irrigation reservoir, the overflow channel, or the field itself, or by the destruction of sown seeds, they shall pay compensation according to the extent of the injury.
In cases of mutual damage to fields, gardens, and embankments, the fine shall be double the value of the damage.
A lower reservoir constructed subsequently shall not flood the fields of an upper reservoir with water.
One situated on higher ground shall not obstruct the flow of water from the fullness of a lower tank,
except in the case of one whose work has been suspended for three years.
In the event of its violation, the first amercement shall be imposed,
and the dam shall be filled up.
Ownership of a dam whose construction has been abandoned for five years shall be forfeited,
except in cases of distress.
For the new construction of tanks and embankments, there shall be a tax remission for five years;
for those that were broken or abandoned and have been restored, a remission for four years; and for those that were overgrown and have been cleared, a remission for three years.
The [period of ownership] for land is two years.
In the case of giving oneself away or selling oneself.

They shall provide the proceeds from the cultivation of excavations, as well as from non-river-dependent irrigation works, tanks, fields, gardens, groves, and sown lands— either according to the specific share of the crop or color, or otherwise according to the benefit received— from those other than themselves.
Those who have purchased, leased, or received as a pledge a share of these [animals], as well as those who have been granted their use or are currently enjoying them, shall make restitution for them.
In the case of failing to provide medical treatment for a king, the fine shall be one and a half times the minimum.
For one who releases water from embankments when there is no need for it, the fine is six paṇas;
likewise for one who, through negligence, obstructs the water of others when they have need of it.
(Regarding damage to pastures:)
KAZ03.10.01: For one who blocks or creates an improper watercourse for fields and roads, or conversely, one who creates a proper one where it is improper, the first amercement shall be imposed;
as shall it be for one who establishes embankments, wells, sacred sites, shrines, or temples on another's land.

KAZ03.10.02: For one who brings about, or causes to be brought about, the transfer by gift or sale of a bridge of dharma that has been maintained since ancient times, the middle amercement shall be the punishment;
for those who hear of it, the highest amercement, except in the case of what is broken or abandoned.
In the absence of an owner, the villages or those of virtuous character shall provide compensation.
The measurement of roads has been explained in the section on the construction of forts.
For one who blocks a path for small animals or humans, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for a path for large animals, twenty-four paṇas;
and for a path for elephants or fields, fifty-four paṇas.
The road through a forest or a wilderness shall be six hundred [dhanus] wide; the road to a cremation ground or a village shall be two hundred;
the road at a port or a river crossing shall be five hundred.
For the destruction of a local settlement, a kingdom, or a pasture-land path, the fine is one thousand panas.
And for excessive extraction of these [revenues], the fines shall be one-fourth of the standard fines.
Regarding cultivation, those previously mentioned [rules apply].
If the owner of a field does not sow it, or if the tenant abandons it at the time for sowing, he shall be fined twelve paṇas,
except in cases of defects, calamities, or insuperable obstacles.
Taxpayers may pledge or sell their property to other taxpayers; those who hold land granted by a Brahmin may pledge or sell it to others who hold land granted by a Brahmin.
Otherwise, the first amercement shall be imposed.
Or [the fine shall be imposed] on a tax-payer who enters a village that is not subject to taxes.
But for one who enters as a tax-payer, there shall be freedom of choice regarding all goods,
except for his own house.
He should also give that to him.
If another person enjoys for five years property that should not be taken (anādeya) while its owner is not cultivating it, he shall restore it upon receiving compensation for his labor.
Those who do not pay taxes but reside elsewhere may subsist on the usufruct [of their property].
When the village headman departs on behalf of the village, the villagers should follow him in turn by means of fasting.
Those who do not follow along shall pay one and a half panas per yojana.
If a village headman expels from the village one who is neither a thief nor an adulterer, the fine shall be twenty-four paṇas; for the village, it shall be the highest fine.
The entry of one who has been expelled is explained by the rules regarding [the entry of] a suitor.
KAZ03.10.20: One should cause a rampart to be constructed all around the village at a distance of one hundred bows from the pillars.
They may subsist by means of cutting down the *vivīta* forest for the purpose of grazing cattle.
KAZ03.10.22. For camels and buffaloes that have grazed upon pasture lands and then fled, they shall collect a tax of one-quarter of a rūpa;
for cows, horses, and donkeys, half of a quarter-rūpa; and for small animals, a sixteenth part of a rūpa.
For those who have eaten and are sitting [drinking], these same fines shall be doubled; for those who are staying overnight, they shall be quadrupled.
A village deity, a bull, a cow within ten days of calving, oxen, and breeding bulls are exempt from punishment.
KAZ03.10.25: In the case of eating standing crops, having calculated the damage to the crop according to its actual yield, he shall cause double that amount to be paid.
For one who grazes [cattle] without informing the owner, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for one who releases them, the fine is twenty-four paṇas.
For those who protect [the goods], the fines shall be half.
One should perform that very same rite in the case of eating from a barren field.
In the case of breaking a fence, the fine is double; likewise for the consumption of grains located within houses, threshing floors, or enclosures.
He shall provide a remedy for injury.
If animals in a sanctuary (*abhayavana*) that have been taken into custody are eating [the crops], they should be restrained after informing the owner, provided they are not to be killed.
Cattle should be kept at bay with a rein and a goad.
If they cause injury in any other manner, the punishments for physical assault shall be applied.
Those who are making improper demands, or those whose offenses have been observed, shall be restrained by all possible means.
Thus ends the section on damage to fields and roads.
(KAZ 3.10.35) If a cultivator, having entered a village, does not perform his work, the village itself shall impose a fine upon him.
KAZ03.10.36: In the case of not performing the work, one shall pay double the wages for the work;
in the case of not giving gold, double the share;
and in the case of not providing food and drink at festive gatherings, one shall give double the share.
In a public spectacle,
one who does not pay his share shall not watch it along with his own people.
In cases of secret listening or watching, and in any action for the benefit of all, he shall pay double the share by way of punishment.
Those who speak for the welfare of all shall carry out the command of that one person.
In the case of non-compliance, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
If they should kill him together, their punishment shall be double that for an individual offense.
Among those who cause harm, he is distinguished as the most severe.
And among these, the status of the eldest shall be determined by the Brāhmaṇa.
And at their festivals, Brāhmaṇas shall perform the rites even if they are unwilling,
and they shall receive a share [of the offerings].
By this, the non-violation of the agreements (*samaya*) of regions, castes, families, and guilds is explained.
The king, while constructing embankments for the welfare of the country, bridges on the roads,
village beautifications, and defensive works, should act for their benefit and well-being.
(Non-payment of debts)
A monthly interest of one and a quarter paṇas per hundred paṇas is lawful;
five paṇas is the commercial rate; ten paṇas is for those traveling through wilderness regions.
Twenty paṇas for those from the sea.
Beyond that, the first amercement shall be imposed on both the perpetrator and the instigator,
while each of the witnesses shall be fined half of that amount.
But if it brings about security and prosperity for the kingdom, the king should examine the conduct of both the creditor and the debtor.
The increase on grain shall be one-half when the crop is harvested; beyond that, it shall increase according to the market price.
Interest on a deposit shall be half of the rate of increase; it may be paid annually when the amount has accumulated.
One who has been away on a long journey or is confined by paralysis shall pay double the value.

KAZ03.11.07: For one who recovers a debt without having stipulated interest, or for one who increases the amount, or for one who announces a price by adding on interest, the fine shall be four times the value of the pledge.
In the case of empty hearing, there is no real possession of the four qualities.
Of that [fine], the receiver shall pay one-third, and the giver shall pay the remainder.

One shall not increase the debt of a minor who is engaged in a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*), or who is afflicted by disease, or detained in the household of a teacher, or who is destitute.
If one does not accept a debt being discharged, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
Under the pretext of a legal cause, it may remain elsewhere with its interest suspended.

A debt neglected for ten years shall not be recoverable, except in cases involving minors, the elderly, the sick, those afflicted by calamity, those who have gone abroad, those who have abandoned their country, or during a revolution in the kingdom.
The sons of the deceased shall pay the interest,
or the heirs who take the inheritance, or those who were joint borrowers.
Or [the debt shall be paid by] the sureties.
No other kind of suretyship is valid.
A suretyship entered into by a minor is without substance.
But for a debt whose place and time are unascertained, the sons, grandsons, or other heirs who take the inheritance shall pay it.
But for a guarantee concerning life, marriage, or land, the sons or grandsons shall bear the liability if the time and place were not specified.
KAZ03.11.19: But when there is a combination of various debts, two persons shall not simultaneously sue for one and the same debt, except in the case of one who is departing from the country.
Even in that case, one who has received the sequence of items should first restore the property of the king or of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*).
A debt contracted among a husband and wife, between a father and son, or among brothers who are undivided, is not recoverable from one another.
KAZ03.11.22: Farmers and royal officers shall not be arrested during the times for their work.
And a wife who does not deny it shall pay the debt contracted by her husband, except in the case of herdsmen and sharecroppers.
But a husband shall be held liable for a debt contracted by his wife if he has gone abroad without providing for her.
In the case of mutual agreement, the highest fine is prescribed.
But in our own judicial proceedings, witnesses are the means of proof; they must be trustworthy, pure, and approved, and there should be at least three of them.
Or, when both parties have agreed upon the claim, two may act together, but never just one regarding a debt.

Those prohibited [as witnesses] are the brother-in-law, an associate, a petitioner, a creditor, a debtor, an enemy, one with a physical deformity, one who has been punished, and those previously declared unfit for legal proceedings.

The king, a Vedic scholar, village officials, laborers, those suffering from leprosy or open sores, outcasts, Caṇḍālas, those who perform despicable acts, the blind, the deaf, the mute, those who claim to be so, women, and royal servants— except for their own respective classes— are exempt [from military service].
But in cases of assault, theft, and adultery, those who have enmity with the accused, his brother-in-law, and his associates shall be excluded.
In secret transactions, a single woman or man who has overheard or witnessed them shall be the witness, with the exception of a king or an ascetic.
Masters may give testimony for their servants, officiating priests and teachers for their pupils, and parents for their sons; or conversely, these others may give testimony for them. KAZ03.11.32.
In the case of mutual accusations among them, those of higher status shall pay a fine of ten times the value when defeated, while those of lower status shall pay five times the value.
Thus ends the section on witnesses.
In the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, a water-pot, and fire, he should summon the witnesses.
In that case, he should say to the Brāhmaṇa: "Speak the truth."
A kṣatriya or a vaiśya [should be threatened]: "May you not enjoy the fruit of your sacrifices and charitable works; with a skull in hand, may you go to the enemy's house seeking alms!"
“O Śūdra, whatever fruit of merit you have gained between birth and death shall go to the king; likewise, the king’s guilt shall fall upon you if you speak falsely, and a punishment shall follow.”
"Later it may be known as it was seen and heard;
being of one mind, offer the truth."
For those who do not bring [the goods] within seven nights, the fine shall be twelve paṇas; after three fortnights, they shall pay the legal costs of the suit.
In the case of a conflict among witnesses, they should decide according to those who are numerous, pure, or authorized; or else, they should adopt the middle course.
Or the king may take that property for himself.
If the witnesses should testify to an amount less than the claim, the plaintiff shall pay a fine equal to the excess.
Or if they should state an amount in excess, the king shall take that excess for himself.

If, having considered that the plaintiff’s claim is based on folly, or was wrongly heard, or wrongly written down, or is due to a persistent obsession with the deceased, the case shall depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses.

"A separate examination regarding the place, time, and nature of the case against witnesses and bailiffs shall be punished with the first, middle, and highest fines respectively"—so say the followers of Uśanas.
“False witnesses shall pay a fine ten times the amount of the matter which they have falsely established or destroyed,” so say the followers of Manu (Mānavas).
“Those who cause a breach of trust out of foolishness shall be executed by various methods of torture,” so say the followers of Bṛhaspati.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
For witnesses must certainly hear the case.
For those who do not hear it, the fine is twenty-four paṇas; for those who do not speak out, it is half of that.

One should produce witnesses who reside neither far from the place nor distant in time; or, for those who are distant or unable to travel, one should secure their testimony by means of the depositor’s own statement.
KAZ03.12.01 / A deposit is explained by the rules concerning debt.

Or when a fort or the countryside is devastated by a foreign army or forest-dwellers; or when villages, caravans, or herds are plundered by robbers; or when there is the destruction of a military force.

In the event of an affliction by fire or water in the midst of a village, or when obstructed by the force of a conflagration, or when a boat has sunk or been plundered, one who has rescued himself need not restore a deposit.
The user of a deposit shall pay a fee for its use proportionate to the place and time,
and shall also pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
If he brings back what has been lost or destroyed for the purpose of personal enjoyment,
there shall be a fine of twenty-four paṇas; or the same penalty applies if he fails to produce it otherwise.
One should not bring forth a deposit to a deceased person or one who has fallen into calamity.
In cases of mortgaging, selling, or misappropriating [the property], the fine for him shall be four or five times the value.
In case of exchange or removal, the fine shall be equal to the value [of the article].
By this, the loss, enjoyment, sale, pledge, and seizure of a mortgage are explained.
A mortgage that is accompanied by an additional benefit shall not suffer depreciation, nor shall its value increase,
except in the case of its voluntary relinquishment.
If it provides no benefit, it shall perish, and its price shall increase.
If one who has been summoned fails to deliver the pledged object, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
Or, in the absence of the instigator, having deposited it with the village elders, he may obtain the release of the pledge by paying its redemption value.

Or, when the interest has ceased, the pledge shall remain in that very place with its value fixed at the rate established at that time; or it may be placed under the supervision of a person who ensures its preservation against loss or destruction.
In the absence of the pledge-holder, or out of fear of loss, he may sell the property at a raised price with the permission of the judge,
or upon the testimony of the pledge-guardian.

But immovable property, which is to be enjoyed through labor or enjoyed for its produce, shall be restored after deducting the value of the investment, the interest, and the principal, along with the profits, provided there is no loss in value.
One who enjoys property without authorization shall pay the value of the property, a purification fee, his livelihood, and a fine.
The remainder is explained by the rules concerning deposits (*upanidhi*).
By this, the *ādeśa* (substitute) and the *anvādhi* (mortgage deposit) are explained.
If one who has received a deposit from a caravan fails to reach the designated place, or is robbed or abandoned by bandits on the way, he shall not be liable for the delivery of the deposit.
Or, in the case of one who has died in the interim, even his heir shall not bring [the property] back.
The remainder is explained by the rules concerning deposits (*upanidhi*).
Whatever they may receive—whether on loan or as a deposit—they shall restore it in that very same condition.
They shall not be held liable for what has been given, lost, or destroyed due to negligence or misfortune, provided it was hindered by the constraints of place or time.
The remainder is explained by the rules concerning deposits (*upanidhi*).

KAZ03.12.25 / Regarding sale through commission agents: those acting as commission agents, when selling merchandise according to the appropriate place and time, shall pay the price and the profit exactly as it accrues.
Or, in the case of missing a designated place or time, they shall pay the value and the interest at the price prevailing at the time of delivery.
Or, if they sell according to what was agreed upon but do not obtain a profit,
they shall pay only the purchase price.
Or, in the event of a fall in market price, they shall pay the deficiency in value according to the extent of that decrease.

Or, in the case of those who are trustworthy in their dealings and not subject to the king's direct command, they shall not have to pay even the value of what is lost or destroyed due to negligence or an unforeseen accident.
But for commodities separated by distance or time, they shall pay the price after deducting the loss and expenses, as well as the profit;
and for collective consignments of goods, they shall pay their respective shares.
The remainder is explained by the rules concerning deposits (*upanidhi*).
By this, the sale of articles obtained through service is explained.
And a deposit is treated in the same manner as an open deposit.
If one person, having received a deposit from another, hands it over to a third party, he shall forfeit it.
In the case of the misappropriation of a deposit, the previous history of the matter and the depositors themselves are the authority for proof.
For artisans are indeed impure.
In these cases, the legal rule regarding deposits does not apply when preceded by the use of instruments.
If a depositor denies a deposit that lacks any written record, the depositor should cause secret witnesses placed behind a hidden wall to reveal themselves through a prostration in private,
or by means of an invitation to a drinking party at the edge of a forest where they have been instilled with confidence.
In secret, some elderly or diseased merchant (vaidehaka), having deposited property marked with identifying signs into his [the suspect's] hands, should depart.
Upon receiving notification of this, the son or brother of the depositor shall go there and demand the deposit back.
If he returns it upon request, he is pure; otherwise, he shall pay the penalty for theft and a fine equal to the deposit.
Or, some trustworthy person intending to renounce the world might entrust property marked with identifying signs into his hands and then depart.
Then, having returned after some time, he should make his request.
If he returns it honestly, he is pure; otherwise, he shall pay the penalty for theft and a fine equal to the deposit.
Or he may cause him to be recovered by means of property marked with a distinctive sign.
Or, being of a foolish nature, he might, fearing the opportunity provided by the king's attendants at night, deposit the valuables in his hand and depart.
Having entered the prison, he should entreat him.
If he returns it upon request, he is pure; otherwise, he shall pay the penalty for theft and restore the deposit.
And by means of a token of recognition, one should request both types of people from his house.
Regarding the taking of anything else [than that], it is as previously stated.
He should investigate the source of his acquisitions of goods and wealth, as well as the legal transactions related to that property,
and the financial capacity of the accuser.
By this, mutual association is explained.
Therefore, one should conduct a legal proceeding clearly and with witnesses,
whether against one's own people or others, ensuring it is properly articulated according to place, time, number, and caste.
(Law concerning slaves and laborers)
KAZ03.13.01: For a kinsman who sells or mortgages a Śūdra who is not a slave by birth, who possesses the life-force of an Ārya, and who has not attained legal capacity, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for a Vaiśya, it is double that amount; for a Kṣatriya, it is triple.
For a Brahmin, it is fourfold.
For another person, the punishments for killing are of three degrees— lesser, middling, and highest—
and this applies equally to the buyer and the informant.
For the Mlecchas, there is no offense in selling or mortgaging their offspring.
But there is no such thing as slavery for a noble person.
Alternatively, having placed a noble man as a hostage for the sake of family ties during a time of distress for the nobles,
and having obtained the ransom, they should first redeem a child or one who provides assistance.
One who has established his own fire (ātma-ādhātṛ) shall sit [in penance] if he has fled once; one whose fire has been established by another (anyenāhitaka) twice;
and both shall sit if they have fled toward a foreign territory once.
Or, for a slave who steals his master's property or deprives him of his status as a free man (āryabhāva), the fine shall be half [of the standard].
In the case of those who have fled, died, or met with misfortune, the depositor shall receive the value [of the pledge].

For a man who has taken a wife, making her handle the feces, urine, or food-leavings of a dead person; bathing her naked; sending her on punitive expeditions; or allowing her to transgress [proper conduct], results in the loss of the bride-price.
Furthermore, it results in the release of nurses, female attendants, concubines, and maidservants from their service.
KAZ03.13.10: Once the child has been born, the departure of the attendant is accomplished.

For one who approaches a nurse or a female attendant against her will when she is under his own authority, the first amercement shall be the punishment; if she is under the authority of another, the middle amercement.
If a man defiles a maiden or a betrothed girl, either by himself or through another, he shall forfeit her price, pay the bride-price, and be fined twice that amount.
One should know that the offspring of one who has sold himself is an Ārya.
He shall receive what he has acquired himself, provided it does not conflict with his master's business,
as well as his paternal inheritance.
And by means of payment, one may attain the status of an Ārya.
By this, the *udara-dāsa* (slave by the belly) and the *āhitaka* (slave for maintenance) are explained.
And his ransom shall be proportional to the amount deposited.
One who has been sentenced to punishment shall perform labor as his means of paying that fine.
A person whose life is noble, or one captured under a banner, shall be released for half the price, in accordance with the time required for his labor.

KAZ03.13.20: For one who sells or mortgages any of the following types of slaves— a slave born in the house, one acquired as a portion of inheritance, one received as a gift, or one purchased— namely, one under eight years of age, one without relatives, or one unwilling [to work], or for one who does so with a female slave who is pregnant or unable to provide for the pregnancy due to lack of provisions, the punishment shall be the first amercement.
And [it is so] for the buyers and the listeners.
For one who makes a slave an Ārya by paying an appropriate ransom, the fine is twelve paṇas, and there shall be confinement until the act is undone.
The heirs of a slave who is property are his kinsmen;
in their absence, the owner [is the heir].
One should know that a son born to a master by his own female slave is not a slave, provided he is born together with the mother.
If she is a housewife who manages the affairs of the family, her mother, brother, and sister shall not be liable for her debts, provided they are not slaves.
For one who, having ransomed a male or female slave, subsequently sells or mortgages them again, the fine is twelve paṇas,
except in cases where the parties themselves have agreed otherwise.
Thus ends the section on slaves (dāsa-kalpa). Those close to a laborer shall know his connection to his work.
One who has agreed upon a wage shall receive it as stipulated; one for whom no wage was stipulated shall receive it in accordance with the duration of the work performed.

A cultivator shall receive a tenth part of the crops; a cowherd, a tenth part of the clarified butter; and a merchant, a tenth part of the merchandise he has traded himself—provided that his wages were not previously agreed upon.
But one whose wages have been agreed upon shall receive them exactly as agreed.

Artisans, craftsmen, actors, physicians, professional storytellers, attendants, and others who provide services for wages shall receive their remuneration according to what another of that same class would do, or as experts may determine.
It must be based solely on the testimony of witnesses.
In the absence of witnesses, one should interrogate the person from whom the action originated.
For the non-payment of wages, the fine shall be ten times the amount, or six paṇas.
If one denies a debt, the fine shall be twelve paṇas,
or a surety of five [times the amount].

One who, beset by the force of a river, a conflagration, thieves, or wild beasts, has been rescued from distress by offering all his property, his children, his wife, and even himself, shall, having called upon his rescuer, pay the fee prescribed by experts once he has safely crossed over.
By this, the remorse regarding gifts given out of distress in all cases is explained.
A wanton woman may obtain enjoyment through the pretext of a sexual union;
however, she shall be defeated by excessive begging or by her own wickedness and lack of discipline.
(Duties of Servants)
(Kinds of Partnership) KAZ03.14.01: A hired laborer who, having received wages, fails to perform the work shall be fined twelve paṇas and shall be detained until the work is completed.
If he is incapable due to a loathsome task, illness, or misfortune, he may obtain a rescission of the contract or have it performed by another.
The master may either take his share through that expenditure or cause him to perform it.

KAZ03.14.04: “No one else shall be made to work by you, nor shall anyone else do work for me”—in the event of such an agreement, if the employer does not cause work to be done or the hired laborer does not perform the work, the fine shall be twelve *paṇas*.
When the completion of the work depends on the employer, one who has received wages shall not perform it against his will, except in other circumstances.
"The teacher should consider it as already performed by one who causes [the pupil] to perform what has been presented," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Wages are due for work performed; there are none for work not performed.
If, after having caused even a small portion to be executed, he should not have it completed, one should consider that work as already finished for him.
If a task is performed by missing the proper place or time, or if it is executed otherwise than intended, one who did not consent to it shall not be held to have authorized its performance.
If the work performed exceeds what was agreed upon, one should not let the effort go to waste.
By this, those maintained by a corporation (saṃgha) are explained.
Their pledge shall remain [in effect] for seven nights.
Then he should appoint another person, and [ensure] the completion of the work.
And the community shall not, without having informed the master, exclude anyone or initiate anyone [into the order].
In the event of its violation, the fine shall be twenty-four paṇas.
For one who has been protected by a corporation, the fine shall be half.
Thus concludes the section on hired laborers.
Those supported by a corporation, or those who have entered into a joint undertaking, shall divide their wages equally, either according to what was agreed upon or in equal shares.

Alternatively, cultivators and merchants shall pay a share of the work as it was performed during the interval between the commencement and completion of the cultivation or trade of crops, for one who has withdrawn from the undertaking.
In the case of attendance by a male slave, they shall pay the full share.
But when the merchandise has been successfully completed and extracted, they shall pay him his share immediately upon his arrival.
For success and failure on the road are common to all.
But if one who is in good health abandons work once it has commenced, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
And there shall be no arbitrary departure.
But a thief he should first reassure with a promise of safety and then compel him to accept a share of the proceeds from his crime;
he should give him that share and grant him safety.
In the case of stealing again, there shall be banishment,
as well as for going elsewhere [to commit the offense].
But in the case of a great offense, he should deal with him as with a traitor.
The officiating priests shall divide their fee equally, or as previously agreed upon, with the exception of the materials used for their own ritual activities.
In the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, after the initiation (dīkṣā), one should give a third part;
after the middle pressing (madhyama-upasad), a half-part;
and after the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) on the day of the Soma-pressing (sutya), a part less a quarter.
After the midday libation, he shall receive his full share.
For the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) have indeed been led away.
KAZ03.14.32: With the exception of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are indeed given at each pressing of the Soma.
By this, the sacrificial fees for the series of days are explained.
For those who have been hired for a period of ten days or nights, they shall perform the work as long as their wages remain unpaid; or others may do so, provided they are personally trustworthy.
But if the sacrificer should perish while the ritual is incomplete,
the officiating priests shall complete the rite and take their sacrificial fee.
But if one abandons either the sacrificer or the officiating priest while the ritual is not yet completed, the first amercement shall be imposed.
One who has not maintained the sacred fires, one who has performed a hundred sacrifices, and one who has performed a thousand sacrifices;
a drinker of spirituous liquor, a husband of a Śūdra woman, a slayer of a Brahmin, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
One who is intent on accepting gifts from the unworthy, a thief, or a contemptible officiating priest—
there is no fault in their mutual abandonment of one another, because it is certain that their professional activities have become intermingled.
(Rescission of Sale and Purchase)
If one has sold a commodity but does not deliver it, the fine shall be twelve paṇas,
except in cases of defects, accidents, or insurmountable obstacles.
A defect in the merchandise constitutes a defect [in the sale].
KAZ03.15.03: An impending calamity consisting of oppression by the king, thieves, fire, or water.
Or that which is deficient in many qualities, or performed by one who is distressed, or otherwise unbearable.
For merchants, the period for rescission is one night;
