for cultivators, three nights; and for cattle-herders, five nights.
In the case of mixed castes and the highest castes, there shall be a seven-night period of impurity for the sale of their means of livelihood.
For perishable commodities, a penalty shall be imposed by prohibiting their sale elsewhere with the declaration: "This may not be sold anywhere else."
In case of its violation, the fine shall be twenty-four paṇas,
or else a tenth part of the merchandise.
For one who has purchased merchandise but does not accept it, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
Except in cases where the onset of a fault is unbearable.
And the rescission [of the sale] is subject to the same conditions as the rescission by the seller.
But for the three preceding castes, the completion of marriage is established by the grasping of the hand; and for Śūdras, it is by the performance of sexual intercourse.
Even for those who have already taken each other's hands in marriage, it is established that they may separate upon seeing a fault related to their private life.
But this is certainly not the case for those who have already given birth.
If one gives away a maiden without disclosing a defect related to her private life, the fine is ninety-six paṇas,
and he must also return the bride-price and the woman's property.
Or, if the giver of the bride takes her without disclosing a defect in the groom, he shall pay double the fine and forfeit both the bride-price and the woman's property.
In the case of bipeds and quadrupeds, however, for reporting those that are dull, diseased, or unclean as being energetic, healthy, or clean, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
The recall of quadrupeds occurs within three fortnights; that of humans occurs within one year.
For within that much time, it is possible to determine both purity and impurity.
The members of the assembly should so manage the rescission of a gift or a purchase that neither the giver nor the receiver shall be harmed. (Non-conveyance of gifts)
(Ownership without possession) (Possession with ownership): KAZ03.16.01 / The non-delivery of what has been given is explained by the rules concerning the recovery of debts.
What has been given shall not be subject to legal dispute; it remains valid as long as the donor’s regret persists.
One who has expressed regret may offer his entire property, his wife and children, or even himself, as restitution.

The gift of righteousness (dharma-dāna) consists of engaging in unrighteous acts or harmful deeds; the gift of wealth (artha-dāna) consists of bestowing it upon those who do not help or even those who cause harm; and the gift of pleasure (kāma-dāna) consists of giving to those who are unworthy.
And the experts should determine the legal settlement in such a way that neither the giver nor the receiver shall suffer harm.
For one who accepts a gift out of fear— whether from fear of punishment, fear of verbal abuse, or fear of some misfortune— the penalty for theft shall apply both to the recipient and to the giver.
The giving of gifts out of anger for the purpose of harming another, as well as the giving of gifts out of pride toward kings, [is a cause of ruin].
In that case, the highest fine shall be imposed.
A son, an heir, or an inheritor of the estate need not pay against his will for a suretyship, the remainder of a fine or a toll, or debts incurred through gambling or drinking.
Thus ends the section on the non-recovery of what has been given.
Regarding sale by one who is not the owner: having recovered property that was lost or stolen, the owner shall cause it to be seized by the magistrate.
Or, in the event of a lapse regarding place or time, he should seize it himself and bring it back.
And the judge shall interrogate the owner, saying: "From whom did you obtain this?"
If he should demonstrate the traditional succession of ownership but not the seller,
he would be released by the relinquishment of that property.
If the seller is found,
he shall pay both the price and the fine for theft.
If he finds an opportunity to escape, he shall flee until that opportunity for escape is exhausted.
In the event of loss, he shall pay the value of the goods and the penalty for theft.
And the owner who has lost [the property] shall recover it once he has provided proof of ownership.
In the absence of his own instruments, the fine shall be five times the amount.
And that property shall belong to the king.
If one fails to report property that has been lost or stolen, the owner shall be punished with the first amercement for each day it is withheld.
At the customs station, any goods that are lost, stolen, or found should be kept in custody.
After three fortnights, if he does not return, the king shall take him [the property],
or the owner may do so by means of his own proof of ownership.
One shall pay a ransom of five paṇas for a two-hoofed animal, four paṇas for a single-hoofed animal,
and two paṇas for a cow or a buffalo.
For small animals, it shall be one-quarter [of a pana].
One should pay five percent as a premium on precious stones, raw materials, forest produce, and base metals.
But having recovered what has been seized by a foreign army or forest tribes, the king shall restore it to its respective owners.
He shall provide from his own property what has been stolen by thieves if it is not available, or if he is unable to recover it.
Having brought back what was seized by his own men, he shall restore it, or pay its ransom.
Or, he may enjoy what has been brought back by force from a foreign territory as directed by the king,
except for the lives of noble beings and the property of gods, Brahmins, and ascetics.
Thus ends the section on sale by one who is not the owner (asvāmi-vikraya).

As for the relationship between property and its owner: in the case of lands whose possession has been interrupted, ownership of the respective goods is established through the continuity of enjoyment.

If one neglects one's own property being enjoyed by others for ten years, it shall be lost to him, except in the cases of minority, old age, disease, misfortune, absence from home, exile from the country, or political upheaval.
One shall not pursue a claim regarding a building site that has been neglected for twenty years or over which no residence was established.
KAZ03.16.32 Relatives, Vedic scholars, or heretics dwelling in the houses of others in the absence of the king shall not acquire ownership through mere possession;
this applies also to deposits, pledges, treasure-troves, sealed deposits, women, boundaries, and the property of the king or Vedic scholars.
Ascetics or heretics shall dwell in a large open space, not obstructing one another.
They should endure minor harassment.
Or, one who has arrived earlier shall provide a turn for lodging.
One who fails to pay [the fine] shall be expelled.

KAZ03.16.37: For forest hermits, ascetics, and lifelong students, the heirs to the inheritance are, in order: the teacher, the pupil, a spiritual brother, and those belonging to the same religious order.

In cases of dispute among these [offenders], they shall undergo for as many nights as there are panas of their fines the following penances: fasting, ritual bathing, fire-rites, and the practice of severe austerities (mahākacchavardhana) under the king.
Those who possess neither silver nor gold, the Pāṣaṇḍas, are virtuous.
They shall propitiate them according to their respective fasts and vows,
except in cases of verbal abuse, theft, violence, and adultery.
Against them, the punishments as previously described shall be inflicted.
The king should restrain by means of punishment those who follow improper conduct within the orders of renunciation;
for dharma, when struck down by adharma and neglected, destroys the ruler himself.
KAZ03.17.01: Sāhasa (violence) is an act committed by force accompanied by a claim of right.
Theft is [punishable] when there is no claim of ownership,
as is the act of misappropriation.
“Regarding gems, raw materials, forest produce, and base metals, the fine for violence shall be equal to their value,” so say the followers of Manu.
“The fine shall be double the value,” so say the followers of Auśanasa.
"According to the offense," says Kauṭilya.

KAZ03.17.06: For small articles such as flowers, fruits, vegetables, roots, tubers, cooked food, leather, bamboo, earthenware, and the like, the fine shall be no less than twelve paṇas and no more than twenty-four paṇas.

For the theft of articles such as iron, copper, wood, rope, raw materials, small animals, cloth, and other similar coarse goods, the fine shall be no less than twenty-four paṇas and no more than forty-eight paṇas.

For the theft of coarse goods such as vessels made of copper, brass, bronze, glass, or ivory, the first amercement (pūrva-sāhasa) shall be imposed, ranging from a minimum of forty-eight paṇas to a maximum of ninety-six paṇas.

For large animals, humans, fields, houses, gold, bullion, fine garments, and other such bulky goods, the middle amercement consists of a fine ranging from no less than two hundred to no more than five hundred [paṇas].

For one who, having overpowered a woman or a man, binds them, causes them to be bound, or releases them from bondage, the punishment shall be the highest amercement, ranging from no less than five hundred panas to no more than one thousand.
Thus say the teachers.
KAZ03.17.11: “He who causes another to commit an act of violence by saying, ‘I am the perpetrator,’ shall pay double the fine.”
“If I shall give as much gold as will be used,” he should pay a fine four times that amount.
"He who causes [work] to be done by specifying a limit, saying, 'I will give this much gold,' shall pay the gold as stated and a fine," so say the followers of Bṛhaspati.
If he should plead anger, intoxication, or delusion as an excuse, Kauṭilya maintains that one should inflict upon him the punishment as previously prescribed.
In all cases of fines for punishment, the fee (rūpa) shall be one hundred and eight paṇas;
for fines exceeding one hundred, one should know that the commission (vyājī) shall be one hundred and five paṇas.

Due to the abundance of faults among the subjects, or because of the moral corruption of kings, the people may appear to be unrighteous under the pretext of their outward form; however, the true nature of the subjects is traditionally held to be righteous.
(Verbal Injury)
Verbal cruelty consists of slander, reviling, and threatening.

KAZ03.18.02: Regarding the body, physical constitution, learning, occupation, and the inhabited territory, if one makes a true accusation concerning the body by means of charges such as being one-eyed or lame, the fine is three paṇas;
if the accusation is false, the fine is six paṇas.
KAZ03.18.03: For using such phrases as "those with beautiful eyes" in order to praise or disparage those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise disabled, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
In cases of contempt due to leprosy, insanity, impotence, and so forth, as well as for true or false praise or blame among equals, the fines shall start from twelve paṇas and increase progressively.
In the case of superior persons, the fines are doubled; for inferior persons, they are half the fine;
and for the wives of others, they are doubled.
For those [offenses] committed through negligence, intoxication, delusion, and so forth, the punishments shall be halved.
In cases of leprosy and insanity, physicians and nearby male relatives are the authorities;
in the case of impotence, women are the authority, as well as the appearance of foam in the urine and the sinking of feces in water.

In cases of defamation regarding natural status, for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Antas, and Āvasāyins, the fines shall be three paṇas higher for each subsequent person when defaming a preceding one,
and two paṇas lower for each preceding person when defaming a subsequent one;
the same applies in cases of contemptuous abuse involving "wicked Brāhmaṇas" and similar terms.

By this, the censure of livelihoods among those who live by their speech, the censure of the livelihoods of artisans and actors, and the censures of various regions such as Prāgjyotiṣa, Gāndhāra, and others, are explained.
If one should threaten another with an act by saying, "I will do this to you," he shall pay half the fine that would be imposed for actually committing that act.
If the threat is not carried out, he shall pay half of the fine prescribed for its commission.
If he is unable [to pay], he shall plead anger, intoxication, or delusion as his excuse and shall pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
One who harbors a sense of enmity and is capable of doing harm should be given a lifelong maintenance allowance.

For verbal abuse against one’s own country or village, the first amercement is prescribed; for that against a caste or a guild, the middle amercement; but for abusing the king or a sacred shrine, one deserves the highest amercement.
(Physical Injury)
Assault with a staff consists of touching, threatening with a blow, or striking.

For one who touches the body below the navel with mud from the hands, ashes, or dust, the fine is three paṇas; for touching it with those same impure substances, or with the feet or spittle, the fine is six paṇas; and for touching it with vomit, urine, feces, and so forth, the fine is twelve paṇas.
Above the navel they are double [the strength], and on the head they are fourfold, in the case of equal [distances].
In the case of superior persons, the fines are doubled; for inferior persons, they are half the fine;
and in the case of other men's wives, they are doubled.
In cases involving negligence, intoxication, delusion, and so forth, the penalties shall be halved.
In cases of pulling at a person's foot, garment, hand, or hair, the fines shall start from six paṇas and increase progressively.
For causing pain, binding, bending, pulling, or sitting upon [another], the first amercement shall be the punishment.
If he causes it to fall and then flees, the penalty is half of the fine.
If a Śūdra strikes a Brāhmaṇa with any limb, that limb of his shall be cut off.
For threatening with a blow, there is a ransom; for actual contact, half the fine.
By this, the impurity of Caṇḍālas is explained.
For striking with the hand, the fine shall be no less than three paṇas and no more than twelve paṇas; for striking with the foot, it shall be double that amount;
and for causing pain with any object, the first amercement shall be imposed.
If it causes obstruction to the vital breaths, it is a middling offense.
For one who inflicts pain without drawing blood by means of any one of the following— wood, clods of earth, stones, metal rods, ropes, or other objects— the fine shall be twenty-four paṇas;
if blood is drawn, the fine shall be double,
except in the case of "vicious blood" (i.e., where the victim is already suffering from a wound).
For one who strikes someone nearly dead or bloodless, or who inflicts mutilation by cutting off a hand or foot,
or for breaking a hand, foot, or tooth, or for cutting off an ear or nose, or for tearing open a wound— except in the case of malignant sores— the first amercement shall be the punishment.
In cases of breaking a leg or a neck, piercing the eyes, or obstructing speech, movement, or food, the middle amercement shall be imposed, along with the expenses for recovery.
In the event of misfortune, he should be led away for the purpose of clearing out the thorns.
For one who kills a member of a large group, the fine shall be double for each individual victim.
“An old quarrel or an internal dispute should not be prosecuted,” so say the teachers.
"There is no escape for one who has done harm," says Kauṭilya.
"In a quarrel, he who arrives first wins, for he who cannot endure runs away"— so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.

In the case of one who has approached [as a witness] either before or after [the event], the witness is the authority; in the absence of a witness, there shall be punishment for the assault or evidence of the quarrel.
If one accused of murder fails to provide a defense, the subsequent legal procedure shall take place on that very same day.
In a quarrel, for one who steals property, the fine is ten paṇas;
for damage to minor articles, the fine is that article itself plus an equal amount; for damage to substantial articles, the fine is that article itself plus double its value.
In the case of injury to clothing, ornaments, silver, gold, or vessels, the fine shall be both that [specific penalty] and the first amercement.
For one who agitates another's wall by striking it, the fine is three paṇas;
for cutting or breaking it, the fine is six paṇas, and the damage must be repaired.
For one who throws a substance that causes pain into another's house, the fine is twelve paṇas; for a substance that threatens life, the first amercement shall be imposed.
For causing pain to small animals with sticks or similar objects, the fine shall be one *paṇa* or double that;
for drawing blood, it shall be double.
In the case of large animals, the fine at these same locations shall be double, as well as the expenses for their recovery.
For cutting the sprouts of trees in city gardens that possess flowers, fruit, and shade, the fine is six paṇas;
for cutting small branches, twelve paṇas;
and for cutting thick branches, twenty-four paṇas.
For the wounding of a limb, the first amercement shall be imposed; for the complete severance [of a limb], the middle amercement.
For cutting shrubs and creepers that possess flowers, fruits, and shade, the fines shall be half those prescribed;
the same applies to trees in sacred sites, penance groves, and cremation grounds.
In the case of boundary trees, sacred trees, marked trees,
and likewise in royal forests, those same fines shall be doubled.
(Miscellaneous) KAZ03.20.01:
The superintendent of gambling shall conduct gambling through a single center.
For one who gambles elsewhere [than in the authorized place], a fine of twelve paṇas shall be imposed for the purpose of revealing those who live by clandestine means.
KAZ03.20.03: “In a lawsuit concerning gambling, the victor shall be punished with the first amercement, and the defeated with the middle amercement.”
"For this man is of a childish nature; desiring victory, he cannot endure defeat," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
If one who has been defeated were to be made to pay double the fine, no one at all would approach the king.
For gamblers are generally cheats who play with fraudulent dice.
Their supervisors, being pure, shall establish *kākaṇīs* and dice.

KAZ03.20.09: For the fraudulent substitution of *kākaṇī* dice, the fine is twelve *paṇas*; for the use of false dice, the first amercement shall be imposed, along with the restoration of the winnings;
and in the case of deception (*upadhā*), the punishment for theft shall also be applied.

The superintendent shall take five percent from the winnings of those who have lost their wealth, as well as the fees for the use of the dice, the axle-weights, the ivory pieces, and the counting-sticks, along with the charges for water, land, and labor.
He shall carry out the mortgaging and the sale of goods.
And for failing to prohibit the faults of the dice, the gaming ground, or the hands, the fine shall be double.
By this, a formal challenge for a match is explained, except in the case of challenges involving knowledge or artistic skill. Thus it is said.
KAZ03.20.14 / Miscellaneous cases, however, are as follows: failing to return items that have been borrowed, purchased for use, pledged, or deposited at the proper place and time;
violating the regulations regarding the duration of stay or the permitted time for sitting in the shade;
and one who compels a Brāhmaṇa to pay a toll on a ferry.
For inviting one's immediate neighbor or next-door neighbor [to a meal], the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
For one who fails to deliver a promised object,
who violates the hand of his brother's wife, or who approaches a courtesan who is under the protection of another;
For one who purchases goods that should not be sold by others,
for one who breaks through the house [of another] to reach the sea,
and for one who causes injury to the forty families of the neighboring district, the fine shall be forty-eight paṇas.
For one who misappropriates the family dowry; for one who forcibly violates a widow living at her own will; and for one who touches an Ārya woman while being a Caṇḍāla.
For one who does not run to assist when a calamity is imminent, for one who runs without a valid reason,
or for one who feeds low-caste renunciants such as Śākyas and Ājīvakas during rites for the gods or ancestors, the fine shall be one hundred [paṇas].
For one who administers an oath or interrogation without authorization;
for one who performs work while not appointed to it;
and for one who destroys the virility of small livestock or bulls.
And for those who cause an abortion in a female slave by means of medicine, the first amercement shall be imposed.

If a father abandons his son, a husband his wife, a brother his sister, a maternal uncle his nephew, a pupil his teacher, or vice versa— provided they have not fallen from their caste— and abandons them while traveling with a caravan or in the middle of a village, he shall be punished with the first amercement; if he abandons them in a wilderness, he shall be punished with the middle amercement.
If they cause a failure for that reason, the leader shall receive the highest fine; among the others who set out together with him, the fine shall be half.

For one who binds, causes to be bound, or releases from bondage a person who should not be imprisoned, or who binds or causes to be bound a minor who has not attained legal capacity, the fine shall be one thousand [paṇas].
A specific punishment must be imposed according to the specific nature of the offender's transgression.

A pilgrim, an ascetic, one who is diseased, one exhausted by hunger, thirst, or travel, one who has entered a foreign territory, one afflicted by punishment, and one who possesses nothing—these are to be shown favor.
The judges shall carry out the legal affairs of gods, Brahmins, ascetics, women, children, the elderly, the diseased, and the helpless who do not have anyone to represent them;
nor shall they delay these matters by pretexts regarding place, time, or enjoyment.
Men are to be honored on account of their excellence in learning, intellect, prowess, lineage, and deeds.
Thus, those established in dharma, perceiving without deception, should carry out their duties; being impartial toward all conditions, they shall be trustworthy and beloved by the world.
(Suppression of Criminals)
(Supervision of artisans) KAZ04.1.01: Three ministers each shall act as supervisors to carry out the eradication of thorns (the suppression of criminals).

KAZ04.1.02: Those who are capable of providing remedies for losses, artisans, teachers, depositors, and artisans using their own capital may receive deposits, provided they are authorized by their respective guilds.
In the event of misfortune, the guild shall share the deposit.
They shall perform the work as specified regarding place, time, and nature;
however, if no place or time is specified, they may perform it under the pretext of the work itself.
If there is a delay in the time [of payment], the wages shall be reduced by one-quarter, and the fine shall be double that amount.
Except in cases of negligence or misfortune, they shall make good whatever has been lost or destroyed.
If one performs a task otherwise than prescribed, there shall be forfeiture of wages and a fine twice that amount.
Weavers shall increase the thread by ten or eleven [parts].
In the case of cutting down a growth, the fine shall be double the amount of the cut.
The price of the thread is the wages for weaving; for linen and silk fabrics, it is one and a half times the value of the thread,
while for leaf-fiber, wool, blankets, and fine muslin, it is double.
If the measure is deficient, the wages shall be reduced by one-quarter or one-half, and the fine shall be double that amount;
if the scale is deficient, the fine shall be four times the deficiency; and in the case of substituting the measuring cord, the fine shall be double the value of the goods.
By this, the weaving of double-cloth is explained.
For one *tulā* of wool, the deduction for beating and the deduction for clipping the fibers shall each be five *palas*.
Washermen shall wash clothes on wooden boards or smooth stone slabs.
In other cases, those who wash clothes shall pay a fine of six paṇas for any damage to the garments.
Those wearing garments other than those marked with the mallet-sign shall pay a fine of three paṇas.
In cases of selling, letting on lease, or pledging another's garment, the fine shall be twelve paṇas;
in the case of exchanging it, the fine shall be twice its value, and the garment must be returned.
They shall provide [the cloth] that is as white as a flower bud, pure as a stone slab, the color of washed thread, or polished white, for a period of one night or more.
A garment that is light-colored fades after five nights; a blue one, after six nights;
and a cloth dyed with flowers, lac, or madder—which requires extensive processing and careful maintenance—is of superior quality and lasts for seven nights.
Beyond that point, they shall suffer a reduction in their wages.
In disputes arising from passion, experts who are trustworthy should determine the compensation.
For those of the highest quality, the wage is one paṇa; for those of middle quality, half a paṇa;
for those of inferior quality, a quarter paṇa.
For coarse [cloths], the fine is one *māṣaka* or two *māṣakas*;
for dyed [cloths], it is double that amount.
In the first washing, there is a loss of one-fourth; in the second, a loss of one-fifth.
By this, the subsequent [case] is explained.
Weavers and dyers are explained by the same rules as washermen.

For goldsmiths who purchase silver or gold from the hand of an impure person without declaring its true nature: if it is of the same quality as what was received, the fine is twelve paṇas; if it is of a different quality, the fine is twenty-four paṇas;
if purchased from the hand of a thief, the fine is forty-eight paṇas.

In cases of purchasing goods while they are concealed, of defective appearance, or at an undervalued price, as well as in the case of fraud regarding manufactured goods, the punishment for theft shall be imposed.
For one who steals a *māṣaka* of gold, the fine is two hundred *paṇas*;
for one who steals a *māṣaka* of silver *dharaṇa*, the fine is twelve *paṇas*.
By this, the subsequent [case] is explained.
For one who effects an improvement in caste, an escape, or the acquisition of a [new] status, the fine is five hundred [paṇas].
KAZ04.1.31: One should recognize that when these two do not act [as required], it is a deprivation of passion.
KAZ04.1.32: One māṣaka is the wage for a dharaṇa of silver, and it is one-eighth part of a suvarṇa.
KAZ04.1.33: In case of exceptional skill, the increase in wages shall be double.
By this, the subsequent [case] is explained.
The wage for copper, round brass, bell-metal, vaikṛntaka, iron, and brass is five per cent.
A lump of copper suffers a ten-percent loss [in weight during processing].
If it is deficient by one *pala*, the fine shall be double the deficiency.
By this, the subsequent [case] is explained.
A lump of lead or tin suffers a loss of one-twentieth part.
And one *kākaṇī* shall be his wage for a *pala*.
A lump of iron from Kāla loses one-fifth of its weight.
And two kākaṇīs shall be his wage for a pala of work.
By this, the subsequent [sūtra] is explained.
For one who subverts a fixed and unalterable rate of exchange established by the superintendent of coinage, or fails to subvert one that ought to be subverted, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
KAZ04.1.45: When the commission has been cleared, the payment of the toll shall take place.
For one who lives off a single *māṣaka* from every ten *paṇas*, the fine shall be twelve *paṇas*.
By this, the subsequent [sūtra] is explained.
For one who causes counterfeit coins to be made, or accepts them, or exports them, the fine is one thousand panas; for one who deposits them in the treasury, the punishment is death.
Carakas and pāṃsudhāvakas shall receive one-third of the value of the essence; the king shall take two-thirds and the gem itself.
For the theft of gems, the highest fine shall be imposed.
In the case of reporting a mine, a jewel-mine, or a treasure-trove, the informant shall receive a sixth part,
while the hired laborer shall receive a twelfth part.
A treasure exceeding one hundred thousand [paṇas] belongs to the king.
KAZ04.1.53: If the amount is less than that, one-sixth part shall be paid as a fine.
A pure local official shall, by means of his own investigation, receive in its entirety a treasure-trove discovered to have belonged to a previous generation.
In the absence of his own instrument, the fine shall be five hundred;
in the case of taking it by stealth, the fine shall be one thousand.

KAZ04.1.56: For a physician who undertakes treatment without declaring that it may cause danger to life, the first amercement for violence shall be imposed if death occurs; if death occurs due to professional negligence, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
KAZ04.1.57: One should understand that for causing injury or impairment by striking a vital organ, the punishment is that prescribed for physical assault.
Actors and performers shall stay together in one place during the rainy season.
They should avoid granting excessive gifts to a single person and the use of excessive speech toward him.
In the event of its violation, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
KAZ04.1.61: They may freely engage in jesting by means of mockery regarding country, caste, lineage, school of thought, or sexual intercourse.
By [the rules concerning] actors, wandering performers, and mendicants are explained.
For those who should falsely declare the amount of panas [stolen] by means of an iron spike, there shall be as many lashes with a whip as the number of panas declared as punishment.
KAZ04.1.64: For the remaining types of work, the superintendent shall determine the wages for artisans based on the completion of the task.

In this manner, he should prevent thieves who go by the names of non-thieves— merchants, artisans, actors, mendicants, jugglers, and others— from oppressing the country. (KAZ04.1.65ab–66cd) (On the Supervision of Traders)
KAZ04.2.01: The superintendent of manufactories shall establish the pledge or sale of old goods that have been cleared by the payment of their respective duties.
And he shall inspect the weights, measures, and vessels to prevent fraud in the department of weights and measures (pautava).
KAZ04.2.03: In the case of a measuring vessel and a *droṇa*, a deficiency or excess of half a *pala* is not considered a fault.
For a deficiency or excess of one *pala*, the fine shall be twelve *paṇas*.
By this, the increase of the fine by one *pala* for each subsequent [offense] is explained.
In the case of a balance scale, a deficiency or excess of one *karṣa* is not considered a fault.
For a deficiency or excess of two karṣas, the fine shall be six paṇas.
By this, the increase of the fine for each subsequent *karṣa* is explained.
In the case of an *āḍhaka*, a deficiency or excess of half a *karṣa* is not considered an offense.
For a deficiency or excess of one *karṣa*, the fine shall be three *paṇas*.
By this, the increase of fines for those who exceed one *karṣa* is explained.
KAZ04.2.12: From this, one should infer the specific weights and measures for other items not mentioned here.
KAZ04.2.13: For one who buys with weights and measures that are excessive and sells with those that are deficient, the same fines shall be doubled.
For one who steals an eighth part from commodities that are counted or from the prices of goods, the fine is ninety-six *paṇas*.

KAZ04.2.15: For one who brings for sale or deposits as collateral an article made of wood, metal, or gems, or made of rope, leather, clay, thread, bark, or hair, which is of inferior quality when it should be of superior quality, the fine shall be eight times its value.

KAZ04.2.16: For one who brings for sale or pledge goods that are substantial but are actually unsubstantial, or which are of that origin but are not of that origin, or which are of good quality but are actually fraudulent, or which have been swapped with a covered container, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas if the price is low, and double the price in paṇas if the price is high.
Two hundred [paṇas] is the price for two paṇas.
By this, the increase of the fine in the event of an increase in price is explained.

KAZ04.2.18: For those who, acting in concert, cause a decline in the quality of work or the livelihood of artisans and craftsmen, or cause an obstruction to their buying and selling, the fine shall be one thousand [paṇas].
For merchants who, acting in concert, withhold merchandise or sell it at an improper price, the fine shall be one thousand panas.

KAZ04.2.20: For a weigher or a measurer who, through the deception of his hand, causes a discrepancy in weight or measure, or a discrepancy in price or quality, the fine shall be two hundred panas for an offense involving a value of one pana or more, plus an eighth part of that value.
KAZ04.2.21: By this, the increase in fines for amounts exceeding two hundred panas is explained.
KAZ04.2.22: For the adulteration of grains, oils, alkaline substances, salts, perfumes, and medicinal drugs by means of substances of similar appearance, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
Whatever they may earn from what has been assigned to them, the merchant, having calculated that which was produced during the day, shall set it aside for them.
KAZ04.2.24: That which falls between the buyer and the seller becomes the property of the one who seizes it.
With that [permission], they may, having obtained authorization, carry out the accumulation of grain and merchandise.
The Superintendent of Commerce shall confiscate the merchandise of those who have packed it otherwise than prescribed.
By means of that [measure], he should conduct transactions involving the sale of grain and merchandise for the benefit of the subjects.
After the purchase has been authorized, he shall fix a five percent profit on these domestic commodities and a ten percent profit on those from foreign lands.
KAZ04.2.29: Beyond that, for those who increase the price or cause it to rise during purchase or sale, the fine shall be five paṇas for every hundred paṇas, up to two hundred paṇas.
By this, the increase in fines resulting from an increase in price is explained.
And in the case of a joint purchase, until their share has been sold, one shall not provide another joint purchase.
And in the event of damage to their merchandise, he should grant them relief.
KAZ04.2.33: Due to the abundance of merchandise, the Superintendent of Commerce shall sell all commodities through a single outlet.
KAZ04.2.34: While those [goods] have not been sold, others shall not sell them.
They should sell those [articles] for daily wages, as a favor to the subjects.
But for commodities separated by distance or time, the expert in pricing, having calculated the outlay, the production cost of the commodity, the duty, the interest,
the rent, and other expenses, shall fix the price.
(Remedial Measures during Calamities)
KAZ04.3.01: There are eight great calamities caused by fate: fire, water, disease, famine, rats, wild beasts, snakes, and demons.
From them, he should protect the inhabited territory.
In the summer, the villagers shall perform the outdoor cooking of food,
or they may do so under the supervision of a collector of the ten roots.
The prevention of fire has been explained in the section on the appointment of city officials,
as well as in the sections on the royal palace and the king's private quarters.
On the festival days, he should cause the worship of the sacred fire to be performed with offerings, oblations, and the recitation of auspicious prayers.
During the rainy season, villages situated in low-lying areas should evacuate at the onset of the flood tide and reside elsewhere.
And they shall also take up wooden and bamboo boats.
They should cross over by means of gourds, leather bags, rafts, floats, or bamboo mats while being carried along.
For those who do not come to the rescue, the fine shall be twelve paṇas,
except in the case of those lacking a boat.
And on the festival days, he should cause the worship of the rivers to be performed.
Those who know the application of illusion or those who know the Vedas may perform a year-long rite of malevolent magic.
During a drought, one should cause worship to be performed for Śacīnātha, Gaṅgā, the mountains, and the great marshlands.
They shall counteract the danger of disease with secret remedies: physicians with medicines, or perfected ascetics (siddha-tāpasa) with rites for pacification and expiation.
By this, the procedure for causing death is explained.

He should cause the ceremonial bathing at sacred fords (*tīrthābhiṣecana*), the enlargement of great marshlands, the milking of cows in cremation grounds, the burning of headless trunks (*kabandha*), and the "Night of the Gods" (*devarātri*) to be performed.
In the event of disease or a plague among livestock, he should cause the performance of a lustration ceremony for the site and its wealth, as well as the worship of its tutelary deity.
In times of famine, the king should provide relief by supplying seed-corn and food, or by undertaking works for fortifications and irrigation through the distribution of food,
or by sharing out his own stores of food.
Or the entrustment of the region.
Or he should seek the protection of allies,
or he should carry out the policy of emaciation or evacuation.
When the crops have ripened, he should march to another territory containing people,
or take refuge in the ocean, lakes, or tanks.
Or he may establish sowings of grain, vegetables, roots, and fruits on the embankments, or engage in the capture of wild animals, cattle, birds, beasts of prey, and fish.
In the event of fear from rats, cats and mongooses shall be released.
For their capture or injury, the fine shall be twelve paṇas;
and for failing to restrain dogs, except in the case of those roaming in the forest.
One should scatter grains smeared with the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant, or those treated with secret formulas and yogic applications.
Or he may employ the "rat-tax."
Or accomplished ascetics may perform a rite for peace.
And on the festival days (parvan), he should cause the worship of mice to be performed.
By this, the remedies against the danger of locusts, birds, and insects are explained.
In the event of fear from wild beasts, one should scatter the carcasses of animals mixed with the juice of *madana*, or fill the bellies of dead animals with *madana* and *kodrava*.
Hunters or those with packs of dogs should operate using concealed snares, cages, and pitfalls.
Those equipped with shields and holding weapons in their hands shall strike at the wild beasts.
For one who does not go forth to meet [the claimant], the fine is twelve paṇas.
That same profit belongs to one who kills a predatory beast.
And on the festival days, he should cause the worship of the mountains to be performed.
By this, the methods for dealing with herds of wild animals, domestic cattle, and flocks of birds are explained.
In times of fear from snakes, those skilled in the science of *jāṅgulī* (snake-remedies) shall move about using mantras and medicinal herbs.
Or even by acting together, they may slay serpents.
Or those who know the Atharvaveda may perform rites of malevolent magic.
And on the festival days, he should cause the worship of the Nāgas to be performed.
By this, the measures for countering danger from water and living beings are explained.
In the event of fear from demons, those learned in the Atharvaveda or those skilled in the application of magic should perform rites that slay demons.
And on the festival days (parvan), he should cause the worship of the Caityas to be performed with awnings, umbrellas, canopies, hand-banners, and offerings of goats.
KAZ04.3.42: In all cases of danger, they should move about day and night with the thought, "We are moving like a sacrificial oblation."
And in all cases, he should favor those who have been wronged, just as a father would.

Therefore, accomplished ascetics who are experts in the application of *māyā* (illusion) should dwell within the king's domain, honored by the monarch and acting as a remedy against calamities sent by fate.
(Guarding against those with secret means of income)
In the section concerning the duties of the Collector-General, the protection of the inhabited territory has been explained.
We shall now describe the removal of thorns (the suppression of criminals) for that [kingdom].

KAZ04.4.03. The Collector-General shall station as secret agents (*vyañjana*) in the countryside accomplished ascetics, mendicants, wandering performers, spies, bards, magicians, actors, fortune-tellers, astrologers, soothsayers, physicians, madmen, the mute, the deaf, the dull-witted, the blind, merchants, artisans, craftsmen, actors, prostitutes, vintners, cake-sellers, sellers of cooked meat, and sellers of boiled rice.
They shall ascertain the purity and impurity of the villages and their superintendents.
And whoever therein he might suspect of living in secret, him he should cause to be spied upon by means of an agent-in-disguise.

KAZ04.4.06: An agent provocateur should say to a judge who has gained his confidence: "This relative of mine has been prosecuted; let this misfortune of his be remedied, and let this wealth be accepted."
If he should act in such a manner, being a receiver of bribes, he shall be banished.
By this, the commissioners (pradeṣṭāraḥ) are explained.
A secret agent should say to the village headman or the superintendent: “This man is a rogue who possesses abundant wealth; this is his undoing, so cause him to be seized by means of that.”
If he should act in such a manner, he shall be branded as a bribe-taker and banished.
Or, one who has been accused of a crime committed by himself may begin his defense by exposing false witnesses through the extensive nature of their well-known misconduct.
If they should act in such a manner, they shall be declared false witnesses and banished.
By this, those who cause false testimony to be heard are explained.

Or, if he should suspect someone of being an intermediary through the use of spells, magical applications, or rites performed at cremation grounds, the secret agent (sattrī) should say to him: “I desire the wife, daughter-in-law, or daughter of so-and-so;
let her desire me in return.”
"And let this matter be accepted."
If he should act in that manner, he shall be banished as a "mediator" (*saṃvadanakāraka*).
By this, those who are habitually inclined toward ritual magic and malevolent sorcery are explained.

Or, if the spy should believe that someone who is a maker, buyer, or seller of poison, or a dealer in medicinal herbs and foodstuffs, is a poisoner, he should say to him: "This man is my enemy; let his destruction be carried out, and let this wealth be accepted."
If he should do so, he shall be branded as a poisoner and banished.
By this, the practice of administering aphrodisiacs (madana-yoga) is explained.

Or, one who frequently purchases various metals, alkalis, charcoal, ashes, tongs, pincers, crucibles, molds, hammers, and furnaces; whose hands, clothes, and personal effects are smeared with soot, ash, and smoke; and who is associated with the tools of a smith—one should suspect him of being a forger of counterfeit coins.
An undercover agent, having gained his confidence through the guise of a student and by engaging in trade with him, should expose him.
One who is identified as a forger of counterfeit coins shall be banished.
By this, the one who steals gold and the dealer in counterfeit gold are explained.
But those thirteen types of persons living by secret means who have already begun acts of violence shall be banished; or,
depending on the specific nature of their offense, they may be made to pay a fine as an atonement.
After the employment of the secret agents (*sattrin*), those who have attained the status of spies (*siddhavyañjana*) should entice young men with the knowledge of youth,
obstructors with mantras for inducing sleep, invisibility, and opening doors,
and adulterers with mantras for summoning [their partners].

KAZ04.5.02. When they have been thus incited, he shall take a large band of them at night, go toward another village that has been prepared with artificial men and women, and say: "Let the power of our knowledge be seen right here;
the other village is difficult to reach."
Then, having opened the doors with the mantra for opening the doors, they should say, "Enter."
With the *antar-dhāna* mantra, they should cause the young students to pass through the midst of the watchmen while they are awake.
Having put the guards to sleep with a lulling mantra, they should cause them to be moved about by young men lying down.
Using the greeting-mantra, those disguised as wives should exchange friendly greetings with the young men of the enemy.
For those who have acquired knowledge and power, one should prescribe preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth for the purpose of identification.
Or, they may cause work to be performed in houses where the property has been marked with identifying signs.
Or, having entered [the enemy's territory], they should cause [the enemy] to be captured at a single location.
In cases of transactions involving goods marked with identifying signs, or in sales and mortgages, they should cause those intoxicated by liquor or drugs to be apprehended.
Once they have been apprehended, one should interrogate them regarding their prior criminal records and their accomplices.
Or, spies disguised as old-time thieves, having infiltrated the bandits, should cause them to perform the same kind of work and cause it to be captured.
The Collector-General shall show the captured individuals to the citizens and country-folk, saying: "The King studies the science of catching thieves;
by his instruction these thieves have been caught, and I shall catch many more."
"You must restrain your own kinsmen who practice evil deeds."

And whoever among them he should discover, through the instruction of his spies, to be a thief of the sacrificial pins, the goad, or other such items, him he should point out to those [spies], saying, "This is the power of the king."

Ancient thieves, cowherds, hunters, and dog-keepers, having infiltrated forest-thieves and forest-dwellers, should incite them against caravans, herds, and villages by means of abundant counterfeit gold, base metals, and goods.
When an attack is launched, they should cause [the enemy] to be killed by means of concealed forces,
or by means of food for the journey mixed with *madana* poison.

They should cause those who have carried loads of stolen property to be apprehended when they are traveling long distances and exhausted, or while they are sleeping at festive gatherings, or when they are intoxicated by drugs or liquor.
And having apprehended them as previously described, the Collector-General shall cause them to be interrogated,
proclaiming the king’s omniscience among the inhabitants of the realm.
(Arrest on Suspicion)
After the completion of the operation, the apprehension of the suspect occurs through the possession of the stolen article and the indications of the act. (KAZ 04.6.01)
One whose family's inheritance is exhausted, who receives a meager livelihood, and who provides false accounts regarding his country, caste, lineage, name, and occupation;
One who conceals his livelihood and activities,
who is addicted to meat, liquor, various foods, perfumes, garlands, clothing, and ornaments,
and who incurs excessive expenditure;
One who is addicted to prostitutes, gambling, and taverns;
one who frequently travels abroad; and one whose place of residence is unknown.
One who frequents solitary forests, groves, or remote places at improper times;
one who assembles many counselors in a secluded place or where there is a lure of wealth;
and one who causes secret treatment to be administered for fresh wounds or sores.
One who is constantly inside the house, one who seeks to gain [wealth], and one who is devoted to his beloved—
One who frequently inquires about the property, women, or houses of others; one who associates with those of reprehensible conduct, scriptures, or implements;
and one who wanders at night in the shadows of concealed walls—[these are persons to be watched].
One who sells deformed goods at an improper place or time, one harboring a sense of enmity, or one of low occupation or birth—
One who conceals his true appearance,
one who does not wear the insignia of an ascetic though he possesses them, or one who wears the insignia of an ascetic but follows a different mode of conduct; KAZ04.6.02g.
One who has a history of past offenses,
who is pointed out by his own past deeds,
who hides himself upon seeing a city magistrate or a high official, who sits unable to breathe, who is agitated, and whose voice and facial complexion are parched and altered—

One should suspect anyone who causes terror by the presence of men with weapons in hand, or who is one of those who are violent, thieves, misappropriators of treasure-troves or deposits, practitioners of magic for others, or those who live by secret means.
Thus ends the apprehension of suspicion.
KAZ04.6.03: Regarding the seizure by appearance, however—one who has lost or had stolen property that is no longer present shall report it to those who deal in goods of that kind.
If, having received that which was reported, they should conceal it, they shall incur the guilt of being accomplices;
if they were unaware, they shall be released by the forfeiture of that property.
And they shall not carry out the mortgaging or sale of old articles without first reporting them to the superintendent of the establishment.
If that which has been reported should be found, he shall question the person apprehended on the basis of his appearance regarding the source of the goods, asking: "From whom did you obtain this?"
If he should say, "It was obtained as an inheritance, received from such-and-such a person, purchased, made over, or recovered from a pledge;
this is its place and time of acquisition."
"This is its value, its measure, its characteristic, and its price"—
if one reflects thus, one will be liberated in the meditative concentration of traditional scripture (āgama-samādhi).
If the owner of the lost property should recognize it, one should know that the object belongs to him who has had prior and long-term possession of it, or whose location is pure.

For even among quadrupeds and bipeds there exists a commonality of form and gender; how much more so, then, among articles of base metal, ornaments, and vessels produced from the same source, material, and maker?

If he should say, "This was borrowed, hired, deposited as a pledge, placed in trust, or given for the purpose of business on behalf of such-and-such a person," he shall be acquitted by proving the source of that claim.
KAZ04.6.12: Or, he may offer a defense by saying, "It is not so.

If his character is challenged, he should corroborate the reason for the other's gift, the reason for his own acceptance, or the circumstantial evidence, by means of the giver, the one who caused the gift, the recorder, the receiver, the witnesses, or the overhearers.
One who has been found after being abandoned, lost, or escaped shall be cleared of suspicion by means of evidence regarding the place, time, and circumstances of his recovery.
If it is impure, he shall pay both that [item] and a fine of the same amount.
Otherwise, he shall incur the punishment for theft.
Thus ends the apprehension of physical form (rūpābhigraha).
As for the apprehension of action (karmābhigraha), it consists of: entering or exiting a plundered house by means other than the door;
or the breaking open of a door by means of a joint or a bolt.
The piercing of the lattice-windows, air-ventilation holes, and eaves of the upper chamber;
the piercing of the wall for ascending and descending;
or the method of digging a tunnel for the purpose of depositing or seizing hidden goods.
One should know that which is obtainable through instruction, involving internal cutting, digging out, and rubbing, as being "internally produced."
In the opposite case, it is caused by external factors;
when both conditions are present, it is caused by both.
In the case of an internal offense, [the king shall punish] a man who is addicted to vice, has cruel associates, or is in contact with the implements of a thief;
or a woman from a poor family, or one who is attached to another; or a servant of such conduct.
Excessive sleep, exhaustion from drowsiness,
agitation, and a parched, broken voice and complexion.
One who is unstable,
excessively talkative, and whose limbs are agitated by climbing high; KAZ04.6.18c.
With body and clothing torn, rubbed, pierced, and split;
with hands and feet scarred and calloused;
with hair and nails covered in dust, or with hair and nails shorn and broken. (KAZ 4.6.18d)
One should examine him who has properly bathed and been anointed, whose limbs have been rubbed with oil, or whose hands and feet have just been washed;

one should observe whether his footprints leave identical impressions in dusty or muddy places, and whether there is no change in his garlands, the scent of his wine, his clothing, his ornaments, his ointments, or his perspiration during his entry and exit.
One should recognize him as either a thief or an adulterer.

The Superintendent of the Outskirts, together with the Gopas and Sthānikas, shall conduct the search for thieves in the external regions; likewise, the City Prefect shall do so within the fort, using the specified grounds for investigation.
(Inquest of sudden deaths)
One should examine a recently deceased person who has been anointed with oil.

One should recognize as killed by suffocation (pīṭana) one whose urine and feces have been discharged, whose internal organs and skin are distended with wind, whose hands and feet are swollen, whose eyes are closed, whose throat is choked with secretions, and whose breathing is obstructed.
One should recognize him as killed by hanging if his arms and thighs are found contracted.
One should recognize that a prisoner has been removed from custody when his hands, feet, and belly are swollen, his eyes have disappeared, and his navel is protruding.
One should recognize a person as killed by water if their anus and eyes are motionless, the tongue is bitten, and the abdomen is distended.
One should recognize a person as killed by sticks or stones if they are drenched in blood and have broken or mangled limbs.
One should recognize a person whose limbs are broken, split, or torn as being "overthrown" (avakṣipta).
One should recognize a person killed by poison by their hands, feet, teeth, and nails being dark-brown; their flesh, hair, and skin being loose; and their mouth smeared with foam.
One should recognize that very person as killed by a snake or an insect if there is a bite mark accompanied by blood.
One should recognize him as killed by the application of *madana* (emetic poison) if his clothes and limbs are disheveled and he has vomited excessively or purged.

Having killed one who has been killed for any one of these reasons, or having killed him out of fear of punishment, one should know him as "one whose neck was strangled or cut" (*udbaddhanikṛttakaṇṭha*).
In the case of one killed by poison, one should examine the remains of the food with birds.
One should know that poison has been administered when, after being extracted from the heart and thrown into the fire, it makes a crackling sound (*ciṭiciṭāyat*) and takes on the color of a rainbow;
or when one sees the heart of the victim burnt while the rest remains unburnt.
He should seek out his attendants who have become insolent through verbal or physical abuse;
or women afflicted by suffering, or those attached to another man; or a kinsman who covets his inheritance, livelihood, or women.
One should examine that very same case of a person who has been killed and then hanged.
Or, he should investigate the improper mistreatment of one who has hanged himself.

KAZ04.7.17: For all [of these], the grounds for anger are either the fault regarding the inheritance of women, rivalry in work, hatred toward an adversary, a gathering at a marketplace, or any one of the points of dispute. KAZ04.7.18: Killing caused by anger [is the offense].

One should investigate the killing of a person who has been slain by men commanded by himself, or by thieves for the sake of wealth, or by enemies of others due to a resemblance [to the victim], by questioning those nearby.
He against whom he was summoned, with whom he stood together, with whom he set out, or with whom he was brought to the battlefield—him he should interrogate.

And he should question those who were in his immediate vicinity on the site where he was killed, one by one: "By whom was he brought here, or by whom was he killed? Who saw him with a weapon, concealing it, or in a state of agitation?"
He should question them in accordance with what they say.

Upon seeing the personal effects, belongings, clothing, attire, or ornaments belonging to the body of a person who has died without heirs, the officials dealing with such property [shall investigate].
He should inquire into his associations, his place of residence, the reason for his stay, his occupation, and his conduct; thereafter, he should carry out the search.
Or he who, under the sway of lust or anger, causes his own death by means of a rope, a weapon, or poison; or a woman, deluded by sin, brings about her own destruction.
A Caṇḍāla shall drag them away by means of a rope onto the royal highway;
for them there is no funeral rite, nor likewise any rites for their relatives.
But whichever relative of theirs performs the ritual procedures for the funeral rites,
he shall later follow their destiny or be released from his own kin.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for one year;
this applies to officiating at sacrifices for them, teaching them, or forming a matrimonial alliance with them— and also to anyone else who associates with such persons in those same ways.

KAZ04.8.01: In the presence of the victim of the theft, the interrogator shall examine the accused regarding the external and internal witnesses, as well as his country, caste, lineage, name, occupation, property, associates, and residence.
And he should reconcile them by means of pretexts.
Then, one should inquire about the movements of the previous day and the location of the night's encampment, starting from the time of capture.
If he can provide proof of his escape, he shall be cleared;
otherwise, he shall undergo the prescribed punishment.

After three nights have passed, a person suspected [of being a spy] may not be apprehended due to the absence of grounds for interrogation, except in the case of the discovery of incriminating implements.
For one who falsely accuses a non-thief of being a thief, the punishment shall be equal to that for a thief;
and the same applies to one who conceals a thief.
One who has been accused by the core (the king) but is pointed out as being motivated by enmity or hatred shall be considered pure.
For one who causes a pure person to be exiled, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
When a charge has been substantiated, he shall cause the instruments, the confederates, the helpers, the accomplices, and the attendants to be produced.
And one should reconcile the work with the distribution of the place, the materials taken, and the division of shares.
If, in the absence of these motives, one speaks incoherently, he should be known as a non-thief.

For it is observed that even one who is not a thief may be seized on a path frequented by thieves due to a chance encounter, by virtue of his resemblance in dress, weapons, or equipment to a thief, or by the possession of a thief’s goods;
or as in the case of Aṇīmāṇḍavya, who, out of fear of the pain of torture, though not a thief, said, "I am a thief."
Therefore, one should restrict the completion of the ritual action.

KAZ04.8.14: One should not compel a child, an elderly person, one who is ill, intoxicated, insane, exhausted by hunger, thirst, or travel, one who has overeaten, one who has eaten uncooked food, or one who is weak to perform labor.
KAZ04.8.15: One should cause them to be diverted by those of similar character, by prostitutes, by storytellers, by those providing shelter, and by those providing food.
In this manner he should outwit [the enemy], just as it was explained in the section on the misappropriation of deposits.
One may compel a person who has committed an offense to perform labor,
but never a woman who is pregnant or one who has given birth within the past month.
But for a woman, the penalty is half the fine,
or she may be subjected to interrogation.
A Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas and ascetic may accept the property of a Sattrin.
In the case of its violation, the highest fine shall be imposed on both the perpetrator and the instigator, by means of forced labor and physical torture.
KAZ04.8.21: The fourfold set of judicial punishments consists of six types of flogging with a rod, seven strokes with a whip,
and two types of suspension from office.
And a water pipe.
For those who commit further evil deeds, there shall be nine strokes with a cane,
twelve lashes with a whip, and two wrappings of the thighs [with leather].
Twenty *naktamāla* creepers,
thirty-two *tala* trees,
and two *vṛścikabandha* knots.
And there are two types of hanging: [the sin] of one who has a needle in his hand,
and the burning of a single joint of a finger by one who has drunk gruel.
For one who has drunk an emollient [oil], there is heating for one day,
and sleeping on a bed of the tips of *balbaja* grass during the cold nights.
Thus ends the eighteenfold set of duties.
KAZ04.8.24: He shall cause the equipment, the size, the striking weapon, the support, and the grip of that [missile] to be obtained from a workshop.
Every day, he should cause each person to perform one task.

Having promised to restore property previously misappropriated, one who then conceals it; or one caught in the act or by physical evidence while stealing goods seen in a certain place; or one who embezzles the royal treasury; or one condemned to death by the king’s command—such a person shall be made to perform labor either collectively, individually, or repeatedly, according to the king’s decree.
Even in the case of all offenses, a Brāhmaṇa must not be subjected to physical punishment.
He shall have a mark branded upon his forehead for the purpose of identifying him in legal proceedings:
a dog for theft,
and a headless trunk for homicide.
For violating the bed of the Guru, a female organ;
for drinking liquor, a sign of a tavern.
Having publicly proclaimed a Brāhmaṇa who has committed a sinful act and having branded him with a scar,
the king shall banish him from the realm or settle him in mines.
(Supervision of officials of all departments)
KAZ04.9.01: The collectors and supervisors shall first carry out the regulation of the superintendents and the subordinate officials of the superintendents.
For one who steals valuable timber or precious gems from mines or manufactories, the punishment is execution by burning.
KAZ04.9.03: For stealing articles of small value or tools from those who deal in articles of small value, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
KAZ04.9.04: For one who steals royal merchandise from the marketplaces, if its value is above one *māṣa* but not reaching one *pāda*, the fine is twelve *paṇas*;
if up to two *pādas*, the fine is twenty-four *paṇas*;
if up to three *pādas*, the fine is thirty-six *paṇas*.
"Up to a value of eight paṇas" refers to forty-eight paṇas;
"up to a value of two paṇas" refers to the first amercement (pūrva-sāhasa);
"up to a value of four paṇas" refers to the middle amercement (madhyama).
For theft up to a value of eight paṇas, the highest fine is prescribed; for theft up to a value of ten paṇas, the punishment is death.

KAZ04.9.05: For the theft of raw materials, vessels, implements, or weapons from the storehouse, the merchandise warehouse, the forest produce warehouse, or the armory, these same fines apply when the value of the items stolen is half that [of those specified in the preceding rule].
KAZ04.9.06: For those who steal from the treasury, the storehouse, the armory, or the workshop, the fines shall be double those prescribed for items of one-fourth value.
For the violent assault of thieves, the punishment is various forms of execution.
Thus it has been explained regarding the royal possessions.

But regarding outsiders: for one who steals base metals, vessels, or utensils—concealed during the day—from fields, threshing floors, houses, or marketplaces, if the value is above one *māṣa* and up to one *pāda*, the fine is three *paṇas*.
Or, if the theft is committed by smearing it with a coating of cow-dung or by concealing it under a public announcement, if the value is up to two *pādas*, the fine is six *paṇas*.
Or, having smeared it with cow-dung ashes, it shall be publicly proclaimed;
for up to three-quarters of its value, the fine is nine paṇas, or, having smeared it with cow-dung ashes, it shall be publicly proclaimed.
For an offense involving a rim made of a shallow dish (*śarāva-mekhalā*), up to a value of twelve *paṇas*, the fine is twelve *paṇas*;
for shaving the head or banishing [the offender], up to a value of two *paṇas*, the fine is twenty-four *paṇas*;

for banishing one who has been shaved with a fragment of brick, up to a value of four *paṇas*, the fine is thirty-six *paṇas*; [and] up to a value of five *paṇas*... [the fine is forty-eight *paṇas*].

Thus, for a value of up to forty-eight paṇas, the first amercement (pūrva-sāhasa) is the punishment; for a value up to twenty paṇas, the fine is two hundred; for a value up to thirty paṇas, five hundred; for a value up to forty paṇas, the middle amercement (sāhasra); and for a value up to fifty paṇas, the punishment is death.
KAZ04.9.10: For one who forcibly steals goods that have been stored overnight, whether by day or by night, these same fines apply to items worth half the original value.
KAZ04.9.11: For one who forcibly carries off property, whether by day or by night, while armed, these same fines shall be doubled when the value of the items is four times the [standard] share.

For those who forge royal edicts or seals— whether they be householders, superintendents, chiefs, or masters— the punishments shall be death in the first, middle, or highest degree, or as the offense may warrant.
If a judge threatens, reviles, drives away, or intimidates a person who is litigating, he shall first impose upon him the fine for physical assault;
if the offense involves verbal abuse, the fine shall be double.
He does not question what should be questioned, he questions what should not be questioned,
or having questioned, he dismisses [the matter].
He instructs, he reminds,
or he gives first.
Thus, he should impose upon him the middle fine for violence.
He does not inquire about a place that ought to be granted, he inquires about a place that ought not to be granted,
and he carries out a matter by means of an improper place.
He carries him away by means of deception;
he diverts the weary one through procrastination;
and he causes one who has entered upon the right path to deviate from his speech.
If he provides assistance through his intellect to witnesses,
or takes up again a case that has already been decided and instructed,
the king shall impose upon him the highest fine for violence.
In the case of a repeated offense, the punishment shall be double and include removal from his position.
If the scribe does not write what has been told, writes what has not been told, or writes down what was wrongly stated;
If he cites a well-spoken verse or speculates on the origin of its meaning,
one should first inflict upon him the punishment for rashness.
Or according to the offense.
If a judge or a commissioner imposes a monetary fine on one who is exempt from punishment, the king shall impose on him a fine double the amount of that improper imposition,
or eight times the difference between the lesser and greater fines.
If one inflicts corporal punishment, he shall undergo corporal punishment himself,
or pay double the amount of the ransom.
Or, whoever destroys an existing fact or fabricates a non-existent fact shall pay a fine eight times that amount.

KAZ04.9.21: In the judicial department, regarding confinement in a guard-house or a prison, for the acts of obstructing or binding someone while they are lying down, sitting, eating, or moving about for defecation, fines of three panas each incrementally higher shall be imposed upon both the perpetrator and the instigator.
For one who releases or causes to escape an accused person from prison, the middle amercement shall be imposed,
as well as the payment of the legal claim;
for one who does so from a place of confinement, the forfeiture of all property and the death penalty shall be imposed.
KAZ04.9.23: For the superintendent of the prison who causes a person under detention to wander without reporting it, the fine is twenty-four paṇas;
for one who makes him perform labor, the fine is double that;
and for one who moves him to another location or withholds his food and drink, the fine is ninety-six paṇas.
For one who causes suffering or extorts by means of a bribe, the middle amercement shall be imposed; for one who kills, the highest amercement.

For one who has sexual intercourse with a female slave who is under protection, or with a woman held in confinement, the first amercement shall be imposed; for one who has intercourse with the wife of a thief or a bandit, the middle amercement; and for one who has intercourse with a noblewoman held in confinement, the highest amercement.
Or, he may be executed right there while he is under siege.
One should know that the same applies when a noble woman has been seized by force;
in the case of a slave woman, the first amercement shall be the punishment.
For one who escapes from a prison without breaking through the walls, the middle amercement shall be imposed;
for one who escapes by breaking through the walls, the penalty is death; and for one who escapes from a house of confinement, the penalty is death and the confiscation of all property.
In this manner, the king should first purify those who move about for their own interests by means of punishment;
and once purified, they in turn shall purify the citizens and country-dwellers through disciplinary measures.

For those who destroy a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), break a knot, or carry [goods] on their shoulders, the punishment for the first offense is the cutting off of a finger or a fine of fifty-four *paṇas*;
for the second, the cutting off of a hand or a fine of one hundred *paṇas*; and for the third, the amputation of the right hand or a fine of four hundred *paṇas*.
In the fourth case, execution may be carried out according to one's will.

In cases of stealing or injuring cocks, mongooses, cats, dogs, or pigs, when their value is less than twenty-five panas, the fine shall be fifty-four panas, or the cutting off of the tip of the nose; for Caṇḍālas and forest-dwellers, the fines shall be half of these amounts.

For the seizure of wild animals, domestic cattle, birds, beasts of prey, or fish that have been caught in snares, nets, traps, or pits, the fine shall be equal to the value of the animal and the cost of the snare or trap.
KAZ04.10.04: For the theft of game-animals or forest produce from a game-preserve or a forest, the punishment shall be one-eighth of the value.
In the case of theft or injury to images, monasteries, wild animals, or birds, the fine shall be double.
KAZ04.10.06: For artisans, craftsmen, actors, and ascetics, the fine for stealing small articles is one hundred [paṇas];
for stealing large articles, it is two hundred;
and likewise for stealing agricultural implements.

KAZ04.10.07: For one who enters a fort without authorization, or who carries off a deposit through a breach in the rampart while escaping, the death penalty shall be carried out by the commander (*kāṇḍarāvadha*), or a fine of two hundred [*paṇas*] shall be imposed.
For one who steals a boat equipped with wheels or a small animal, there shall be the amputation of one foot,
or a fine of three hundred [paṇas].
Those who employ fraudulent kārṣāpaṇas, false dice, crooked pieces, or cheat with the hand by using secret signals shall have one hand cut off,
or be fined four hundred paṇas.

KAZ04.10.10: For the act of assisting a thief or an adulterer, the punishment for a woman who has been apprehended is the cutting off of her ears and nose, or a fine of five hundred panas; for a man, the punishment is double.

For one who steals a large animal, a male slave, or a female slave, or sells the funeral goods of a deceased person, the punishment is the same as for the killing of a human being, or a fine of six hundred panas.

KAZ04.10.12: For those of the highest castes and for elders, in the case of overstepping their hands or feet, or for climbing onto a royal carriage, vehicle, or similar object, there shall be the amputation of one hand and one foot, or a fine of seven hundred [paṇas].

For a Śūdra who speaks like a Brāhmaṇa, who misappropriates the property of the gods, who incites hatred toward the king, or who pierces both eyes, the punishment shall be blindness induced by a medicinal ointment,
or a fine of eight hundred [paṇas].
For one who releases a thief or an adulterer; for one who writes a royal edict as deficient or excessive;

for one who abducts a maiden or a female slave along with her gold; for one who engages in fraudulent transactions; and for one who sells meat that is unfit for consumption—the punishment is the amputation of the left hand and two feet, or a fine of nine hundred [paṇas].
For the sale of human flesh, the punishment is death.
For those who steal images of deities or animals, humans, fields, houses, gold, bullion, gems, or grain, the highest fine shall be imposed,
or they shall be put to death without qualification.
Having carefully considered the person involved, the offense, the motive, its gravity or lightness, the consequences, the immediate circumstances, as well as the place and the time; KAZ04.10.17ab–cd.

The Pradeṣṭṛ, standing as an intermediary between the king and the constituent elements of the state, shall determine the severity— whether highest, lowest, or middling— of the infliction of punishment in judicial proceedings. (Law of Capital Punishment)
KAZ04.11.01: For one who kills a man in a quarrel, the punishment shall be varied and severe.

KAZ04.11.02: If death occurs within seven nights, the purification is as prescribed for murder; if within a fortnight, the highest amercement; if at the end of a month, five hundred panas, plus the expenses for recovery.
For one who strikes with a weapon, the highest fine shall be imposed.
For killing with the hand out of intoxication, the fine is two hundred; for doing so out of delusion, it is two hundred.
For killing, the punishment is death.

For one who causes an abortion by means of physical violence, the highest fine shall be imposed; for administering medicine, the middle fine; and for causing it through harassment, the first amercement.

KAZ04.11.07: Those who forcibly kill women or men, those who abduct women, those who arrest others, those who issue proclamations [of rebellion], those who attack by surprise, those who bore tunnels, those who obstruct roads or houses, those who injure the king’s elephants, horses, or chariots, or thieves—these they shall impale upon stakes.
And whoever should burn them or remove them shall receive that same punishment, or the highest amercement.

KAZ04.11.09: For those who provide food, clothing, equipment, fire, mantras, or service to murderers and thieves, the highest punishment shall be imposed; however, there shall be a mere reprimand if it was done unknowingly.
In the case of violent criminals or thieves, one should release their children and wives without taking security; one should take them with security.

One who lusts after the kingdom, one who violates the inner apartments, one who incites forest tribes or enemies, or one who provokes rebellion within the fort, the countryside, or the army, shall be executed by having his head and hands set on fire as lamps.
He shall cause that Brāhmaṇa to enter into darkness.
Or, one who kills his mother, father, son, brother, teacher, or an ascetic, he shall cause to be executed by having his skin and head set on fire.
For reviling them, the tongue shall be cut off; for biting their limbs, he shall be deprived of those same limbs.
In the case of killing a man unintentionally, and in the theft of herds of cattle, there shall be execution by simple death.
And one should know that a herd consists of at least ten animals.

For one who breaks a dam that holds back water, there shall be drowning in those very waters; for a dam that does not hold water, the highest amercement; and for one that is broken or abandoned, the middle amercement.

A man who administers poison and a woman who kills a man shall be cast into water, provided she is not pregnant; if she is pregnant, she shall be released once she has given birth after at least one month.
One who kills her husband, her teacher, or her offspring, or who administers poison or fire, or who breaks into a breach in a wall, shall be torn apart by oxen.
One shall cause by fire the burning of pasture lands, fields, threshing floors, houses, goods, elephant forests, and so forth, [if they have been set on fire].
KAZ04.11.21: One shall have the tongue torn out of those who revile the king, those who divulge secret counsel, those who engage in harmful activities, and those who lick the kitchen of a Brāhmaṇa.
One who steals weapons or armor should be executed with arrows, provided he is not himself armed.
For a professional soldier, the highest [fine] applies.
One who causes injury to the penis or the scrotum shall have that very part cut off.
KAZ04.11.25: In the case of injury to the tongue or the nose, the punishment is death by the pincers.
KAZ04.11.26ab: These punishments for those who commit offenses against the high-minded are prescribed in the treatises as afflictive penalties.
KAZ04.11.26cd: However, for those who have committed sins without such affliction, righteous execution is declared to be the pure form of punishment.
(Regarding the violation of maidens)
For one who marries a woman of the same caste who has not yet attained her marriageable age, there shall be the punishment of hand-cutting or a fine of four hundred [paṇas].
If she dies, there shall be the penalty for murder.
For one who causes a woman who has already obtained fruit [of her labor] to perform [the act], there shall be the amputation of the middle and index fingers,
or a fine of two hundred panas.
And he shall pay the father's share that has been withheld.
