And one shall not obtain the fulfillment of one's desires with respect to a woman who is unwilling.
If she is willing, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas; for the woman, however, the fine shall be half.
If a woman has been detained by another's dowry, there shall be the punishment of the hand,
or a fine of four hundred [paṇas],
and the payment of the dowry.
If a man has not obtained a wife after seven menstrual periods have passed since her first menses, he may take another woman of his own accord,
provided he does not pay a reduced bride-price to the father.
KAZ04.12.09: One who obstructs the [proper] season departs from his lordship.
For a woman who has given birth three times and whose menses have ceased, it is no fault to approach her even if she is not his equal; beyond that, however, it is a fault even if she is not adorned.
In the case of taking paternal property, one shall be liable for theft.
If one acquires [property] for another while intending it for someone else, the fine shall be two hundred [paṇas].
And he shall not obtain his desire with a woman who is unwilling.
If one shows one girl and gives another instead, the fine shall be one hundred panas if the substitute is of equal status,
and double that amount if she is of inferior status.
KAZ04.12.15: If a girl who is not yet a maiden has been deflowered, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas;
and he shall also reimburse the costs of the bride-price and the wedding expenses.
Having remained [in that state], he shall subsequently pay double the amount produced by it.
In the case of using the blood of another as a pretext, the fine shall be two hundred panas,
as it shall also be for a man who makes a false accusation.
And he shall suffer loss regarding the customs duties and the performance of his work.
And he shall not obtain his desire with a woman who is unwilling.
A woman who has been approached by a man against her will, but consents when they are of equal status, shall pay a fine of twelve paṇas; if she is the instigator, she shall pay double.
In the case of a woman who is unwilling, the punishment shall be one hundred [paṇas] for the sake of her own gratification,
as well as the payment of the nuptial fee (śulka).
If she has been employed by her own accord, she shall enter into service as a royal slave.
KAZ04.12.23: In the case of a false accusation regarding a matter concerning those outside the village, the fine shall be double that prescribed for the standard offense.
For one who abducts a maiden by force, the fine is two hundred [paṇas]; if she is accompanied by gold, it is the highest amercement.
KAZ04.12.25: For many abductors of maidens, the punishments shall be applied individually as previously stated.
For one who makes the daughter of a courtesan a [common] prostitute, the fine is fifty-four paṇas;
the bride-price shall be the mother’s share multiplied sixteenfold.
For one who makes the daughter of a male or female slave a non-slave, the fine is twenty-four paṇas, as well as the payment of the bride-price and the marriage-fee.
For one who treats a female slave as if she were a free woman in accordance with her ransom price, the fine is twelve paṇas, and she must be given clothing and a marriage-portion.
If one provides assistance or an opportunity [for the offense], the punishment shall be equal to that of the perpetrator.
KAZ04.12.30: If a woman whose husband is away from home commits misconduct, her husband’s kinsman or his agent shall apprehend her.
Once she has been taken in marriage, she shall desire her husband.
If the husband forgives her, both [the property and the woman] shall be released.
If a woman is intolerant, her ears and nose shall be cut off, and her paramour shall suffer the death penalty.
For one who accuses a paramour of being a thief, the fine is five hundred panas;
for one who releases him by paying gold, the fine is eight times that amount.
Adultery consists of seizing each other by the hair,
or from the observation of the marks of sexual enjoyment on the body, or from those born of such acts.
Or [it may be obtained] from the word of a woman.

Having rescued another's wife who has been carried off by a foreign army or by forest-dwellers, or who has been swept away by a flood, or abandoned in the forests or during a famine, or left behind upon the death of her husband, he may enjoy her as previously agreed.
One should give back a wife who is distinguished by her caste, who is unwilling, and who has children, upon payment of a ransom.
Having rescued [the woman] from the hands of thieves, from the current of a river, from famine, or from regional upheaval;
A man may enjoy the wife of others as previously agreed upon,
but he must not do so with one who has been released by royal authority or by her own kinsmen.
One should not take a woman who is of the highest caste, nor one who is unwilling, nor one who already has children;
however, such a woman may be taken away by paying a suitable ransom.
(Punishments for Transgressions)
For one who causes a Brāhmaṇa to drink or eat that which is unfit to be drunk or eaten, the highest fine shall be imposed;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle fine;
and for a Vaiśya, the first amercement.
For a Śūdra, the fine shall be fifty-four paṇas.
Those who seize property for themselves shall be deprived of their offices.
KAZ04.13.03: For entering another's house during the day, the first amercement shall be imposed; at night, the middle amercement.
For one who enters [the royal palace] with a weapon, whether by day or by night, the highest punishment shall be imposed.
Beggars, merchants, those who are intoxicated or insane, and those who have entered by force or during an emergency— even if they are very close to the gate— are exempt from punishment,
except in cases where they have been specifically forbidden.
For one who climbs onto the roof of his own house after midnight, the first amercement shall be the punishment; for one who climbs onto the roof of another's house, the middle amercement;
and the same for those who break into village groves or garden enclosures.
In villages, merchants whose goods have been inspected shall reside within the interior.
The village headman shall restore what has been stolen or carried off by them, provided it has not yet left the village at night.
Or, in the case of anything stolen or carried off in other villages, the superintendent of pasture lands shall make restitution.
For uncultivated lands, the rope-holder shall be held responsible for theft.
Even so, they shall provide for the investigation of those who are unprotected by means of a boundary encirclement.
In the absence of a boundary, a group of five villages or ten villages shall be established.

One should understand that in cases of injury caused by making a house weak, a cart unpropped, a weapon with its handle pointing upward, a pit or well without a railing, or a concealed trap, the offense constitutes "violence through physical assault" (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
In cases of cutting trees, seizing the bridles of draft animals, or failing to attend to or properly driving four-footed beasts;

or when there is the throwing of wood, clods, stones, sticks, arrows, or arms; or when a carriage or elephant causes a collision with a person—provided one cries out "Move aside!"—there shall be no punishment.
One who has been killed by an enraged elephant should offer food belonging to Droṇa, a jar of liquor, garlands, ointment, a tooth-cleaning stick, and a cloth.
Washing one's feet is equal to the killing of an elephant, which is equivalent to the ritual bath at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha-avabhṛtha-snāna).
In the case of killing a neutral person, the highest fine shall be imposed on the assailant.

If an owner does not rescue his property from being harmed by a horned or fanged animal, he shall be punished with the first *sāhasa* fine; if he fails to respond when called out, the fine shall be double.
If two persons cause each other to be killed by means of horned or tusked animals, the punishment shall be both that [for the animal] and that [for the person].
For one who makes a divine animal—a bull, a steer, or a young cow—work, the fine is five hundred panas; for one who causes it to be driven away, the highest amercement.

For the failure to provide small livestock that are useful for their wool, milk, draught power, or breeding, the punishment shall be the value of the animal and an equal amount as a fine; the same applies to driving them away,
except in the case of rites for the gods or the ancestors.

If a vehicle is equipped with wheels but has its nose-rope severed, its yoke broken, or if it comes from the side or from the front, or if it is retreating, or if there is a crowd of animals and humans, the driver is not liable for punishment in the event of injury.
Otherwise, he shall incur the penalty as prescribed for injury to human beings or animals.
In the case of killing a non-human animal, the punishment is the gift of another animal.
If the driver is a minor, the owner who is in the vehicle shall be fined;
if there is no owner in the vehicle,
the driver who has attained legal majority shall be fined.
The king may seize a vehicle that is occupied by a child or one that is unattended by a man.
Whatever harm an enemy might inflict through magical rites or sorcery, that very harm should be inflicted upon him in return.
KAZ04.13.28: At will, there may be a formal agreement between a husband seeking a wife or a wife seeking a husband, even if she is unwilling, provided it concerns a maiden or a wife.
In the case of injury other than this, the middle amercement shall be the punishment for violence.

For one who has sexual intercourse with his mother, his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, the wife of his teacher, his daughter-in-law, his daughter, or his sister, there shall be the cutting off of the male organ and death as punishment.
A woman who has been with her own consent shall receive that very same [property],
as shall a female slave, a female attendant, a pledged wife, and one who has been supported by him.
In the case of an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman, the punishment for a Kṣatriya is the highest amercement;
for a Vaiśya, it is the forfeiture of all property;
and a Śūdra shall be burned by a fire of straw mats.
In all cases of sexual intercourse with the wife of a king, the punishment is the *kumbhīpāka* hell.
Upon approaching a dog-cooker (outcaste woman), he shall go to another kingdom with the mark of a severed head (*kabandha*) branded on him,
or else the Śūdra shall become a dog-cooker himself.
If a Śvapāka approaches an Ārya woman, he shall be put to death,
and the woman’s ears and nose shall be cut off.
For having sexual intercourse with a female ascetic, the fine is twenty-four paṇas.
If she is willing, she shall receive that very same [gift].
In the case of forcible enjoyment of a woman who lives by her beauty, the fine shall be twelve paṇas.
When many men commit adultery with a single woman, each shall be punished with a fine of twenty-four paṇas.
For one who has sexual intercourse with a woman in a place other than the vagina, or for one who urinates over a man, the first amercement shall be imposed.
For one who lacks self-control, the fine for sexual intercourse with animals is twelve paṇas;
for approaching images of deities, it is recorded as double that amount.
When the king punishes those who are exempt from punishment, a fine thirty times the amount [of the unjust penalty] must be paid into the water;
thereafter, it should be offered to Varuṇa and then to the Brāhmaṇas.
By that means, the sin arising from the king’s failure to administer justice is purified;
for Varuṇa is the punisher of kings who behave falsely toward men.
(On the Infliction of Secret Punishment)
The cleansing of thorns in the fort and the countryside has been explained.
We shall now discuss the king and the kingdom.

KAZ05.1.03: When the principal officers who depend upon the king or who are common to both him and his enemy have been seized, success is achieved through the employment of secret agents or by winning over those on the side of the enemy. This includes instigation and subversion as previously described, or as we shall explain in the section on "The Siege of an Enemy's Village."

But regarding those who harm the kingdom—whether they be favorites, acting in concert, or leading figures who cannot be restrained openly—the king, appearing to favor righteousness, should employ secret punishment against such corruptible persons (*dūṣya*). A secret agent (*sattrin*), having incited the disgraced brother of a high minister (*mahāmātra*) who is corruptible, should present him to the king.
The king should cause that [enemy] to attack the seditious person by granting him the enjoyment of the seditious person's wealth.
One who has attacked with a weapon or poison should be executed right there, [the authorities proclaiming] "This man is a fratricide."
By this, the *pāraśava* and the son of a female attendant (*paricārikā-putra*) are also explained.
A seditious person, incited by a secret agent, should have his brother demand his inheritance from a high minister who is susceptible to corruption.

When that [suspect] is lying down at night near the door of the house of a seditious person, or staying elsewhere, a sharp assassin shall say: "This man, who coveted the inheritance, has been killed."
Then, having secured the one whose faction has been destroyed, he should subdue the other.
Or, spies stationed near the person to be corrupted (dūṣya) should threaten with death a brother who is demanding his inheritance.
"He [should do] that at night"—the rest is the same.
Or, when the son of a seditious person or a high official has illicit relations with his father’s wife, or the father with his son’s wife,
or a brother with [his] brother’s [wife],
the resulting quarrel between them, instigated by a spy (kāpaṭika), is explained by the previous [rule].
KAZ05.1.15: A secret agent should instigate the son of a seditious high official, or one who considers himself of noble birth, saying: "You are a prince;
you have been placed here out of fear of the enemy."
KAZ05.1.16: When the prince has agreed, the king should honor him in secret, saying: "I do not consecrate you, though the time for the heir-apparency has arrived, out of fear of the high ministers."
The secret agent should employ him in the assassination of a high official.
If he has attacked, one should have him executed right there, saying, "This man is a parricide."
Or a female mendicant, having established intimacy with the wife of a seditious person by means of aphrodisiac herbs, should overpower her with poison.
Thus concludes the ritual application for the water-offering.

KAZ05.1.21: To destroy a seditious high official, a forest tribe, or a foreign village; or to station a provincial governor or a frontier guard in a region separated by a wilderness; or to suppress a rebellious city-quarter;
or to seize a caravan that has passed through or to recover a loan from a border region—one should dispatch a weak force accompanied by assassins (*tīkṣṇa*).
When a battle has commenced by night or by day, assassins or spies disguised as rebels should kill [the enemy], saying, "He was killed during the assault."
Or, while on a journey or excursion, he may invite the seditious mahāmātras to see him.
Having entered with sharp assassins carrying concealed weapons, they should conduct a self-search in the middle enclosure for the purpose of gaining entry inside.
Then, the assassins (tīkṣṇa), seized by the gatekeepers, should say, "We have been employed by the seditious."
Having proclaimed that to them, they should have the seditious persons executed.
And others who are condemned to death may be stationed in place of the executioners.
Or, having gone outside the monastery, he should honor those seditious persons who reside nearby.
KAZ05.1.29: A female attendant of the queens or a wicked woman may be caught at night in their lodgings; the rest is the same as previously described.
Or, having praised a seditious high official by saying, "Your cook or food-preparer is excellent," he should request solid or soft food;
or, having gone somewhere outside on a journey, he should request water.
Having combined both of those with a sauce, one should employ them exactly as they are when tasting.
Having publicly proclaimed that [crime], he shall have the person executed as a "vendor of poison."

Or, an agent appearing as a perfected ascetic (*siddha-vyañjana*) who is habitually engaged in malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) should induce [the victim] by saying, "You shall obtain your heart's desires by consuming one of these auspicious [fleshless] heads of an iguana, a tortoise, or a crab.
Once he has consented, the agent should have him killed with poison or iron clubs during the performance of the rite, declaring, "He was killed by a failure in the ritual."
Or a spy disguised as a physician, having diagnosed a malady in a seditious person that is either malevolent or incurable, should administer poison through the application of medicine or food.
Or, cooks, kitchen-staff, and secret agents, having been dispatched, should deceive the enemy with poison.
Thus ends the prohibition regarding the Upaniṣads.
But there is the prevention of both types of seditious persons.
KAZ05.1.39: Wherever a seditious person is to be restrained, the king should send that very seditious person, accompanied by weak troops and assassins (tīkṣṇa), with the command:
"Go, raise an army or collect gold in such-and-such a fort or kingdom."
Either cause gold to be brought from a favorite, or forcibly bring back the daughter of a favorite;

or carry out one of the works concerning forts, bridges, trade routes, colonization of uninhabited lands, mines, precious materials, or elephant forests; or [appoint] a provincial governor or a border-guard commander—whosoever shall oppose you.
"Or if he should not give you assistance, he ought to be bound."
In the same manner, he should send word to the others: "The misconduct of so-and-so must be restrained."
When he disputes over these occasions for quarrel or in the face of obstacles to his work, fiery spies should strike him down with weapons and kill him in secret.
On account of that fault, the others are to be restrained.

KAZ05.1.43: When a quarrel has arisen among seditious persons belonging to ancient villages or clans—concerning the boundaries of fields, threshing-floors, or houses; or regarding damage to property, implements, crops, or beasts of burden; or during spectacles, religious rites, or festivals—or when such a quarrel has been instigated by fiery spies, those fiery spies shall strike with weapons and say: "In this manner are those who quarrel with this man being punished."
On account of that fault, the others should be restrained.
Or, when there are seditious persons among whom quarrels have become deeply rooted, spies should set fire to their fields, threshing floors, or houses;
or, having caused assassins to strike with weapons at their kinsmen, relatives, or vehicles, they should say exactly the same thing: "We were instigated by that man."
On account of that fault, the others are to be restrained.
Or, secret agents should cause the fort-dwellers, country-folk, and seditious persons to act as mutual guests in one another's houses.
In that case, those who provide the juice shall give juice in return.
On account of that fault, the others are to be restrained.
Or a female mendicant should instigate a chief of the enemy's territory, saying: "The wife, daughter-in-law, or daughter of the chief of the enemy's territory desires you."
Having taken the ornament from one who has been won over, he should show it to the owner, saying: "This man of yours, arrogant in his youth, lusts after your wife, daughter-in-law, or daughter."
"The quarrel between the two at night" is the same [as the previous case].

Regarding those who have been won over by sowing dissension or by the employment of force: the crown prince or the commander-in-chief, having committed some offense and then fled, should launch an attack.
Then the king should dispatch only those who are seditious, punished, or submissive, joined with a weak force and fiery spies; thus all these applications are the same.
And among their sons who remain after others have died out, he who is free from defects shall receive the paternal inheritance.
In this way, his kingdom—freed from the faults of men—continues through his sons and grandsons.
Whether against his own faction or that of another, he should apply silent punishment;
being patient and free from suspicion, he should do so both for the future and for the present.
(The replenishment of the treasury)
KAZ05.2.01: One who lacks a treasury, facing a present financial crisis, should collect funds.

KAZ05.2.02: He should demand from a large or small district that is not dependent on rain (adevamātṛka) and rich in grain, either a third or a fourth part of the grain, according to its quality—whether it be middling or inferior.

KAZ05.2.03: One should not request from a border region that is of small extent, nor from one that is beneficial for the construction of forts, bridges, trade routes, and settlements, for mining operations, timber forests, and elephant forests.
One should provide grain, cattle, gold, and so forth to one who is settling there.
One should purchase with gold a fourth part of the grain, after deducting what is required for seed and food.
One should avoid forest-grown produce and the property of a Vedic scholar.
He should also purchase that [land] by means of a favor.
If this is not done, or if it is neglected, the officers of the Collector-General should cause the farmers to clear the weeds during the summer.
KAZ05.2.09: Those who declare a double fine for grain that has been spilled through negligence shall, at the time of sowing, prepare a written record of the seed.

Once the crop is ripe, they shall prevent the gathering of green or ripened grain, except for handfuls of vegetables, broken stalks, or ears of grain intended for offerings to the gods and ancestors, for acts of charity, or for the sake of cattle.
And they shall avoid the base of the heap for the sake of mendicants, village servants, and laborers.
For one who steals another's grain, the fine is eightfold the value of the crop.
For one who steals another's standing crops, the fine for the loss of the field is fiftyfold;
however, for one from among his own group, the penalty is a fine, but for an outsider, it is death.

They shall take a fourth part of grains, a sixth part of forest produce, and [a sixth part] of cotton, lac, linen, bark, cotton-wool, silk, wool, medicines, perfumes, flowers, fruits, vegetables, and merchandise;
as well as of wood, bamboo, meat, and dried meat; and half of ivory and skins.
For one who sells such property without authorization, the punishment is the first amercement.
Thus ends the section on the conciliation of cultivators.
Gold, silver, diamonds, gems, pearls, coral, horses, and elephants as articles of trade shall be subject to a fifty-fold tax.
Those who trade in thread, cloth, copper, round vessels, bell-metal, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and spirituous liquors shall pay a tax of forty kārṣāpaṇas.
Those who trade in grain, liquids, and metals, as well as those who deal in carts, shall pay a tax of thirty *karas*.
Glass merchants and master craftsmen shall pay a tax of twenty *karas*.
Minor artisans and those who maintain prostitutes shall pay a tax of ten *kārṣāpaṇas*.
Merchants dealing in wood, bamboo, stone, earthenware, cooked food, and green vegetables shall pay a five-percent tax.
Actors and those who live by their appearance shall pay half of their wages.
They should cause those who produce gold and those who are skilled in their work to bring it forth,
and they should not overlook any offense committed by them.
For they might sell it after having brought in an unclaimed animal.
Thus is the rule regarding legal proceedings among litigants.
(KAZ05.2.26) One should pay half the value for a cock or a pig; small animals, one-sixth. (KAZ05.2.27)
And for cows, buffaloes, mules, donkeys, and camels, the tax shall be one-tenth.
Keepers of prostitutes shall collect revenue for the treasury by means of royal messengers who possess supreme beauty and youth.
Thus ends the section on the treatment of those who nourish the source [of the crime].
It should be employed only once, not twice.
If he fails to do so, the Collector-General, under the pretext of some public duty, shall solicit contributions from the citizens and country-dwellers.
And in this matter, the agents employed by the yogas should first give excessively large amounts.
By this method, the king shall solicit alms from the citizens and the rural folk.
And spies disguised as fraudulent mendicants (kāpaṭika) should revile those who give them only a small amount.
Or he should solicit gold from the wealthy according to their means, or in proportion to the benefit received, or whatever they might offer of their own accord.
He should provide them with their respective positions, parasols, head-dresses, and ornaments by means of gold.

KAZ05.2.37: Secret agents (kṛtyakarāḥ) should surreptitiously deliver the property of heretical sects (pāṣaṇḍa-saṃgha), or the property of deities (deva-dravya) that is not to be used by those learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya-upabhogyam), under the pretext that it was placed in the hand of a deceased person or one whose house has burned down.

KAZ05.2.38: The Superintendent of Deities (devatādhyakṣaḥ) shall consolidate the treasury of the deities of the fort and the countryside into a single place according to their respective categories, and he shall make surrenders in the same manner.
KAZ05.2.39: Having raised at night a temple of a deity, a shrine of a perfected being, a holy place, or a miraculous manifestation, he may make his living through pilgrimages and festivals.
Or one may indicate the visitation of a deity by means of a tree in a sacred grove or garden that bears flowers and fruit out of season.
Or, having fabricated a threat from demons upon a tree by means of human labor, agents disguised as perfected ascetics (siddhas) should ransom the citizens and country-dwellers with gold.
Or, in the case of a well connected to a tunnel, he should show a snake with its head concealed by means of an offering of gold.

KAZ05.2.43: In an image of an elephant, or one concealed within a hollow of a sacred tree, or in a hole in an anthill, one should show a snake whose consciousness has been bound by food to those who possess faith.

KAZ05.2.44: For those who lack faith, one should administer poison during the acts of sipping water or sprinkling, under the pretext of a ritual offering to the gods, or by having them bitten by a venomous creature after it has been incited.
Or, he may effect the accumulation of treasury by means of countermeasures against the philosophy of Yoga.
Or a spy disguised as a merchant from Videha may carry on trade under the guise of being a student of a large quantity of merchandise.
When that [debt] has been augmented by means of the sale of merchandise, deposits, and loans, he should then rob him at night.
By this, the examiner of form and the goldsmith are also explained.
Or a spy disguised as a merchant, well-known for his business dealings, may take on loan or purchase various vessels of silver and gold under the pretext of a festival.
Or, in a marketplace, he may borrow a large amount of gold and bullion as a loan by means of a collection of all kinds of merchandise, as well as the value of goods in exchange.
One should plunder both of those at night.
Having caused the seducible men to become infatuated with virtuous women, they should seize them in the very houses of those women and confiscate all their property.
Or, when a dispute arises among the families of seditious persons, poisoners stationed there should administer poison.
On account of that same fault, the others are to be excluded from office.
Or, one who has been accused of being a seditious person may request from the suspect goods, a deposit of gold, the repayment of a loan, or an inheritance under a credible pretext.
Or, he may incriminate the person to be corrupted by using the word "slave" for him,
or by using the word "slave" or the word "wife" for his wife, daughter-in-law, or daughter.
When that [agent] is lying down at night at the door of the seditious person's house, or staying elsewhere, a sharp agent (tīkṣṇa) shall kill him and say: "This seeker of wealth has been killed."
On account of that same fault, the others should be deprived of their property.

Alternatively, one who has mastered the art of disguise may entice a seditious person with the sciences of sorcery (jambhakavidyā) and say: "I know a ritual that yields inexhaustible gold, gains access to the royal court, captivates the hearts of women, or cures the diseases of enemies; it also promotes longevity or the birth of a son."
And at night, he should cause an offering consisting of abundant perfumes of liquor and meat to be made at the site of a shrine frequented by those who have entered [the heretical path].

KAZ05.2.61. Furthermore, in this case, he should show him gold of a single form that was previously buried where a corpse’s limb or a child’s corpse had been placed, and he should say of it, "This is far too little."
"Since a further offering must be made for the sake of abundant gold, you yourself must purchase a large quantity of items for the offering with this very gold on the following day."
He shall be apprehended with that gold for the purpose of purchasing articles intended as offerings.
Or, by means of a female spy disguised as a mother, she may be made to feel provoked, saying: "My son has been killed by you."

KAZ05.2.65: When he has already achieved his objective and is engaged in a night-sacrifice, a forest sacrifice, or a forest game, the *tīkṣṇas* (assassins) should kill him and carry him away as if he were a discarded corpse.
Or, an agent appearing as a hired servant may insert counterfeit coins into the wages and gold of a seditious person and cause them to be examined.

Or a spy disguised as a laborer, while performing work in a house, may place there the tools of a thief or a forger; or a spy disguised as a physician may administer poison under the pretext of medicine.
Or, a spy stationed near a seditious person may, through the mouth of a fraudulent agent, announce that the equipment for consecration and an enemy's command have been dispatched,
and he should state the reason for this.
In this manner, one should behave toward those who are corruptible and those who are unrighteous, but not toward others.
Just as one might obtain ripe fruit from a garden, so should one obtain [revenue] from the kingdom, ripening it bit by bit.
Out of fear of self-destruction, one should avoid that which is unripe and provocative of anger.
(Salaries of State Servants)

KAZ05.3.01: He should establish the labor of servants according to the strength of his fortresses and territories, based on one-quarter of the total revenue, or according to the acquisition of servants that is sufficient for accomplishing his tasks.
One should look after one's own body;
one should not cause harm to virtue or wealth.
The sacrificial priests, teachers, ministers, domestic chaplains, army commanders, crown princes, the king’s mother, and the king’s queens receive forty-eight thousand [paṇas] each.
By this much maintenance, they become unassailable and free from provocation.
The door-keeper, the officer of the inner apartments, the chief magistrate, the collector-general, and the treasurer shall each receive twenty-four thousand [paṇas].
By this much they become fit for ritual action.

The prince, the prince’s mother, the commander-in-chief, the city magistrate, the superintendent of manufactories, the minister, the council of ministers, the provincial governor, and the frontier guard shall each receive twelve thousand [paṇas].
For it is by this much that one possesses the support of a master, the strength of an army, and the assistance of allies.
The heads of guilds, the chiefs of the elephant, cavalry, and chariot corps, and the commissioners shall receive eight thousand [paṇas] each.
For by this much, they become those who attract their own group.
The superintendents of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants, as well as the keepers of timber forests and elephant forests, shall receive four thousand [paṇas] each.
Charioteers, elephant-keepers, physicians, horse-trainers, carpenters, and breeders of animals shall receive two thousand [paṇas] each.

Astrologers, fortune-tellers, experts in auspicious moments, reciters of the Purāṇas, bards, and heralds, as well as the attendants of the domestic chaplain and all superintendents, shall each receive one thousand [paṇas].
Skilled artisans as foot soldiers, along with the class of accountants, scribes, and so forth, shall number five hundred.
The actors shall number two hundred and fifty, and those who play musical instruments for them shall receive double wages.
Artisans and craftsmen shall pay a tax of twenty *paṇas*.

Quadrupeds, bipeds, attendants, laborers, personal servants, guardians, and forced laborers shall receive a wage of sixty [paṇas]; likewise, noble officials, riders, young novices, stone-cutters, and all types of attendants.
Teachers and those possessed of learning shall receive honoraria according to their merit, with a minimum of five hundred and a maximum of one thousand [paṇas].
A messenger of middle rank shall receive ten paṇas per yojana;
for every ten yojanas beyond that, his wages shall be doubled, up to a distance of one hundred yojanas.
In sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, the king shall provide three times the sacrificial fee compared to those of equal learning.
The king's charioteer is worth one thousand.
Spies disguised as fraudulent ascetics, wandering mendicants, householders, merchants, and forest hermits constitute a force of one thousand men.
Village laborers, secret agents, assassins, poisoners, and female mendicants shall receive five hundred [paṇas].
Spies moving about shall number two hundred and fifty, or they may be provided with increased wages according to the effort required.
The superintendents of groups of one hundred and groups of one thousand shall determine the food rations, wages, profits, orders, and disbursements.
And he should remain undistracted in the supervision of the royal household, the fortifications, and the protection of the realm.
There should be those who are permanently chief and those who are chiefs for multiple purposes.
KAZ05.3.28: The wives and sons of those who die while on duty shall receive food and wages.
Among them, children, the elderly, and the diseased are to be shown favor.
KAZ05.3.30: And in the case of the rites for the deceased, the sick, or women who have recently given birth, one should perform their work with respect to wealth and honor.
One with a small treasury should give base metals, livestock, and fields, as well as a small amount of gold.
Or, if he has set out to settle a deserted area, he should give only gold,
not a village, for the purpose of establishing the legal proceedings customary to that village.
By this same principle, one should determine the distinction between food and wages for those who are hired and those who are not, based on their learning and their work.
KAZ05.3.34: For one whose salary is sixty [paṇas], having calculated an āḍhaka as the measure, one should provide food corresponding to the amount of gold.
KAZ05.3.35: Infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants shall perform training in their respective crafts outside the city at sunrise, except on the day of the peace treaty.
The king should be constantly devoted to these [arts],
and he should frequently inspect their craftsmanship.
He shall cause the weapons and armor marked with the insignia of the king to enter the armory.
They shall move about unarmed, except when authorized by a seal.
He shall pay double the value for what is lost or destroyed.
And he should carry out a census of those who have been dispersed.
The frontier guards shall seize the weapons and armor of merchants,
or they may allow them to pass through the sea route.
Or, having set out on a military expedition, he should mobilize his army.
Then, spies disguised as merchants shall provide all types of merchandise to the armed soldiers at the time of their expedition on the condition that it be returned with double the value.
In this manner, the sale of royal merchandise through association and the recovery of wages are accomplished.
Thus, one who has scrutinized income and expenditure does not suffer from calamities regarding the treasury or the army.
Thus ends the section on the alternatives regarding food and wages.
Spies, armed soldiers, courtesans, artisans, actors,
and those advanced in age shall, remaining vigilant, ascertain the purity and impurity of the [king’s] dependents. (KAZ05.3.47)

One who knows the ways of the world should seek refuge with a king who is endowed with personal wealth and constituent elements (prakṛtis), by means of those who are both dear to him and act for his welfare.

Or, if he should think, "Just as I am desirous of a refuge, so is this person desirous of discipline and endowed with the qualities that lead to approaching [the king]," he should seek shelter with him even if he is deficient in wealth and natural resources, but never with one who is devoid of self-cultivation.
For one who lacks self-control, due to an aversion to the science of policy or through association with harmful things, does not remain in power even after attaining great sovereignty.
When one possesses self-control, having found the opportunity, one should apply oneself to the study of the scriptures.
For through non-contradiction, one attains stability in one's position.

In matters requiring deliberation, he should speak—when questioned—concerning both the present and the future, in a manner consistent with righteousness and material interest, being capable, acting like an expert, and unafraid of an assembly.

KAZ05.4.07: One who is desired as a candidate for appointment should bargain: "In matters concerning dharma and artha that are not contested, and in cases involving those allied with the powerful, you shall administer punishment; likewise, in my own affairs and in immediate matters, you shall administer punishment. You must not undermine my faction, my livelihood, or my secrets;
and by means of a secret signal, I shall restrain you from the infliction of punishment driven by desire or anger."
Having been commanded, he should enter when the ground has been assigned to him; having been permitted, he should sit down at the side, neither too near nor too far from the seat of the other.

KAZ05.4.09: One should not engage in contentious speech, nor utter words that are indecorous, indirect, untrustworthy, or false; nor should one laugh loudly except in jest, nor make noise while coughing or spitting.
Mutual conversation with another; speaking in pairs during public rumor;
and [speaking of] the king's dress and that of arrogant impostors.
He makes a request for the manifestation of the excellence of jewels; while speaking with the enjoyment of one eye and lip, and with the knitting of eyebrows and the casting aside of words,
he displays a powerful and joined contradiction.

He should avoid association with women, those who frequent women, envoys from neighboring kings, and those cast off by his enemies' faction; he should also avoid socializing with wealthy men, acting for a common purpose with them, and forming groups with them.

One should speak at the appropriate time for the sake of the king’s interests, for one’s own interests along with those who are dear and beneficial, for the interests of others, and regarding place and time, all in accordance with righteousness and material gain.
When questioned, one should speak what is pleasant and beneficial; one should not speak what is unpleasant even if it is pleasant.
Or, one may speak what is beneficial though unpleasant, provided the listener is attentive and has given his private consent.
Or he should remain silent when a reply is expected, and he should not describe the dress and other attributes [of his enemies].
Even those who are disliked may be capable; therefore, one should not exclude those who are excluded from that [faction] because of their disposition.
One should observe those who are unpleasant yet beloved, as well as those who are attentive to one's thoughts;
one should laugh at things that provoke laughter and avoid those who laugh with a terrifying laugh. One should direct one’s own severity toward others, but one must not speak harshly to others.
Being patient and possessing forgiveness, he should endure even his own suffering, remaining equal to the earth.
For one who understands, self-protection must always be performed first;
for the livelihoods of those who depend upon the king are said to be like [a life] within a fire.
If fire, having reached another's body, should burn a portion of it,
the king should either have the offender executed along with his sons and wife, or he should punish him by mutilation.
(Proper conduct for a courtier)
An official appointed to duties shall present the revenue with the expenditures fully accounted for and cleared.
He should specify whether a matter is internal, external, secret, public, urgent, or to be neglected, stating, "This matter is thus."
One should not follow with praise a king who is addicted to hunting, gambling, intoxicants, or women.
And when he is close to being struck by a calamity, he should strive to avert it and protect himself from the intrigues, deceptions, and fraudulent conditions of his enemies.
And one should observe his gestures and facial expressions.
A wise person practices the concealment of counsel by means of gestures and facial expressions, [thereby masking] desire, hatred, joy, dejection, resolve, fear, and the reversal of dualities.
Upon seeing him, he is pleased;
he accepts his words and offers him a seat.
He shows himself secluded; he does not feel excessive suspicion toward grounds for suspicion; he delights in discourse.
He examines those things that should be fully understood, he endures what is spoken for his benefit, and he issues commands with a smile.
He touches her with his hand,
does not mock what is praiseworthy, and speaks of her virtues in her absence.
He remembers [the friend] during meals,
goes along with him in his dwelling,
and assists him in times of misfortune.
He honors those devoted to him,
reveals secrets to them,
and increases their esteem.
"It accomplishes what is beneficial and strikes down what is harmful"— this is the knowledge of contentment.
The opposite of this applies to one who is dissatisfied;
furthermore, we shall explain this more fully.
Anger upon seeing him, refusing to hear or obey his words, and not offering him a seat or one's gaze.
Alteration of complexion and voice; knitting of one eyebrow and distension of the lips; and the untimely manifestation of perspiration, labored breathing, and smiles.
Secret consultation,
departing suddenly,
and the promotion of another.
Scratching the ground or one's limbs, poking another, and disparaging knowledge, caste, or locality.
Censure of faults in general,
censure of specific faults,
and praise by way of inversion.
Disregarding good deeds,
proclaiming evil deeds,
and turning one's back [on others].
Excessive generosity,
false speech, and for those who attend upon the king, behaving otherwise than their true character.
And one should observe even the changes in the behavior of non-human beings.
"This one sprinkles loudly," said Kātyāyana as he went forth;
"the curlew [sings] counter-clockwise," said Kaṇiṅka Bhāradvāja; "grass," said Dīrgha Cārāyaṇa.
“‘A cool cloth! said Ghoṭamukha; ‘The elephant sprinkled [it]! said Kiñjalka;
‘He praised the chariot-horse! said Piśuna.”
At the howling of the dog, the son of Piśuna.
And there shall be forfeiture of wealth, honor, and position.
Or, having perceived the character of the master and his own guilt, he may remedy the situation.
Or his ally, being drawn away, may go over to him.
Remaining there, he should, together with his allies, effect the removal of faults from his master;
then, whether the master is alive or dead, he may return again.
(Continuance of the Kingdom)
(Kingdom-wide Sovereignty) KAZ05.6.01: In this manner, the minister should counteract the calamities of the king.

Even before the danger of death or illness arises, he should arrange for an audience with the king once every month or two by means of pleasing and beneficial services, under the pretext that "the king is performing a ritual act that removes distress from the country, destroys enemies, prolongs life, or bestows sons."
He should display the insignia of royalty to the subjects at an improper time,
as well as to the envoys of friends and enemies.
And through them, he should conduct the appropriate conversation with the ministers' chief as his intermediary.
The doorkeeper, the officer of the inner apartments, and the chamberlain shall carry out the king’s instructions as previously prescribed.
Toward those who have done him harm, he should display either resentment or favor as is pleasing to his subjects; however, toward those who have been helpful, he should show only favor.
He should cause the treasury and the army to be stationed together, either under the supervision of trustworthy men or located in the fort and the border regions;
and he should station the heads of noble families and princes under some other pretext.
And whoever, being a leading person with partisans, or residing in a fort or forest, should fall into a state of weakness, he should be made to surrender.
Or he should dispatch him on a journey fraught with many dangers,
or to the family of a friend.

And from whichever neighbor he perceives a threat, he should cause that neighbor to be restrained by means of the pretext of providing for festivals, weddings, the tethering of elephants, the sale of horses, or the granting of land,
or else through his own ally.
Thereupon, he should conclude a peace treaty that cannot be violated.
Or he should cause him to incur enmity with forest-dwellers or enemies.
He should cause a man of noble birth or one who has been deposed to be won over by means of a portion of the greater [territory].
Or, having won over the chief of the royal princes, he should show the prince as already consecrated.
Or, like a magistrate administering punishment, he should rule the kingdom after having uprooted the thorns of the state.
Or, if any one among the principal feudatories and others should fall into a state of rebellion, he should be summoned with the words, "Come, I shall make you king," and then have him killed.
Or he should accomplish it by counteracting the calamity.
Or, having gradually transferred the burden of the kingdom to the crown prince, he should announce his royal misfortune.
KAZ05.6.19: When there is a calamity for the king on foreign territory, he should conclude a treaty with the enemy through a friend disguised as an enemy and then withdraw.
Or, having stationed one of his neighbors or others in his fort, he should depart.
Or, having consecrated the prince, he should arrange a counter-array.
Or, when attacked by an enemy, he should take measures to counteract the calamity as previously described.
"In this manner, the minister should exercise sole authority," says Kauṭilya.
"It is not so," says Bhāradvāja.
KAZ05.6.25: Or, when the king is dying, the minister should cause the principal kinsmen and princes to attack one another, or cause them to attack the leading nobles.
One should have a man who has shown valor executed when his own subjects are incensed against him.
Or, having subdued the chief kinsmen and princes by silent punishment (secret execution), he should seize the kingdom himself.

For it is for the sake of the kingdom that fathers betray their sons and sons betray their fathers; how much more so, then, the ministerial element, which is the single point of support for the kingdom?
One should not disregard that which has presented itself of its own accord.
“For a woman who has ascended of her own accord, if she is abandoned, brings a curse upon herself”—this is a popular proverb.
Time comes but once to the man who awaits his time;
that same time is difficult for him to obtain again when he wishes to perform his duty.
"This [policy] provokes the subjects, is most unrighteous, and is uncertain in its outcome," says Kauṭilya.
One should establish a prince endowed with personal excellence upon the throne.

In the absence of a suitable candidate, he should place before the high officials a prince who is free from vices, or a princess, or the queen who is pregnant, and having assembled them, he should say: "This is your trust;
look after his father, as well as your own character and noble lineage.
He is merely a symbol; you yourselves are the masters."
Or else, how should it be done? he asked.
To him who speaks thus, the agents of discipline (*yoga-puruṣas*) should say: "Who else but this king, led by you, is worthy to protect the fourfold order of society?"
"In the same manner," the minister shall appoint a prince, a princess, a pregnant queen, or a [junior] queen [to oversee the matter],
and he shall present them to the relatives and kinsmen as well as to the envoys of friends and enemies.
He should arrange for a specific increase in food and wages for his ministers and soldiers,
saying, "This man, now grown old, will perform even more [in the future]."
In this manner, he should address the chiefs of the fortresses and the countryside,
as well as those on the side of his friends and enemies, according to their respective status.
And he should strive for the prince's discipline in matters of conduct.
Or, having procreated offspring with a maiden of the same caste, he should have her consecrated.
Out of fear of agitating the mother's mind, he should present a relative of little strength and a student of distinguished appearance as a substitute.
And he should protect her during her fertile period.
And he should not cause anyone to provide him with any superior luxury for his own sake.
But for the sake of the king’s interests, he should cause to be made vehicles, mounts, ornaments, garments, women, dwellings, and attendants.
One should request a truce from one who is in the prime of youth for the sake of gaining time;
however, one should abandon one who is dissatisfied and maintain one who is satisfied.
Having reported to the king that he possesses secret stores of wealth for the sake of protecting his sons,
he may retire to the forest or undertake a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) when he has become weary of worldly life.
Or, one who knows the science of polity (arthaśāstra), relying on what is dear to him, should awaken a king who has been seized by his chief ministers by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Or, having assumed the appearance of a perfected spy (*siddha-vyañjana*), he should employ a stratagem against the king;
having gained [his trust], he should carry out punitive measures (*dāṇḍakarmika*) among those who are corruptible.
(The Circle of States: The Sixth Book)

(Ninety-sixth Section – The Excellence of the Constituent Elements) KAZ06.1.01: The sovereign, the minister, the territory, the fort, the treasury, the army, and the ally are the constituent elements (*prakṛtis*).
In that regard, the excellence of the master [is as follows].

KAZ06.1.03: Being of noble birth, endowed with a divine intellect and courage, having seen many elders, righteous, truthful in speech, non-deceptive, grateful, liberal, possessed of great energy, not procrastinating, capable of subduing neighboring vassals, firm in resolve, having a retinue that is not mean-spirited, and desiring discipline— these are the qualities of approachability.
The qualities of wisdom (prajñā) consist of: the desire to hear, hearing, grasping, retention, comprehension, reasoning, critical examination, and firm adherence to the truth.
Bravery, impatience, speed, and dexterity are the qualities of energy (*utsāha*).

He is eloquent, bold, endowed with the strength of memory and intelligence, exalted, self-controlled, skilled in the arts, free from vice, capable of inflicting punishment, one who returns favors and injuries with visible retaliation, modest, a manager of both calamities and the constituent elements of the state, far-sighted, one who prioritizes place, time, human effort, and the objective, and one who discerns the divisions of peace, military expedition, cession, restraint, and the vulnerabilities of the enemy.

Self-perfection consists in being restrained; having no frowning brow or momentary glance of derision; being free from desire, anger, greed, arrogance, fickleness, affliction, and slander; being pure; speaking with a joyful smile; and following the conduct of the instructions of the elders.
The qualifications of a minister have been stated previously.
A territory that is well-provided with positions both in the center and at the borders; one that sustains itself and sustains others in times of distress;

one that protects itself, provides its own livelihood, and hates its enemies; one whose neighboring vassals are manageable; one free from swamps, rocks, saline soil, uneven terrain, rows of thorns, predatory beasts, wild animals, and forests;

one that is pleasant, possesses fertile land, mines, raw materials, and elephant forests; one rich in cattle, populated by men, with protected pastures, abundant in livestock, and free from excessive worship of goddesses or mother-goddesses.

Provided with both water and land routes, possessing abundant and diverse commodities of high value, capable of bearing the burden of taxes and military service, having farmers who are industrious, a ruler who is not foolish, a population consisting mostly of the lower castes, and men who are loyal and pure— this is the excellence of a territory.
The requirements for a fort have been stated previously.

KAZ 6.1.10: Wealth acquired through righteous means by ancestors, or acquired by oneself, consisting primarily of gold and silver, along with various large gems and bullion—this constitutes the excellence of the treasury (*kośasaṃpat*), which can withstand even a long-standing calamity and future adversity.

KAZ 6.1.11: [The excellence of the army consists of] troops inherited from father and grandfather, who are permanent, obedient, whose wives and sons are well-satisfied, who have not been betrayed during expeditions, who are everywhere irresistible, who endure hardship, who have fought many battles, and who are experts in the science of all types of warfare and weapons.
Because it increases and decreases together with [the king], it is non-divisive and consists primarily of the kṣatriya class; such is the excellence of the army.
KAZ06.1.12: An ally who is hereditary from father and grandfather, loyal, undivided in purpose, and capable of rising to both great and small tasks—this is the excellence of an ally.

KAZ06.1.13: One who lacks the seed of royalty, is greedy, has a base assembly of ministers, whose subjects are disaffected, who acts unjustly, is undisciplined, addicted to vices, lacking in energy, one who relies on fate, who proceeds haphazardly in his undertakings, who lacks foresight, is impotent, and is constantly harmful— this is the nature of an enemy.
For an enemy in such a state is easy to utterly destroy.

Excluding the enemy, these seven constituent elements (prakṛtis), arising from their own respective qualities, have been described as the subordinate limbs; they constitute the essential attributes of a king.
A self-possessed king brings his incomplete constituent elements to completion; a king lacking self-mastery destroys his constituent elements even when they have grown strong and are loyal.
Therefore, even if he rules over the four quarters of the earth, that king of wicked character and lacking self-control is either slain by his own subjects or falls under the power of his enemies.

But one who possesses self-control, even if he rules over a small territory, being endowed with the excellence of his constituent elements and skilled in policy, surely conquers the entire earth and does not suffer decline. (The Chapter on Peace and War)
Tranquility and exertion are the source of acquisition and security.
KAZ06.2.02: For undertakings of action, exertion consists in the practice of yoga.
Peace is the means for securing the enjoyment of the fruits of one's actions.
The sixfold policy is the source of both tranquility and exertion.
Decline, stability, and growth are its outcomes.
Human [fortune] consists of policy and impolicy; divine [fortune] consists of luck and ill-luck.
For it is both divine and human action that sustains the world.
Destiny (daiva) is that which is brought about by the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
In that regard, union with a desired result is *ayaḥ* (gain), while union with an undesired result is *anayaḥ* (loss).
Human evidence is that which is produced by what has been perceived.
KAZ06.2.11: In that regard, the accomplishment of acquisition and preservation is *naya* (policy); failure to do so is *apanaya* (mismanagement).
That is to be reflected upon;
fate is inconceivable.
KAZ06.2.13: A king who is endowed with his own self, resources, and constituent elements is the foundation of policy and is one who desires victory.
Surrounding that [neutral king] on all sides, forming a circle, is the enemy constituent (ari-prakṛti), whose territory is immediately adjacent to his own.
In the same way, a territory separated by one intervening state is of the nature of a friend.

A neighboring king endowed with the excellence of an enemy is an *ari* (enemy); one who is beset by calamities is a *yātavya* (one to be marched against); and one who is without support or has a weak support is to be destroyed (*ucchedanīya*).
In the opposite case, he should be subjected to oppression or emaciation.
Thus end the specific types of enemies.

Therefore, the friend, the enemy’s friend, the friend’s friend, and the enemy’s friend’s friend follow one after another as the immediate territories in front; behind them follow, respectively, the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the ally of the rear-attacker (*ākranda*), the ally of the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāhāsāra*), and the ally of the ally of the rear-attacker (*ākrandāsāra*).
The neighbor whose territory is immediately adjacent is the natural ally;
one of equal lineage is the innate ally;
and one who is hostile or acts as an adversary is the artificial enemy.
A neighbor separated by one territory is a natural friend; one related through mother or father is a born friend; and one who has taken refuge for the sake of wealth or life is an acquired friend.

KAZ06.2.21: The king whose territory is adjacent to both the enemy and the conqueror, who is capable of favoring them whether they are united or disunited, and of suppressing them when they are disunited, is the middle king.

KAZ06.2.22: An *udāsīna* (neutral king) is one who is stronger than the external constituent elements of the enemy, the conqueror, and the middle king; who is capable of supporting the enemy, the conqueror, and the middle king when they are united, and of suppressing them when they are disunited.
Thus end the constituent elements [of the state].
KAZ06.2.24: For one who desires victory, the ally, the ally’s ally, and the ally’s ally are his three constituent elements.
When these [five] are each combined with the five constituent elements of sovereignty—ministers, the territory, the fort, the treasury, and the army—they constitute a circle of eighteen [states].
By this, the distinctness of the circles of enemies, middling kings, and neutral kings is explained.
Thus is the summary of the four circles.
There are twelve constituent elements of the state, sixty constituent elements of material resources;
in brief, there are seventy-two.
KAZ06.2.29: Their success depends on their respective circumstances.
Power and success.
KAZ06.2.31: Force is power.
Success is happiness.

KAZ06.2.33: Power is threefold: the power of knowledge (*jñānabala*) is the power of counsel (*mantraśakti*); the power of the treasury and the army (*kośadaṇḍabala*) is the power of lordship (*prabhuśakti*); and the power of valor (*vikramabala*) is the power of energy (*utsāhaśakti*).
KAZ06.2.34: Thus, success (siddhi) is indeed threefold: success achieved through the power of counsel is counsel-success (mantra-siddhi);
success achieved through the power of the sovereign is sovereign-success (prabhu-siddhi); and success achieved through the power of energy is energy-success (utsāha-siddhi).
By these [means], one who is augmented becomes superior; one who is diminished becomes inferior;
and one whose power is equal remains the same.
Therefore, he should strive to instill power and success within himself,
whether as a common factor among the material constituents or through immediate proximity or by means of purification.
Or he should strive to alienate him from his seditious subjects and enemies.

Or if he should perceive: "My enemy, though possessed of power, will harm my subjects through verbal and physical violence and the misappropriation of wealth; or, though successful, he will fall into negligence due to hunting, gambling, wine, and women; being thus alienated by his subjects, depleted, or intoxicated, he will become vulnerable to me."

"Or, one engaged in war, standing alone with his entire force at a single point, whether in a fort or not in a fort, will remain there; he, with his army concentrated and separated from the fort of an ally, will become easy for me to overcome.

Or, "A powerful king, desiring to destroy an enemy further away, might destroy that [enemy] and then destroy me"; thus, assistance is given to one who is sought by a powerful king or whose undertakings have failed.
And in cases such as the desire for a middle course, one should seek the power and success of even an enemy for these reasons.
Having made the kings one degree apart as the rim and those immediately adjacent as the spokes,
the leader should fix himself as the nave within the circle of constituent elements.
For an enemy placed between both the leader and his ally, even if he is powerful, becomes one who must be either destroyed or suppressed.
(The Section on the Sixfold Policy: Determining Decline, Stability, and Growth)
The circle of constituent elements (*prakṛtimaṇḍala*) is the source of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
“Peace, war, sitting encamped, marching, seeking shelter, and duplicity constitute the sixfold policy,” so say the teachers.
“Dvaiguṇyam” refers to the disease of wind (vāta-vyādhi).
"For it is through peace and war that the sixfold policy is accomplished."
Kautilya maintains that this very sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) is [the same] despite the differences in its states.
In that case, peace is made by means of a wager.
KAZ07.1.07 / War is injury.
Neglect is the posture.
An increase in strength is marching.
KAZ07.1.10: Seeking the protection of another is seeking refuge.
KAZ07.1.11: The adoption of peace and war constitutes the state of double-dealing (dvaidhībhāva).
Thus end the six measures of policy.
One who is being defeated by another should make peace.
When being overpowered, one should wage war.
"One is incapable of harming another, nor is another capable of harming me"—thus one should remain.
One who possesses excellence of qualities should march.
One who is deficient in power should seek refuge.
When a task is to be accomplished with the assistance of allies, one should resort to a double policy (dvaidhībhāva).
Thus concludes the determination of the qualities.

Among those [qualities], he should abide in whichever quality, remaining there, he perceives: "Staying here, I shall be able to carry out for myself the works of fortifications, bridges, trade routes, the settlement of uninhabited lands, mining, and the management of timber and elephant forests, and I shall be able to destroy these same works of the enemy. He should then persist in that state.
That is interest.
"Knowing that 'my growth will be swifter, more abundant, or yield a higher rate of interest than my opponent's, while the opposite will be true for him,' one should disregard the opponent's growth."
Or, when interest has accrued such that the principal and the interest have become equal, he should enter into a peace treaty.
Or, if he perceives that by remaining in a particular quality (guṇa) his own duties will be impaired, while those of another are not, he should not remain in that quality.
This is the depletion.

Having realized, "I shall exhaust [the enemy's resources] in a longer time but with less effort, or with greater profit and growth, whereas the opposite will be the case for my opponent," one should disregard the depletion [of one's own resources].
Or, when the rise of results at the same time is equal, he should enter into a peace treaty upon the reduction [of the enemy's power].
Or, that particular quality in which one is situated such that he perceives neither an increase nor a decrease in his own undertakings—this is the state [of stability].
"Having realized, 'I shall remain shorter or with less increase in prosperity than my rival, while the opposite shall be true for him,' one should disregard the position."
"Or, when the arising of the fruits is simultaneous, one should enter into peace while remaining [in one's current position]," so say the teachers.
"This is not an optional rule," says Kauṭilya.

Or if he should perceive: "Remaining in peace, I shall frustrate the undertakings of others through my own highly fruitful actions, or I shall enjoy my own highly fruitful undertakings, or those of others."
"Either I shall destroy the enemy's undertakings through a treaty based on trust, or by means of secret yogic incantations and spies;

or else, by making my own undertakings easy to carry out through the granting of favors and exemptions, I shall cause the people to flock to them because of the abundance of their rewards, thereby inducing them to engage in the enemy's undertakings."
Or, "The enemy, when allied with one who is excessively powerful, will suffer damage to his own undertakings;
or, being attacked by one with whom I have made peace, he will enter into a long conflict with that person;
or, while allied with me, he will harass the territory of one who hates me."—KAZ07.1.32b.
"Or, his territory being oppressed by another, it will come to me;
then I shall achieve growth in my undertakings.
Or, with his undertakings ruined or being in a precarious state, the enemy will not exert himself against me in his operations."

Or, having begun an undertaking against another, he may, in conjunction with those two, achieve success in his undertakings; or, having made peace with an enemy who is obstructing him, he may break the circle of states.

"I shall obtain him when he is divided," or "by means of punishment or favor, having won over the enemy, I shall cause him to be hated by the circle of states (*maṇḍala*) during their desire for acquisition,
and once he is hated, I shall have him killed by that very circle"— with such thoughts, one should pursue prosperity through peace (*saṃdhi*).

Or if he should perceive: "My territory consists mostly of martial men or mostly of guildsmen; or it is protected by mountains, forests, rivers, and passes with a single entrance; or, having taken refuge in an impassable fort on the frontier, I shall be able to withstand the enemy's attack; or I shall be able to strike at the enemy's operations."

Or, if the enemy’s enthusiasm is struck down by the pain of calamities, or if he has reached a time when his undertakings are being frustrated, [the king] should maintain an attitude of expansion while remaining in a state of war, thinking: "I shall be able to drive the enemy's people away from their territory, either because he is engaged elsewhere or because of my own position."

Or if he should think: "The enemy is not capable of obstructing my undertakings, nor am I an obstructor of his undertakings; moreover, he is beset by calamity, like the quarrel between a dog and a boar."
"Or, devoted to the performance of my own duties, I shall prosper"—thus one should establish growth through the posture (āsana).

Or, if he should think, "The enemy's impairment of his undertakings can be accomplished through marching, and I am one who has provided for the protection of my own undertakings," he should pursue progress by means of marching.
Or if he should think, "I am not capable of destroying the enemy's undertakings, nor of protecting my own undertakings from destruction," then,
having sought refuge with one who is powerful, he should desire stability from decline and growth from that state of stability by means of the performance of his own duties.

Or if he should think, "By means of peace with one [party] I shall carry out my own operations, and by means of war with the other I shall destroy the enemy's operations," he should pursue prosperity through the policy of double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*).
Thus, established in the circle of constituent elements by means of these six expedients,
he should seek stability from decline and growth from stability in his undertakings.
(The Conduct of Seeking Shelter)
When the increase resulting from peace and war is equal, one should resort to peace.
For in war, there occur loss, expenditure, exile, and misfortune.
By this, the treatment of the seat and the vehicle is explained; [first] the seat is explained.
Between the policies of double-dealing and seeking shelter, one should adopt the policy of double-dealing.
For one who has become divided, being intent on his own duty, benefits himself alone;
whereas one who is dependent benefits another, not himself.
One should seek refuge with one whose strength is superior to that of the neighboring king who possesses such strength.
In the absence of such superior strength, one who has taken refuge with him should strive to assist him unobserved by means of any one of his treasury, army, or territory.
For kings, an alliance with one of distinguished power is a great danger, except when they are already engaged in hostilities with an enemy.
When it is impossible [to achieve one's goal], one should behave as if toward one who has been brought under punishment.

And when he perceives that a life-threatening disease, internal unrest, the rise of an enemy, or the misfortune of an ally has befallen him— or that his own prosperity will result from such causes— then, under the pretext of attending to the treatment of the illness or performing religious duties, he should withdraw.
Or, remaining within his own territory, he should not go to meet him.
Or, being close at hand, he should strike him during his moments of vulnerability.
Or, situated between two more powerful kings, he should seek refuge with one capable of protecting him, or with whichever one might provide him concealment, or with both.
He should remain sheltered within the shards, while the other, who has seized his property, remains elsewhere under some pretext.
Or he should employ mutual accusations between the two factions to cause division, and then apply secret punishment against those who have become divided.
Or, standing by the side, he should provide assistance to the two powerful parties out of fear of imminent danger.
Or, taking refuge in a fort, he should remain in a state of double-dealing.
Or he should act by means of the sequence of causes for peace and war.
He should win over the seditious, the enemies, and the forest tribes for the sake of both parties.
Going against either one of these two, he should strike at the other whenever the latter falls into misfortune.
Or, one who is oppressed by two kings should remain dependent on a circle of states, or seek refuge with a middle king or a neutral king.
Having won over one of them along with him, he should destroy the other, or both.

Or, one who has been uprooted by two kings should seek refuge with a middle king or an indifferent king, or with those kings who belong to their factions, provided they follow a righteous course of conduct.
Or, among equals, he should go to one whose subjects would favor him,
or where, being situated, he would be able to extricate himself,
or where there is a path customary for his ancestors or a nearby alliance.
The allies may be numerous or exceedingly powerful.
Between one who loves another and one who is loved by another, which of these two is superior?
He to whom the other is dear shall go to him; such is the supreme course of seeking refuge.
(The attachment to qualities of those who are equal, inferior, or superior—concerning treaties with the inferior.)
A king desirous of victory should employ the sixfold policy in accordance with his own power.
One should make peace with those who are equal or superior, and wage war against those who are inferior.
For one who is at war with a superior power enters into a conflict like that of a foot-soldier fighting an elephant.
And when one uses an unbaked vessel with an unbaked [substance], it causes destruction on both sides, as if with something that has not yet been fired.
Just as a stone with a hollow at its base sinks, so too one who is deficient attains success in only one direction.
If the superior king does not desire peace, he should adopt the conduct of one who has submitted to force or employ the strategy of the stronger power.
If the other party is equal and does not desire peace, one should retaliate against him to the same extent as he has caused injury.
For fire is the cause of rejoining.
"Heated iron does not join with unheated iron."
If he is inferior and remains submissive in every respect, he should enter into a peace treaty.
For, like a forest fire, the energy born of the indignation of suffering impels one to valor.
And he becomes one who is to be favored by the circle [of kings].

If he perceives that the allied forces—being greedy, depleted, or disaffected—are not coming forward because of fear of being reclaimed, then even if he is inferior in strength, he should still wage war.
If, while at war, he perceives that "the enemy's subjects— whether greedy, impoverished, disaffected, or distressed by the conflict— are not coming over to me," then even if he is superior in power,
he should seek peace or alleviate the distress caused by the war.

Even when calamities occur simultaneously, if one perceives that "I am beset by a heavy calamity while my opponent has a light one, and having easily remedied his own calamity, he will attack me," even a superior king should make peace.
If, in the case of peace or war, he does not perceive the weakening of the enemy or his own advancement, even if he is superior, he should remain seated [in neutrality].
If he perceives that the enemy's calamity is incurable, even one who is inferior should march against him.
Or, if his calamity is imminent and cannot be remedied, even a superior king should seek protection.
If one perceives that the accomplishment of an objective can be achieved through peace with one party and war with another, then even a superior king should remain divided.
Thus is the application of the six measures of policy in combination.
But in that case, there is a specific distinction.
When a weak king is attacked by a powerful king who has set his wheel in motion,
he should quickly seek peace through the offering of treasury, army, himself, and territory.
"‘One must present oneself with a self-calculated fine, or by means of the distribution of the army’— this peace treaty is considered one where the enemy is the bait."
"The commander-in-chief and the crown prince must present themselves [to the king]"—this is a treaty with another person, not with oneself; thus it serves for self-protection.
"Either one should go elsewhere alone, or with the army oneself"—
this is the "unseen-person" treaty (*adṛṣṭapuruṣa-saṃdhi*), which provides protection for the commander of the army and for oneself.

In the first two cases, he should effect the capture of the enemy's chief queen; in the last case, however, he should secretly subdue the enemy. These are the treaties concluded with one who has submitted to force.
The liberation of the remaining constituent elements [of the state] by the granting of treasury is a purchase; that indeed is peace, and it may be concluded as desired.
The alliance that can be brought about by the army is to be understood as manifold; it is an "acquisition" (upagraha).
When obstructed by place and time, that acquisition becomes a "transgression" (atyaya).
By giving after enduring [the enemy's force], one becomes capable in the future even when bound by women;
through a golden peace, one attains unity based on mutual trust.
The *kapāla* (the "broken pot") is the opposite of these two: he who takes excessively and speaks with arrogance.
Against these two, one should send base metals or elephants and horses mixed with poison.
In the third year, he should bring wealth while explaining the exhaustion of his undertakings;
he should remain in the fourth year—these are the treaties concluded with one who has surrendered his treasury.
By the surrender of a portion of the territory, the protection of the remaining subjects is ensured;
this is known as the "designated peace" (ādiṣṭasaṃdhi), intended for cases involving secret thieves and assassins.
When territories have been stripped of their resources, the payment of tribute— excluding the root—
is desired from one who has severed his alliances and awaits the calamity of the enemy.
The release of lands through the payment of their produce constitutes a lease;
when the produce is waived, that treaty with respect to the lands is termed "corruption."
One should conduct inspections during the first two watches of the night, but the last two should be spent in vigilance against powerful enemies;
having thus secured the fruits [of policy], these are the treaties concluded with local subjects.

These three types of inferior treaties (*hīna-saṃdhi*), pertaining to the state of one weaker than the enemy (*ābalīyasika*), are prescribed according to place and time, and in accordance with the requirements of one's own objectives. (Thus ends the section on:
sitting after declaring war; sitting after making peace; marching after declaring war; marching after making peace; and marching in concert.)
The states of sitting and marching in the context of peace and war have been explained.
Staying, sitting, and indifference—these are synonyms for *āsana*.
The specific details, however, are as follows: remaining in a single part of the enemy's territory;
sitting down for the purpose of attaining one's own growth;
and indifference, which is the non-employment of strategic means.

When two kings, the enemy and the seeker of conquest, both desire to outmaneuver each other but are unable to strike one another, they should remain on the defensive after either declaring war or making peace.

Or when he perceives: "I am capable of weakening one who is equal or superior by means of my own forces or through the forces of my allies and forest tribes," then, having completed his external and internal preparations, he should remain in a state of war.
