Or when he perceives: "My constituent elements (prakṛtis) are endowed with energy, united, prosperous, and will carry out their own duties without obstruction, or will strike at the undertakings of the enemy," then he should remain in a state of war.

Or when he should perceive: "The subjects of my enemy have been mistreated, impoverished, greedy, or oppressed by their own army, thieves, and forest-dwellers; they will come over to me either spontaneously or through instigation; my own economic resources are flourishing, while those of my enemy are failing."
His subjects, afflicted by famine, will come to me; my means of livelihood have failed, while that of the other has prospered.
"The constituent elements will not desert me;
having declared war, I shall seize his grain, cattle, and gold, or I shall block his foreign merchandise that harms my own trade."
"Or, they will flow from the enemy's trade route and come to me when I am at war, but not otherwise; or, being at war, he will not carry out the suppression of traitors, enemies, or forest tribes."
Or he will encounter conflict with those very same people.

"My ally, being friendly toward me, having marched forth, will acquire wealth with little time, effort, and expenditure, or he will obtain a territory that is excellent and worth seizing."— KAZ07.4.07d.

"Or, if [the enemy], disregarding me, desires to advance with his entire force, how could he not go? Thus, for the sake of checking the enemy's growth and for the sake of demonstrating one's own majesty, one should remain at peace after having declared war.
"For he, once turned back, will surely devour him," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
One should merely cause the emaciation of one who is not in distress; however, when one has grown powerful through the enemy's increase, one may effect total destruction.
In this manner, one who is to be attacked by another should provide assistance to him without being ruined.
Therefore, having seized that which constitutes the source of all gathered forces, one should remain in a state of siege.
When the reasons for remaining encamped after declaring war are reversed, one should make peace and remain encamped.
When he has been strengthened by the causes for remaining in a state of war, he should march after declaring war, with the exception of the mobilization of the entire army.

Or when he should perceive: "The enemy is in distress, or his ministerial distress cannot be remedied by his other ministers; or his own subjects are oppressed by his army, disaffected, weakened, lacking enthusiasm, or divided among themselves, and can thus be enticed."

"Furthermore, when there is a threat from fire, water, disease, pestilence, or famine, and the enemy has depleted his stores of draft animals and men and is engaged in defensive measures, then one should march after declaring war."

Or when he perceives: "My ally and my rear-ally have subjects who are brave, experienced, and loyal, whereas the enemy's rear-ally and his own rear-supporters have subjects of the opposite character; I shall be able to march by engaging the rear-supporter with my ally and the rear-ally with my rear-ally," then he should march after declaring war.

Or, when he perceives that the fruit is to be secured by one party alone and for a short duration, then he should march after having made a formal declaration of war against both the rear-attacker (pārṣṇigrāha) and the ally of the rear-attacker (āsāra).
In the opposite case, he should march after making a treaty.

Or, when he perceives that "it is not possible for me to march alone, yet it is necessary to march," then he should march in conjunction with confederates— whether they be equals, inferiors, or superiors—
with a specified share of the spoils if there is only one confederate,
or with an unspecified share if there are many.
In the absence of their assembly, he should demand a fine from one of them in proportion to the share assigned to him.
Or, they may enter into a joint undertaking and receive their share after the work has been completed; in the case of a certain profit, by the specified portion,
and in the case of an uncertain profit, by a share of that profit.
The share [of the spoils] shall be equal to the army for the first [type of ally], equal to the effort for the best;
or it may be a forfeiture according to the profit, or exactly equal to the investment.
(Considerations regarding the attack on the one to be marched against and the enemy—causes of the decline, greed, and disaffection of the constituent elements—the deliberation on the confederacy.)

KAZ07.5.01: When there is an equal calamity among neighboring kings, one should march against either the *yātavya* (the one to be attacked) or the *amitra* (the enemy); one should march against the *amitra*, and once that is accomplished, [march against] the *yātavya*.
For when an enemy achieves success, the one who is to be attacked should provide assistance; but an enemy does not provide assistance when the one to be attacked achieves success.

Regarding whether one should march against an enemy with a heavy calamity or an ally with a light calamity, the teachers say: "One should march against the one with the heavy calamity because of the ease [of victory]."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
One should march against an enemy who is suffering from a minor calamity.
For even a minor calamity becomes difficult for one who is under attack.
Truth, even if heavy, becomes even heavier.
But an enemy who has not been attacked and whose calamity is slight, having easily remedied his own misfortune, may march against the one to be attacked or seize his rear.

When there is a simultaneous opportunity to march against two enemies—one who is powerful but suffers from a calamity and acts justly, and another who is weak but suffers from a calamity and acts unjustly—the king should march against the one whose subjects are disaffected.
When a ruler who conducts himself according to justice is beset by great calamity, his subjects support him; when one who acts unjustly is beset by minor calamity, they neglect him;
and when they are alienated, they overthrow him even if he is powerful.
Therefore, one should proceed only toward a nature that is dispassionate.

"Between a state whose constituent elements are exhausted and greedy, or one whose constituent elements are rebellious, one should march against the one whose elements are exhausted and greedy; for exhausted and greedy subjects easily succumb to subversion or to oppression, whereas those who are merely rebellious can only be subdued by suppressing their leaders," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
For subjects who are impoverished yet remain affectionate toward their lord will persist in his welfare or frustrate the intrigues of others;
indeed, when there is devotion, all virtues are present.
Therefore, one should proceed only against a constituent who has acted improperly.
Between a strong man who acts unjustly and a weak man who acts justly, one should march against the strong man who acts unjustly.
When one who is powerful but acts unjustly is attacked, the subjects do not support him;
they cause him to fall,
or they resort to his enemy.
But when a weak king conducts himself with justice, the subjects embrace him or follow him even into exile.
By the disparagement of the virtuous, by the promotion of the wicked,
and by the instigation of unjust acts of violence that do not exist [in reality].
By the abandonment of customary practices, by the turning away from those most devoted to dharma, through the pursuit of unrighteousness, and by the suppression of dharma; KAZ07.5.20ab–cd.
By the commission of improper acts, by the neglect of duties that ought to be performed, by the non-payment of what must be given, and by the enforcement of what must not be given; KAZ07.5.21cd.
By failing to punish those deserving of punishment and by punishing those not deserving of it;
by arresting those who should not be arrested and by failing to arrest those who should be arrested.

By causing harm to those who do not seek it, by obstructing those who do, by failing to protect them from thieves, and by personally plundering them; KAZ07.5.23ab/ anarthyānāṃ ca karaṇair arthyānāṃ ca vighātanaiḥ / KAZ07.5.23cd/ arakṣaṇaiś ca corebhyaḥ svayaṃ ca parimoṣaṇaiḥ //
By the failure of human efforts, by the vitiating of the qualities of actions,
by the injury of principal elements, and by the insulting of those worthy of honor.
By opposing the elders, by partiality, by falsehood, by failing to requite what has been done, and by not performing what is established; KAZ07.5.25ab–cd.
Due to the king’s negligence or indolence, or through the destruction of the security and well-being [of the subjects],
the depletion, greed, and alienation of the constituent elements arise.
When the subjects are impoverished, they fall prey to greed; being greedy, they become disaffected.
Once disaffected, they either go over to the enemy or kill their own master themselves.
Therefore, one should not cause the causes of decay, greed, or alienation among the subjects to arise;
or, if they have arisen, one should remedy them immediately.
"The subjects are impoverished, greedy, or disaffected."
Those who are weakened, out of fear of oppression or destruction, immediately favor peace, war, or flight.
Those who are greedy, being dissatisfied due to their greed, seek to instigate treachery against others.
Those who are disaffected rise up against an attack by an enemy.
Among these, the depletion of gold and grain causes total destruction and is difficult to remedy; whereas the loss of draft animals and men can be compensated for by means of gold and grain.
KAZ07.5.34: Greed that is localized and dependent on a specific person can be countered or appropriated when it concerns the wealth of others.
Dispassion is to be accomplished by the restraint of the primary cause (pradhāna).
For when the constituent elements are devoid of a sovereign, they become objects of enjoyment for others and cannot be instigated by them; however, they are unable to endure times of calamity.
But when protected by means of securing the subjects and the chiefs in various ways, they remain secure and capable of enduring calamities.
KAZ07.5.38: Even among those who have formed an alliance, having examined the causes for peace and war, he should march in concert with those who possess both power and integrity.
For one who possesses power is capable of seizing the rear or providing assistance during a march; moreover, being pure, he acts as he has promised whether success is achieved or not.
Regarding those [allies], one should march together with the superior one, or with two equals; between these options, it is better to march with two equals.
For one who is held in check by a superior king acts [submissively], or else, when there is an excess of overreaching by equals, he acts [to counter it].
For it is easy to cause dissension between those two,
and it is easy for one who is wicked to be restrained by the two, as well as to win over their favor through the means of sowing dissension.
KAZ07.5.43: Whether with one equal [ally] or with two inferior ones—it is better to have two inferior ones.
For these two accomplish both objectives and remain under one's control.
But upon the accomplishment of the task—[the spy] should, under a pretext, depart secretly from one who has achieved his purpose and is superior;
however, from one who is impure but behaves with purity, he should wait until his dismissal.
One should withdraw from a confederacy with diligence, having either removed one's wife or the entire force;
for even from a confederacy that has achieved its objective, there may arise danger through misplaced trust.
Even one who has achieved his objective is considered equal to a superior;
moreover, one who is over-extended is untrustworthy, for prosperity causes a change of heart.
Having received even a small share from a superior, he should depart with a satisfied countenance;
or, if he receives no share at all, he should strike at his weak point and seize double the amount.
But when his purpose has been achieved, the leader himself should dismiss his confederates;
even if he should suffer defeat, he must not seek victory, for in this way he remains desired by the circle of states.
(The section on marching in alliance: treaties concluded with or without stipulations, and those involving withdrawal.)
A conqueror seeking victory should thus overreach the second constituent power.
KAZ07.6.02: In a joint expedition, he should engage a neighboring king with the words: "You go from here; I shall go from here;
the gain shall be shared equally."
When the gains are equal, there should be peace; when they are unequal, there should be military action.
KAZ07.6.04: Peace is both negotiated and non-negotiated.
“Go to this place;
I shall go to this place”—this is a contract regarding a specified location.
“You shall exert yourself for this much time, and I shall exert myself for this much time”— this is a contract with a fixed period.
“‘You accomplish this much work;
I shall accomplish this work’—this is a matter of a stipulated agreement.”

Or if he should think: "The enemy will march to a region that is difficult due to mountains, forests, and rivers; obstructed by wilderness; deprived of grain, men, supplies, and reinforcements; lacking fodder, fuel, and water; unknown; remote; of a different character or alien to his own people; or one where the ground is unsuitable for military maneuvers."
If the specific point [of the enemy] is "I am superior," he should enter into a peace treaty with a stipulated territory.

Or if he should think: "The enemy will exert himself during a time that is deficient or excessive for the accomplishment of his tasks— a period characterized by heavy rain, heat, or cold, prone to disease, with food and supplies depleted, and obstructive to military maneuvers—
whereas my own efforts will be directed toward the opposite conditions," then, in view of this distinction, he should enter into a peace treaty with a stipulated time.

Or if he should think: "The other will accomplish an undertaking that is liable to be revoked, provocative of internal unrest, long-lasting, involving great loss and expense, yielding little benefit, followed by harm, unwholesome, contrary to righteousness, opposed by intermediate and neutral powers, or destructive to his allies."
If the specific point "I am the opposite" is staked as the object of the agreement, one should enter into a peace treaty.
Thus, by establishing the conditions of place and time, time and action, place and action, and place, time, and action, the counter-stipulation (paripaṇita) is of seven kinds.
In that situation, having already commenced and established his own operations, he should exert himself against the operations of the enemy.

KAZ07.6.13: One who desires to overreach an enemy—whether that enemy is beset by calamity, haste, humiliation, or indolence, or is simply ignorant—should not fix a specific place, time, or task, but rather declare, "We are allied," and having gained the enemy's confidence through this treaty, strike when an opportunity for a weakness is found; this is the "unpledged" (aparipaṇita) treaty.
In this regard, the following occurs:
Having engaged one neighbor in hostilities by means of another neighbor, the wise king should then seize the land of the other, having cut off his support from all sides.

KAZ07.6.16: Regarding peace, there is the desire not to conclude it, the consolidation of what has been concluded, the subversion of what has been concluded, and the action against one who has fallen away.
KAZ07.6.17: Of the three types of military prowess, there is open battle, treacherous battle, and silent battle.
Thus end the sections on peace and military expedition.

KAZ07.6.19: Seeking peace through means such as conciliation (*sāman*) and others, along with their respective adjuncts, for a peace not previously concluded; and the stabilization of equals, inferiors, and superiors according to their relative strength—this is "the desire to act where none has been done."

The consolidation of what has been done consists of protecting both sides through favors and benefits, following through on the agreements as they were discussed, and ensuring their preservation so that "he may not be alienated from the other," thereby cementing the alliance.
Having established the enemy's untrustworthiness by means of deceiving his own seditious elements, one commits a transgression; this is "the act of creating a pretext" (*kṛtavidūṣaṇa*).
KAZ07.6.22: Reconciliation with a servant or a friend who has departed due to an offense constitutes the act of mending what is broken.
Regarding that [attainment], there are four types of going and returning: one who goes and returns for a reason;
the opposite;
one who goes for a reason but returns without a reason; and—
And it is also contrary.

One who has gone away due to the fault of his own master but returned due to his merit, or who has gone away due to the merit of another but returned due to his fault—such a person is one who has "gone and returned for a specific cause," and he should be made peace with.
One who has come and gone due to his own fault, having abandoned the merits of both sides, and who comes and goes without cause, being of fickle intellect, is not to be allied with.

KAZ07.6.26: One who has come from another due to his master’s fault, yet has returned due to his own fault, should be scrutinized on the grounds that he left for a reason but returned without one: "Is he instigated by the enemy or acting out of his own malice, wishing to cause harm;
or has he come out of fear of retaliation, knowing me to be an enemy intent on destroying him; or has he abandoned the enemy, who desires to destroy me, and come out of compassion?"
Having ascertained that he is of noble intent, one should honor him; if he is of contrary intent, one should cause him to dwell in a degraded place.

"He departed due to his own fault and has returned due to the fault of another"; thus, one who left without cause and returns for a cause should be scrutinized [with the thought]: "He will fill my vulnerability; he is accustomed to living here; people there do not please him."
"I am allied with my friends, at variance with my enemies,
and alarmed by one who is greedy and cruel, or by another who is allied with the enemy."
Having ascertained [the truth], he should be established according to his understanding.

“Loss of what has been done, loss of power, making knowledge a commodity for sale, despair regarding expectations, longing for another country, lack of trust, or conflict with a stronger power—these are grounds for abandonment,” so say the teachers (KAZ 7.6.30).
Fear, lack of livelihood, and resentment, says Kauṭilya (KAZ 7.6.31).

In this case, one who has done harm is to be abandoned; one who has done harm to the enemy is to be made peace with; and one who has done harm to both is to be scrutinized—this is the same [as previously stated].
But when one must necessarily make peace with a person with whom it should not be made, one should provide a counter-measure from whichever side possesses superior power.

One should provide shelter for a member of the enemy's faction who has been assisted, separated, or protected, on the grounds that his life is at its end, under the pretext of performing funeral rites for one who has passed away.
Or he may incite his master against him, or instigate a successful spy who is moving with the army.
One should employ them against enemies or forest tribes, or else cast them out to the frontiers.
He may sell merchandise that is either unprepared or prepared, provided it is covered by that [deposit].
Because of that very fault, even though he himself is blameless, he must be reconciled with the enemy for the sake of a strategic purpose.
Alternatively, one should pacify him through secret means for the sake of the future.
And seeing one who intends to kill him in the future, he should slay that person even if they have merely come and gone.
A danger arising from an enemy who has arrived from abroad is caused by living in association with that foe.
Because his nature is like that of living with a snake, he is perpetually defiled by agitation.
It arises from eating the seeds of a *plakṣa* tree, just as [lac] comes from the *śālmali* tree because of the pigeon.
It constantly produces agitation and brings fear even later on.
Open warfare is the display of prowess at a specified place and time.
A surprise attack causes terror and afflicts those who are negligent or in distress.
Abandoning one side and striking the other is the fundamental principle of treacherous warfare.
The characteristics of silent war (*tūṣṇīṃ-yuddha*) are for the purpose of secret maneuvers and instigation. (Thus end the methods of peace and war pertaining to the dual policy.
The conqueror should win over the second constituent power (*prakṛti*) in this manner.
KAZ07.7.02: He should march in concert with a neighboring king, or if he should think: "He will not seize my rear, or he will ward off the one who seizes my rear."
The one to be marched against will not come to his aid;
my own forces will become doubled; and he will provide me with supplies and reinforcements.
He will ward off the enemy;
he will crush the thorns on my path, which is beset by many afflictions; and he will move with his army through difficult terrains, forests, and retreats.
"Having incurred an intolerable fault, he will either enter into peace or,
having secured a share of the spoils, he will inspire confidence in my other enemies."
Or, having divided his forces, he may seek to obtain the army from one neighbor by means of his treasury, or the treasury from one neighbor by means of his army.

Among them, a treaty made with one superior on the basis of a larger share, with an equal on the basis of an equal share, and with an inferior on the basis of a smaller share, is called a "treaty of equality" (*sama-saṃdhi*).
In the opposite case, it is an unequal treaty.
An over-reach occurs when one of those two gains a specific advantage.
A weaker king should bargain with a stronger king who is beset by calamities, stuck in a disadvantageous position, or unwilling to act, by offering a gain equal to his own strength.
If one who has been purchased is capable of harming him, he should exert force;
otherwise, he should enter into an alliance.

In such a situation, a weaker king, for the purpose of replenishing his deficient power and majesty, or to secure support from a reliable ally, or to protect his base and rear, should bargain with a superior king by offering a gain distinguished by its strength.
One who has been purchased should favor a person of virtuous intent;
otherwise, he should act with force.

When a weaker king—whether his superior enemy has met with a calamity, has weaknesses among his constituent elements, or is beset by impending misfortune; or whether the weaker king himself is blocked by a fort or an ally and desires to travel a short distance; or when he wishes to seize a gain that is certain and requires no battle from the enemy—he should bargain for peace with the superior power using a force inferior to what he possesses and accepting a gain less than his full strength.
If one who has been purchased is capable of harming him, he should exert force;
otherwise, he should enter into a treaty.

KAZ07.7.13: Or, one who is superior and free from vulnerabilities or calamities—desiring to further burden with loss and expense an inferior who has undertaken difficult tasks; desiring to send away the army of a seditious person; desiring to bring in the army of a seditious person; desiring to afflict or destroy an inferior; or a superior of virtuous intent who prioritizes peace with an inferior—[should act accordingly].
One should accept the gain.
One who possesses a virtuous disposition should seek to acquire wealth by joining with others;
otherwise, he should employ forceful action.
In this manner, one who is equal should either outmaneuver or favor an equal.

KAZ07.7.16: One should bargain for an equal share of the booty with one of equal force, whether for the purpose of providing a counter-force against the enemy's army or for forest tribes, or for a guide to the enemy's various territories, or for the protection of the base and the rear.
A suitor should favor one who possesses a virtuous disposition;
otherwise, he should proceed with force.

One who is equal in strength to another, or one who is weaker, should make a pact for gain with a superior power if that superior is suffering from a calamity, has vulnerable subjects, or is opposed by many others, or if he can obtain support from elsewhere.
If one who has been made an offer is capable of harming the other, he should display his prowess; otherwise, he should enter into a treaty.
Or, being thus situated, he should remain neutral while entrusting his affairs to his neighbors; or, having prepared his forces, he should bargain for a gain superior to that of his rival army.
A suitor should favor one who possesses a virtuous disposition; otherwise, he should proceed with force.

One who desires to strike at the enemy’s vulnerabilities—such as those arising from calamities or internal weaknesses—or one who wishes to frustrate the enemy’s own undertaken enterprise that is certain of success;

or one who wishes to strike at the enemy’s base or during his expedition; or one who, obtaining more than expected from the enemy to be attacked, seeks further from a superior, inferior, or equal power—should demand more.

Or, having been requested further, if he desires to crush by means of the enemy's army another fort that is difficult to attack, a supply base, or a forest region for the sake of protecting his own forces; or if he desires to subject the enemy's army to loss and expense over a long distance or time; or if, having grown strong by means of the enemy's army, he desires to destroy that very same enemy; or if he desires to seize the enemy's army for himself—he should give more.
Or, a superior king who desires to bring an inferior one under his control under the pretext of a campaign against another, or who desires to destroy that very person after first destroying another,
or who, having made a cession, desires to recover it, should bargain for a gain distinguished by superior force.
If one who has been made an enemy is capable of inflicting harm upon him, he should exert military force;
otherwise, he should enter into a treaty.
Or he may remain allied with the enemy to be attacked, or he may provide him with a force consisting of seditious persons, enemies, forest tribes, or a punitive expedition.
Or, a superior king who has suffered a calamity or whose constituent elements are in disorder should bargain with an inferior king for an equal share of the force in exchange for a gain.
If one who has been made an enemy is capable of inflicting harm upon him, he should attack;
otherwise, he should enter into a treaty.
When such a person is inferior, a superior king should bargain with that inferior for a gain equal to his own strength.
If one who has been insulted is capable of retaliating against the offender, he should strike back; otherwise, he should make peace.
At the outset, both the one who has offered a wager and the one who is accepting it should ascertain the underlying reason.
KAZ07.7.31cd: Having deliberated on both sides, he should proceed toward that which is more beneficial.

(The Conduct of the Invader; Specifics Regarding Allies to Be Favored) KAZ07.8.01: An invader who is about to march, desiring to secure the cause for peace or wishing to disrupt [the enemy], should bargain with one of the confederates by offering double the profit.
While bargaining, he should describe to him the loss, expenditure, travel, legal obstacles, services rendered to others, and physical hardships involved.
One should provide the one who has approached with the object.
Or, having caused them to incur enmity with others, he should cause them to be betrayed.
One who has joined with an enemy (the *yātavya*) may, desiring to further subject an opponent whose undertakings have begun poorly to greater loss and expense,

or wishing to frustrate the success of an expedition already begun by him, or intending to strike at his base or during his expedition, or desiring to request [terms] again after having been reconciled, or being in difficulty regarding present resources, or lacking confidence in him, may seek only a small immediate profit from that [enemy].
Abundant in the future.

Considering the benefit to a friend, the injury to an enemy, and the subsequent consequences for wealth, one who wishes to cause a former benefactor to act again should, disregarding a great immediate gain, desire only a small gain in the future.

If one desires to protect a king who is at war with a seditious person, an enemy, or a superior power that seizes his very roots; or if one desires to cause such a king to perform a service in return; or if one considers the relationship and sees a benefit both in the present and for the future, one should not accept a gift from him.

KAZ07.8.08: Having made a treaty, one who wishes to violate it—desiring to weaken the enemy's constituent elements, or wishing to cause a breach between the enemy's ally and foe, or fearing an attack from the enemy—should demand a profit not yet obtained, or one that is excessive.
The other [party] should consider the sequence of that [action] both in the present and in the future.
By this, the preceding cases have been explained.

But between the enemy and the conqueror, both of whom are favoring their respective friends, the distinction lies in whether those friends undertake feasible, timely, and promising enterprises, whether they possess steadfastness in action, and whether their subjects are loyal.

One who undertakes what is possible begins a task that can be endured; one who undertakes with vigor begins a faultless task; one who undertakes with capability begins a task that results in auspiciousness.
One of steady action does not desist from his task until it has been completed.
One whose subjects are devoted accomplishes his task even with a small favor, because of the assistance provided by them.
These, having achieved their purpose, serve him both easily and abundantly.
Therefore, those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) are not to be favored.
KAZ07.8.17: Of these two, when favoring one person, he who favors a friend or a closer friend gains the advantage.
For from a friend one obtains personal advancement, whereas the other [the enemy] suffers loss, expense, exile, and assistance rendered to another.
And an enemy whose purpose has been achieved falls into a state of deficiency.
KAZ07.8.20: But of two who favor the middle [king], he who favors the middle king as a friend or as a closer friend gains the advantage.
For from a friend one obtains personal advancement, whereas the other incurs loss, expense, exile, and service to another.
If the middle king is favored but becomes deficient in quality, the enemy overreaches him.
For one obtains a middle enemy who has exerted effort, retreated, and then approached for a common purpose.
By this, the favoring of a neutral king is explained.

KAZ07.8.25: When providing a portion of the army to either a middle king or a neutral king, he who gives an army that is brave, skilled in weapons, capable of enduring hardship, or loyal, is overreached.
One who acts in the opposite manner gains the upper hand.

But where an army has been dispatched and it accomplishes that objective as well as others, there he should provide one of the following forces— hereditary troops, hired troops, guilds, allies, or forest-dwellers— having secured the appropriate place and time;
or else he should provide the force of enemies or forest-dwellers when the place and time are distant.
But regarding one whom he might think: "Having achieved his purpose, he would seize my army,
or he would station it in enemy territory, in forest regions, or on ground unsuitable for the season,
or he would render it fruitless," [he should act accordingly].
He should not favor him under the pretext of being occupied with the administration of justice.
KAZ07.8.29: Thus, if he must necessarily be favored, one should give him a punishment that can be endured at that particular time.
And until the conclusion [of the campaign], he should cause him to dwell there, make him fight, and protect him from calamities to his army.
And once his purpose has been accomplished, he should cause him to depart under some pretext.
Or he should provide him with a force consisting of seditious persons, enemies, and forest tribes.
Or, having made peace with the one who is to be attacked, he should overreach him.
For when the gain is equal, peace should be made; when it is unequal, military action is considered appropriate.
The treaties and military expeditions of those who are equal, inferior, or superior have thus been described.
(This concludes the section on treaties for allies, gold, land, and undertakings;
therein, the treaty for an ally and the treaty for gold.)
KAZ07.9.01: In an expedition undertaken with a confederate, each subsequent gain among the acquisition of a friend, gold, or territory is superior to the preceding one.
For both an ally and gold result from the acquisition of land; an ally results from the acquisition of gold.
Or rather, whatever profit has been established accomplishes one of the two remaining [goals].
“Both you and I shall obtain a friend”—this and similar [formulations] constitute a treaty of equality (*sama-saṃdhi*).
“Thou art my friend,” and so forth—this is an unequal treaty (*viṣama-saṃdhi*).
A superior bargain results from obtaining a specific advantage over those two.
But in a treaty of equality, he who acquires a prosperous ally, or an ally in the midst of a friend's distress, overreaches the other.
For adversity indeed produces steadfastness in friendship.

Regarding whether one should choose a constant but unsubmissive ally or an occasional but submissive one even when faced with difficulty, the teachers maintain: "A constant but unsubmissive ally is better, for even though he does not provide assistance, he does no harm."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Control is transient; self-mastery is better.
One is a friend only so long as one provides assistance;
for a friend is defined by the characteristic of being helpful.
Even between two submissive [wives], there is a choice between one who provides great enjoyment but is unstable and one who provides little enjoyment but is constant.
"Greater wealth, though impermanent, is better; for by providing great assistance in a short time, it compensates for large expenditures," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
It is better to have constant, meager enjoyment.
One who possesses great wealth may depart out of fear of providing assistance,
or having provided assistance, he may seek to recover it.
That which yields little enjoyment constantly, by providing small assistance continuously, renders great assistance over a long period of time.
"Is a great ally arising from a superior source better, or a small one arising from an inferior source? "A great ally arising from a superior source brings about prestige;
and when he rises up, he accomplishes the task," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
That which arises with little effort and is small is better.
A minor ally produced by force does not let the time for action pass by, and due to its weakness, it can be enjoyed at will;
the other type, one rooted in superior territory, is not so.
Regarding whether the army is scattered or under control, the teachers maintain: "A scattered army can be rallied because it remains obedient."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
An army that is under one's own control is better.
For it is certainly possible to bring [the enemy] under control by means of conciliation and the other [strategic measures],
but it is not possible to withdraw [one's own force] when it is already engaged in action.

Regarding whether a friend who provides human resources or one who provides financial resources is superior, the teachers maintain: "A friend who provides human resources is better; such a friend brings about prestige, and when he rises up, he accomplishes the task. (KAZ07.9.26)
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A friend who provides wealth in gold is better.
For the possession of gold is constant, whereas that of the rod [of punishment] is occasional.
For through punishment, gold and other desired objects are obtained.

Regarding whether a friend should be one who provides wealth or one who provides land, the teachers say: "A friend who provides wealth is preferable because, being mobile, he can counteract all expenditures."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
It has been stated previously that both an ally and gold result from the acquisition of land.
Therefore, an ally who provides land-enjoyment is better.
When the enjoyment of men is equal, the distinction [of one over another] arises from valor, endurance of hardship, loyalty, or the acquisition of all types of forces from the circle of allies.
When the enjoyment of gold is equal, the distinction lies in the attainment of desired objects, abundance, the smallness of effort required, and continuity.
In this regard, the following occurs:
Constantly submissive, quick to rise, inherited from father and grandfather, great, and free from duplicity— a friend endowed with these qualities is said to possess the six attributes.
That which is protected out of affection even when it serves no purpose, and which one protects because of a previously established relationship— that friend is called "constant."
All types of diverse and great enjoyments are said to be of three kinds of subjugation:
those enjoyed from one side, those enjoyed from both sides, and another which is enjoyed from all sides.
Whether as a receiver or even as a giver, one who lives by harming enemies possesses a friend that is constant, indispensable, and capable of escaping from forts and forests.
That ally who is attacked by another, or is in a minor state of distress,
and makes peace for the sake of assistance, is submissive but unstable.
Furthermore, that which is connected with a single objective and does not change its nature even when the beneficiary changes—
this becomes a "friend-like" ally (*mitrabhāvin*), an ally who remains undivided in times of calamity.

A friend is certain [to remain] a friend because of his friendly disposition, but he is unstable because of his commonality with the enemy. One who is neutral belongs to neither; he may become either of the two.
For a seeker of victory, that enemy who has become a friend through mediation,
or one who is either uncommitted to providing assistance or incapable of doing so, is of no benefit.
That friend whom one favors— whether it be someone dear to another, worthy of protection, deserving of honor, or even merely connected to them— is indeed common to both friend and foe.
That which possesses excellent territory, is contented, powerful, and yet indolent becomes indifferent [to the conqueror] when it is afflicted by calamity or treated with contempt.
That which, due to weakness, follows the growth of both the enemy and the leader,
and is disliked by neither— know that it will belong to both.
He who neglects a friend who has been ruined by causes or non-causes, or who has come from causes or non-causes, embraces his own death.

Regarding whether a small gain quickly is better than a large gain after a long time, the teachers say: "A small gain quickly is better, for it accords with the requirements of the task, the place, and the time."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A great gain that comes after a long time but is not subject to failure is superior, being like a seed; in the opposite case, the former [immediate gain] is better.
Having thus observed that gain is certain and that an increase in merit will arise from both the gain itself and its portion,
one intent on achieving one's own objective should march forth in alliance with the confederates.
(The treaties concerning allies, gold, land, and undertakings.)
In that regard, (the treaty for land:
KAZ07.10.01 / “Both you and I shall acquire land”—this is a treaty for land.
Of these two, he who achieves his objective as it presents itself and attains the desired ground overcomes the other.
KAZ07.10.03: When the acquisition of wealth is equal for both, he who seizes the territory by attacking the stronger party achieves over-reach (*atisaṃdhatte*).
For he indeed attains the acquisition of territory, the weakening of enemies, and majesty.
KAZ07.10.05: When land is acquired from a weak ruler, there is indeed ease.
Moreover, the acquisition of territory is indeed weak;
furthermore, its neighboring king becomes an enemy to one's friend.
KAZ07.10.07: When the strength is equal, he who, having uprooted an enemy, acquires the land, gains a superior advantage.
For the acquisition of a fort indeed effects the protection of one's own territory and the suppression of enemies and forest tribes.
In the acquisition of land from a mobile enemy, there is a distinction [to be made] regarding a conquerable neighbor.
For a weak neighbor has resources for security and prosperity that can be quickly replenished.
Conversely, a territory that possesses powerful neighbors and is subject to the depletion of its treasury and army is unfavorable.

Regarding whether land that is well-endowed but has permanent enemies is better than land that is less endowed but has temporary enemies, the teachers maintain: "Land that is well-endowed but has permanent enemies is superior; for such land produces both the treasury and the army, and these two are the means for repelling enemies."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
KAZ07.10.14: When one fails to obtain a constant enemy, there arises the acquisition of many enemies.
A natural enemy remains an enemy whether one does him a favor or an injury;
however, an incidental enemy is pacified by a favor or by the absence of injury.

For that territory whose borders are constantly occupied by many forts belonging to bands of thieves, barbarians, or forest-dwellers is a permanent enemy; however, in the opposite case, it is a temporary enemy.
Regarding land that is either small and nearby or large and distant, the small and nearby is better.
For it is indeed easy to acquire, to protect, and to mobilize [an army].
The contrary [type] is the interrupted one.

KAZ07.10.20: Even between two lands that are distant from one another, both may serve as a basis for maintaining the army or for maintaining oneself; however, a land that maintains itself is superior.
For it is supported by its own treasury and army.
KAZ07.10.22: The application of punishment in a manner contrary [to the rules] is a ground for the infliction of punishment [upon the king].
Regarding the acquisition of territory from either a fool or a wise man, the acquisition of territory from a fool is better.
For it is easily acquired, easy to maintain, and cannot be taken back.
One who is devoted but contrary to a wise man is the opposite [of a good wife].
Between one who is to be oppressed and one who is to be destroyed, the acquisition of territory from the one who is to be destroyed is better.
For one who is to be exterminated—being without support or having weak support—and who, when attacked, desires to flee after seizing his treasury and army, is abandoned by his subjects;
however, one who is to be harassed, being obstructed by a fort and allies, is not so abandoned.
KAZ07.10.28: Even between two [forts] that are equally well-established, the acquisition of territory from one situated on land is better than from one situated by a river.
For this [fortress] situated on a plateau is easy to defend, difficult to crush, and hard to storm, and its enemy cannot be heard of.
A river-fort, however, causes double the hardship;
moreover, the water must be drunk by the enemy and serves as his means of sustenance.
Between gains of territory from those situated in river-fortresses and mountain-fortresses, gain of territory from a river-fortress is better.
For a river-fortress can be overcome by means of elephant-trappings, pillars, bridges, embankments, and boats; its depth is unstable, and its water can be drained away.
But a mountain fort is self-defending, difficult to besiege, and hard to scale;
when one part is broken, there is no total destruction,
and stones and trees can be hurled at great wrongdoers.
KAZ07.10.34: For those who fight in low ground or marshy terrain, the acquisition of land is better than for those who fight on level ground.
For those who fight in low ground are restricted by place and time, whereas those who fight on firm ground can fight at all places and times.
Between those who fight from underground and those who fight from the open air, it is better for the conqueror to gain the land from the underground fighters.
For miners fight both with their excavations and with weapons, whereas those who fight in the open air fight with weapons alone.
A knower of the science of polity who acquires land from such persons as described above gains a distinct advantage over others who have formed alliances for the sake of wealth, gold, or territory.
(Alliances for friends, gold, land, and undertakings; therein, the alliance for land that is not yet settled.)
“Both you and I shall cause the settlement to become empty”—this is a negotiation whose conclusion has not been finalized.
Of these two, he who settles upon a territory possessing the aforementioned qualities when the opportunity has presented itself gains the advantage.
In that case as well, between dry land and water, dry land is better than a small amount of water,
because its fruits are constant and reliably available.
Between two tracts of land, that which has abundant crops from both the previous and subsequent seasons, requires little rain for ripening, and can be cultivated without difficulty is superior.
KAZ07.11.05: Even between two types of watered land, sowing grain is better than sowing non-grain.
KAZ07.11.06: Regarding the relative quantity of these two, a large area that is not favorable for grain is better than a small area that is favorable for grain.
For in a large space, both cultivated plants and wild herbs grow in a cooking pot.
Furthermore, works such as fortifications and the like are carried out with abundant resources.
For the qualities of the land are indeed artificial.
Between the enjoyment of mines and the enjoyment of grain, the enjoyment of mines produces revenue for the treasury,
whereas the enjoyment of grain produces revenue for both the treasury and the granary.
For the undertakings of works such as fortifications have grain as their foundation.
Alternatively, the sale of a large territory or the enjoyment of a mine is better.
“Between the enjoyment of timber forests and elephant forests, the enjoyment of timber forests is the source of all undertakings and is capable of providing abundant stores;
the enjoyment of elephant forests is the opposite,” so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
It is possible to plant various kinds of timber trees on various plots of land,
but not so with elephant forests.
For the destruction of the enemy's army depends primarily upon elephants.
Between the enjoyment of water routes and land routes, the enjoyment of water routes is unstable, whereas the enjoyment of land routes is stable.
Between land inhabited by alien people and land inhabited by guildspeople, that inhabited by alien people is better.
When the people are divided, she becomes enjoyable [to the conqueror], cannot be instigated by others, but is unable to endure calamities.
Guilds and common people who have become hostile are a source of great danger when provoked to anger.

In that settlement of the four castes, one consisting mostly of the lower castes is better because it can endure all types of exploitation; one with many cultivators is better due to the abundance and stability of agriculture;
and one with many cattle-herders is better because they provide the impetus for both agriculture and other undertakings.
It is like a wealthy merchant who has acquired riches through the accumulation of merchandise, the granting of loans, and acts of favor.
Among the qualities of land, having a place of refuge is the best.
Between land that relies on fortifications and land that relies on men, land that relies on men is superior.
For a kingdom is indeed like a person.
KAZ07.11.25: How could a cow that has no owner yield milk, any more than a barren woman?

But one who desires to acquire land involving great destruction, expense, and settlement should first negotiate with a buyer who is weak, lacks royal lineage, is devoid of energy, lacks supporters, is unjust in conduct, addicted to vices, superstitious, or acts impulsively.
For when a weak scion of royalty settles on land characterized by great destruction, expense, and hardship, he perishes along with his allied subjects due to that destruction and expense.
A powerful man who lacks royal lineage is abandoned by his subjects, even if they are otherwise loyal, out of fear of the loss of territory and the depletion of resources.
But one who lacks energy, even if he possesses an army, fails to employ it; thus, though possessing an army, he is consumed by loss and expense.
Even one who possesses a treasury, if he lacks allies, achieves nothing because he is deprived of the benefits of reducing losses and expenditures.
One who acts unjustly may cause even a settled person to rise up [in revolt].
How, then, should he settle those who have not yet settled?
By this, one who is addicted to vices is explained.
One who relies solely on fate, lacks human effort, or fails to undertake or properly completes his undertakings, comes to ruin.
One who does whatever comes along achieves nothing at all.
And he is the most wicked among them.
“Whatever a seeker of victory undertakes, he may at some point encounter a vulnerability,” so say the teachers.
"Just as there is a vulnerability, so too may destruction be incurred," says Kauṭilya.
In their absence, he should station his troops on the ground in the manner we shall describe regarding the seizure of a rear-ally (*pārṣṇigrāha*).
Thus concludes the treaty concluded under compulsion.
If he is requested by a powerful person for fertile or revenue-yielding land at a purchase price, he should establish a treaty and grant it.
Thus ends the section on unstable peace.

Or, when requested by an equal, he may grant it after considering the cause, thinking: "This land is recoverable by me or is under my control; through this [gift], my enemy will be obstructed and thus come under my control; or, from the sale of the land, I shall obtain friends and gold that will enable me to accomplish my objectives."
By this, the purchaser who is deficient [in the required qualities] is explained.

In this manner, one who knows the treatise, while obtaining a friend, gold, and cattle— whether with or without their owners— outmaneuvers his confederates. (The Treatises on Peace through Friends, Gold, and Land)
Among these, the treaty of joint action (*karma-saṃdhi*) is as follows:
"You and I shall both construct a fort"—this is a treaty of joint action.
Of these two, he who constructs a fort that is divinely ordained, impregnable, and requires little expenditure and effort, gains the advantage.
Even among those, each subsequent type of fort—land, river, and mountain—is superior to the preceding one.
Between a dam and a water-diversion channel, that which has its own water source is superior to one that relies on water drawn from elsewhere.
Even between two fields that are equally well-watered, the one with a larger area for sowing is superior.

KAZ07.12.06: Furthermore, between a source of raw materials and a forest, he who cuts down a forest of raw materials located at the border of the territory—which possesses large and high-quality materials and is sustained by rivers—gains a superior advantage.
For a livelihood dependent on rivers provides both one's own means of subsistence and a refuge in times of distress.

KAZ07.12.08: Furthermore, he who binds an elephant forest at the edge of his territory—one that contains many brave wild animals, has weak neighbors, and causes endless harassment—secures a great advantage.
Even in that case, between one who has many cowards and one who has few heroes, the one with few heroes is better;
for battle is fought among heroes,
and few heroes can break many cowards.
"Once broken, they become destroyers of their own army," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.

KAZ07.12.11: Many who are blunt [in spirit] are superior, for by being assigned to specific divisions they perform various tasks; they provide support for their own side in battle, and they are difficult for enemies to overcome and cause them terror.
For when many are dull-witted, valor can be instilled through disciplinary action; however, it is not possible to achieve the same by merely increasing the number of those who are already brave.
Between two mines as well, he who causes a mine to be excavated that possesses abundant minerals, lacks difficult access, and requires little expenditure and effort, gains the advantage.

In that regard as well, concerning whether [an item] is of great value and small in quantity, or of little value and abundant, the teachers say: "A small amount of great value is better; for a large quantity of little value—such as diamonds, gems, pearls, coral, gold, silver, and ores—is swallowed up by its high price."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
After a long time, a buyer for high-quality goods is found to be few, whereas buyers for low-quality goods are numerous due to their constant demand.
By this, the merchant's route is explained.

Regarding that as well, the teachers say: "Between the water-route and the land-route, the water-route is superior, as it involves less expenditure and labor, and yields a greater profit from merchandise."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The water-route has its passage obstructed, is not available at all times, is a source of great fear, and is beyond remedy;
the land-route is the opposite of this.
Regarding water routes, between the coastal route and the river route, the coastal route is superior due to the abundance of market towns;
or else, the river route is preferable because of its continuity and because it is free from oppressive disturbances.

Regarding the land route as well, the teachers maintain that "the region of the Himalayas is superior to the Deccan, for its commodities— elephants, horses, sandalwood, ivory, skins, silver, and gold— are more substantial."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
KAZ07.12.24: With the exception of blankets, skins, and horses, commodities such as conch shells, diamonds, gems, pearls, and gold are more abundant in the Deccan.

KAZ07.12.25: Even in the Deccan region, a trade route that has many mines, valuable merchandise, established access, low expenses and effort, or one with abundant territory and light goods, is preferable.
By this, the eastern and western trade routes have been explained.
In that case as well, between a cart-track and a footpath, the cart-track is superior because it involves a large-scale undertaking;
or else, a path for donkeys and camels is preferable when considering the requirements of the place and time.
By these two, the shoulder-paths (aṃsapatha) are explained.
When the leader undertakes the work of another, there is loss; in the opposite case, there is gain.
When the course of action is equal, the seeker of victory should know that his own position is superior.
When income is small and expenditure is excessive, there is depletion; in the opposite case, there is growth.
Balance between income and expenditure is to be understood as one's own standing in undertakings.
Therefore, among forts and other such works, one should undertake that which involves little expenditure but yields great profit.
KAZ07.12.34: "By performing his duty, one may become distinguished"—thus have been explained the conjunctions of action (*karma-saṃdhayaḥ*). (The consideration of the rear-attacker).
KAZ07.13.01: When two enemies, both seeking victory and attacking another, join together and attack from the rear, he who attacks the rear of the one endowed with superior power gains the advantage.
For one endowed with power, having destroyed the frontal enemy, may then destroy the rear-attacker; but one who is deficient in power and has not yet gained his objective cannot do so.
When power is equal, he who takes the rear of one who has undertaken a vast enterprise gains the advantage.

For one who undertakes a vast enterprise, having destroyed the enemy, may then destroy the rear-attacker; but one who undertakes a small enterprise cannot do so, being hindered by the wheel of the enemy's forces.
KAZ07.13.05: When the initial undertaking is equal, he who seizes the rear of one who has marched forth with his entire host gains the advantage.
For one whose base is depleted is easy to overcome,
unlike one who has marched with a portion of his army and has already made arrangements for the protection of his rear.
When the acquisition of force is equal, he who seizes the rear of one who has marched against a mobile enemy achieves the superior advantage.
For one who marches against a mobile enemy achieves success with ease and can destroy the rear-attacker, whereas one who marches against a stationary enemy cannot do so.
For he, having been repelled by a fort and turned back toward his rear-guard, is hemmed in by the enemy who remains stationed there.
By this, the preceding [cases] have been explained.
When there is equality between two enemies, he who seizes the rear of the one attacking the righteous king gains the advantage.
For one who brings a righteous accusation becomes hateful to both his own people and to others, whereas one who brings an unrighteous accusation is well-liked.
By this, the seizure of the rear by those who seize the root, those who act for immediate gain, and the miserly litigants is explained.
The same reasons apply for seizing the rear of two kings who are attacking their ally.
KAZ07.13.15: Of two kings attacking each other—one a friend and the other an enemy—he who seizes the rear of the one attacking his friend achieves a superior advantage.
For one who attacks an ally, having easily achieved his objective, may destroy the rear-attacker.
For peace with a friend is easy to achieve, but not so with an enemy.
Of two who are rescuing both a friend and an enemy, he who seizes the rear of the one rescuing the enemy gains the advantage.
For one who has many aged friends and can extricate himself from enemies will destroy the rear-attacker,
whereas the other, who harms his own side, will not.

KAZ07.13.20: Of these two, in the event that neither gains what they have not yet obtained, he whose enemy is deprived of a great gain or incurs excessive loss and expense shall overreach the rear-attacker (pārṣṇigrāha).
KAZ07.13.21: When a gain has been acquired and subsequently lost, he whose enemy is deprived of that gain and its power gains the advantage over the rear-attacker;
or rather, he against whom the one to be marched against is capable of waging war and inflicting injury upon the enemy gains the advantage.
Between the two rear-attackers as well, he who possesses superior resources for undertaking what is feasible and has an entrenched enemy or one stationed at his side gains the advantage.
For one who stands at the side is both an ally to the enemy to be marched against and a harasser of the [attacker's] base;
whereas one who stands in the rear is merely a harasser of the base.
KAZ07.13.24ab: Three rear-enemy types (pārṣṇigrāhas) are to be known as those who obstruct the enemy’s movements:
the neighbor (sāmanta) from behind, the group (varga) from the rear, and the two neighbors on the flanks (prativeśas).
A weak king situated between the enemy and the leader is called a "hiding place" (antardhi);
he serves as a defense for the powerful one by providing forts, forests, and places of retreat.

KAZ07.13.26: When the conqueror and the one seeking conquest both desire the middle king, and while seizing the middle king's rear, one prevents the middle king from losing what he has gained, thereby separating the middle king from his friend and securing an enemy as a friend, that king overreaches the other.
An enemy who is providing assistance should be made peace with,
but not a friend who has overstepped the bounds of friendship.
By this, the desire for neutrality is explained.
But in the cases of seizing the rear or launching an attack, there is an advantage over a war of intrigue.
For in a war of physical exertion, there is no gain for either side due to the loss of men and the expenditure of resources.
"Even after winning, one whose army and treasury are exhausted is defeated," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Even at the cost of immense loss and expense, the destruction of the enemy must be pursued.

When the loss and expenditure are equal, he who first causes the enemy's treacherous forces to be destroyed and, being free from internal thorns, subsequently fights with his own loyal forces, gains the superior advantage.

Between two [kings] who both intend to strike the enemy's forces from the front, he who causes the death of the more numerous, the more powerful, and the most corruptible [faction] achieves the superior advantage.
By this, the destruction of the forces of enemies and forest tribes is explained.
When the rear-attacker, the aggressor, or the one to be attacked becomes desirous of conquest, then the conqueror should employ this guiding policy therein.

The rear-guard leader should become the guide for the enemy who is attacking an ally; having first caused a conflict between the rear-guard leader and the rear-attacker, he should then strike the ally's rear.
By employing an ally (ākranda), one should ward off a rear-attacker (pārṣṇigrāha);
likewise, by employing an ally's ally, one should ward off the rear-attacker’s ally.
One should cause an enemy’s ally to clash with one’s own ally from the front;
likewise, one should prevent an enemy’s friend of a friend from joining by means of one’s own friend of a friend.
When attacked by an assailant, one should cause an ally to seize the rear of that assailant;
and through the ally’s own ally, one should cause the ally’s rear-seizer to be restrained.
In this manner, the seeker of victory should establish his circle for his own sake,
both behind and in front, through the excellence of his allies and constituent elements.
He should always station envoys and secret agents throughout the entire circle of states; acting as a friend to his enemies, he should strike them down repeatedly while remaining concealed.
The undertakings of one who lacks self-restraint, even when particularly well-attained,
undoubtedly perish like a leaking boat in the ocean.
(Fulfilling Deficient Power)
KAZ07.14.01 When a seeker of victory is thus attacked by his confederates, he should say to their leader: "I have an alliance with you; here is gold for you, and I am your ally."
“Your interest has doubled; you ought not to increase enemies with the faces of friends at the expense of your own self, for once they have grown wealthy, they will surely treat you with contempt.”

Or he may sow dissension by saying: "Just as I, though innocent, have been attacked by these acting in concert, so too will they attack you when they are united in strength, whether in times of prosperity or in times of calamity;
for power indeed alters the mind, therefore destroy their cohesion."
When they are divided, he should win over the principal one and exert pressure on the inferior ones;
or, having favored the inferior ones, he should turn them against the principal one; or he should act in whatever way he deems best.
Or, having caused them to incur enmity with others, he should cause them to be betrayed.
Or, having incited the principal [party] by means of the abundance of the fruits [of peace], he should cause a treaty to be made.
Then, those receiving wages from both sides, demonstrating the greater abundance of rewards, should incite the confederates by saying, "You have been overreached."
One should corrupt the peace treaty with those who are wicked.
Then those who receive wages from both sides should further create dissension among them, saying, "That which was pointed out by us has come to pass."
When they are divided, he should act by securing the support of one of them.

KAZ07.14.10: In the absence of a primary [ally], one should win over—starting from the first and proceeding to the last in their absence—the instigator among the constituent members, one who is steadfast in action, whose subjects are loyal, who has joined the confederacy out of greed or fear, one who is afraid of the conqueror, one connected to the kingdom, a friend, or a fickle enemy: the instigator by surrendering oneself;
One who is steadfast in action by means of conciliation and prostration; one whose subjects are devoted by means of giving a daughter in marriage and procrastination;
and one who is greedy by means of doubling his share.
One who is afraid of these [enemies] should be reassured by the granting of treasury and army; one who is afraid of his own [king] should be reassured by providing a surety;
and one connected to the kingdom should be won over by entering into a state of alliance.
A friend is one who is dear and beneficial on both sides, or by virtue of providing assistance; a wavering enemy is one who is determined to neither harm nor assist.
Or, whoever should serve according to his fitness, one should treat him accordingly,
whether by means of conciliation, gifts, sowing dissension, or force, as we shall explain in the section on times of distress.
Or, if urgent due to the onset of a calamity, he should enter into a peace treaty determined by the treasury and the army, or by place, time, or purpose.
Having made peace, one should remedy any weakness in oneself.
If he is weak in his own faction, he should secure the support of kinsmen and friends, or take refuge in an impregnable fortress.
For one who is supported by both forts and allies is honored by his own people as well as by others.
One who is deficient in the power of counsel should cultivate the company of wise men or associate with those advanced in learning.
For in this way, one attains immediate well-being.
One who is deficient in power should strive for the accomplishment of the natural security and well-being of his constituent elements.
The countryside is the source of all undertakings;
from it comes power.
Its location is a fortress for oneself in times of calamity.
The construction of embankments is the source of crops.
For in the case of irrigation works involving embankments, the acquisition of the benefits of rain is a constant and continuous occurrence.
The trade route is the source of deception by others.
For by means of the merchant route, the secret passage of troops and spies is accomplished, as well as the purchase of weapons, armor, vehicles, and draft animals, along with their entry and exit.
A mine is the source of materials for warfare; a timber forest is the source for fortifications, as well as for vehicles and chariots;
and an elephant forest is the source of elephants.
And the herd of cattle, horses, donkeys, and camels.
In the absence of these, they shall be acquired from the families of kinsmen and friends.

One who is deficient in energy should, according to the opportunities available, increase the number of guild-leaders, heroic men, groups of thieves, forest-tribesmen, Mleccha tribes, those who do harm to the enemy, and secret agents.
He should employ against enemies a stratagem that is mixed with others, provides no remedy, or is superior in strength.
Thus, endowed with a [favorable] faction, counsel, resources, and power, he should march forth to overcome the enemy's obstruction of himself.
(Causes for Siege; The Conduct of One Who Has Submitted with an Army)
A weak king who is attacked by one more powerful should seek refuge with someone whose strength exceeds that of his attacker, such that the latter cannot overcome him through the power of counsel.
Among those who possess equal power of counsel and whose prosperity is dependent on others, superiority arises from association with the aged.

In the absence of superior forces, one should stand together with those of equal strength or with groups of equal strength against a powerful foe, such that they cannot outmaneuver him through the powers of counsel (*mantra*) and majesty (*prabhāva*). Among those who possess equal powers of counsel and majesty, superiority is determined by the scale of their undertakings (*vipulārambha*).

In the absence of an equal force, he should stand together with those who are inferior in strength but pure and energetic, acting as a counter-force against the powerful one, such that he cannot be outmaneuvered by the latter's powers of counsel, majesty, and energy.
Among those who possess equal energy and power, the distinction arises from the acquisition of terrain favorable for one's own mode of warfare.
Among those of equal status, the distinction arises from obtaining the opportunity for battle at a time favorable to oneself.
Among those who are equal in terms of place and time, the distinction is made by means of their draft animals, weapons, and armor.

In the absence of allies, he should take refuge in a fort where even an enemy with a vast army would be unable to cause a shortage of food, fodder, fuel, and water, and where the enemy himself would be forced to suffer from loss of life and expenditure of resources.
Among those possessing equal fortresses, the distinction lies in the abundance of stores and means of escape.
Kautilya maintains that one should desire a human fort (manuṣyadurga) to be well-supplied with stores and means of retreat.
Therefore, he should rely on these black [strategies]: "I will provide a rear-attack, reinforcements, or support for a neutral king;
or, through one of his neighboring kings, forest-dwellers, members of his own family, or those in rebellion, I will cause him to lose his kingdom or have him killed."
"By winning over his faction of agents, I shall incite a revolt against him in his fort, his kingdom, or his camp;
or, by means of secret applications of weapons, fire, and poison, I shall destroy him as desired when he is near."
"Or, by means of a personally supervised application of strategic measures, I shall bring about his depletion and expenditure;
or, when his circle of allies or his army is afflicted by depletion, expenditure, and long-distance travel, I shall gradually succeed in instigating internal dissension."
"Either by destroying his supplies, reinforcements, and foraging parties, I shall bring about the siege of his camp;

or, having opened a vulnerability in him by bringing my own army against him, I shall strike with my entire mobilized force; or, when his enthusiasm is thwarted, I shall obtain a peace on my own terms."
Or, if [the mind] is bound to me, hostilities will arise from all sides.
"Or, I shall cause his base, which lacks reinforcements, to be struck down by my allies, forest tribes, and punitive forces;
or, staying here, I shall protect the security and prosperity of a vast territory;
or, my own army scattered abroad or that of an ally scattered abroad will become irresistible when concentrated here under my command."
Or, my army—skilled in fighting from low ground, in trenches, and at night, and free from the afflictions of the road—will perform its task when it is near [the enemy].
Or, having arrived here at an unfavorable time and place, he will perish of his own accord due to loss and expenditure;
for this country is accessible only at great cost and loss because of its many forts, forests, and places of retreat.
"His army will mostly suffer from disease and lack the ground for military maneuvers;
thus, having fallen into calamity, he will enter [the territory], or having entered, he will not emerge."
KAZ07.15.13: “In the absence of a cause for conflict, or when the enemy’s power has increased, one should abandon the fort and depart.”
Or he may enter into the enemy like a moth into a fire.
"For the attainment of one or the other belongs to one who has abandoned the self," so say the Teachers (ācāryāḥ).
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Having ascertained that he himself and his enemy are both capable of making peace, he should conclude a treaty.
In the opposite case, he should seek peace or a retreat through valor.
Or he may send an envoy to one with whom he ought to make peace.
Or, having honored with wealth and honors a messenger sent by him, he should say: "This is the king’s warehouse; this belongs to the queen and the princes;
by the command of the queen and the princes," and so forth.
"This kingdom and I myself are placed at your disposal."
Having obtained shelter, he should behave toward his master like one who follows the customary conduct of the agreement.

KAZ 7.15.22–23: He may carry out works such as fortifications, as well as marriages, the installation of a son, the capture of horses or elephants for sale, sacrificial sessions, military expeditions, and journeys for recreation, provided he has obtained permission.

Furthermore, he may carry out all measures regarding peace with constituent elements stationed on their own territory, or the infliction of injury upon them when they have withdrawn, provided he has obtained permission.
Or, if the citizens and country-folk are wicked, one who conducts himself according to justice may request another piece of land.
Or he should counteract it by means of secret punishment, as in the case of a seditious person.
Or, he should not accept suitable land being offered by a friend.
When the king is absent, he should look after one among the minister, the domestic priest, the commander-in-chief, or the crown prince,
and assist him to the best of his ability.
During the recitations for divine blessings and auspiciousness, he should cause those intent upon that [deity] to pronounce the benedictions.
In all circumstances, one should speak of the excellence of the king's own natural disposition.
Serving those who are powerful and allied with him, avoiding those who are hostile or suspected of treachery,
and remaining submissive to his master’s army— thus should one conduct himself while stationed under the command of the army.
(The Conduct of One Leading the Army)

KAZ07.16.01: A powerful king desiring conquest, having obtained permission for the peace-treaty and its terms, and being free from agitation, should march from that direction where his own territory and the favorable season for his troops are located, provided the enemy lacks a fort or a place of retreat, has no flank protection, and has no reinforcements.
In the opposite case, he should march after having taken countermeasures.
One should win over the weak by means of conciliation and gifts, and the strong by means of dissension and force.
By means of the application, alternation, and combination of these expedients, he should win over the constituent elements of the state, whether they are immediate or separated by one degree.
He should employ conciliation by protecting the villages, forest-dwellers, herds, and trade routes, and by handing over those who have abandoned their posts, fled, or acted as enemies.
One should practice the giving of land, goods, a daughter, and the granting of safety.

One should employ the tactic of sowing dissension by instigating any one of the following—neighboring kings, forest-dwellers, members of the enemy's family, or those who have been deposed—to demand the treasury, the army, territory, or hereditary grants.
One should employ force by means of open warfare, treacherous warfare, silent warfare, and the methods for seizing forts to capture the enemy.
Thus, he should appoint those who possess energy as assistants for the army, those who possess personal influence as assistants for the treasury,
and those who possess wisdom as assistants for the territory.

That which benefits [the state] extensively through gems, valuable goods, forest produce, and base metals produced in their market-towns, villages, and mines; or through vehicles and draft animals arising from their timber forests and elephant herds; or through whatever else provides frequent assistance, is termed "varied enjoyment" (citra-bhoga).
That which greatly benefits [the state] through either the army or the treasury is called "great profit" (mahābhoga).
That which benefits [the state] through the army, the treasury, and the territory is called "all-enjoying" (sarvabhoga).
That which one counteracts against an enemy on one side is "beneficial on one side."
That which counters both the enemy and the ally from both sides is called "benefiting both sides."
That which counters enemies, reinforcements for the enemy, neighbors, and forest tribes from all sides is called "benefiting on all sides" (*sarvatobhogi*).

If a rear-attacker, a forest-dweller, a chief enemy, or some other enemy who can be managed by the gift of land should be encountered, one should cause him to accept land that is of no value; if he is stationed in a fort, land that is not contiguous with his territory.
A forest region that cannot be subsisted upon.

One should win over an enemy's kinsman by means of a woman who can be reclaimed; an enemy's imprisoned son by means of one whose lineage has been severed; the strength of a guild by means of a woman who is a constant source of enmity;
and the combined force of allied powers by means of a woman belonging to a powerful neighbor.
In battle, [the formation] is reversed by both.
One who is discouraged by lack of exertion,
one on the enemy's side by pride,
and one who has been driven away by being emaciated; KAZ07.16.16c.
If she has incurred great loss, expense, and ruin, or has gone away and returned,
or has withdrawn without any support,
she should herself cause her husband to take her back, provided he cannot endure her presence with another woman.
One should follow their great assistance and remain free from any change of heart toward them.
One should accomplish it in the reverse order by means of the whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*).
One should satisfy a benefactor according to the extent of his capacity to provide benefit.
And he should provide wealth and honor according to the effort expended, as well as grant favors during times of misfortune.
He should grant audiences as desired to those who come of their own accord and provide them with appropriate treatment.
One should not employ insults, injuries, contempt, or harsh words toward them.
And having granted them security, he should favor them like a father.
And whoever should do him harm, having publicly proclaimed that offense, he should have that person executed openly.
Or, for the sake of causing alarm to the enemy, he should act as described in the section on the employment of punishment.
And he should not covet the land, property, sons, or wives of one who has been slain.
He should also cause his kinsmen to be established in their own rightful positions.
If one dies while on active service, the king shall establish his son in the kingdom.
In this way, those who have submitted to his punishment follow after his sons and grandsons.
