But he who, having attacked or captured those who have surrendered, treats their land, wealth, sons, and wives with contempt, against him the circle of states rises up in agitation for his destruction.
And those ministers of his who are dependent on their own territories, being alarmed, seek refuge with the Circle of States.
Or they themselves covet his kingdom or his life.

Therefore, kings who are protected by conciliation (*sāman*) in their own territories become favorable to the monarch and continue to follow him through his sons and grandsons. (End of *saṃdhikarma*: the attainment and maintenance of peace.)
Tranquility (śama), peace (saṃdhi), and composure (samādhi) have one and the same meaning.
For kings, gaining trust, tranquility, alliance, and composure constitute peace.
“An alliance based on truth or an oath is unstable, whereas one based on a surety or a gift is stable,” so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Truth or an oath is a stable treaty for both this world and the next;
however, a surety or a gift is intended solely for this world and depends upon one's power.
“We are united,” saying this, the kings of old, true to their word, entered into alliances through truth.

In the event of its violation, they shall touch by oath fire, water, a furrow, a clod of earth from a rampart, the shoulder of an elephant, the back of a horse, the seat of a chariot, weapons, gems, seeds, perfumes, liquids, gold, and bullion, with the declaration: "May these destroy and abandon him who violates this oath."
KAZ07.17.08: In the event of a violation of an oath, a *pratibhū* (surety) is one who provides a guarantee (*prātibhāvya*) or a pledge for great men, ascetics, or leaders.
In that situation, he who takes sureties capable of resisting an enemy's attack gains the advantage.
One who acts contrary to this is deceived.
Acceptance [of gifts] from the leaders of one's kinsmen is *pratigraha*.
In that situation, he who gives a seditious minister or a seditious son [to the enemy] gains the upper hand.
The opposite person is deceived. For when one has been made confident by the acceptance of gifts, the enemy strikes at his vulnerabilities without hesitation.
Regarding the securing of offspring, however, in the giving away of a daughter or a son, he who gives away a daughter overreaches [the other party].
For a maiden is indeed not an heir; she exists for the sake of others and is free from affliction.
The opposite is the case with a son.
Even between two sons, he who gives one who is noble-born, wise, brave, skilled in weapons, or an only son, is overreached.
One who acts contrary to this is deceived.
For a man of low birth is better than one of high birth for the purpose of adoption, because he lacks a lineage of heirs;
an unwise man is better than a wise man, because he lacks the power of counsel;
and a coward is better than a hero, because he lacks the power of enterprise.

One who has not mastered weapons should be avoided because of the loss of the capacity to strike, and one with many sons should be avoided because of his lack of concern for the welfare of the father.

Between one who is noble by birth but lacking in wisdom and one who is not noble by birth but possesses wisdom, royal power follows the nature of the former; however, the authority for counsel belongs to the latter, even if he is not of noble birth.
Even when authorized to give counsel, one born of noble lineage outwits a wise man through association with the elderly.
Between a wise man and a hero, the application of thought and action follows the wise man who is not a hero; the authority for valor belongs to the hero who is not wise.
Even in matters of prowess, a wise man overreaches a brave one, just as a hunter overreaches an elephant.

Between one who is brave but untrained in weapons and one who is trained in weapons but not brave, the latter’s superior effort follows from his mastery of weapons; whereas for the former, the advantage lies in his physical prowess and resolve.
However, against one who is trained in weapons but not brave, the decisive factor is the ability to hit the target.
Even in the matter of hitting a target, a hero surpasses one skilled in weapons through steadiness, successful execution, and lack of confusion.
Between one who has many sons and one who has only one son, the one with many sons, having given away one son, remains supported by the remainder and thus transgresses the treaty; the other does not.
If a treaty is made for the gift of a son along with all one's possessions, the distinction lies in the fruit resulting from the son.
Between two [offenders] who have committed equal offenses, the distinction is made based on their capacity and procreative power.
Even between one who is capable of procreation and one whose procreative power has already manifested, there is a distinction based on whether procreation has actually occurred.
But if he has a single son who is capable [of performing rites], yet whose own offspring would fail to continue the lineage, he may offer himself [into the fire] provided that it is not his only son.
When being attacked, he should effect the release of his concentration.
Spies in the guise of artisans and craftsmen, stationed near the prince, should carry out their work at night and, having dug a tunnel, carry off the prince.
Actors, dancers, singers, instrumentalists, storytellers, bards, acrobats, or jugglers, previously employed for this purpose, shall present themselves before the enemy.
They should attend upon the prince with the utmost devotion.
He should establish for them fixed times for entering, staying, and departing.
Then, disguised as one of them, he should set out at night.
By this, those who live by their appearance and those whose sexual organs are like those of a wife are explained.
Or, taking their musical instruments, vessels, or baskets, he should depart.

Or it may be carried out by cooks, confectioners, bath-attendants, massagers, bed-spreaders, hairdressers, decorators, or water-attendants, using their own goods, clothing, vessels, baskets, beds, seats, and articles of personal enjoyment.
Or, under the guise of an attendant, he may take something and depart at an improper time or place; or he may exit through the mouth of a tunnel by means of a nocturnal offering.
Or, at a reservoir of water, he should employ the Varuṇa yoga.
Or, spies disguised as merchants may administer poison to the guards under the pretext of trading cooked food and fruit.
On the occasion of offerings to the gods, ancestral rites, or festive gatherings, he should administer food, drink, or liquor mixed with *madana* (datura) to the guards and then depart,
or else by instigating the guards [to revolt].
Or, spies disguised as citizens, actors, physicians, or cake-sellers may set fire at night to wealthy houses or to the guards.
Or spies disguised as merchants may set fire to the merchandise warehouse.
Or, having deposited another body [in place], he may set fire to his own house out of fear of pursuit.
Then he should escape by means of breaking through a wall, digging a tunnel, or a secret passage.
Or, disguised as a carrier of loads of glass, jars, and vessels, he should set out at night.

Or, having entered among those with shaven heads or matted hair who are subject to banishment, he should remain there at night disguised as one of them; or he may do so under any other pretext, such as assuming a deformed appearance, feigning a disease, or pretending to be a forest-dweller.
Or he may be carried out secretly by spies disguised as hungry ghosts.
Or she may follow a corpse while dressed in women's clothing.
And spies disguised as forest-dwellers should represent him as going in one direction when he is actually traveling in another.
Then he should go elsewhere.
Or, he may withdraw by means of wagon-paths along with his mobile units.
And when the enemy's approach is imminent, he should either undertake a defensive encampment (*sattra*).
In the absence of a caravan, he should leave behind gold, or mercury-infused foodstuffs, along both sides of the road.
Then he should depart elsewhere.
Or, once captured, he should deceive his pursuers by means of conciliation and other such methods,
or by food mixed with poison.
Or, during a conjunction with the planet Varuṇa, or in the event of a fire, he should place another body [on the funeral pyre] and attack the enemy, saying, "My son has been killed by you."
Or, having concealed his weapon and approached at night, he should attack the guards.
He should retreat quickly with those who have been secretly dispatched by means of swift-footed messengers.

(The Conduct of the Middle King; The Conduct of the Neutral King; The Conduct of the Circle of States) The middle king’s own self, his third constituent power, and his fifth constituent power are [the primary] constituents.
The second, fourth, and sixth are the modified forms (vikṛtis).
If the middle king should favor both of these, the conqueror should act in accordance with the middle king.
If he should not favor him,
he should act in accordance with the nature of the people.
If the middle king should desire to seize the conqueror’s friend who is likely to become his own,
the conqueror should protect that friend by mobilizing the friends of both himself and his friend, and by alienating the friends of the middle king.
Or he should incite the circle of states, saying: "This Middle King has grown excessively powerful and has risen up for the destruction of us all; let us join together and thwart his expedition."
If he should favor that circle,
he should strengthen himself by means of the middle restraint.
If he should not favor [the enemy],
then by favoring the ally with treasury and army, those kings who are hostile to the middle king— or many who stand together in mutual support—
should be dealt with; for when one is accomplished, many may be accomplished.
Or, if they should not rise up because they suspect one another,
he should win over their leader or someone close to them by means of conciliation and gifts.
The second [fine] shall be double, and the third shall be triple.
When thus strengthened, he should seize the middle king.

Or, in the event of the loss of territory or time, he should form an alliance with the middle king and provide assistance to his friend, or else conclude a treaty for joint action against the seditious elements.
Or, if the Middle King should desire to weaken an ally of his, he should support that ally, saying, "I shall protect you," until the weakening is accomplished.
One should protect him when he has been emaciated.
Or, if the middle king should desire to seize an ally who ought to be destroyed by [the conqueror],
the conqueror should protect that ally when he is weakened, out of fear of the middle king's expansion.
Or, by means of a favor of land, he should bring back into his own hand one who has been uprooted, unless there is fear of his escaping elsewhere.
If the allies of both the one to be weakened and the one to be destroyed should provide assistance to the middle king,
he should make peace with another person.
Or, if the friends of either of those two [rivals] seeking victory are capable of obstructing them,
he should enter into a peace treaty.
Or if the middle king should desire to win over his enemy,
he should enter into a treaty.
In this way, his own interest is accomplished and the middle king is gratified.
If the middle king should desire to win over his own friend who is likely to become a friend [of the conqueror], he should enter into an alliance with him through an intermediary person.
Or, out of consideration for him, he should dissuade him by saying, "You ought not to destroy a friend."
Or he may ignore him, thinking: "Let his circle of allies be provoked by the slaughter of its own side."
If a neutral king should desire to win over an enemy or himself,
he should assist him with treasury and army while remaining invisible.
Or, the middle king might seek to win over a neutral king, providing him with assistance [with the thought]: "Let him be alienated from the neutral king."
Between the middle king and the neutral king, he should seek refuge with whichever one is favored by the circle of states.
The conduct of the neutral king is explained by the conduct of the middle king.
If the neutral king should desire to win over the middle king,
he should turn toward that direction from which he may outmaneuver the enemy, provide assistance to his ally, or obtain the support of the army of the neutral king.
Having thus strengthened himself, he should weaken the enemy's constituent elements and win over the constituent elements of his allies.

Even though he may not be an enemy by nature, one who lacks self-control and is constantly harmful is an enemy; likewise, an ally of an enemy, a rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), or one who attacks when the leader is in distress or during an expedition—these possess the nature of an enemy. Furthermore, there are those who march with a common purpose, those who march for separate purposes, those who march in concert, and those who march in alliance.

One who has set out for his own interest, one who acts for a common purpose, one who is a buyer or seller of either the treasury or the army, and one who practices double-dealing—these are the types of potential friends.

A neighboring king who is a counter-attack against a powerful one, one who is hidden away, one who is a neighbor, one who is a rear-attacker, one who has surrendered of his own accord, one who has submitted out of fear, or one who has submitted with troops— these are neighboring kings who may become servants.
By these, those separated by one intervening territory are explained.
Among them, when a friend enters into a common purpose during a conflict with an enemy,
one should favor that friend with such power as would enable him to withstand the adversary.

When a friend, having assisted one against an enemy, becomes powerful and falls under the influence of others, one should cause him to fall out with his immediate neighbor and the king situated beyond that neighbor— his two constituent powers.
He should cause the land to be taken away from one who is of that lineage or from one who has been deposed;
or he should act in such a way that the person remains submissive, depending on the favor [he may require].

A man who understands statecraft should not assist an enemy, nor should he go to one who is excessively weakened; rather, he should establish that friend in a position that is neither diminished nor overgrown with power.
When a fickle ally enters into a treaty due to some material interest,
one should eliminate the cause for his departure so that he does not waver.
Or, whatever [territory] may be common to both the enemy and himself, he should cause that rogue to be alienated from the enemy;
having caused the split, he should destroy him, and thereafter the immediate enemy.
One should cause a neutral king who remains indifferent to be at variance with his neighbors;
then, when he is distressed by that conflict, one should bring him into a state of service.
When a weak king moves between an enemy and a conqueror,
the conqueror should support him with force so that he does not turn his back [on the conqueror].
Having removed them from there, he should settle them on another piece of land;
or, having first settled others there for the purpose of rewarding the army with punishment or favor, he may then settle them.
If a friend should do harm, or if he should fail to provide assistance in times of distress,
one should utterly destroy that ally who has placed himself within the lap of trust.
If an enemy should rise up, unrestrained, due to the calamity of an ally,
he must be dealt with by that very ally once his own calamity has been concealed.
When a friend who has risen due to the calamity of an enemy becomes alienated because of the success of that enemy's misfortune,
he is effectively won over by that very enemy.
One should consider growth, decline, and stability, as well as emaciation and destruction.
He who knows the treatise on statecraft (*artha-śāstra*) should employ all these expedients;
likewise, he who perceives the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) as mutually interchanging [in application].
He plays at will with kings who are bound by the chains of their own intellects.

(The Section on the Calamities of the Constituent Elements) When calamities occur simultaneously, the consideration of these calamities concerns whether it is easier to march against an enemy or to remain on the defensive.
Calamity arising from the nature of things, whether divine or human, occurs through both sound policy and bad policy.
KAZ08.1.03: Vice consists of the reversal of virtues, their absence, transgression, addiction, or affliction.
It is called a *vyasana* because it casts one away from what is better.
"Among the calamities of the sovereign, the minister, the territory, the fort, the treasury, the army, and the ally, each preceding one is more serious than the following," so say the teachers.
"No," said Bharadvāja.
Between the calamities of the sovereign and the minister, the calamity of the minister is more serious.
KAZ08.1.08: Counsel, the attainment of the fruits of counsel, the performance of rituals, the management of income and expenditure,

the infliction of punishment, the suppression of enemies and forest tribes, the protection of the kingdom, the remedying of calamities, the protection of princes, and the consecration of princes depend upon the ministers.
In their absence, those [other elements] also cease to exist;
and for the king, there is a loss of effective action, like that of a bird whose wings have been clipped.
And when [the enemy] is beset by calamities, there is the risk of instigation by an external power.
"And in case of misconduct, there shall be a threat to life, because the king moves within the range of one's life."
"No," says Kauṭilya.

KAZ08.1.13: The king himself manages the group of servants consisting of ministers, domestic priests, and others; the administration of superintendents; the remediation of calamities affecting men, material resources, and the constituent elements of sovereignty; and their augmentation.
Or, when ministers are in distress, he appoints others who are free from such distress.
He remains constantly engaged in honoring those worthy of honor and in restraining those who are corruptible.
And a master who is himself endowed with his own excellences brings about the excellence of his constituent elements.
The subjects adopt the character of whatever character he possesses,
because their own exertion or negligence is dependent upon his.
For the master is indeed like the immovable pivot of that [wheel].
"Between a calamity affecting the ministers and a calamity affecting the people, a calamity affecting the people is more serious," says Viśālākṣa.
“Treasury, army, raw materials, labor, transport, and stores—all these arise from the inhabited territory.”
Their absence [is determined] by the absence of the people,
as well as by the immediate proximity of the sovereign and the minister."
"No," says Kauṭilya.

KAZ08.1.23: All undertakings have their root in the minister—the accomplishment of the works of the realm, both by one's own efforts and through others; the securing of acquisition and protection (*yoga-kṣema*); the remedying of calamities; the settlement and expansion of waste lands;
and the granting of favors regarding the army and taxes.
"Between the calamity of the territory and the calamity of the fort, the calamity of the fort is more serious," so say the followers of Parāśara.
"For in a fort, there is the production of treasury and army, and it serves as a refuge for the population in times of calamity."
Moreover, the citizens are more powerful than the country-dwellers and are constant allies of the king in times of distress.
"But the subjects, however, are common to both friend and enemy."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The undertakings of forts, treasuries, armies, irrigation works, and agriculture have their foundation in the people.
Bravery, steadfastness, skill, and abundance are found among the inhabitants of the countryside.
Mountains, interior valleys, and islands that are difficult of access are not inhabited due to the absence of people.
But if the population consists mostly of cultivators, there is a calamity for the fort; if the population consists mostly of those armed with weapons, there is a calamity for the territory.
“Between a calamity of the fort and a calamity of the treasury, the calamity of the treasury is the more serious,” says Piśuna.

KAZ08.1.34: For the fortification of a fortress, the protection of the fortress, the suppression of the people, friends, and enemies, the encouragement of those in distant regions, and the administration of the army and the treasury are all rooted in the treasury.
KAZ08.1.35: A fortress can be subverted by enemies through the use of the treasury.
"Moreover, having taken the treasury, it is possible to retreat in times of calamity,
but not from a fort."
"Not so," says Kauṭilya.

The treasury, the army, silent warfare, the suppression of one's own faction, the employment of the force of punishment, the recruitment of reinforcements, and the warding off of enemy armies and forest tribes constitute the surrender of a fort.
Furthermore, in the absence of a fort, the treasury belongs to the enemies.
For it is observed that those possessing a fortress do not suffer total destruction.
"Between the calamities of the treasury and the army, the calamity of the army is more serious," says Kauṇapadanta.
KAZ08.1.42: For the suppression of friends and enemies is rooted in punishment; it consists of inciting others to inflict punishment and receiving punishment from one's own side.
And in the absence of punishment, the destruction of the treasury is certain.
In the absence of treasury resources, the army can be maintained by means of forest produce, land, or the seizure of enemy territory;
and conversely, the treasury can be replenished by means of the army.
"And because it functions in close proximity to the master, the army (daṇḍa) shares the same nature as the minister."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
For the army has its root in the treasury.
In the absence of treasury funds, the punishment passes to another or destroys the master himself.
And the treasury, which enables all undertakings, is the cause for both righteousness and pleasure.
However, depending on the requirements of place, time, and the task at hand, either the treasury or the army becomes the primary authority.
For the acquisition and preservation of the treasury is the purpose of the army;
the treasury, moreover, serves both the treasury and the army.
Because it involves the expenditure of all resources, a depletion of the treasury is more serious [than a depletion of the army].
"Between a calamity involving the army and a calamity involving an ally, a calamity involving an ally is the more serious," says Vātavyādhi.
“An ally who is unpaid and distant performs service;
he counters the rear-attacker, the rear-supporter, the enemy, and the forest-dwellers; and he assists with treasury, army, and territory during times of calamity.”
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The friend of one who possesses the power of punishment remains in the state of friendship, or even an enemy may remain in the state of friendship.
But between the staff and the friend, when the task is common to both, the distinction lies in their relative strength and the advantages of terrain, time, and opportunity for independent action.
But in a rapid expedition, or when there is provocation from enemies, forest tribes, or internal rebels, no ally is to be found.
When calamities occur simultaneously and when the enemy prospers, an ally remains steadfast in pursuit of self-interest.
Thus, the determination of the calamities of the constituent elements has been explained.
But among the constituent elements of a state, it is specifically their misfortune that is significant;
or else, their great number, their loyalty, or their strength is what accomplishes the task.
But when two [allies] are equally in distress, the distinction [between them] is based on their qualities and the extent of their depletion;
provided that the excellence of the remaining constituent elements is not subject to control by the other.
But where the destruction of the remaining constituent elements occurs due to the misfortune of a single one,
that misfortune would be more serious, whether it concerns the principal element or the other.
(Consideration of the misfortunes of the king and the kingdom)
"The king and the kingdom"—this is the summary of the constituent elements.
KAZ08.2.02: Is the internal or external the source of the king's provocation?
Internal unrest arising from fear of snakes is worse than external unrest,
and internal unrest caused by the ministers is worse than general internal unrest.
Therefore, he should establish the power of his treasury and army within himself.

Regarding the two forms of dual kingship—*dvairājya* and *vairājya*—the teachers maintain that *dvairājya* perishes through mutual hatred and partiality toward each other's factions, or through their internal rivalry; whereas *vairājya*, depending on its ability to capture the hearts of the constituent elements (*prakṛtis*), is enjoyed by others as it stands.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A dual kingship between father and son, or between brothers, which maintains equal security and prosperity and is free from the interference of ministers, functions successfully.
But when one seizes the sovereignty of another while he is still alive and, thinking "this is not mine," causes it to waste away, diverts it, or treats it as a commodity for sale; this is *vairājya*.
Or, having become dispassionate, he abandons it and departs.

"Whether a king is blind or one who has deviated from the scriptures," [it is said]. Regarding this, the teachers maintain: "A blind man, lacking the eye of the scriptures, acts haphazardly, is stubbornly dogmatic, or is led by others, and thus destroys the kingdom through injustice; however, one who has deviated from the scriptures—though his mind has strayed from the teachings—is still capable of being persuaded."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A blind king can be established here or there by means of a successful assembly of allies.
But one who has deviated from the treatises, whose intellect is fixed on what is contrary to the treatises, ruins both the kingdom and himself through unrighteousness.

"Whether the king is diseased or newly installed," [says the text]. Regarding this, the teachers hold that "a diseased king incurs either an injury to the kingdom rooted in his ministers, or a threat to his life rooted in the kingdom; whereas a newly installed king conducts himself by pleasing and benefiting the subjects through the performance of his own duties, favors, remissions, gifts, and honors."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
When the king is afflicted by illness, he continues to carry out the royal administration as it has been established.
But a new king, having secured his power through force, acts as he pleases without restraint, thinking, "This kingdom is mine."
Or, one who has been restrained by those acting in concert may tolerate injury to the kingdom.
"One who has not taken root among the subjects is easy to uproot," so it is said.
Regarding the sick, there is a distinction: one who is wicked yet healthy, and one who is healthy yet wicked.
Even among those born into new families, there are those who are well-born and those who are not.

Regarding the statement, "A weak king who is of noble birth, or a strong king who is of ignoble birth," the teachers say: "The subjects, out of regard for the weakness [of the former], find it difficult to respond to the instigation of a weak but noble-born king; however, they do so easily in the case of a strong but ignoble-born king, as they rely on his strength."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The subjects themselves approach one who, though weak, is of noble birth;
for the nature of sovereignty follows the person of noble birth.
And they cause the sowing of dissension against one who is powerful but of low birth,
asserting that all virtues reside in [the one who possesses] popular affection.
The destruction of crops through the killing of laborers is worse than the destruction of a handful; lack of rain is worse than excessive rain because it results in total loss of livelihood.

The relative strength and weakness of the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) in each pair of calamities has been explained according to their successive order; this constitutes the cause for marching or remaining stationary. (Section on the Calamities of Men)
The discipline of ignorance is the cause of human calamity.
For one who is undisciplined does not perceive the faults inherent in calamities.
We shall explain them.
The threefold group arises from anger;
the fourfold group arises from desire.
Of these two, anger is the more serious.
For anger indeed moves everywhere.

Moreover, it is heard that kings who generally succumb to anger have been destroyed by the provocation of their subjects, while those who succumb to passion have met their end through enemies or diseases caused by their own depletion.
"No," says Bhāradvāja.
KAZ08.3.09: “The conduct of a virtuous man [is as follows]: anger, retaliation for enmity, killing out of contempt, and treating people with fear.”
And the constant connection with anger is for the purpose of prohibiting evil.
Desire, attainment of success, conciliation, a disposition toward renunciation, and a state of being well-liked.
"Furthermore, for one who has performed their duty, there is a constant connection with desire for the purpose of experiencing the fruits [of that action]."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Being hated, the discovery of an enemy, attachment to suffering, and anger [are the causes of fear].
KAZ08.3.15: Disrespect, loss of property, association with undesirable persons such as thieves, gamblers, hunters, singers, and musicians, and lust [are the causes of the ruin of a kingdom].
Between these two, being held in contempt is more serious than being hated.
One who is treated with contempt by his own people and seized by his enemies becomes hated and is utterly destroyed.
The suffering caused by an enemy is more grievous than the loss of wealth.
The loss of wealth is a detriment to the treasury;
the provocation of an enemy is a threat to life.
KAZ08.3.20: The connection with suffering is more serious than the connection with what is useless.
KAZ08.3.21: Association with what is harmful is countered only momentarily; it causes long-lasting affliction and is an attachment to sufferings.
Therefore, anger is more serious.
Verbal cruelty, injury to property, and physical assault.
"Between verbal cruelty and the defilement of wealth, verbal cruelty is the more serious offense," says Viśālākṣa.
For a spirited man, when addressed with harsh words, rises up in response with his own spirit.
"A harsh word is like a thorn driven into the heart; it inflames one's spirit and afflicts the senses."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Honor accorded to wealth removes the thorn of harsh speech, whereas the deprivation of one's livelihood is an injury to wealth itself.
Non-payment, taking [what is not due], destruction, or abandonment of wealth—this is the corruption of wealth.
“Between the corruption of wealth and violence by punishment, the corruption of wealth is more serious,” so say the followers of Parāśara.
“Dharma and kāma have their root in artha.”
And the world proceeds in dependence upon wealth.
"The injury to that [the king] is more serious," so it is said.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
No one would desire the destruction of their body, even for the sake of a very great object.
And from violence with the rod, he incurs that same offense toward others.
Thus ends the triad born of anger.
But that which arises from desire consists of the fourfold group: hunting, gambling, women, and drinking.
Regarding that, Piśuna says: "Between hunting and gambling, hunting is the more serious."

In that [forest], there is the danger of thieves, enemies, wild beasts, forest fires, and stumbling; the delusion of distress during times of famine; and the affliction of hunger and thirst to one's life.
But in gambling, that which is won by one skilled in dice is valid, as in the case of Jayatsena and Duryodhana.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
It has been explained by Nala and Yudhiṣṭhira that even for those two, there is defeat by either one of them.
That very wealth acquired from the conquered territory is both a source of material gain and a cause for the persistence of enmity.

KAZ08.3.45: The faults of gambling are the loss of existing wealth, the acquisition of non-existent wealth, the destruction of what has not been enjoyed, and the contracting of diseases through the suppression of urine and excrement, hunger, and so forth.

KAZ08.3.46: In hunting, however, there is physical exercise, the reduction of phlegm, bile, fat, and sweat; proficiency in hitting targets whether moving or stationary; knowledge of the mental states of wild animals in situations of anger, fear, or stillness;
and the practice of riding on unstable vehicles.
"Between the vices of gambling and women, the vice of gambling is the more serious," says Kauṇapadanta.
"For indeed, when the lamp is extinguished at night and his mother has died, the gambler continues to play incessantly."
And when questioned about what is difficult, he becomes angry.
But in the case of a woman's addiction, there shall indeed be an inquiry into matters of dharma and artha during her bathing, her toilet, and at the time of her meals.
"Moreover, a woman can be employed for the king's benefit,
or she can be turned away or caused to flow [semen] by means of secret punishment or disease."
"Not so," says Kauṭilya.
Gambling can be remedied; addiction to women cannot be remedied.
KAZ08.3.54: Disappearance [of the king], weariness with the task, loss due to the lapse of time, neglect of duty, weakness of the state administration, and addiction to drink [are the disadvantages].
“Between the addiction to women and the addiction to drink, the addiction to women is the worse,” says Vātavyādhi.
KAZ08.3.56: For the various kinds of folly regarding women have been explained in the section on the duties of the harem.
"But in drinking, there is the enjoyment of sense objects such as sound and the rest, the giving of pleasure, the honoring of attendants, and the removal of fatigue from labor."
"Not so," says Kauṭilya.

In the vice of women, there may arise the birth of offspring and the protection of oneself among one's own wives; however, the opposite occurs with outside women, and with forbidden women, there is total ruin.
Both of these [faults] exist in the vice of drinking.

KAZ08.3.61: Perfection of drinking consists of the loss of consciousness for one who is not insane, the state of insanity for one who is not insane, the state of being dead for one who is not dead, the exposure of one's private parts, the loss of learning, wisdom, vitality, wealth, and friends, separation from the virtuous, association with the undesirable, and addiction to lute-playing, singing, and other arts that destroy wealth.
Between gambling and drinking intoxicants, gambling [is the more serious offense].
According to some, victory or defeat resulting from a wager among living beings or inanimate objects causes a disturbance of the constituent elements of the state through the division of factions.

Furthermore, specifically regarding the division of *saṃghas* and royal families that follow the customs of *saṃghas* caused by gambling, and the resulting destruction thereof— it is the most wicked of vices,
namely the "wrongful seizure" (*asat-pragraha*), because it causes weakness in the administration of the state.
The favoring of the wicked is desire, and the suppression of the virtuous is anger;
both are considered by the wise to be extreme vices due to the abundance of their faults.

Therefore, one who possesses self-control, serves the elders, and has conquered his senses should abandon anger, lust, and the undertaking of vices that destroy the very root [of the state]. (The Section on Oppression; The Section on Obstruction; The Section on the Blockage of the Treasury)
KAZ08.4.01 / Calamities caused by fate—namely, fire, water, disease, famine, and pestilence.

Regarding fire and water, the teachers say: "The affliction caused by fire is unavoidable and consumes everything; the affliction caused by water can be avoided by departing, provided one is capable of doing so."
Not so, says Kauṭilya.
Fire burns a village or half a village, whereas the force of water can sweep away a hundred villages.

"Between disease and famine, disease destroys works through the obstruction of labor caused by the dead, the diseased, and those afflicted by illness, as well as by attendants; famine, however, does not destroy works and yields gold, cattle, and taxes," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A disease that afflicts only one region and can be remedied is preferable; whereas a famine that afflicts the entire country leads to the loss of life for living beings.
By this, the procedure for causing death is explained.

"Between the loss of minor and major elements, the loss of the minor causes the failure of the security and prosperity of undertakings, whereas the loss of the major has as its characteristic the obstruction of the execution of undertakings"— so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The destruction of the minor elements can be repaired because of the abundance of minor elements,
but not the destruction of the principal elements.
For among thousands, there is indeed one who becomes preeminent, or perhaps none at all, because of the superiority of his character and wisdom; for the common folk depend upon him.
“Between one's own circle and an enemy's circle, one's own circle oppresses with excessive punishment and taxes and is impossible to restrain;
however, an enemy's circle can be fought against or liberated through conciliation or by means of a strategic retreat,” so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The oppression by one's own army can be prevented through the seizure of its leaders and the disruption of its recruitment of subjects; furthermore, it oppresses only a single region.
However, the enemy's army oppresses the entire country through plunder, slaughter, burning, destruction, and deportation.
"Between a dispute among the constituent elements of the state and a dispute with the king, a dispute among the constituent elements causes division among them and brings about attacks by enemies;
however, a dispute with the king results in the constituent elements receiving double their food, wages, and exemptions," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A conflict among the constituent elements can be prevented by winning over the leaders of those elements or by removing the cause of the quarrel.
But when the constituent elements are at variance, they assist one another through mutual rivalry.
But a dispute with the king, because it leads to the oppression and destruction of the subjects, can only be accomplished through twice the effort.
“Between the interests of the country and those of the king, the interests of the country cause the destruction of the fruits of action throughout the three periods of time,
whereas the interests of the king provide assistance to artisans, craftsmen, actors, those who live by their speech, those who live by their appearance, and merchants,” so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The king’s pleasure-ground consumes little of the laborers’ toil for the sake of rest, and having consumed it, they again apply themselves to their tasks;

but the royal pleasure-park, however, oppresses them through the king himself and his favorites by means of forced labor, personal favors, the requisitioning of goods from shops, and the imposition of official duties.

"Between a fortunate woman and a young man, the young man afflicts her through his own seizures, favors, love-tokens, pleasure-houses, and acts of service, whereas the fortunate woman afflicts him with amorous dalliance and enjoyment," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The prince can be restrained by the minister and the domestic priest, but not by a courtesan, due to her frivolity and her association with undesirable people.

"Between the guild-leader and the guild-members, the guild, due to its numerical strength, oppresses through theft and violence; the leader, however, oppresses by obstructing business and withholding favors," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
A guild is easy to turn away from its purpose because its members share common character and vulnerabilities;
or, it can be turned by winning over a portion of the guild leaders.
A chief official who is arrogant afflicts [the people] by destroying the lives and property of others.
"Between the *samnidhātṛ* (the treasurer) and the *samāhartṛ* (the collector-general), the *samnidhātṛ* causes suffering through the concealment of revenue and the infliction of fines;
the *samāhartṛ*, however, being established over the instruments of collection, enjoys the fruits as they are assigned," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.

The *samnidhātṛ* (the treasurer) receives from others what has been determined as payable into the treasury; however, the *samāhartṛ* first secures wealth for himself and only afterwards performs the king’s business, or else causes it to perish, and he conducts himself with confidence in seizing the property of others.

"Between the frontier-guard (antapāla) and the merchant (vaidehaka), the frontier-guard afflicts the trade route by inciting thieves and by the excessive seizure of what is due; the merchants, however, maintain it through the favor of providing goods and counter-goods," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The frontier guard maintains himself by favoring the arrival of merchandise;
however, the merchants, acting in concert, manipulate the prices of goods by raising or lowering them, living off a profit of one hundred paṇas per paṇa and a hundred kumbhas per kumbha.

Regarding land occupied by high-born persons or occupied by cattle-pens: "Land occupied by high-born persons, even if it yields great fruit, is beneficial to the armed forces and is not fit to be released; however, land occupied by cattle-pens, being suitable for agriculture, is fit to be released."
"For pasture land is obstructed by [cultivated] field-land," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.

Land occupied by high-born persons, even if it provides immense benefit, may be released from occupation out of consideration for the fear of distress and calamity; however, land occupied by herds of cattle, which is beneficial for the treasury and transport, may not be released, except when its occupation obstructs the sowing of crops.

KAZ08.4.41: Of the highway robbers (*pratirodhaka*) and forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*), the highway robbers move openly and visibly; they travel by night, lie in ambush, attack persons directly, are permanent, carry provisions for a hundred thousand days, cause great provocation, and operate from remote locations.
The forest-dwellers, on the other hand, move within the intermediate forests and are not easily seen.
"And they destroy only a portion [of their object]," say the Teachers (Ācāryas).
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Robbers strike at one who is negligent; they are few, weak, and easy to detect and apprehend.
Forest-dwellers (*āṭavika*), however, being numerous, courageous, and fighting openly, are plunderers and destroyers of countries, possessing the same nature as kings.
KAZ08.4.44: Between deer and elephants, deer are more numerous, provide abundant meat and hides that are useful, require little fodder and cause little distress, and are easy to manage.
Elephants captured while in a contrary state, as well as those that are vicious, lead to the destruction of the country.

KAZ08.4.46: Between assistance provided for one's own position and assistance provided for another's position, assistance for one's own position—consisting of grain, cattle, gold, and forest produce—is what sustains the inhabitants of the countryside in times of calamity.
The opposite of this is the assistance rendered to one who occupies the position of an enemy.
Thus are the obstructions: the internal obstruction consisting of the chief minister, and the external obstruction consisting of enemies and forest tribes.
[Thus ends the section on Obstruction.
KAZ 08.4.49: One who is oppressed by those two [the king and the minister] and by the aforementioned forms of harassment, yet remains attached to the principal officials, [is termed "obstructed"].
One that is impaired by avoidance,
one that is scattered, and one that is falsely collected.
"Carried off by neighboring kings or forest tribes" refers to the section concerning the depletion of the treasury.

One should strive for the non-occurrence of oppressions and for the prevention of those already arisen; one should likewise strive for the prosperity of the territory and for the destruction of paralysis and congestion. (The section on calamities of the army; the section on calamities of allies.)
KAZ08.5.01 / The calamities of the army are: being dishonored, being insulted, and not being maintained.
one who is ill, one who has newly arrived, and one who has come from afar.
Exhausted, depleted, and frustrated.
With its forward momentum destroyed, arriving out of season, and reaching an unfavorable ground.
Despair,
wandering about,
and pregnancy of the wife.
With an internal splinter,
with a provoked root, and with a ruptured interior;
withdrawn, overthrown, and settled nearby;
completed,
obstructed,
and encompassed.
One where the transport of grain and men has been cut off;
one abandoned by its own people; one abandoned by allies.
Beset by seditious persons, with a hostile rear-guard, and with its root (the capital) empty.
One that is without a master, one that is disunited, and one that is blind.
Among those [three types of troops], between one who has been honored and one who has been insulted or undisciplined, the one who has been honored but whose purpose has been achieved should fight;
not the one who has been insulted, for he harbors internal resentment.
Of those who are neither hired nor diseased, the one who is not hired shall fight after receiving wages for the immediate present,
but not the diseased person who is incapable of action.
Between one newly arrived and one who has traveled from afar, the newly arrived should fight— having obtained a position from elsewhere and being unmixed with others—
not the one who has traveled from afar, who is exhausted by the long journey.
Between two armies that are both exhausted and depleted, one should fight against the exhausted army once it has obtained rest through bathing, eating, and sleeping,
but not against the depleted army— except in the case of a battle where its draft animals and men have already been worn out.

Between two forces, one whose front-line momentum has been repelled and one whose front-line momentum has been destroyed, one should fight with the one whose front line has been repelled but broken by the enemy's advance and which still contains a concentration of pre-eminent warriors; not with the one whose front-line momentum is destroyed and whose leading heroes have been killed by the enemy's advance.

KAZ08.5.07: Of two forces that have reached an unfavorable season or unfavorable ground, one that has reached an unfavorable season but possesses vehicles, weapons, and armor suited to the season should fight; not one that has reached unfavorable ground, as its expansion and maneuvers will be obstructed.

Between one who has retreated out of despair and one who has retreated out of fear, one should fight against the one who has retreated out of despair once his purpose has been achieved, but not against the one who has retreated out of fear whose chief leaders have fled.

Between one whose wife is pregnant and one who has an internal thorn (a secret enemy), it is better to fight one whose wife is pregnant after having released her, rather than one with an internal thorn who has a hidden ally within.

KAZ08.5.10: Between one whose root is provoked and one whose internal core is split, one should fight the one whose root is provoked after pacifying his anger through conciliation and other means, but not the one whose internal core is split, as he is divided from within by mutual dissension.

Between the "withdrawn" (apasṛta) and the "over-thrown" (atikṣipta) types of enemy, one should fight the withdrawn enemy who has crossed into a single kingdom by means of counsel and military exertion, provided he relies on a confederacy or an ally; but not the over-thrown enemy who has crossed into many kingdoms, because of the great difficulty involved.

Between the "encamped" (upaniviṣṭa) and the "concluded" (samāpta) forms of battle, one should fight the enemy by deceiving him regarding the separate movement and positioning of the encamped army, but not the concluded army, which moves and stays in a single location together with the enemy.
Between a besieged city and a surrounded city, one should fight against the besieger by exiting from elsewhere, rather than fighting against a surrounded city which is blocked on all sides.

Between a supply line cut off for grain and one cut off for men, one should fight by bringing grain from elsewhere or by using mobile and stationary food supplies; one should not fight against a supply line cut off for men that lacks reinforcements.

Between an army scattered within one's own territory and one scattered among the allies, that which is scattered within one's own territory can be mobilized in times of emergency, whereas an army scattered among the allies cannot, because of the great distance in space and time.
Between an army joined with traitors and one beset by a treacherous rear-guard, one should fight that which is joined with traitors but commanded by trustworthy men and is not disorganized;
one should not fight that which is beset by a treacherous rear-guard and is terrified by an attack from the rear.

Between an army whose root is depleted and one that is leaderless and disorganized, the one whose root is depleted should fight with its entire mobilized force after providing protection for the city-dwellers and country-folk;
it should not fight the leaderless and disorganized army, which lacks a royal commander-in-chief.
Between a broken peak and a blind one, a broken peak that is under the command of another should fight, not a blind one that lacks a guide.
Purification of faults, the reinforcement of forces, the siege of a fortified position,
and peace with the opposing party constitute the means for overcoming the calamities of one's own army.
Ever vigilant, he should protect his own army from enemies during times of calamity;
ever vigilant, he should strike at the vulnerabilities in the armies of his enemies.
One should vigilantly counteract, even beforehand, that very cause from which one’s subjects might suffer calamity.
Whether an ally has been attacked by oneself, by another ally, or by the power of others in concert, [one should act accordingly].

When one who has abandoned [the territory] due to incapacity, greed, or affection, or one who has sold it, is attacked by an adversary in battle or acts treacherously; ||| KAZ08.5.23ab ||| [then the conqueror shall act accordingly].
Or, while proceeding against an enemy by means of a double policy, or while marching toward another from a different direction,
he may be overreached through misplaced trust, whether traveling separately or together.
Or one who has not been released from calamities due to fear, humiliation, or indolence;
or one who has been confined from his own lands, or has fled from nearby out of fear.
Whether by seizure or by non-payment, or having been given and then insulted;
or whether wealth has been over-exacted, either by oneself or through another.

Or one who has been assigned an excessive burden, or who has approached the enemy after breaking [his own side], or who has been neglected due to incapacity, or who has been made hostile after being solicited; KAZ08.5.27ab.
A friend is acquired with difficulty, and once acquired, he quickly becomes alienated.
A friend who has exerted effort, or one who is worthy of honor but has been neglected through delusion,
or one who was honored but not in a manner befitting him, or one who was restrained despite his power— [such a friend becomes estranged].

A friend who is terrified by an attack from another ally, or apprehensive of an alliance with an enemy, or who can be alienated by seditious persons—such a friend is one to be won over; once won, he remains loyal.
Therefore, one should not produce these faults that destroy friends;
or, if they have arisen, one should pacify them by means of qualities that counteract those faults.
(Knowledge of power, place, time, strength, and weakness—[and] the times for marching.)

KAZ09.1.01: A conqueror, having ascertained the relative strength and weakness of himself and his enemy—taking into account power, place, time, the timing of the expedition, the mobilization of forces, internal revolts, depletion, expenditure, gains, and calamities—should march forth if he possesses superior strength;
otherwise, he should remain stationary.
KAZ09.1.02: “Between energy and power, energy is superior.”
For a king who is himself brave, powerful, healthy, and trained in weaponry is capable of defeating even a powerful monarch, provided he has his army as his second.
Moreover, even a small punishment inflicted by him becomes effective through his majesty.
"But a king who possesses power yet lacks energy perishes when overcome by his own valor," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
One who possesses power overcomes a king who possesses energy by means of his own power; having summoned, hired, or purchased men of proven heroism from another king superior to him.
And his army, endowed with abundant power and equipped with horses, elephants, chariots, and implements, moves everywhere unimpeded.
And it is said that those possessed of energy and power, having conquered or purchased women, children, the lame, and the blind, have thereby conquered the earth.
KAZ09.1.10: “Between power and counsel, power is superior.”
For one who possesses the power of counsel but lacks fruitful intellect becomes powerless.
"Moreover, his ritual action performed with mantras is rendered ineffective; it destroys the grain in the womb [of the field], just as a lack of rain does," so say the teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
The power of counsel is superior.

For a king who possesses the eye of wisdom and the treatises is capable of formulating counsel with even a small amount of effort, and he is able to outmaneuver enemies who possess energy and power through the means of conciliation and so forth, as well as through the secret application of strategic methods.
In this way, one who possesses a greater degree of each successive power—namely energy, majesty, and the power of counsel—gains the upper hand over his opponent.
KAZ09.1.17: Place is the earth.
Within that region, extending from the Himalayas to the ocean, there is a transverse area measuring one thousand yojanas, which constitutes the domain of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
In that regard, the specific types [of terrain] are: forest, village, mountain, watery, earthy, level, and uneven.
Among these, one should employ such actions as will increase one's own respective strength.
Where the terrain is suitable for one's own troops to exercise and maneuver, but unsuitable for those of the enemy,
that is the best location.
The contrary is the inferior;
the common is the middling.
Time consists of cold, heat, and rain.
Its specific divisions are night, day, fortnight, month, season, solstice, year, and the yuga.
Among these, one should employ measures that increase one's own strength according to the specific circumstances.
Where it is the season for one's own troops to exercise but the wrong season for those of the enemy,
that is the best time; the opposite is the worst.
The common [person] is the middling one.
“Among power, place, and time, power is the most important,” say the teachers.
For one who possesses power is capable of countering a terrain characterized by lowlands and plateaus, as well as a season characterized by cold, heat, and rain.
“Place is more important,” say some.
"For a dog on dry land can drag out a crocodile,
whereas a crocodile in deep water can drag out a dog."
“Time is superior,” say some.
"By day the crow kills the owl; by night the owl kills the crow."
"No," says Kauṭilya.
For power, place, and time are mutually supportive of one another.
Strengthened by those [allies], he should set aside a third or a fourth part of his army for defense at the base, in the rear, and against frontier forest tribes; then,

taking with him a treasury and an army sufficient for accomplishing the task, he should set out on an expedition in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa to destroy the enemy's autumnal crop and his winter store of grain— provided that the enemy’s food supplies are exhausted, no new supplies have been gathered, his fortifications and allies are not yet prepared, and his winter harvest has been ruined.
And he should set out on an expedition in the month of Caitra to destroy the winter crops and the spring handfuls of grain belonging to him.
He should undertake an expedition in the month of Jyeṣṭha or Mūla to destroy the enemy's unprepared fortifications, his friend, his spring crops, and his winter stores of grain;
or he should march in the winter against a region that is excessively hot and deficient in fodder, fuel, and water.
In summer, one should march through a region that is covered in frost and mist, characterized by deep depressions, or one that is dense with grass and trees.
When it rains, he should march if his own army is capable of training and exertion while that of the enemy is not.
Between the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa and that of Taiṣa, he should undertake a long-term expedition;
between Caitrī and Vaiśākhī, a medium-term one;
and between Jyeṣṭhāmūlīyā and Āṣāḍhī, a short-term one.
One who intends to observe the fast should do so on the fourth [lunar day] even in times of misfortune.
An expedition during a calamity has been explained under the heading of marching after declaring war.
And for the most part, the teachers instruct that one should march against an enemy when he is in distress.
Kauṭilya maintains that one should march when power arises, because calamities are uncertain in their occurrence.
Or rather, when he is able to weaken or destroy the enemy by marching against him, then he should march.
KAZ09.1.45: During the season when [the crops] have been destroyed by excessive heat, one should march with an army consisting primarily of elephant forces.
For elephants that have internal sweat become afflicted with leprosy.
Not plunging into the water and yet drinking it, they become blind due to the internal alkaline salt.
Therefore, one should march with a preponderance of elephant forces through a region that has abundant water and while it is raining.
In the opposite case, the terrain will be dominated by asses, camels, horses, and wild beasts, with little rain and much mud.
While it is raining, one should march with the fourfold army through a region that is mostly desert.
Or, one should divide the march along a route according to whether it is even or uneven, low or high ground, and short or long.
Alternatively, all [expeditions] may be of short duration, depending on the lightness of the task;
or they may be long, depending on the gravity of the task, with the rainy season serving as the time for encampment elsewhere.
(Bases of Force, Qualities of Equipment, and the Operations of an Enemy Force)
KAZ09.2.01: The times for mobilizing the hereditary troops, hired troops, guilds, allies, enemies, and forest tribes.

KAZ09.2.02: The hereditary army (*maula-bala*) may exceed [the enemy's] by virtue of protecting its own base; or, the hereditary troops, being joined with reinforcements (*atyāvāpa*), might revolt at the base; or the opponent may possess a hereditary army that is numerous and loyal, or a core army (*sāra-bala*).
One must fight with exertion,

because the hereditary troops (*maula*) are capable of enduring loss and expense over long distances or times; furthermore, when there is a large gathering of devoted troops, there is fear of instigation (*upajāpa*) by the enemy, and there is no trust in other types of forces, such as hired troops (*bhṛta*), and so forth.
Or when there is a depletion of the strength of all the troops—this is the time for the hereditary army (*maula-bala*).

“KAZ09.2.03: ‘My hired force is large, while my hereditary force is small. ‘The enemy’s hereditary force is small or disaffected; his hired army consists mostly of weaklings or is lacking in substance. ‘War must be fought through counsel with little exertion. ‘The terrain is narrow or the time is short, resulting in minimal loss and expenditure. ‘My army has few reinforcements, intrigue has been quelled, or it is full of confidence.’”
“The enemy’s small expansion must be destroyed”—this is the time for employing hired troops.
“‘My guild-force is abundant and capable of being deployed both at home and on an expedition; the campaign shall be short;
the opponent consists primarily of a guild-force and desires to fight by means of counsel and physical exertion. (KAZ09.2.04)
The administration of force through punishment—this is the time for the power of guilds.

“KAZ09.2.05: ‘My allied force is abundant and can be deployed both at home and on the expedition; ‘The absence will be brief, and there is more scope for physical combat than for war of intrigue; ‘Or, having first caused the forest tribes, the city garrison, or the ally’s reinforcements to fight with my allied force, I shall afterwards cause them to fight with my own force; ‘Or, my objective is one shared with my ally.’”

"Is the accomplishment of my task dependent upon my ally? "Is my ally nearby and worthy of being favored? "Or shall I cause his enemy to suffer a great calamity?"—these constitute the time for the power of an ally.
“‘My enemy’s force is vast;
I shall make them fight with that enemy force in the city or in the forest.
There, like a *caṇḍāla* in a fight between a dog and a boar, my success will be achieved through the destruction of either side. [This is the strategy] regarding the reinforcements.”

"Or I shall perform this 'crushing of the thorns' in the forests"— or, out of fear of excessive accumulation [of troops], he should station the enemy force constantly nearby, except when there is apprehension of internal rebellion; and this is the time for fighting the enemy or for a secondary battle.
— thus ends the section on the time for attacking the enemy's forces.
By this, the time for forest troops has been explained.
It provides guidance on the road,
is suitable for enemy territory,
and is favorable for fighting the enemy.

When the enemy consists primarily of forest troops, one should think, "Let the *bilva* be struck down by the *bilva*"; a small foraging party must be destroyed—this is the time for using forest troops.

KAZ09.2.09: An army that rises up for the purpose of plunder—whether it be numerous, stationed in many places, or previously mentioned or unmentioned—is called *autsāhika* (voluntary). Such an army, which provides no food or wages and acts through plunder, forced labor (*viṣṭi*), and intimidation, is to be sown with dissension among enemies; however, an army consisting mostly of men from the same region, caste, and craft, who are united and large in number, is not to be divided.
[Thus end the times for recruiting forces.
KAZ09.2.10: Of these, he should employ the enemy's forest-dwellers as a force maintained by providing raw materials (kupya), or as a force maintained by plunder (vilopa).
Or, when the time for military action against an enemy has arrived, he should seize the enemy's force, or send it elsewhere,
or render it fruitless.
Or he should cause it to be stored away when scattered,
or release it once the proper time has passed.
And one should frustrate this accumulation of forces by an enemy and accomplish it for oneself.
And among these, each preceding one is better to arm than the following.
Because it exists only when that [king] exists and because it follows him with constant devotion, the hereditary army is superior to the hired army.
A hired force that is permanent, immediately available, and obedient is better than a guild-force.

The strength of guilds (śreṇī-bala) consisting of local people who have come together for a common purpose, and who possess equal rivalry, resentment, success, and gain, is superior to the strength of allies (mitra-bala).
KAZ09.2.17: An ally’s force is superior to an enemy’s force because it can be employed for a single purpose at any time and place without limit.
An enemy force commanded by noble leaders is better than a forest-dwelling force.
Both of these are for the purpose of confiscation.
If there is no destruction or misfortune caused by those two, there will be danger from snakes.
"Among the armies of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, each preceding one is better to mobilize because of their preeminence in spirit," so say the Teachers.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
An enemy should attack the strength of the Brāhmaṇas by means of prostration.
However, an army of Kṣatriyas trained in the science of weaponry is superior, or else an army of Vaiśyas and Śūdras that is large in number and possesses great strength.
Therefore, knowing that the enemy possesses such strength and that this is the counter-force required against him, one should mobilize the collection of forces.
Against an elephant force, the counter-force consists of elephants equipped with mechanical devices, carts, concealed shafts, spears, javelins, gold-plated bamboo, and barbed missiles.
That same force, consisting primarily of stones, clubs, shields, goads, and hair-seizing hooks, is the counter-force for the chariot army.
That same force is the counter-force for cavalry;
or else, armored elephants are the counter-force for cavalry, and armored horses are the counter-force for elephants.
Chariots equipped with armor and infantry equipped with shields constitute the counter-force for a fourfold army.

In this manner, one should effect the mobilization of forces and the repelling of the enemy's army according to the distribution of one's own troops, by means of various tactical dispositions of the constituent parts [of the army]. (Consideration of internal rebellion—
remedies against the provocation of external and internal constituents.)
Between a small provocation from behind and a great gain from the front, the small provocation from behind is more serious.
If he marches against one who has little internal dissension, his seditious persons, enemies, forest tribes, or the subjects' own agitation will indeed augment that dissension from all sides.
Moreover, even a great acquisition previously obtained is swallowed up by the loss and expenditure of servants and friends when things have come to such a state.

Therefore, because there is no acquisition of gain from the front for one who possesses a thousand [men], or because there is internal rebellion from behind for one who possesses only a hundred, he should not march.
"For misfortunes are like the point of a needle," so runs the popular proverb.
If the enemy provokes him later, he should employ conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force.
If one is obtained beforehand, he should appoint either the commander-in-chief or the crown prince as the leader of the army.
Alternatively, a powerful king, capable of suppressing a rearward rebellion, may march to seize a gain in the front.
If there is suspicion of internal rebellion, he should march taking those suspected persons with him; or, if there is suspicion of external rebellion, he should take their sons and wives.
Having established internal outposts and appointed a commander for the empty fort with many troops and many leaders, he may march, or he may not march.
It has been stated previously that internal rebellion is more evil than external rebellion.
KAZ09.3.12: An internal rebellion consists of the provocation of any one among the ministers, the domestic chaplain, the commander-in-chief, or the crown prince.
One should settle that matter either by abandoning one's own faults or by virtue of the power of the other party and their transgressions.

KAZ09.3.14: Even in the case of a high offense committed by the domestic priest, the successful resolution is either confinement or expulsion; in the case of the crown prince, it is confinement or suppression, provided there exists another son endowed with virtuous qualities.

One should win over a son, a brother, or another relative who has seized the king by means of energetic action; in the absence of such energy, one should do so through compliance with what has been seized and the performance of conciliation, out of fear of an alliance with the enemy.
Or he should inspire confidence in him by means of land-grants from other persons of similar character.

He should send someone distinguished to seize [the enemy's] property or to levy a fine, or he should dispatch neighboring kings and forest-dwellers; once the enemy is engaged by them, he should strike him down.
He should employ the seizure of a person under arrest or the stratagem concerning an enemy village.
By this, the counselor and the commander-in-chief are explained.
The provocation of any one of the internal ministers, excluding the counselor and others, is termed "internal ministerial provocation."
In that case as well, he should employ the appropriate means according to what is fitting.
KAZ09.3.22: An internal rebellion among any of the following—leaders of the realm, frontier guards, forest-dwellers, or those who have submitted to military service—is termed an external rebellion.
He should cause him to be seized by one another.

Or, if it is held by one who is extremely difficult to overcome, he should cause it to be seized by one among the neighboring kings, forest tribes, members of the king's own family, or those who have been deposed.
Or, he should cause him to be won over by a friend in such a way that he does not go over to the enemy.

Or, an agent provocateur (sattrin) should cause him to be alienated from his enemy, saying: "This man, regarding you as a mere instrument (yoga-puruṣa), will incite you against your own master; once his purpose is achieved, he will employ you as a leader of the army (daṇḍa-cārin) against enemies or forest tribes, or subject you to arduous labor, or leave you at the end with your wife and children like one who has no son."
Having seen your prowess frustrated, he will treat you as a commodity for sale to his master;
or, having made peace with you, he will propitiate your master himself.
"Go to a friend or one who is close to him."
One should honor those who have approached with gifts according to their desired intentions.
He should cause the one who has not yet submitted to break off his alliance by saying, "That man of yours is a spy sent by us."
And an agent provocateur should have him killed by means of forged edicts, or by secret agents.
Or, he should win over those brave men who have set out with him by having them carry out his intentions.
By means of that, the secret agent (sattrin) should speak to those who have been dispatched.
Thus is the established conclusion.
And he should incite these provocations in others, while pacifying them in himself.
KAZ09.3.36: Against one who is capable of either inciting or suppressing anger, secret instigation (upajāpa) should be employed.

KAZ09.3.37: One who is true to his word, capable of assisting in the execution of an undertaking and in obtaining its fruit, and capable of protecting one in times of misfortune—against such a person, a secret agreement should be made; however, one must first deliberate whether he is of noble intent or, on the contrary, a rogue.

KAZ09.3.38: For a deceitful outsider may thus instigate an insider: "If he kills his master and hands him over to me, I shall achieve a twofold gain—the destruction of the enemy and the acquisition of territory.

Or else, the enemy will slay him; then, with his kinsmen and faction destroyed, my own faction of those who would not commit such an act will become greatly alarmed by the punishment for such a crime, and he will become suspicious even of others like himself."
"And by means of a forged edict, I shall have him executed, one after another."
Or an internal traitor, being deceitful, may thus instigate an external one: "I shall seize his treasury,
or I shall destroy his army,
or I shall have this wicked master killed by him."

I shall employ against external enemies, such as hostile kings and forest-dwellers, one who is already engaged [in hostilities], thinking: "Let his wheel be set in motion; let his enmity be intensified;
then he will come under my control."
Then I shall either propitiate my husband,
or I shall seize the kingdom myself, or else, having bound both the foreign territory and my husband's territory, I shall obtain both.
"Or, having instigated an enemy, I will have him killed when he has become trusting;
or I will seize his base while it is empty."
But one of virtuous intent, however, instigates [the enemy] for the sake of living together.
One should form an alliance with one who is of noble intent;
however, having received a deceitful person with the words "so be it," one should overreach him.

Having understood this— [that] among others, those who are higher than others [should be protected] by their own [subordinates], and those who are lower than others [should be protected] by themselves—
the wise man must always protect himself from both his own people and from others.
(The consideration of loss, expenditure, and gain)
KAZ09.4.01: A decrease in draft animals and personnel constitutes depletion.
KAZ09.4.02: The depletion of gold and grain constitutes expenditure.
He should march toward a gain that is distinguished by many superior qualities compared to those two.

KAZ 9.4.4–5: Acquirable (ādeya), recoverable (pratyādeya), pleasing (prasādaka), provocative (prakopaka), short-term (hrasvakāla), small loss (tanukṣaya), small expenditure (alpavyaya), great increase in profit (mahānvṛddhyudaya), auspicious (kalya), righteous (dharmya), and leading (puroga)—these are the excellences of gain.
That which is easily acquired and maintained, yet not recoverable by enemies, is "acquirable" (ādeya).
In the opposite case, it shall be returned.
Taking it up, he meets with destruction either while remaining there or while departing.
Or if he should perceive: "Having seized what is recoverable, I shall cause the treasury, the army, the stores, and the defensive arrangements to flow away;
I shall extract the essence from mines, commodities, elephant forests, irrigation works, and trade routes;
and I shall weaken his subjects."
"I shall cause them to be led away, or I shall win them over through strategic means;
furthermore, he will incite them against their opponent through counter-measures."
"Or I shall make this person my merchandise as a counter-measure against him; or I shall provide him with a friend who is currently under siege;
or, while staying here, I shall protect my own country or that of my friend from the afflictions caused by thieves and enemies."
"I shall cause his friend or his refuge to perceive his deficiency;
then that person, being alienated from the enemy, will join him, or I shall grant him land with due honor."
"An ally arisen from a coalition will be mine for a long time"—thinking thus, one may accept even a profit that ought to be returned.
Thus, what may be taken and what may not be taken have been explained.
When a righteous person acquires wealth from an unrighteous person, it becomes a source of confidence for both his own people and those of others.
The opposite is the provoker.
KAZ09.4.12: A gain that is not obtained despite the advice of ministers becomes a cause for anger, [the ministers thinking], "We were made to incur loss and expense by this [king]."

When a gain is being obtained from seditious ministers due to their disregard [for others], it becomes a cause for provocation, [the thought arising]: "This man, having accomplished his purpose, will destroy us."
The opposite of this is conciliatory.
Thus, the means of conciliation and provocation have been explained.

(KAZ 9.4.15) Because it is accomplished merely by going [to the enemy], it is short in duration. (KAZ 9.4.16) Because it is accomplished through secret counsel (*mantra*), there is little loss [of resources]. (KAZ 9.4.17)
It involves little expenditure because its expenses are limited solely to food; it involves great expenditure because of the abundance of immediate requirements.
Interest arises because it is connected with profit.
He is fit for office because he is free from obstacles.
KAZ09.4.22: Because it involves the acquisition of what is praiseworthy, it is righteous (dharmya).
Because the members of the confederacy do not proceed with fixed determination, there must be a leader. Thus it is said.

When gains are equal, one should deliberate upon the place and time, strength and means, the pleasant and unpleasant, speed and lack of speed, proximity and distance, immediate results and future consequences, substantiality and continuity, as well as abundance and the quality of being possessed of many virtues; having thus reflected, one should accept the gain that is endowed with the greatest number of virtues.

KAZ09.4.25 / Obstacles to profit are: desire, anger, timidity, compassion, shame, ignobility, pride, pity, regard for the next world, piety, lack of firmness, wretchedness, envy, humiliation regarding what is in hand, wickedness, distrust, fear, lack of remedy, inability to endure cold, heat, and rain, and the insistence on auspicious days, lunar mansions, and sacrifices.
Wealth passes by the child who asks too much about the constellations;
for wealth is the constellation of wealth—what will the stars do?

Men who possess no wealth do not attain their objectives even with hundreds of efforts; objectives are secured through wealth, just as elephants are captured by means of decoy elephants. (External and internal calamities.)
KAZ09.5.01: *Apanaya* (removal) consists of the improper placement of the stages of peace and the others, contrary to their prescribed order.
Therefore, calamities arise from it.
External origin with internal counter-espionage; internal origin with external counter-espionage; external origin with external counter-espionage.
Internal uprisings and internal conspiracies—these are the internal calamities.
Where outsiders instigate insiders, or insiders instigate outsiders,
there the success of one who responds to both sides is particularly distinguished.
For those who respond with a counter-message are often well-disguised, whereas those who instigate the message are not.
When they have been pacified, the instigators would not be able to instigate others.
