For those outsiders who instigate internal strife against their own people are the most dangerous, as are those insiders who do so against outsiders.
And there is the destruction of great effort by enemies,
as well as a connection with wealth for oneself.
When those within [the enemy's circle] are whispering [against him], he should employ conciliation and gifts.
Position, honor, and work constitute conciliation.
Favor, remission of taxes, assignment for labor, or a gift [constitutes the means of acquisition].
When outsiders are engaged in secret correspondence, one should employ the tactics of sowing dissension and the use of force.
Secret agents or those disguised as friends should report the activities of outsiders to them, saying: "This king of yours wishes to deceive you through the agency of seditious persons;
be on your guard!"
Or, spies disguised as traitors, having been dispatched among the traitors, should cause the traitors to be divided from outsiders,
or the outsiders from the traitors.
Or, having infiltrated among the seditious persons, the assassins (tīkṣṇas) should kill them with weapons or poison.
Or, having summoned outsiders, they should have them killed.
Where outsiders instigate other outsiders, or insiders instigate other insiders,
there the success of the instigator through secret union in a secluded place is particularly distinguished.
For when the fault has been purified, those who were corrupted no longer exist.
For if a corruptible person is not purified, the fault will again corrupt others.
Therefore, when outsiders attempt to instigate rebellion, one should employ the tactics of sowing dissension and the application of force.
Secret agents or spies disguised as friends should say: "This king of yours wishes to seize [the territory] himself; you are at odds with the king—be on your guard!"
Or, sharp agents who have infiltrated the ranks of the messengers of the instigator of the conspiracy should strike them with weapons, poison, and other means at their points of vulnerability.
Then the secret agents should accuse the person who has instigated the conspiracy.
When those within [the enemy's circle] instigate those within [his own], he should employ the appropriate stratagem against them as the situation requires.
One should employ conciliation (sāman) characterized by signs of satisfaction when [the opponent] is dissatisfied, or the opposite when he is satisfied.
Giving consists of honoring [the recipient] by citing one's own capacity for purification, or by showing regard for their misfortune or prosperity.
Or an agent appearing as a friend may say to them: "The king will test you to ascertain your thoughts; therefore, you must report this to him."
Or, he should cause dissension among them by means of one another, saying: "Such-and-such a person and such-and-such a person are making this kind of proposal to the king"—this is dissension.
And the punishment shall be as prescribed for the superintendent of criminal justice.
Of these four types of calamities, one should first settle the internal one.
It has been stated previously that internal unrest arising from fear of snakes is more harmful than external unrest.
One should recognize that among calamities, each preceding one is lighter than the following;
however, a calamity arising from powerful enemies is heavy, while the opposite case is light.
(Calamities involving traitors and enemies).
From among the seditious and from among the enemies, there are two kinds of pure [persons].
KAZ09.6.02: When the enemy's seditious elements have been cleared out among the citizens or the country people, he should employ the strategic means, with the exception of punishment.
For punishment cannot be cast upon the great multitude.
Or, when rebuked, he may fail to carry out that matter and instead produce some other disadvantage.
But regarding their principal officers, he should act as prescribed for those who have committed offenses involving punishment.
KAZ09.6.06: When there is a purification of enemies, one should seek success through conciliation and other means from whichever enemy is the primary one or the one who must be dealt with.

The accomplishment of the primary objective depends upon the master; the accomplishment of the dependent depends upon the ministers; and the accomplishment of the dependent objective depends upon both.
It is "mixed" because of the intermingling of those who are corruptible and those who are incorruptible.
In the case of a mixed [offense], there is the accomplishment [of the punishment] for one who is not at fault.
For in the absence of an object of perception, there are no perceivers.
KAZ09.6.11: Because of the unification of friends and enemies, it is "mixed with others" (paramiśrā).
In the case of a woman who has been mixed with another, success is achieved through a friend.
For an alliance with a friend is easy to accomplish, but not so one with an enemy.
If the ally does not desire peace, one should repeatedly incite him [to rebellion].
Then, having caused a rift between the enemy and [the ally] by means of secret agents, he should obtain an ally.
Or he should seize that member of the ally's confederacy who stands as an intermediary.
When those stationed at the extremities have been won over, those stationed in the middle are divided.
Or he may obtain one who remains neutral.
When those situated in the middle have been obtained, those situated at the extremes do not combine.
And just as there is a distinction among their bases, one should employ those same means accordingly.

One should conciliate a righteous person by praising his birth, lineage, learning, and conduct, as well as his relationship with ancestors, and by citing benefits or harms received from him in the past, present, or future.

One should win over by conciliation an enemy who has lost his enthusiasm for war, who is exhausted by conflict, whose stratagems have been thwarted, who is afflicted by loss of men and wealth, by expenses, and by living abroad; or one who seeks purity through another, or who suspects another, or who is primarily friendly and possesses a virtuous disposition.
One should win over a greedy or impoverished person by means of gifts, preceded by establishing them in the status of a preeminent ascetic.

That is of five kinds: the relinquishment of what is to be given, the continuation of what has been received, the restoration of what was taken, the gift of one's own property, and the gift of seizing for oneself from the property of others that had not been previously granted.
Thus ends the section on the act of giving.
One should cause a split by means of one or another [of these causes] in a case where there is mutual hatred, enmity, or apprehension regarding the seizure of land.
Or, by means of intimidation, he may deter a coward, saying: "This man has made a treaty with you and will carry out his work for you;
his ally has been dispatched, or he is not even internally committed to the treaty."

Or, when merchandise from his own country or another country should arrive at his commercial warehouses, spies should circulate the rumor that these goods have been seized by him from an enemy to be attacked.
When [the enemy's] power has become extensive, he should send a message with a hostile intent: "This merchandise or this warehouse has been sent to you by me;
sell it to the confederates, or else depart."
"Then you shall obtain the remainder of the wager."
Then, secret agents (sattrins) should cause it to be seized by the enemies, saying, "This was given by the enemy."
Or, a commodity well-known to the enemy, but unknown to the conqueror, should be sent to him.
His agents disguised as merchants should sell that [merchandise] to the chief enemies.
Then, secret agents (sattrins) should cause it to be seized among the enemies, saying, "This merchandise was given by the enemy."
KAZ09.6.34: Having won over those who have committed great offenses with wealth and honors, he should employ them against the enemy by means of weapons, poison, or fire.
Then, he should cause one minister to go into exile.
Having seized his wife and children, he should proclaim at night that they have been killed.
Then the minister should cause each of those [enemies] of the foe to be exposed one by one.
If they should act as prescribed, he should not cause them to be apprehended.
Or, he should cause one who is incapable [of resistance] to be seized.
Having gained the confidence of the king, he should tell the king that his own life must be protected from the chief [minister].
Now, if an enemy's edict sent for the purpose of harming a chief official is received, one who receives wages from both sides should cause it to be seized.
Or he should send an envoy to one who possesses the power of energy, saying: "Seize the kingdom of so-and-so; our treaty remains as it was."
Then, secret agents should cause this to be reported among the enemies.
They should cause the destruction of one [king's] divisional camp, his supplies, or his reinforcements.
In the case of others, pretending to be friends, they should instigate them by whispering, "You must have these men killed."

Or, when an eminent man, an elephant, or a horse belonging to [the enemy] dies, or is killed or carried off by secret agents, the spies (sattrins) should declare that it was destroyed by mutual conflict.
Then he should send an edict to the accused: "Do it again; then you shall recover the remainder of the wager."
Those who receive wages from both sides should cause that to be seized.
When they have become divided, he may obtain any one of them.
By this, the rules for the commander-in-chief, the prince, and the army officers are explained.
And he should employ stratagems to create dissension among those allied with the enemy.
Thus ends the section on the act of sowing dissension.
Secret agents should eliminate a fierce, energetic, or addicted enemy, or one who is entrenched, by means of weapons, fire, poison, and the like; or else, one of those [agents] may do so with ease.
For a single sharp man can accomplish [his goal] by means of weapons, poison, and fire.
This person performs either all the collective tasks or those that are particularly distinguished.
Thus ends the fourfold group of means (upāya-caturvarga).
And each preceding one among these is lighter than the next.
Conciliation possesses a single quality.
A gift preceded by conciliation is twice as effective.
Sowing dissension is threefold, preceded by conciliation and gifts.
Punishment, preceded by conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension, is fourfold in its application.
Thus it has been stated regarding those who bring accusations.
But regarding those situated on their own territory, those same means [of policy] apply.
But there is a specific distinction: KAZ09.6.64.
He should frequently dispatch chief envoys, well-known for their trade depots, to any one among those stationed in their own territories.
They may employ him at a time of peace or for the purpose of harming an enemy.
If he does not agree, they should inform him, saying, "The peace treaty has been concluded with us."
Those who receive wages from both sides should cause him to be transferred among the others, saying, "This king of yours is wicked."

Or, they should cause division between one who has fear, enmity, or hatred toward another and that other person, saying: "This man is making peace with your enemy; before he overreaches you, make peace even more quickly."
"And strive for his suppression."
Or, having established a connection through marriage alliances, he should cause those who are not allied to become divided.

He should cause their kingdoms to be destroyed by neighboring kings, forest-dwellers, members of their own family, or those who have been deposed; or he should destroy their caravans, herds, and forest settlements, or their army when it has marched forth.
And their caste-groups, relying on one another, should strike at vulnerable points, while those in hiding should attack with fire, poison, and weapons.

Like a bird-catcher or a swallow-wort plant, a deceitful man should cause his enemies to be killed by means of practiced stratagems, using confidence and bait when they are gathered together with others.
(Disasters involving doubt as to whether they are beneficial or harmful; the successes arising from various alternative means to deal with them.)
Excess of passion and the like provokes one's own subjects;
misconduct provokes those who are external.
Both of these constitute the demonic way of life.
Anger is a transformation of one's own mind.
KAZ09.7.04: Among the causes for the enemy's growth, that which is undertaken for the sake of a calamity is harmful and doubtful.

That objective which, when unattained, causes the enemy's growth; which, when attained, becomes recoverable by the enemies; or which, while being attained, results in loss, expenditure, and no gain—[should be abandoned].
That exists for the sake of misfortune.
KAZ09.7.06: Just as gain arising from the calamity of a neighbor is like a source of food for neighboring kings;
or gain that is naturally attainable when sought by an enemy; or gain from the front when one is attacked from behind by an ally who has become enraged or is acting as a rear-guard harasser.
A gain that is contrary to the circle of states (maṇḍala) due to the destruction of a friend or the violation of a treaty is termed "gain for the sake of an emergency."
The arising of fear from oneself or from another is misfortune.
Regarding these two, [one must consider]: whether it is beneficial or not,
whether it is harmful or not,
and whether it is both beneficial and harmful.
The doubt is whether what is non-beneficial is actually beneficial.
KAZ09.7.09: There is a doubt as to whether it is beneficial or not to incite an enemy or a friend.
Whether it is disadvantageous or not to induce the enemy's forces by means of wealth and honor is a matter of doubt.
KAZ09.7.11: There arises a doubt as to whether it is beneficial or harmful to seize land belonging to a powerful neighbor.
KAZ09.7.12: Traveling together with one's wife is a matter of doubt as to whether it results in harm or benefit.
He should investigate their doubts regarding the matter.
Profit with a profitable consequence;
profit without a consequence; profit with an unprofitable consequence.
Misfortune followed by misfortune,
misfortune without consequence,
and misfortune followed by further misfortune— this is the group of six regarding consequences.
Having uprooted an enemy, the acquisition of a rear-ally is a gain followed by a calamity.
For one who is neutral, the application of force or the granting of favor for the sake of a reward is a purpose that lacks further consequence.
The destruction of another's internal [support] is a gain that is followed by a calamity.
Favoring an enemy neighbor by means of treasury and army is a calamity that results in further calamities.
Withdrawal after having incited one who is weak in power [to act] is a calamity that leaves no consequences.
To turn back after having provoked a superior power is a calamity that leads to further calamities.
Among these, each preceding one is superior to the one following it for the purpose of attaining [the goal].
Thus ends the determination of the status of legal proceedings.
The simultaneous occurrence of matters from all sides is called "the arrival of matters from all sides."
That same [state], when attacked by a rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), becomes a crisis involving uncertainty regarding resources from all sides.
The success of these two depends upon securing the support of their allies and their rear-ally.
When there is the arising of fear from enemies on all sides, it constitutes a calamity of misfortune occurring from every direction.
That same [state], when attacked by a friend from all sides, becomes a calamity involving uncertainty regarding disaster.
The success of these two depends upon winning over a mobile enemy or an ally;
otherwise, there will be a joint operation with the enemy or a lack of counter-measures.
"Gain from this side, gain from that side"—this is a calamity regarding wealth arising from both sides.
When that [fortress] is surrounded on all sides and its resources are exhausted, he should march forth to seize wealth that is endowed with the quality of profit.
When the advantages of the gain are equal, he should march to seize that which is the principal, nearby, and not liable to escape, or that by which he might become superior.
"Disaster from this side, disaster from that side"—this is the occurrence of disaster on both sides.
When that [hostile power] is surrounded on all sides and poses no threat, one should seek success through allies.

In the absence of an ally, one should counteract a minor calamity from one side among the constituent elements; a calamity from both sides by means of a superior element; and a calamity from all sides by means of the root (the king himself).
If it is impossible [to achieve the objective], one should abandon everything and withdraw.
For the return of those who were thought dead has indeed been observed, as in the cases of Suyātra and Udayana.
When there is gain from this side and the seizure of the kingdom from the other side, there occurs a calamity involving both profit and loss.
In that situation, he should march to seize that wealth which, though it may lead to disaster, accomplishes his purpose.
For otherwise, he would prevent any assault upon the kingdom.
By this, the occurrence of gain and loss from all sides has been explained.
"From this side there is harm, from the other side there is doubt regarding gain"—this is the situation where there is harm on both sides and doubt regarding gain on both sides.
In that situation, one should first accomplish what is disadvantageous; once that is achieved, one may then pursue what is doubtful as to its benefit.
By this, the cases concerning loss, gain, and doubt on all sides are explained.
When there is gain from this side and a doubt regarding loss from the other side, that is a crisis involving a doubt regarding both gain and loss.
By this, the matters concerning benefit, harm, and doubt on all sides are explained.
In that situation, he should strive to liberate each preceding constituent of his state from danger and uncertainty.
For a friend is better than punishment when one stands in doubt regarding a calamity; or rather, punishment is better than the treasury.
In the absence of the liberation of the entire population, he should strive to liberate the constituent elements of the subjects.
In that regard, among the human constituents, one should secure those who are numerous or deeply devoted, excluding the violent and the greedy;
among the material constituents, one should secure the essential or that which provides great assistance.
Those that are light are to be managed by means of peace, neutrality, or double-dealing; those that are heavy are to be managed by the opposites of these.
And one should seek to attain each subsequent stage among decline, stability, and growth.
Or, by means of the reverse order, he should perceive a distinction in the future regarding decline and the other factors.
Thus ends the determination of place.
By this, the occurrence of gains, losses, and doubts at the beginning, middle, and end of an expedition and other undertakings is explained.
And because gain, loss, and doubt arise in immediate succession, in matters such as military expeditions, it is better to secure gain;
for gain serves to repel rear-enemies and allies of the enemy, to manage depletion, expenditure, absence from home, and the recovery of debts, and to protect the very foundation of the state.
Likewise, loss or uncertainty is endurable for one who remains on his own territory.
By this, the occurrence of gains, losses, and uncertainties during the course of a military expedition is explained.

At the end of an expedition, however, it is better to obtain wealth by either weakening or destroying the enemy—after having weakened or destroyed them—rather than encountering misfortune or doubt due to the fear of provoking the adversary.

But for one who is not the leader among the confederates, it is better to encounter misfortune or doubt at the midpoint or the end of the expedition, because such a course does not lead to a state of being obstructed.
Wealth, virtue, and pleasure constitute the triad of aims.
Of these, each preceding one is better to attain than the one following it.
Misfortune, demerit, and sorrow constitute the triad of misfortunes.
Of these, each preceding one is better than the following for retaliating.
"Profit is loss," "Dharma is adharma," and "Pleasure is sorrow"— this is the triad of doubt.
If the defendant's case is established, it is better for the plaintiff to reach a settlement.
Thus ends the determination of time.
Thus end the calamities; this is their resolution.
Success is achieved through conciliation and gifts among sons, brothers, and kinsmen;
through gifts and sowing dissension among the leaders of the townspeople and the country-folk; and through sowing dissension and the use of force against neighboring kings and forest tribes.
This is the *anuloma* (direct order); in the reverse case, it is the *pratiloma* (inverse order).
Success among friends and enemies is mixed.
For the means are mutually supportive of one another.
In the case of a rival king's suspected ministers, conciliation employed prevents the application of other measures;
toward corruptible ministers, gifts are used; and against confederacies, sowing dissension is applied.
"Punishment [is applied] toward those who possess power."
Furthermore, due to the combination of gravity and lightness [of the circumstances], there arise application, option, and conjunction in relation to calamities.
“By this very means and not by any other”—this is the restrictive injunction (*niyoga*).
“Either by this or by another” constitutes an option (*vikalpa*).
“By this and by another” indicates a conjunction (samuccaya).
Among these, there are four combinations of one [term], four combinations of three,
six combinations of two, and one combination of four.
Thus end the fifteen expedients.
There are as many [sons] born in the reverse order (pratiloma).
Among these, success by means of one expedient is "single success" (*eka-siddhi*);
by two, "double success" (*dvi-siddhi*); and by three, "triple success" (*tri-siddhi*).
Through four [means], there is the fourfold accomplishment.
Because wealth is the root of dharma and the fruit of desire, the attainment of wealth—which is connected to dharma, artha, and kāma—is the attainment of all goals.
KAZ09.7.82: Fire, water, disease, pestilence, panic, famine, and demonic visitations—these are the calamities arising from fate.
Their success comes from prostrating before the deities and Brahmins.
Excessive rain, drought, or any calamity that may arise from the Asuras—
against these, the rites of the Atharvaveda and the accomplishments resulting from successful undertakings are effective.
(The Laying Out of the Encampment)

On a site approved for construction, the chief architect, the carpenter, and the astrologer shall measure out the camp— whether circular, oblong, or square according to the nature of the terrain— with four gates, six roads, and nine divisions; it shall be provided with a moat, an embankment, a wall, gates, and watchtowers for use in times of danger or security.
In the ninth part to the north of the center is the royal residence, one hundred *dhanus* in length and half that in width;
in its western half is the inner apartment (*antaḥpura*).
And the army of the prince of the harem should encamp at the rear.

In front is the place for attendance; to the right are the treasury, the records office, and the offices for carrying out business; to the left is the station for the king's state vehicles—elephants, horses, and chariots.
Beyond this, at intervals of one hundred bows, there shall be four enclosures consisting of wagons, boundary-poles, thorny hedges, pillars, and walls.
In the first [hall], the minister and the domestic priest shall be in the front; to the right, the storehouse and the kitchen; and to the left, the warehouse for forest produce and the armory.
In the second [section], there is the stationing of the hereditary and hired troops, the cavalry and chariots, and the commander-in-chief.
In the third [year], the elephant-herds and the Praśāstṛ [are appointed].
In the fourth [expedition], the commander shall employ forced laborers and his own troops stationed under trusted officers, along with the forces of allies, enemies, and forest tribes.
Merchants and those who live by their appearance shall follow the great roads.
Outside, there shall be hunters and keepers of packs of dogs, accompanied by musical instruments and fires, as well as secret guards.
Upon the approach of enemies, one should place concealed wells, pitfalls, and thorny obstacles.
He should cause the eighteen classes [of spies] to carry out their protective duties in rotation.
And he should cause the measurement of the day's duration to be made for the purpose of knowing the spies' movements.
He shall also cause the prevention of disputes, debt, social gatherings, and gambling,
as well as the protection of seals.
The officer in charge of the vacant city (śūnyapāla) shall arrest any soldier who has returned from the army without orders.
At the front of the march, the commander-in-chief shall ensure proper security measures;
he should proceed with carpenters and laborers and cause water-supply points to be established.
(The march of the camp and the protection against calamities, assaults, and the proper timing for defense.)

KAZ10.2.01: Having calculated the number of halting places along the road between villages and forests according to the availability of fodder, fuel, and water, and having determined the time for standing, sitting, and marching, he should set out on his journey.
He shall cause twice as much food and equipment to be transported as the cost of that remedy.
Or, if he is unable, he should employ them among his own troops or station them in the intervals between his divisions.
In front is the leader; in the middle are the wife and the master;
on the two sides are the horses, with the arms serving as the clearance.
At the ends of the wheels, there should be an expansion of elephants; behind them, the commander-in-chief should march or encamp.
The forest-based livelihood is the expansion [of the state] in every direction.
KAZ10.2.06 / Vīvadha is the transport of goods from one's own country.
KAZ10.2.07: The ally's force is the reinforcement.
The place for the wife is the place of retreat.
When the enemy's attack is from the front, one should march with the Makara formation;
from the rear, with the Śakaṭa formation; and from the flanks, with the Vajra formation.
On all sides with the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], and on the single path with the needle.
In the event of a fork in the road, one should proceed from one's own territory.
For those who are not established on their own ground are at a disadvantage when fighting against those established on their own ground.
One *yojana* is the lowest [speed], one and a half *yojanas* is the middle, and two *yojanas* is the highest.
Or, the destination is conceivable.
One who provides shelter, one who destroys what has been acquired, a rear-ally, an auxiliary force, a middle king, or a neutral king must be countered;
the narrow path must be cleared;
and the treasury, the army, the forces of friends, enemies, and forest tribes, as well as forced labor and the season, must be awaited.

The maintenance, protection, and depletion of the stores for the construction of fortifications will be exhausted; there will be weariness among the hired troops and weariness among the allied troops;
or the recruiters will not urge haste;
or the enemy will fulfill his intended purpose.
Thus he should proceed slowly;
in the opposite case, quickly.

KAZ 10.2.14: One should cross waters by means of elephant-bridges, walkways, causeways, embankments, rafts made of wood and bamboo, and by means of gourds, skins, baskets, leather bags, floats, rafts, and bamboo-floats.
KAZ 10.2.15: When the crossing point is guarded, one should have elephants and horses carry the troops across elsewhere at night and then seize the camp.
KAZ10.2.16: On a waterless road, he shall transport wheeled vehicles and quadrupeds according to the distance of the journey and according to his capacity, providing them with water.
When the enemy is exhausted by a long journey through a waterless wilderness or a difficult road lacking fodder, fuel, and water;

when they have been overwhelmed by an assault; when they are worn out by hunger, thirst, and the fatigue of the march; when they are occupied with crossing or retreating across rivers, caves, or deep mountains;
when they are concentrated on a single narrow path; or when they are crowded together in a mountain defile or at their camp.

When his own army has set out, is without armor, is preoccupied with eating, is exhausted from a long march, is asleep, is afflicted by disease, pestilence, or famine, or when its infantry, cavalry, and elephants are diseased, or when it is on unfavorable ground, or is beset by calamities, he should protect his own forces and strike the enemy's army.

KAZ10.2.18: Knowledge of the enemy's strength is obtained by counting the number of troops dispatched on a single route, as well as the number of foraging parties, meals, beds, bedding, fire-pits, banners, and weapons.
At that time, he should conceal his true self.
Having secured a mountain fort or a forest stronghold that provides both means of retreat and supplies,
he should fight and encamp, keeping his own territory behind him. (Options for treacherous warfare – encouraging one's own troops – deploying one's forces against the weak).
One who is superior in strength, has successfully carried out secret instigations, and has made arrangements for the seasons, should engage in open battle on his own territory.
In the opposite case, it is a treacherous war.

One should strike the enemy at times when his army is in distress or during a sudden attack; or, being established on one's own ground, one should strike him who is not on his own ground; or, having secured the support of the enemy's constituent elements, one should strike him even while he is established on his own ground.
Or, having caused a rout by means of the forces of seditious persons, enemies, or forest tribes, he should strike them down once they have reached unfavorable terrain.
He should break a compact formation with elephants.
Having previously caused a division by offering a breach, one who is undivided himself should strike back after returning to the enemy who has been divided and absorbed.
Having struck it from the front, one should strike a moving or averse elephant with elephants and cavalry from the rear.
Having struck from the rear, one should strike from the front with the elite force (*sārabala*) against an enemy that is wavering or has turned its back.
By these two, the approaches from the flanks are explained.
Or else, one should strike from the direction where the enemy's treacherous and weak forces are located.
If the ground is uneven in front, one should strike from behind.
If the ground is uneven behind him, he should strike from the front.
If the ground is uneven on one side, he should strike from the other side.
Or, having first caused [the enemy] to fight with the forces of seditious persons, enemies, or forest tribes, one who is rested should strike the exhausted enemy while remaining unexhausted.

Or, having himself given way to a defeat by means of the force of a seditious army, he—remaining distrustful while appearing trustworthy—should strike when the enemy has become confident, taking refuge in an ambush.
Being vigilant, he should strike down one who is negligent regarding the plundering of caravans, herds, military camps, market towns, and transport convoys.
Or, one whose strong forces are concealed by weak forces may enter among the enemy's heroes and slay them.
Having lured the enemy's warriors away by means of cattle or by the slaughter of dogs and other animals, he should strike them while concealed within an ambush.
Having kept them awake at night by means of a surprise attack, one should strike them during the day while they are exhausted by sleep or already fast asleep.
Or he may carry out a night attack using elephants equipped with leather bags containing explosives.
In the afternoon, he should strike those who are exhausted from their day-long preparation and exertion.

KAZ 10.3.22–23: With dry hides, circular shields, pebbles, and quivers, or with herds of cattle, buffaloes, and camels that cause terror, one who has not yet broken his own ranks should strike back at the enemy's broken troops as they retreat;
or he should strike the entire force when it is facing the sun or the wind.
A desert, a forest, a narrow pass, a marsh, mountains, low ground, uneven terrain, boats, cattle, a wagon-array, mist, and night—these are the forms of the *sattra* (protracted siege).
And the earlier times for striking are the occasions for treacherous warfare.
But a battle in which the place and time are specified is righteous.
Having united the army, he should say: "I am on equal pay with you; this kingdom is to be enjoyed by us together;
the enemy must be struck down by those commanded by me."
It is also heard in the Vedas regarding the final purificatory baths (*avabhṛtha*) of sacrifices when the sacrificial fees have been completed: "That is your goal, O hero."
Moreover, there are also two verses on this point:
“Those worlds which Brahmins seeking heaven attain through multitudes of sacrifices, through austerity, and by means of the collection of sacrificial vessels—
heroes who relinquish their lives in well-fought battles surpass even those in an instant.”

“May he who does not fight for the sake of his master’s sustenance never possess a new bowl filled with water, well-prepared and covered with a cloth of *darbha* grass; and may he go to hell!”—thus it is said.
The minister and the priest should inspire the warriors by means of the excellence of the battle array.
And his group, consisting of fortune-tellers and the like, should encourage their own faction and intimidate the opposing faction by proclaiming his connection with omniscient deities.
“Tomorrow there will be battle”: having observed a fast, he should lie down with his weapons and vehicles.
And one should also offer oblations with the Atharva verses.
One should cause him to recite benedictions that are associated with victory and lead to heaven.
And he should surrender himself to the Brāhmaṇas.
One should make those endowed with heroism, skill, noble birth, and loyalty the core of the army, ensuring they are not dissatisfied by means of wealth and honor.
KAZ10.3.39: For the armed forces consisting of fathers, sons, and brothers, the royal station shall be a troop with shaven heads and no banners.
An elephant or a chariot used by the king as a vehicle is followed by horses.
He should cause him to mount that [elephant] which has a large troop of attendants or where he himself is well-trained.
A royal spy should be stationed at the headquarters of the battle array.
Charioteers and bards shall describe heaven for the brave and the lack of heaven for the cowardly, and they shall extol the lineage, guild, family, deeds, and conduct of the warriors.
The chaplains and their attendants shall announce the success of magical rites and incantations;
the mechanics, carpenters, and astrologers shall announce the success of their own crafts and the failure of those of others.
The commander-in-chief, having honored the army with wealth and honors, should address it as follows: "The reward for slaying the king is one hundred thousand [panas];
for slaying the commander-in-chief or the prince, fifty thousand;
and for slaying a leading hero, ten thousand."
The destruction of five thousand elephant-chariots, the destruction of one thousand horses, and the destruction of one hundred leading foot-soldiers.
"The head-fine shall be twentyfold, the doubling of the profit, and the forfeiture of the property itself."
The heads of groups of ten among them should know this.

Physicians with surgical instruments, machines, antidotes, oils, and bandages in hand, as well as women who guard the food and drink, and those capable of inciting the men's spirits, should stand behind them.
One should deploy the army on its own ground with its face turned away from the south, with the sun at its back, and with the wind blowing in its favor.
And in a battle formation on foreign territory, they should cause the horses to move about.
Where there is neither a firm position nor mobility, and it is unsuitable ground for an array, one who remains stationary or attempts to advance will be defeated in both ways.
In the opposite case, one wins;
in both cases, one stands firm, whether in stability or in rapid movement.
Whether the terrain is level, uneven, or mixed, it should be ascertained from the front, the flanks, and the rear.
On level ground, one should employ the staff and circular arrays; on uneven ground, the snake and compact arrays; and on mixed ground, the irregular arrays.
Having broken the enemy's superior force, he should request peace.
When requested by one of equal strength, he should enter into an alliance.
One should strike down one who is inferior,
but never one who has reached his own ground or one who has abandoned his life.

For one who returns again and has lost all hope for life, an irresistible impulse arises; therefore, one should not harass a broken enemy. (Battle grounds – the operations of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants)
KAZ10.4.01: One's own territory is desirable for infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants, both for battle and for encampment.

KAZ10.4.02: For men who fight in deserts, forests, lowlands, or highlands; for those who fight as miners, in the open air, by day, or by night; and for elephants and horses of the river-born, mountain-born, marsh-born, or lake-born breeds—their respective preferred battlefields and times [are to be determined].

Level, firm, well-illuminated, free from pits, wheels, and hoof-marks, not obstructing axles, and not broken by trees, shrubs, creepers, thickets, fields, chasms, anthills, sand, or mud— and devoid of fissures— such is the ground for chariots; it is beneficial for elephants, horses, and men alike in battle and in encampment, whether on level or uneven ground.
A horse-training ground should have small stones and trees, contain shallow pits that can be easily leaped over, and be free from the defect of excessive cracking.
Ground with large trunks, stones, trees, creepers, anthills, and shrubs is terrain for infantry.

An elephant’s terrain consists of mountains, valleys, and uneven ground that are accessible; it contains trees suitable for crushing, creepers suitable for cutting, mud that is soft enough to break, and is free from fissures.
A terrain that is free of thorns, not excessively uneven, and suitable for retreat is the excellence for infantry.
A ground that has a double-layered approach path, is free from mud, water, and splashing, and is devoid of pebbles—this is the excellence for horses.
KAZ10.4.09: Abounding in dust, mud, water, reeds, and *śara* grass; free from dog bites; and devoid of blows from the branches of large trees—these are the superior conditions for elephants.
KAZ10.4.10: A terrain that has water reservoirs as its support, is free from ravines, lacks fields, and is capable of being turned back—this is the excellence for chariots.
The land for all [the officials] has been described.
By this, all deployments of the entire army and battles are explained.

KAZ10.4.13: Surveying the terrain, dwellings, and forests; securing level ground, water sources, fords, winds, and sunlight; destroying or protecting the enemy's supplies and reinforcements; the purification and stationing of one’s own force; the extension of the front, the increase of the flank, the clearing of the rear, the first strike, the penetration, the piercing, the rallying, the seizing, the releasing, the exchange of routes, and the seizure or escorting of the treasury and the prince.
Striking with the hindquarters, following those that are inferior, pursuing, and performing social duties—these are the functions of horses.

KAZ10.4.14: Leading the vanguard; clearing paths not yet made, establishing camps, and performing rites at sacred fords (*tīrtha*); crossing waters by swimming with the arms, and descending into them; halting and marching; entering uneven and narrow passes; setting fires and extinguishing them; victory through a single limb (or division);
reuniting those who have broken away; sowing dissension among those who are united; providing protection in times of calamity; assault; creating terror; frightening the enemy; and magnanimity.
Seizing, releasing, breaking down walls, gates, and watchtowers, and the bringing forth and driving away of treasure-troves—these are the duties of elephants.

KAZ10.4.15: Protecting one's own forces, repelling the fourfold army of the enemy, capturing [the enemy] in battle, releasing [one's own troops], reuniting broken ranks, sowing dissension among those who are united, causing terror, displaying magnanimity, and making a fearsome noise—these are the duties of the chariot.
Carrying weapons at all times and in all places, and physical exercise—these are the duties of the infantry.

The clearing of camps, roads, bridges, wells, and watering places; the transport of machines, weapons, armor, equipment, and provisions; and the removal of struck-down weapons and armor from the battlefield—these are the duties of forced labor (viṣṭi-karmāṇi).
A king with few horses should employ oxen and horses in the *vyāyoga* (maneuvering) on chariots;
likewise, one with few elephants should employ donkeys, camels, and carts as the core of his force.

(Section 18: The division of the army into wings, flanks, and center according to strength; the division of the force into strong and weak units; the battles of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants.)
Having established the fort at a distance of five hundred bows, one should engage in battle,
or according to the nature of the terrain.
Having relieved the army, which has been divided with its main force out of sight, the commander-in-chief and the leader should deploy it in battle formation.
One should station a foot soldier at an interval of one *śama*,
a horse at an interval of three *śamas*,
and a chariot or an elephant at an interval of five *śamas*.
He should deploy [the army] with a double interval or a triple interval between the units.
In this manner, he should fight at his ease and without constraint.
A bow is five aratnis long.
In that [space], he should station an archer; at a distance of three bows, a horse;
and at five bows, a chariot or an elephant.
The interval between the wings, the flanks, and the center of the army shall be five bow-lengths.
KAZ10.5.09: Three men are the combatants against a single horse.
For a chariot or an elephant, there are fifteen attendants and five horses.
An equal number of foot-guards should be assigned to the horses, chariots, and elephants.
One should station three triads of chariots as the central division (urasya), and an equal number in both the flanks (kakṣa) and the wings (pakṣa).
In this manner, there are exactly forty-five chariots in the chariot-array (rathavyūha),
two hundred and twenty-five horses,
and six hundred and seventy-five men as combatants.
There are as many guardians of the quarters.
This is the even array.
Its increase consists of two additional chariots up to twenty-one chariots.
Thus, there are ten basic forms of the even array (*samavyūha*) for the odd-numbered forces (*ojas*).
When the wings, flanks, and center have an uneven number of units relative to one another, it is an "uneven array" (*viṣamavyūha*).
For that [debt] as well, the interest increases by two chariots up to twenty-one chariots.
Thus, there are ten types of uneven battle arrays (*viṣamavyūha*) based on the *ojas* formation.
Therefore, the *āvāpa* (supplementary reinforcement) should be formed from the remainder of the troops after the battle array (*vyūha*) has been established.
One should cause two-thirds of the chariots to be deployed in the wings, and station the remainder in the center.
In this manner, the filling-in of chariots should be performed with a reduction of one-third.
By this, the method for the placement of elephants and horses is explained.
As long as it does not cause an obstruction to the combat of horses, chariots, and elephants, so long should the *āvāpa* (the deployment of troops) be carried out.
KAZ10.5.25: An abundance of punishments is the "sowing" (āvāpa).
KAZ10.5.26: An abundance of infantry is a means of recovery.
KAZ10.5.27: The repetition of a single component [of the army] is called *anvāvāpa*.
KAZ10.5.28: An excessive number of seditious persons constitutes *atyāvāpa* (an overabundance of infiltrators).
KAZ 10.5.29: The reinforcement of troops may be fourfold or up to eightfold, depending on the capacity for further recruitment from enemy or friendly territories.
The array of elephants is explained by means of the array of chariots.
Or, it may be a mixed formation of elephants, chariots, and horses: elephants at the ends of the wheels, horses on the flanks, and chariots in the center.
The center-piercing array consists of elephants in the breast, chariots in the flanks, and horses in the wings.
The opposite of this is one who causes dissension among the enemy's subjects.

But for elephants alone, the pure array is as follows: the breast-position for those used for war-equipment (*sāmnāhya*), the rear for those used for riding (*aupavāhya*), and the flanks for the rogue elephants (*vyāla*).
The horse-array consists of armored troops in the center and unarmored troops in the flanks and wings.
KAZ 10.5.36: The infantry array—shield-bearers in front and archers in the rear.
Thus end the pure [sons].

Infantrymen are on the two wings, horses on the two flanks, elephants at the rear, and chariots in front; or there may be a reversal of this arrangement according to the requirements of the enemy's battle array.
Thus ends the distribution of the two types of forces.
By this, the distribution of the three components of the army is explained.
KAZ 10.5.41: The excellence of the army consists in the strength of its men.

KAZ 10.5.42: Regarding elephants and horses, the specific qualities are lineage, breed, spirit, maturity, vitality, stature, speed, brilliance, skill, steadfastness, courage, tractability, and the possession of auspicious marks and proper conduct.
KAZ 10.5.43: One should station one-third of the elite troops (sāra) of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants in the center (urasya).
Two-thirds [of the circumference] form the girth and the wings on both sides; the *anuloma* is the second layer, and the *pratiloma* is the third layer.
The *phalgu* [mantra] is recited in reverse order.
In this manner, he should bring everything to its proper application.
By stationing weak forces at the extremities, one becomes a "sweeper" who strikes with speed.

Having placed the core force (*sārabala*) at the front, one should station the secondary force (*anusāra*) in the wings (*koṭi*), the third-tier core force in the rear (*jaghana*), and the weak force (*phalgubala*) in the center (*madhya*).
In this way, it becomes enduring.
Having formed the battle array, however, one should strike with one or two of the wings, flanks, or center,
while the remainder should hold their ground.
That which is weak for an enemy—devoid of elephants and horses, with corrupt ministers, or subject to internal intrigue—he should strike with his own abundant resources.
Or else, he should strike the enemy's most vulnerable point with twice that amount of strength.
Whatever limb of one's own is weak, that one should augment with much.
One should deploy the army close to that side where the enemy's weakness lies,
or from that direction where danger may arise.

KAZ10.5.53: Charging forward (*abhisṛta*), circling around (*parisṛta*), charging past (*atisṛta*), retreating (*apasṛta*), seizing by force (*unmathya*), fixing the aim (*avadhāna*), the circle (*valaya*), the cow’s urine pattern (*gomūtrikā*), the circular formation (*maṇḍala*), the scattered formation (*prakīrṇikā*), turning back with the back exposed (*vyāvṛttapṛṣṭha*), following the line of the body (*anuvaṃśa*), [attacking] from the front, from the flanks, or from behind, protecting the broken [unit], and pursuing the broken— these are the modes of horse combat.

KAZ 10.5.54: With the exception of the miscellaneous [stratagems], these same [measures] constitute the destruction of the four constituent elements (aṅgas), either individually or collectively; as well as the breaking of the wings, the flanks, and the center, along with surprise attacks and night assaults—these are "laughable battles" (hasitayuddha).

KAZ 10.5.55: These same types of combat—attacking, retreating, standing one's ground, and engaging in battle—excluding those involving crushing and seizing by force, when conducted on one's own terrain, constitute chariot warfare.
Attacking at all places and times, and the silent strike—these are the modes of combat for infantry.
By this rule, one should form arrays (vyūhas) consisting of odd and even numbers of units,
as far as the resources permit, so that they remain symmetrical with respect to their four constituent parts.
Having advanced two hundred bows’ distance, the king should remain in the reserve (*pratigraha*).
Therefore, he should not fight without a reserve, for that would prevent the reintegration of broken ranks.
(On the formation of the staff, wagon, circle, and detached arrays; and the stationing of counter-arrays.)
The wings, the center, and the reserve constitute the division of the array according to the school of Uśanas.
According to Bārhaspatya, the two wings, the two flanks, the breast, and the reserve constitute the army.
KAZ10.6.03: The *daṇḍa*, *bhoga*, *maṇḍala*, and *asaṃhata* are the natural battle arrays (*prakṛti-vyūha*) for both wings, flanks, and center.
In that case, the punishment shall be one of transverse movement.
The enjoyment [of property] by all [members of the family] together constitutes their inheritance.
The *maṇḍala* (circle) is the movement of those who are advancing in every direction.
For those who remain stationary, operating in separate divisions is the detached formation.
The *daṇḍa* (the army) is that which operates with equal strength through its wings (*pakṣa*), flanks (*kakṣa*), and center (*urasya*).
That which has passed beyond the thicket is a ravine.
That same [wrestler], having advanced with his flanks and armpits, is the *dṛḍhaka*.
That very same person, when he has transgressed against both factions, becomes unbearable.
Having fixed its wings and passed over the breast, it is the hawk (śyena).
In the reverse case, there are Cāpa, Cāpakukṣi, Pratiṣṭha, and Supratiṣṭha.
Saṃjaya was the one with the bow as his wing.
That same [victory] when it has passed beyond the chest is called *atikrānta-vijaya*.
One with thick ears and broad sides is called *sthūṇākarṇa*.
The *viśālavijaya* has pillars twice as thick as those of the *pakṣa* type.
The commander of the army should advance against the enemy when his own side has been tested for its strength.
In the opposite case, it is the mouth of a crocodile.
A staff with vertical lines is called a *sūcī*.
Two *daṇḍa*s make one *valaya*.
Four [kinds of kings] are difficult to conquer.
Thus end the arrays of the army.
Bhoga is that which proceeds unevenly by means of the wings, the flanks, and the center.
It may be either a *sarpa-sārī* or a *go-mūtrikā*.
That [formation] with paired flanks and staff-like wings is the *śakaṭa* (cart).
In the opposite case, it is Makara.
A cart strewn with elephants, horses, and chariots is called the *pāripatantaka*.
Thus end the arrays for enjoyment.
When the wings, the flanks, and the center act in unison, it is the *maṇḍala* (circular) array.
That [fort] has openings on all sides and is auspicious in every respect.
The eightfold army is difficult to conquer.
Thus end the circular battle arrays.
From one who is unallied, he should win over those who are unallied among the allies, the supporters, and the core troops.
By arranging the five divisions (anīkas) into specific formations, that array becomes either the Vajra or the Godhā.
For four [cubits], the *uddhānaka* or *kākapadī* [should be used].
For three [māṣas], it is an *ardhacandraka* or a *karkaṭakaśṛṅgī*.
Thus end the arrays of uncombined forces.
The *rathaurasya*, *hastikakṣa*, *aśvapr̥ṣṭha*, and *ariṣṭa* [are the four types of phalanxes].
Infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants follow behind, forming an immovable array.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry follow behind in an unimpeded manner.
Of these, he should cause a *pradara* to be struck down by a *dṛḍhaka*,
a *dṛḍhaka* by an *asahya*, and a *śyena* by a *cāpa*.
Pratiṣṭha with Supratiṣṭha, Sañjaya with Vijaya, and Sthūṇākarṇa with Viśālavi jaya.
The *pāripatantaka* [is performed] with the *sarvatobhadra*.
With the *durjaya* array, one should counter-array against all [the enemy's formations].

Among infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants, one should cause each preceding unit to be destroyed by the succeeding one; likewise, a unit with fewer components should be destroyed by one with more components.
One lord of ten *aṅgas* is a *patika*;
one lord of ten *patikas* is a *senāpati*; and one lord of ten of those is a *nāyaka*.

He, however, by means of the sounds of musical instruments and the display of standards and banners, shall establish signals for the divisions of the battle array—regarding their separation, their concentration, their halting, their marching, their turning back, and their striking.
When the battle arrays are equal, victory results from the application of the essential factors of place, time, and resources.
By means of mechanical devices, secret applications, sharp assassins stationed in ambush, illusions, alliances with deities, carts, and elephants used for intimidation;
By inciting traitors, by driving off herds of cattle, by setting fire to the camp,
by striking at the rear of the enemy's flank, or by sowing dissension through spies disguised as envoys.
“Your fort has been burnt or captured; your subordinate kinsman has risen in revolt, or a forest-dwelling enemy [has attacked]”—with such words he should cause agitation in the enemy.
An arrow discharged by an archer may kill one person or may not kill anyone at all;
but an intellect directed by wisdom can destroy even those in the womb. (Means of Sowing Dissension – Secret Punishment)
Of the gains from an army, a friend, or a fine, the gain from an assembly is the best.
For assemblies, because they are united, are invincible to their enemies.
He should win over those who are well-disposed through conciliation and gifts, and subdue those who are ill-disposed through dissension and force.
The guilds of Kāmbojas, Surāṣṭras, and Kṣatriyas, and others, subsist by means of both trade and weapons.
The Licchivikas, Vṛjikas, Mallakas, Madrakas, Kukuras, Kurus, Pañcālas, and others are those who subsist on the title of "king."

KAZ11.1.06: Secret agents stationed near all the factions, having identified the grounds for mutual suspicion, hatred, enmity, and quarrels, should instigate a gradual division by saying, "That person is slandering you."
KAZ11.1.07: Thus, for those who are bound by resentment on both sides, spies disguised as teachers should instigate childish quarrels over matters of learning, arts, gambling, or athletics.

Or, in brothels and taverns, fiery spies should incite quarrels among the leaders of the corporations and their followers by praising those of the opposite caste, or by winning over factions through the use of secret agents.
They should encourage the princes who have undergone inferior training by means of superior training.
They shall prevent those of superior status from sharing a single vessel or marrying with those of inferior status.
Or they may unite those of lower status with those of higher status in the sharing of a single vessel or in marriage.
Or, those who have fallen away may be reinstated to an equal status based on their lineage, their personal merit, or a change in their position.
They should investigate a settled legal case by means of a counter-verification.
Or, during disputes over property, cattle, or persons, fiery spies should incite quarrels at night by means of violence against property, cattle, or men.
In all instances of conflict, the king, having supported the weaker party with treasury and army, should employ them for the destruction of the opposing side.
Or he should cause those who have broken away to be led away.
And on the land, he should settle them for cultivation in groups of five families or ten families.
For those who are capable of wielding weapons should be stationed in one place.
And in the event of their assembly, he should establish a penalty for their transgression.
One should establish a noble person of royal lineage who has been confined or cast out by those bearing the title of king in the status of a prince.
And his group, consisting of fortune-tellers and others, should proclaim his possession of royal marks among the assemblies.
And he should instigate the most virtuous leaders of the guilds, saying: "Adopt your own duty toward the son or brother of that king."
When they have submitted, he should send wealth and troops for the purpose of winning over the faction of those who were previously hostile.

At the time of the festival, spies disguised as vintners should offer hundreds of liquor jars mixed with the juice of *madana*, under the pretext that they are for the funeral rites of their sons or wives, claiming they are "for the libation" (*naiṣecanika*).
At shrines, temples, gates, and guard posts, secret agents should display deposits of ritual objects along with gold and signet rings, as well as vessels of gold.
And when crowds are seen gathering, they should announce, "These belong to the king."
Now, one should employ a sudden assault.
Or, having seized the transport animals and gold from guilds for a fixed period, he should bestow well-known property upon the head of the guild.
When they ask for that, he should say: "It was given to such-and-such a principal person."
By this, the division of the army into divisions (skandha), camps (āvāra), and forest-garrisons (aṭavī) is explained.
A secret agent should cause the son of a guild leader, or one who is self-important, to believe: "You are the son of such-and-such a king;
you have been placed here out of fear of an enemy."
Having secured the one who has submitted with treasury and army, the king should cause him to exert his prowess against the confederacies.
Once his purpose has been achieved, the king should also banish him.
Prostitutes' keepers, or acrobats, actors, dancers, and jugglers, being employed as spies, should intoxicate the leaders of the corporations with women of supreme beauty and youth.
Having instilled desire in one of them, they should provoke quarrels by either going elsewhere or by carrying her off by force.
In a quarrel, the assassins (tīkṣṇas) should carry out their work so that people say, "This lover was killed in this manner."
Or, approaching a man who has been deceived but is forgiving her, a woman should say: "That chief [husband] of mine harasses me, for whom you have conceived a desire;
as long as he lives, I will not remain here. Thus, she should incite him to kill him.
Or, if she has been forcibly abducted in a forest or in a pleasure-house, he should have her slayer killed at night by a sharp assassin (tīkṣṇa), or kill him himself with poison (rasa).
Then he should proclaim: "My beloved was killed by this man."

Or, having gained the confidence of one who has conceived a desire [for her], an accomplished spy, after living with her using aphrodisiacs for the purpose of conversation, should deceive him with poison and depart.
When he has departed, the secret agents (sattriṇaḥ) should falsely accuse him of being an enemy's agent.
Wealthy widows, women living in concealment, or women skilled in arts and magic, disputing over inheritance or deposits, may cause the leaders of the guilds to become intoxicated;
likewise, women of the Aditi or Kauśika clans, or female dancers and singers.
The *tīkṣṇas* (assassins) shall kill those who have been identified as having entered secret houses for nocturnal meetings, or they shall seize them after binding them.
Or a secret agent (sattrī) may instigate a leader of a corporation who is lustful for women, saying: "In such-and-such a village, a poor family has emigrated;
his wife is worthy of a king—take her!"

Once she has been apprehended, after half a month, an agent appearing as a perfected ascetic (siddha-vyañjana) shall proclaim in the midst of the leaders of the seditious group: "This leader of yours is violating my wife, daughter-in-law, sister, or daughter."
If the corporation should suppress him, the king, having taken him under his protection, should employ him against those who act contrary to their interests.
When [the enemy] has not been captured, the sharp agents (tīkṣṇas) should cause those who are accomplished spies (siddhavyañjanas) to depart at night.
Then, those who share his caste characteristics should shout out: "This man is a slayer of a Brahmin and a paramour of a Brahmin woman!"
Or a fortune-teller disguised as an astrologer may describe to one man a maiden already betrothed to another, saying: "This man's daughter will become the wife of a king and give birth to a king;
obtain her by means of all your wealth or by force."
If she cannot be obtained, he should incite the rival party.
When [the woman] has been obtained, the quarrel is settled.
Or a female mendicant may say to a man’s favorite wife, "That chief of yours, intoxicated by his youth, sent me to your wife;
out of fear of him, I have come here taking this letter and these ornaments;
your wife is innocent."
"Something must be done against him in secret;
I too shall take action."

In such cases of grounds for quarrel, whether a conflict has arisen spontaneously or has been instigated by *tīkṣṇas*, the king, having supported the weaker party with treasury and army, should cause it to attack those who are disaffected or have them expelled.
In the same manner as [the conduct] toward assemblies, a single king should behave toward [other] kings.
And likewise, confederacies should protect themselves from these [rulers] against overreaching by a single king.

The chief of a corporation, acting with justice toward the corporations, being beneficial and beloved, self-controlled, accompanied by capable men, and conforming to the will of all, should remain [in office]. (The Duties of an Envoy)
KAZ12.1.01: A weak king, when attacked by one who is stronger, should remain submissive in every respect, adopting the nature of a reed.
"He indeed bows to Indra who bows to one stronger than himself," so says Bhāradvāja.
KAZ12.1.03: He should fight with the entire collection of his forces.
For valor indeed destroys calamity.
"Moreover, this is the specific duty of a kṣatriya:
victory or defeat in battle," said Viśālākṣa.
"No," says Kauṭilya.
Subservient to everyone everywhere, like a pet sheep, he lives without hope for his life.
And fighting with a small army, he perishes like one without a boat plunging into the ocean.
But one who has taken refuge with a king superior to him should strive to make his own fortress impregnable or his position invincible.
There are three types of aggressors: those who act out of righteousness, those out of greed, and those out of a desire for conquest.
By their submission, however, the one who conquers through righteousness is satisfied.
He should descend upon him,
even out of fear of his enemies.
But one who conquers through greed is satisfied by the seizure of land and property.
He should assist him with wealth.
One who seizes land, property, sons, wives, or life becomes a conqueror of the Asuras.
Having secured him with land and wealth, one who cannot be captured should take countermeasures against him.
If any one of these rises up [in revolt], he should counter it by means of peace-making, war of intrigue, or treacherous warfare.
He should win over the enemy's faction by means of conciliation and gifts, and his own faction by means of dissension and force.
Secret agents should destroy his fort, kingdom, or camp by means of weapons, poison, and fire.
He should cause his rear guard to be secured from all sides.
Or he should cause the kingdom to be destroyed by forest tribes, or he should cause it to be seized by a scion of that family or by a prince in rebellion.
And when his injuries have reached their limit, he should dispatch a messenger to him.
Or, he may make peace without having caused any injury.
Even so, as he is departing, one should request a treaty for him involving a quarter-part increase in treasury and army, or an increase of one day and night.
If he should request an alliance involving troops,
one should give him inferior elephants and horses, or those that have been encouraged [to fight] but are mixed with poison.
He should request a treaty with the person;
he should provide him with the force of seditious persons, enemies, and forest tribes, commanded by secret agents.
He should act in such a way that there may be the destruction of both.

Or he should provide him with the force of assassins (*tīkṣṇa*) which, when insulted, would revolt; or he should provide him with hereditary troops (*maula*) or those who are loyal, which would strike him down in times of calamity.
He should request a treaty involving the treasury;
he should give him the essential wealth which he cannot find a buyer for, or base metals and goods unfit for war.
He should request a land-peace treaty;
he should give him land that is recoverable, constantly hostile, lacking in support, or situated in a region requiring great loss and expense for its settlement.
Or, he should seek peace with a stronger king by offering his entire property, excluding the royal capital.
KAZ12.1.32ab: Whatever another may seize by force, one should restore that by means of stratagem;
KAZ12.1.32cd: one should protect one’s own person rather than wealth, for what compassion can there be for wealth that is impermanent? (Secret War)
If he does not abide by the treaty, one should say to him: "These kings, having fallen under the sway of the six enemies, have perished;
you ought not to follow the path of those who lack self-control."
Consider both dharma and artha.
For those who persuade you to violence, unrighteousness, and the transgression of your interests are enemies with the faces of friends.
It is a rash act for brave men who have sacrificed their own lives to fight;
it is unrighteous to cause the destruction of people on both sides; and it is a transgression of one's purpose to abandon a visible benefit, a friend, and one who is not at fault.
Moreover, that king is possessed of allies,
and by means of this objective he will further incite those allies so that they shall attack you from every side.
Neither the middle king nor the neutral king has been abandoned by the Circle of States,
yet you have been abandoned; for they look on with indifference while you are striving, thinking, "Let him be further burdened with loss and expense,
and let him be alienated from his ally."
"Then, having abandoned its root, we shall easily uproot it."
"Your Honor ought not to listen to those enemies with the faces of friends;
you ought not to cause your friends to tremble or to bring your enemies prosperity,
nor should you expose yourself to danger to life and calamity"— with these words, he should restrain him.
Nevertheless, he should cause provocation of the enemy's subjects while he is establishing himself, as explained in the sections on the conduct of corporations and the subversion of allies.
And the employment of sharp poisoners and assassins.
Regarding what was stated concerning the "self-protected" [fortress], one should employ fierce agents and poisoners there for the purpose of protection.
Keepers of prostitutes should intoxicate the leaders of the army with women of supreme beauty and youth.
When a desire for a single woman arises among many men, or between two principal rivals, the fierce spies should incite quarrels among them.
In the event of a quarrel, they should urge the defeated party toward fleeing elsewhere or toward providing assistance for their master’s military expedition.

Or, acting under the influence of passion, spies disguised as perfected ascetics (siddhavyañjana) may cause poison to be administered to the principal officials by means of aphrodisiac herbs for the purpose of deception.
Or, under the guise of a merchant, he should shower wealth upon a maidservant in close attendance to the king's favorite queen for the sake of winning her favor, and then abandon her.

A person disguised as an accomplished ascetic (*siddha-vyañjana*), instructed by that very same spy disguised as an attendant (*paricāraka-vyañjana*), should give him a love-charm herb (*sāṃvadanikī oṣadhī*) with the instruction: "It must be applied to the body of a merchant's wife (*vaidehaka-śarīra*)."
Once this is accomplished, he should also instruct Subhagā in this same practice, saying: "It must be applied to the person of the king."
Then, one should overreach him by means of wealth.
Or a fortune-teller disguised as a courtier should tell a high official, who has been gradually won over, that he possesses the marks of a king.
His wife, acting as a female mendicant, says to her: "You shall become the wife of a king or the mother of a king."
Or, a woman disguised as a wife may say to a high official: "The king intends to take me into his harem; this letter and this ornament have been brought for you by a female wanderer."
Or, a cook or a chef acting as a spy may, for the purpose of administering poison, simulate a royal command and represent some desirable object of gain to him.
A spy disguised as a merchant should report this to him and announce the successful accomplishment of the task.
In this manner, by means of one, two, or three methods, he should employ each of his high officials individually for the purpose of attacking or for escaping.

And in his fortresses, secret agents stationed near the *śūnyapāla* (the officer in charge of the vacant city) should proclaim among the citizens and country-folk under the pretext of friendship: "The soldiers and officials have been told by the *śūnyapāla*: 'The king has fallen into great distress; he may yet return alive, or he may not.'"
"Acquire wealth by force, and slay your enemies!"

When this has become widespread, the fierce agents should incite the citizens at night and strike down the principal officials, saying: "In this manner are those treated who do not obey the city-governor."
And in places guarded by sentries, they should leave behind weapons, wealth, and bonds smeared with blood.
Then the secret agents (sattrins) should report: "The guardian of the empty city is causing [the enemy] to be killed and plundered."
In this manner, they should cause the country folk to be divided from the collector-general.

But having killed the men of the *samāhartṛ* at night in the midst of the villages by means of assassins (*tīkṣṇa*), they should say: "In this manner are those punished who oppress the people through unrighteousness."
When a fault has arisen, they may cause the protector of the vacant land or the collector-general to be killed by inciting the anger of the subjects.
They should install someone of that same lineage, or one who has been deposed.
They should burn the inner apartments, the city gates, and the stores of goods and grain,
or they should kill those [guards], or they should utter cries of distress on his behalf.
(The slaughter of the army commander— inciting the circle of states.)

Spies stationed near the king and his favorites should report to the leaders of the infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants—those who stand in the position of friends through the king’s trust—that "the king is angry. They should convey this to those who occupy the status of allies.

When this has become habitual, the fierce agents, having arranged for the countermeasures against their nighttime movements, should say to the people in their houses, "Come at the command of our master."
They should strike them as they are actually departing,
and they should say to those who are nearby, "This is the master's command."
And those who have not been sent away, the secret agents (*sattrin*) should say to them: "This is that which we told you;
one who wishes to live must escape."

And regarding those from whom the king has been requested but does not give, secret agents (sattrins) should say to them: "The king has informed the governor of the frontier: 'So-and-so and so-and-so are requesting from me things that should not be requested; they have been rejected by me because they are allied with the enemy.
Exert yourself in their removal.'"
Thereafter, one should perform [the rites] as previously described.

And regarding those from whom the king has been requested and who have given, the secret agents (*sattrin*) should say: "The guardian of the empty [fortress] was told by the king: 'Such-and-such and such-and-such are requesting from me things that should not be requested; for the sake of establishing trust, I have given that wealth to them. They are allied with the enemy."
"Exert yourself in their deliverance."
Then he should perform [the rites] as before.

And those who do not ask him for the object that should be requested, the secret agents (sattrins) should say to them: "The guardian of the treasury has been told by the king: 'So-and-so and so-and-so do not ask me for the object that should be requested; what else could it be but their fear of some fault on their part?
Exert yourself in removing that [fear] from them.'"
Thereafter, one should proceed as previously described.
By this, the entire category of persons capable of performing a deed is explained.
Or, when he is nearby, the secret agent should cause the king to believe: "This and that high minister of yours is conversing with the enemy's men."
Once he has agreed, the king should show him the seditious persons who are carrying his orders, saying, "This is that very thing."
Or, having enticed the leaders of the army and the principal officers with land or gold, he should cause them to attack his own people or cause them to desert.

KAZ 12.3.15: To whichever of his sons resides near him or in a fort, he should have a secret agent instigate him, saying: "You, my son, are more endowed with personal excellence; yet you remain hidden. Why do you neglect this? Seize power by means of valor!"
"Before long, the young king will destroy you."
Having enticed a person of that same lineage or one who has been deposed with gold, he should say to him: "Crush his internal force, his border-garrison, or his frontier."
Having won over the forest tribes with wealth and honor, he should have them strike down his [the enemy's] kingdom.
Or he should tell the rear-attacker (pārṣṇigrāha) of that king: "This king, having destroyed me, will surely destroy you;
seize his rear!
When he has turned back toward you, I shall seize his rear for you."
Or he should say to his allies: "I am your bridge;
when I am broken, this king will sweep you all away;
therefore, let us join together and frustrate his expedition."
He should send word to those who are united as well as those who are disunited: "This king, having uprooted me, will exact service from you;
take heed!
I am better able to assist you."
One should send [an envoy] to a middle king or to a neutral king, so that by surrendering everything, there may be liberation from one who is nearby.
(The employment of weapons, fire, and poison; the destruction of supplies, the core, and the foraging parties.)
And those of his who are disguised as merchants in the fortresses, as householders in the villages,
and as cowherds and ascetics at the borders of the countryside;
They should send ahead messengers to the neighboring vassals, forest-dwellers, members of that king's own family who have been deposed, and others, announcing: "This country is to be seized."
And when these secret agents have arrived at the fort, they should honor them with wealth and respect and show them the vulnerabilities of the constituent elements of the state.
Among them, they should strike together with those [allies].
Or, at his camp, a spy disguised as a vintner, having stationed a son who has been bribed, should, at the time of an assault, cause him to be expelled by means of poison;
then, under the pretext of a "consecration offering," he should provide hundreds of jars of liquor mixed with *madana* juice.
On one day, he should give either pure liquor or liquor for washing the feet; on the subsequent day, he should provide that which has been prepared with flavoring substances.
Or, having given pure liquor to the chief officers, he should provide it to them at the time of intoxication once it has been prepared with flavoring agents.
Or, an agent disguised as a chief official may [accuse him], saying "this is my abandoned son"; the rest is the same [as previously described].

Or, those dealing in cooked meat, boiled rice, cakes, and sweetmeats, having announced a special variety of their merchandise, may, through mutual rivalry, invite others by proclaiming it to be available for a specific time or at a lower price, and thus cause their own goods to be exchanged for [the others'] by means of flavor.

KAZ12.4.09: Or, women and children, having taken liquor, milk, curd, clarified butter, or oil from the hands of those dealing in such goods, should pour them into their own vessels containing flavored liquids.
"At this price,
or let something more distinguished be given," they should say, scattering [the coins] right there.
These same persons may be employed as spies disguised as merchants, or they may be those who bring goods for sale at a market.
KAZ12.4.12: Those stationed nearby should provide fodder and pasture for elephants and horses according to their specific requirements.
Or spies disguised as laborers may sell fodder or water treated with poison.

Or, cow-merchants who have been long associated with them may, at times when cattle are liable to stray, release herds of cows, goats, or sheep, as well as vicious horses, donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and the like, into places where the enemy is likely to be confused.
Or, disguised as those [same persons], they may have their eyes smeared with the blood of a muskrat.
Or, spies disguised as hunters might release wild beasts from their cages;
or snake-catchers might release snakes of virulent venom; or elephant-keepers might release elephants.
Or those who live by fire may set fire to it.
Or secret agents may strike down the leaders of the infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants who have turned their backs, or they may set fire to the dwellings of these leaders.
