Spies disguised as seditious persons, enemies, or forest-dwellers, having been dispatched, should carry out an attack on the rear or seize the enemy's reinforcements.
Or, hidden in the forest, they may draw out the enemy's rear guard and strike it, or they may attack the enemy's supplies, reinforcements, and foraging parties on a narrow path.
Or, having given a secret signal during a night-battle, they should strike their trumpets loudly and say, "We have entered;
the kingdom has been won!"
Or, having entered the royal residence, they should kill the king during moments of confusion.
Or, as they advance from all sides,
spies disguised as Mlecchas, forest-dwellers, or soldiers on patrol— whether stationed in ambushes or concealed in watchtowers— should strike them down.
Or, spies disguised as hunters may strike them during the confusion of a sudden assault by employing the tactics of concealed warfare.

Or, at a single pass, they should strike [the enemy] by means of their own local forces in a place that is mountainous, obstructed by pillars, enclosed by fences, or filled with water where frogs live.
Or they may cause flooding by the force of breaking dikes of rivers, lakes, ponds, or embankments.
Or they should destroy those stationed in desert forts, forest forts, or lowland forts by means of fire and smoke.
One who has fallen into a narrow pass [is killed] by fire;
one who has gone into a desert by smoke;
and one who has entered a storehouse by poison.
They should have sharp agents eliminate him while he is immersed in water by means of predatory aquatic creatures or water-dwellers,
or while he is fleeing from his dwelling set on fire.
By means of the stratagem of conciliation (*yoga-vāmana*), the stratagem of application (*yoga*), or by any other stratagem,
one should overreach the enemy when he is attached to the aforementioned types of territory.
(Stratagem for Overreaching— Overreaching through Force— Victory by One’s Own Power)
In the case of a sacrifice to the gods,
a journey, or an enemy, there are many occasions for receiving honors out of devotion.
In that regard, he should apply his effort toward this.
For one who has entered the temple of a deity, he should cause a stone or a hidden wall to fall upon him by releasing a mechanical device.
A shower of stones or weapons should be released from the upper chamber;
or a door-panel should be let fall,
or a crossbar fixed against the wall or fastened at one end should be released.
Or he should cause images of deities, bodies, banners, or weapons to fall upon him.
Or, on the ground where he stands, sits, or walks, one should cause the sap to flow by smearing it with cow-dung, sprinkling it with scented water,
or by offering flowers and powders.
Or he should cause a sharp smoke, concealed by fragrance, to enter it.
One should cause him to enter a pit with a stake or a trap-door beneath his bed or seat, by releasing a pin that holds the floor of the mechanism in place.
Or, when an enemy is close at hand, he should lead the people from his territory to a place capable of providing defense.
And from the fort, he should remove those who are incapable of being restrained,
or send them to the enemy's territory as objects to be reclaimed.
And he should establish a single district in mountain, forest, or river fortresses, or in places separated by wilderness tracts, under the protection of his sons or brothers.
The causes for siege have been explained in the section on the conduct of one who has submitted to punishment.
He shall cause grass and wood to be burned within a radius of one yojana.
And he shall pollute the waters and cause them to flow away.
One should cause artificial wells, hidden pits, and thorny bushes to be dug up outside.
Having constructed a tunnel with many openings in the enemy's location, he should cause the seizure of the enemy's stores or the chief officers, or even the enemy himself.
Or, when a tunnel has been employed by the enemy, he should have a ditch dug near the water's edge,
or a well-house, or a series of rooms along the wall.
One should place water-jars or bronze vessels at suspicious locations for the purpose of identifying the excavation site.
Once the path of the tunnel is known, one should have a counter-tunnel constructed.
Having pierced it in the middle, one should provide smoke or water.
Or, having fortified his own fort, he may leave a portion of his forces at the base and march toward an unfavorable direction for the enemy;
or he may join forces with allies, kinsmen, or forest-dwellers, or with the enemy's own enemies, seditious persons, or powerful individuals;
or, having gone there, he may effect a separation between the enemy and his allies, seize his rear, cause him to lose his kingdom, or block his supplies, reinforcements, and foraging parties.
Or he may strike him by means of a sudden assault, like a gambler throwing the dice; or he may protect his own kingdom or increase its fundamental strength.
Or he may go from wherever he might obtain the desired peace treaty.

Or, those who have set out with him may send word to him: "This enemy of yours has fallen into our hands; under the pretext of merchandise or some grievance, send us gold and a core force of troops, so that we may hand him over to you either bound or exiled."
Once he has agreed, the king should collect gold and a force consisting of the best troops.
Or the frontier guard, having led a portion of the army into the surrender of the fort, may cause it to be slain when it has become trusting.
He should cause an enemy force to be drawn into a region where the population is concentrated or located in a single place, in order to destroy it.
Having led him to a secluded place, he should have him killed once he has become confident.
Or, an agent appearing as a friend should send word to the enemy outside: "Grain, oils, alkali, or salt is exhausted in this fort;
it will enter this place at such a time and season;
therefore, seize it."

Then, traitors, enemies, forest tribes, or others who have been abandoned by their own side should cause grain, oil, alkali, or salt impregnated with poison to be introduced [into the enemy's territory].
By this, the seizure of all types of merchandise and transport loads is explained.
Or, having made a treaty, he should give him a portion of the gold while delaying the remainder.
Then he should cause the protective measures to be removed.
Or he should strike with fire, poison, or weapons.
Or he should favor those favorites of his who receive gold [as bribes].
Or, being utterly exhausted, he should surrender his fort to him and depart.
He should escape by means of a tunnel, or through a breach made in the belly [of the wall], or by breaking through the rampart.
Having launched a night assault, one who succeeds should remain;
one who does not succeed should withdraw by a side route.
Under the pretext of being a heretic, he should depart with a small retinue.
Or, disguised as a corpse, he may be carried away by secret agents.
Or, one who assumes the dress of a woman may follow the deceased.
Or, during offerings to the gods, ancestral rites, or festive gatherings, one may distribute food and drink infused with poison.
Having instigated a conspiracy through spies disguised as traitors, he should emerge with secret troops and strike.
Having thus captured the fort, he should establish a sacred tree (*caitya*) as a sacrificial offering and remain hidden, having entered a hollow in the image of a deity,
or behind a concealed wall, or within an underground chamber containing an image of a deity.
If [the enemy] has forgotten [the danger], one should enter the royal residence by night through a tunnel and kill the sleeping adversary.
Or, having disassembled the mechanism, he should cause it to fall down once it has been detached.
By means of a mixture of lac and fire, one should set on fire an enemy who is lying down in a house or a lacquer dwelling that has been smeared with it.

In any one of the pleasure gardens or recreation areas, when the king is intoxicated, assassins who have entered through underground chambers, tunnels, or secret passages in the walls should kill him; or else, spies stationed in hiding may kill him with poison.
Or, while he is sleeping in a confined space, secret women should release snakes, poison, fire, or smoke upon him from above.
Or, when a cause has arisen, whatever may be appropriate, that he should employ through secret agents once the enemy has entered the inner apartments.
Then he should depart secretly and establish himself under the guise of his own kinsmen.

Having summoned the gatekeepers, the umbrella-bearers, and other secret agents stationed by the enemy through signals given by musical instruments, one should cause the remaining enemies to be slain. (Subversion)

KAZ13.1.01: A conqueror desiring to seize another's territory should encourage his own side and intimidate the enemy's side by proclaiming his possession of omniscience and a connection with the gods.

The demonstration of omniscience, however, consists of: the rejection of high-ranking officials through knowledge of the secret activities within their households; the public exposure of those who act hostilely toward the king through the discovery of spies engaged in the removal of "thorns" (enemies); and the proclamation of one's own wisdom and the means for reporting [to the king] by means of secret associations, specialized sciences, signs, and so forth.
Knowledge of events abroad was obtained on that very day by means of a house-pigeon carrying a sealed message.

KAZ13.1.03. As for the disclosure of association with deities: [this consists of] conversing with and worshipping those disguised as fire-deities, shrine-deities, or deity-images who have entered through the openings of underground tunnels;
or conversing with and worshipping those disguised as Nāgas or Varuṇa who have emerged from the water.
At night, having placed a casket of ocean sand within the water, there is the appearance of a garland of fire;
[there is] standing on a raft held by a stone-sling,
[and] with a bladder of water.

Or, with the head covered by the placenta and the nose [stuffed], one may administer oil that has been processed a hundred times (*śatapākyam tailam*) as a nasal application (*nastaḥ prayoga*), using the fat of spotted deer, intestines, crabs, crocodiles, porpoises, or otters.
By means of that, he performs the series of nights.
Thus end the rules concerning water-consumption.
By them [the Nāgas], there shall be the performance of the words of the Varuṇa-nāga maidens and conversation with them; and in instances of anger, they shall emit fire and smoke from their mouths.

In his own territory, astrologers, fortune-tellers, soothsayers, experts in the Purāṇas, physiognomists, and secret agents shall act as his assistants and publicize his visions. In the territory of his enemy, they shall proclaim his visions of deities and the appearance of divine treasure and military forces.
In matters of divination, omens, the science of crows, bodily marks, dreams, and the cries of wild animals and birds, they should proclaim victory for him and the opposite for his enemy.
They should display a meteor accompanied by the sound of drums to the enemy under an auspicious constellation.
Spies disguised as envoys, presenting the enemy's principal ministers as friends, should speak of the honors shown to their own master,
the strengthening of their own side’s forces, and the repulsion of the enemy’s side.
They should report that the security and welfare of the ministers and the armed troops are equal.
Among them, he should apply himself to observing their misfortunes and successes, as well as honoring their offspring.
By that means, he should incite the enemy's faction as previously described.
And we shall speak further on this matter.

By means of a common donkey, he should drive out those who are clever; by means of beating with sticks and branches, those who move about with staffs; and by means of a domestic ram, those who are agitated.

Those whose hopes were shattered by a rain of thunderbolts, by a forest fire, by a swarm of crows, and by a cloud of deceit; those who regarded honors as the fruit of their efforts while they were actually like ornaments on an ill-favored person or like enemies;
and those who were ensnared by tiger skins that were but the snares of death.
By the chewing of a pilu fruit, by a female camel carrying a water-jar, and by the churning of a donkey’s milk—
these are the constant auxiliaries.
He should employ those who have submitted by means of wealth and honor; and he should favor them with gifts of goods and food whenever there are deficiencies in their supplies of goods or food.
They shall present ornaments for women and children to those who do not accept bribes.

During calamities caused by famine, thieves, or forest-dwellers, secret agents (sattriṇaḥ), inciting the citizens and country-folk, should say: "Let us petition the king for favor; without favor, we shall go elsewhere."

When they have agreed, saying "So be it," he should cause them to provide goods and grain through intermediaries; this great success resulting from instigation is known as "the subduing by yoga" (*yogavāmana*).
Shaven-headed or with matted hair, dwelling in mountain caves and claiming a lifespan of four hundred years, he should remain near a city surrounded by many disciples with matted hair.
And his disciples, by bringing roots and fruits, should introduce the ministers and the king to the sight of the Blessed One.
And having met with the king, he should recount the identifying marks of former kings, saying:
"Every hundred years that have passed, I have entered the fire and become a child again;
therefore, here in your presence, I shall enter the fire for the fourth time."
"You must certainly honor me; choose three boons."
He should say to the one who has arrived: "You must stay here for seven nights with your sons and wife, preceded by theatrical performances and festive gatherings."
One should attack during the spring.
Either a shaven-headed man or one with matted hair, appearing as a local ascetic and having many disciples with matted hair,
should smear a bamboo splinter with gold dust and bury it in an anthill for the purpose of tracking a snake’s trail,
or he may use a golden tube.
Then the secret agent should tell the king: "That perfected man knows of a blooming treasure."
When questioned by the king, he should say, "So be it," and he should present that token of recognition,
or else place more gold inside.
And he should say to him: "This treasure is guarded by a nāga; it can be won over by prostration."
He should say to the one who has entered [the fast], "For seven nights," and the rest is the same.

Alternatively, secret agents (sattrins) should report at night to the king that a local spy, carrying a torch and fire and standing in a secluded spot, has been brought before him in due order, saying: "This man is a perfected practitioner of magic."
Whatever matter the king should request of him, he shall perform it for him; the procedure regarding the "seven nights" is the same as before.
Or, one who has mastered the arts of deception may entice the king with the magical sciences of the Jambhakas.
The king [should deal] with him in the same manner as previously described.

Or, one disguised as an accomplished ascetic (*siddha-vyañjana*), having taken refuge in a highly honored local deity, should repeatedly associate with the leaders of the constituent elements through invitations and, by degrees, bring about the king's downfall. Or, spies should report to the king that Varuna or the King of Nagas— disguised as a matted-haired ascetic or a dweller in the waters, entirely white, and appearing in a tunnel, a subterranean chamber, or an underground passage— has been gradually led before him.
The king shall deal with him in the same manner as previously described.
A resident on the frontier of the enemy's territory, or one disguised as an accomplished ascetic, should incite the king to a meeting with the enemy.
Having made an effigy of the enemy who has surrendered and having summoned him into it, one should have him killed in a confined place.
Spies disguised as merchants arriving with horse-merchandise may invite the king— who is either occupied with examining the merchandise or surrounded by horses— and kill him,
or strike him with the horses.

Or, having climbed a sacred tree (*caitya*) near the city at night, fiery spies (*tīkṣṇas*), blowing through reeds or hollow tubes into jars, should speak indistinctly: "We shall eat the flesh of the master or his chief officers;
let our worship proceed!"
Therefore, their astrologers, fortune-tellers, and spies should publicize these [omens].
Or, at night, near an auspicious pool or in the middle of a tank, men disguised as *nāgas*— anointed with *tejana* oil— shall crush iron *śaktis* and maces while speaking in that same manner.

Or, wearing coats of bear-skin and emitting fire and smoke, assuming the form of *rakṣasas*, they shall circumambulate the city three times counter-clockwise and speak in that same manner during the howling of dogs and jackals.
Or, having set fire at night to a shrine, a deity, or a statue using either *tejana* oil or a fire concealed by a layer of clouds, they should report it in the same manner.
Others shall report that matter.
They shall cause excessive bleeding from the images of deities or from those who are highly honored by means of blood.
Others say that in such a case, when there is a flow of divine blood, it portends defeat in battle.
On the nights of the conjunctions, or at the entrance to a cremation ground, they should cause a sacred tree (caitya) to appear as if inhabited by men who have been devoured from above.
Then, assuming the form of a Rakshasa, he should beg from the man.
And whoever among those who boast of their heroism or anyone else should come here to look on, others shall strike him with iron clubs so that it may be known he has been killed by demons.
Spies who have witnessed it should report that marvel to the king.

Then, spies appearing as astrologers and fortune-tellers should declare: "Otherwise, a great misfortune will befall both the king and the country," and they should prescribe propitiatory rites and expiatory ceremonies.
When he has agreed, they should say: "The king himself must perform, for seven nights, the offering of oblations with each of these mantras."
Thereafter, it is the same as before.
Alternatively, having demonstrated these applications within himself, he should perform them for the sake of instructing others.
Thereafter, he should employ the various stratagems.
Or, he may effect the accumulation of treasury by means of countermeasures against the application of spies.
Or, forest-keepers of elephant preserves may entice one who desires an elephant with a well-characterized elephant.
Having led him into a dense forest or a narrow path accessible to only one person, they should have him killed,
or having bound him, they should carry him off.
By this, the case of one who desires to hunt is explained.
KAZ 13.2.42: Spies should entice one who is greedy for wealth or women by means of wealthy widows or women of supreme beauty and youth, presented under the pretext of being inheritance or deposits.
KAZ 13.2.43: Once he has agreed, spies disguised as members of the *sattra* should kill him with weapons or poison at the place of their meeting during the night.

Or, when [the enemy] frequently visits perfected ascetics, monasteries, stūpas, or images of deities, sharp agents— having entered underground chambers, tunnels, or climbed up walls— should strike him down.

In whatever regions the king himself attends various spectacles, or where he delights in excursions and pastimes, or plays in the water; ||| KAZ13.2.45ab/ yeṣu deśeṣu yāḥ prekṣāḥ prekṣate pārthivaḥ svayam / KAK13.2.45cd/ yātrā.vihāre ramate yatra krīḍati vā^ambhasi //
In all cases involving words of reproach and the like, or at sacrifices and invitations; during the birth of a child, death, or illness; or in times of joy, grief, or fear;
or when one falls into negligence due to confidence during a family celebration—[in these instances, the king may take action].
Wherever his movement is unobserved by guards— on a cloudy day, in tumultuous crowds,
in a deserted place, in a conflagration, or even when he has entered a secluded spot—
he may leave behind baskets of garments, ornaments, and garlands, as well as beds and seats.
Accompanied by drums and carrying the dregs of liquor and food,
the assassins (tīkṣṇas), together with those previously stationed there, should strike the enemy;
and they should enter the enemy's camp for the purpose of a sacrificial session (sattra) just as they would otherwise enter.
And in this very manner they should depart; thus has the "Yoga-deception" (yogavāmana) been described.
(On secret agents: KAZ 13.3.01: He should cause a trusted chief of a guild to go forth [as a spy].
Relying upon that supreme [ally] under the pretext of taking his side, he should secure the acquisition of assistants who will act as intermediaries from his own territory.

Or, having carried out the deployment of secret agents (*apasarpas*) and gained the enemy's confidence, he should strike the enemy’s seditious village, his cavalry and elephants, his seditious ministers, his army, or his ally, and send the head to the sovereign.
Or, he should seek refuge with a portion of the enemy’s territory, a guild, or a forest tribe (*aṭavī*) for the purpose of securing allies.
Having gained the master's confidence, he should send him [messages].
Then the master, under the pretext of a tethering post for elephants or a raid on a forest settlement, should strike in secret.
By this, the ministers and forest-dwellers are explained.
Having established friendship with an enemy, he should cause his own ministers to fall into disfavor.
They should send word to that enemy, saying: "Propitiate our master."
Whichever messenger he may dispatch, he should reproach him, saying: "Your master is alienating me from his ministers;
you must not come here again."
Then, he should cause one minister to go into exile.

Having taken refuge with the enemy, he should incite to rebellion against the enemy those who have escaped from imprisonment, those who are disaffected, seditious persons, the weak, thieves, forest-dwellers, or those who harm both sides.

Having gained the confidence of a frontier governor, a forest chieftain, or a commander of an army, he should cause the destruction of that person's brave men by saying: "Such-and-such a man and such-and-such a man are firmly allied with your enemy."
Then, afterwards, he should have them executed by means of forged edicts.
Or, having incited an enemy through the use of force or legal proceedings, he should have him killed.
Or, by winning over the faction of those who favor a course of action, he should cause an enemy king of the other to inflict injury upon himself and then attack him.
Then he should send a message to the other: "This enemy of yours is harming me;
come, let us join together and slay him, and the land or the gold shall be your possession."
Having honored the enemy who has arrived after surrendering, one should cause him to be slain by the enemy himself, either through a surprise attack or in open battle.
To inspire confidence, he should cause [the enemy] to be seized under the pretext of granting land, the consecration of a son, or protection.
Or, if he is impossible to overcome, he should have him killed by means of secret punishment.
If he should pay the fine but not come in person, the king shall have him executed by an enemy.
Or, if he wishes to advance with force rather than with one seeking victory, he should nevertheless cause him to be destroyed by means of pressure from both sides.

Or, if one who is distrustful should wish to march alone, either individually or with a portion of the kingdom, desiring to seize a part of the enemy's realm, even so, he should have him slain by an enemy or by the entire combined force.
Or, when one is beset by an enemy, he should cause the enemy to carry off his base (the treasury) elsewhere by means of applying force.
Or he should bargain with a friend for the enemy's territory,
or with an enemy for the friend's territory.

Then, in the desire to seize the enemy's territory, one should cause harm to oneself by means of a friend and then launch an attack; all these strategic applications are identical to those previously described.
Or, he should support with an army an enemy who has agreed to his desire to seize the territory of a friend.
Then he should overreach the one who has gone over to the ally.
Or, having prepared his defenses, he may feign his own misfortune, incite the enemy against the ally, and thus cause the enemy to attack himself.
Then, by means of oppression, he should have him killed, or else, by taking him alive, he should effect an exchange of kingdoms.

If an enemy, having sought refuge with a friend, should wish to remain in a position from which he cannot be seized, the friend should cause his base to be destroyed by means of neighboring kings and others.
Or, if he should wish to protect him by means of punishment, he should have that [offender] executed.
If those two do not break apart, he should openly bargain with each other for their respective territories.
Then, either spies disguised as friends or double agents should send messengers to one another, saying: "This king of yours, allied with the enemy, desires your territory."
Whichever one of the two suspects that the other has harbored suspicion or resentment should act as previously described.
Or, having publicly proclaimed that the chiefs of the fort, the countryside, and the army are on the side of the enemy through the employment of subversive means, he should cause them to be exiled.
They should deceive the enemy by means of sudden attacks in battle, breaches of siege lines, or during times of calamity.
Or they should create dissension between him and his own factions.
They should cause those who have been branded with the mark of a criminal to be brought back by means of forged edicts.

Or, spies disguised as hunters, by selling meat at the gate while relying on the gatekeepers, may report twice or thrice to another that a band of thieves has arrived; having gained his confidence, they shall station their master’s army in two divisions and, during a village massacre or a sudden assault, say to the enemy: "The band of thieves is close at hand."
"Let there be a great outcry; let a vast army come forth! he said.

Having delivered that [message], the army—leaving behind the force intended for the punishment of a village raid—should take up another position and say at night at the gates of the fort: "The band of thieves has been slain;
this army has arrived with its mission accomplished;
let the gate be opened."
Or those previously stationed there may open the gates.
They should strike together with them.
He should station spies disguised as artisans, craftsmen, heretics, actors, or merchants, or as soldiers, within the enemy's fort.
Among them, those disguised as householders should bring weapons and armor on carts loaded with wood, grass, grain, and merchandise,
or under the guise of divine banners and images.
Then, those disguised as commoners should announce with the sound of conchs and drums from behind, "He has entered," by means of a murderous assault, a surprise attack, or a frontal charge;
they should effect the breaching of walls, gates, and watchtowers, or the breaking up of the enemy's ranks, or their slaughter.

KAZ13.3.48: The passage of spies may be facilitated by those living in caravans or guilds, by escorts, by those who transport brides, by those dealing in horses for sale, by carriers of equipment, by buyers and sellers of grain, or by those bearing the marks of ascetics; they may also act as messengers for the purpose of establishing trust in the execution of a treaty.
Thus end the king's secret agents.
These same persons are the spies for forest-dwellers, as well as those mentioned in the section on the removal of thorns.
Spies should cause a herd of cattle near a forest or a caravan to be attacked by thieves at a place called *vraja-aṭavī-āsanna*.
Having arranged a secret signal and having provided food and drink there that has been infused with *madana* juice, they should depart.
Cowherds and merchants, having seized the loads of plunder from those thieves at a time when they are affected by the intoxication of *madana* juice, should attack them.

Or, one disguised as a Saṃkarṣaṇa devotee, appearing as a shaven-headed ascetic or one with matted hair, might deceive [the enemy] by means of a festive gathering through the application of intoxicating juice.
Now, he should launch a sudden assault.

Or, a spy disguised as a vintner, at festivals, divine rites, funeral ceremonies, or public assemblies, should deceive the forest tribes by means of the administration of intoxicating liquor under the pretext of selling wine;
then, he should launch a sudden assault.

Or, having dispersed those who have entered for the purpose of plundering a village, he should cause them to be slain in various parts of the forest; these are proclaimed as the secret agents (*apasarpas*) among thieves. (The act of siege—*avamarda*).
The practice of attending upon [the teacher] is preceded by the act of emaciating oneself.
He should establish the countryside, as it has been settled, in a state of security.
Once it has risen, he should settle it by means of favors or exemptions,
except for one who is fleeing elsewhere.
He should settle them on land other than the battlefield, or have them reside in a single location.
For there can be no kingdom without people, nor a kingdom without a territory, says Kauṭilya.
One situated in a difficult position may destroy a handful [of grain], or the standing crop, as well as the transport and the supplies.
The depletion of the constituent elements of the state arises from the cutting off of trade routes and supplies, from the destruction of standing crops and grain stores,
from the expulsion of subjects, and from secret assassinations.
“KAZ13.4.08 My army is complete with abundant supplies, bound by many virtues, as well as other forest produce, machines, weapons, armor, laborers, and draft animals; moreover,
the season is favorable for us.”

He should wait upon [the enemy] with the thought: "There is a calamity from another; there is the depletion of stores due to disease, famine, and defense; there is weariness with the hired army and weariness with the ally's army."
Having ensured the protection of the camp, the supply lines, and the roads; having surrounded the fort with a moat and a rampart;
and having contaminated the water supply;
Having drained the moats or having filled them [with water],
he should cause the rampart and the wall to be breached by means of a tunnel and a wooden hut,
and the gate by means of a concealed pit.
Or he should cover a depression with a mound of dust.
In a place with many guards, he should have them killed by mechanical contrivances.
Having drawn them out from the gate, they should strike them with horses.
And during the intervals between military expeditions, he should seek success through the application of strategic means by means of their various combinations, options, and aggregations.

Having caused hawks, crows, naptṛ-birds, vultures, parrots, mainas, owls, and pigeons dwelling within the fortress to be captured, he should release them into the enemy's fortress with fire-impregnated devices attached to their tails.
Or, having withdrawn from the camp, one whose protection consists of raised banners and bows should set fire to the enemy's fort with a human-made fire.

Secret agents serving as guards within the inner fort shall attach incendiary devices to the tails of mongooses, monkeys, cats, and dogs, and release them upon stores of firewood, defensive equipment, and residential buildings.
Or, having placed fire inside the bellies of dried fish or within dried meat, they shall cause birds to carry it away by means of offerings to crows.
Sal tree, deodar, pūtī, grass, guggulu, śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, lac, and pellets, as well as the dung of donkeys, camels, goats, and sheep, serve for maintaining the fire.
Powdered priyāla, the soot of avalguja, beeswax, and the dung of horses, donkeys, camels, and cows—this is the incendiary mixture to be thrown [into the enemy camp].

A mixture of all-metal powder heated to the color of fire, or the powder of bell-metal, lead, and tin, combined with the oil, honey, and wax from the flowers of the *pāribhadraka* and *palāśa* trees, human hair, soot, and *śrīveṣṭaka*, constitutes a fiery application (*agniyoga*) that destroys trust.
Coated with that [poison], wrapped in fibers of hemp or *trapusa*, and fitted with an arrowhead—this is the application of fire.
But one should never release fire while there is still prowess available.
For fire is untrustworthy and a source of divine affliction; it causes the destruction of countless living beings, grain, livestock, gold, base metals, and other goods.
And a kingdom, even if acquired, if its stores are exhausted, leads only to ruin.
(Thus ends the section on the duty of attendance.
KAZ 13.4.25: “I am fully equipped with all undertakings, implements, and laborers;
whereas my enemy is diseased, or his subjects are hostile due to secret subversion, or he has not yet completed the construction of fortifications or the accumulation of stores.”
Whether devoid of reinforcements or possessing them, he first forms an alliance with friends; such is the time for subduing.
When a fire has broken out spontaneously or been intentionally set, during a festival, a public spectacle, a military review, a gathering, a debt-related dispute, or a brawl;

when the enemy force is exhausted from constant warfare, its men are worn out by numerous battles and deaths, its people are drowsy from being kept awake or are already asleep, or during foul weather, a river flood, or a thick mist— then one should strike.
Or, having abandoned the camp and hidden in the forest, he may strike the enemy when he has gone out.
Or, an agent appearing as a chief official of a friend's ally, having established friendship with the besieged, should send a disguised messenger with the message: "This is your vulnerability;
these are your seditious subjects," or "This is the vulnerability of the besieger; this is your faction of enemies."
When the envoy returns with that message and departs, the conqueror should seize him, proclaim his offense, banish him, and then withdraw.
Then, an agent appearing as a friend's ally should say to the besieged: "Come out to rescue me, or else join me in destroying the besieger."
Having captured him, he should have him executed by crushing him between two [objects], or he should have him taken alive and exchanged for the kingdom.
Or he should lay siege to and crush his city.
Or, having caused his core strength to be vomited out, he should strike him down.
By this, the treatment of those who have submitted to punishment and of forest-dwellers is explained.
Either the one who has submitted to punishment or the forest-dweller (āṭavika) should send a message to the besieged [king], saying: "This besieger is ill; he is attacked by a rear-enemy;
another opening has arisen."
"I wish to depart for another realm."
When it has been taken over, the besieger, having set fire to the camp, should withdraw.
Thereafter, one should act as previously described.
Or, having brought together a collection of merchandise, one should overreach him by means of that very merchandise infused with poison.
Or, an agent disguised as a reinforcement might send a messenger to the besieged, saying: "The enemy outside has been struck down by me; come out to strike him."
One should treat one who has submitted as before.
Under the pretext of being a friend or a kinsman, secret agents (yoga-puruṣas) carrying royal edicts and seals should enter the fort and cause it to be seized.
Or, a spy disguised as a messenger from a reinforcement force may send word to the besieged: "At such a place and at such a time, I shall attack the camp;
you too must fight."
Having shown the besieged king that the assault was as described and that it was crowded with danger, one should cause him to be killed when he has gone out from the fort at night.
Or, he may invite a friend or a forest-dweller (āṭavika) and encourage him, saying: "Having attacked, seize his territory when it is besieged."

One should have a man who has shown valor killed by the subjects through the instigation of seditious leaders, or kill him himself with poison once the objective is achieved, saying, "This man is a betrayer of his friend."
Or, one disguised as a friend may incite another who desires to attack against the enemy.
Having gained the confidence of the enemy, he should cause his most heroic men to be struck down.
Or, having made a treaty, he should cause this people to settle in a district.
When his people have settled down, he should destroy them unobserved.
Having caused harm to the seditious persons or the forest-dwellers, or having led a portion of his army into them, he should cause the fort to be lost by means of a surprise attack.

Seduced persons, enemies, forest tribesmen, those who hate [the enemy], and those who have fled from him, having been provided with rewards, honors, signals, and tokens, should launch a surprise attack on the enemy's fort.

Having launched an assault on an enemy fort or a military camp, they should grant safety to those who have fallen, those who have turned their backs in flight, those who are overwhelmed, and those who are disfigured by disheveled hair or weapons; and they should grant safety to all who are not fighting.
Having seized the enemy's fortress and purified the faction of the enemy, he should enter it both from within and from without, having arranged for secret punishment as a countermeasure.
In this manner, a seeker of victory, having acquired the territory of the enemy, should seek to win over the middle king; once that is accomplished, he should seek the neutral king.
This is the first way to conquer the earth.
In the absence of both the middle and neutral kings, one should win over the constituent elements of the enemy through the excellence of one's own qualities,
and thereafter the subsequent elements.
This is the second course of action.
In the absence of a circle of states (*maṇḍala*), one should achieve one's purpose by squeezing both sides—using a friend against an enemy, or an enemy against a friend.
This is the third path.
It is possible to win over one neighboring king; with him as an ally, one can win over a second, being twice as strong, and a third, being three times as strong.
This is the fourth way to conquer the earth.
And having conquered the earth, with its social classes and stages of life well-distinguished, he should enjoy it according to his own duty.
Sowing dissension, secret agents, bribery, siege,
and assault— these five are the means for capturing a fort.
(The pacification of what has been acquired.)
The mobilization of one who desires conquest is of two kinds: that consisting of forest tribes and the like, and that consisting of single villages and the like.
And his acquisition is of three kinds: new, previously possessed, and inherited from ancestors.
Having obtained a new gain, one should conceal the faults of others by means of one's own virtues,
and one's own virtues by doubling them.
And he should pursue what is pleasing and beneficial to his subjects through acts that conform to their own duties, by showing favor, by remitting taxes, and by bestowing gifts and honors.
And he should cause the faction of those acting on his behalf to receive what was promised,
especially after they have exerted further effort.
For one who is untrustworthy and deceptive becomes unreliable both to his own people and to others,
and his conduct is contrary to nature.
Therefore, one should adopt a commonality of character, dress, speech, and conduct.
And he should maintain devotion toward the country, the deities, the assembly, festivals, and recreational excursions.
And secret agents should repeatedly point out the transgressions of the enemy toward the leaders of regions, villages, castes, and guilds,
as well as the high status and devotion the sovereign shows toward them,
and the actual honors bestowed by the sovereign upon them.
And he should enjoy them with appropriate provisions for their maintenance, exemptions from taxes, and supervision regarding their protection.

He should cause the worship of all deities and hermitages to be performed; he should grant lands, goods, and tax exemptions to those who are learned, eloquent, righteous, and heroic; and he should effect the release of all prisoners as a favor for the poor, the helpless, and the diseased.
During the Cāturmāsya festivals, there shall be a cessation of slaughter for half a month;
on full-moon days, for four nights; and during royal or national asterisms, for one night.
He shall prohibit the killing of female animals and young ones, as well as the destruction of virility.
And whatever custom he may consider to be detrimental to the treasury or the army, or to be unrighteous, he shall abolish it and establish a legal system of conduct that is righteous.

He should cause those of criminal disposition and of Mleccha origin to change their places of residence, assigning them to various locations, as well as the chiefs of forts, districts, and military forces.
And he should cause the ministers and domestic priests who have been captured by the enemy to reside in various places on the enemy's frontiers.
If those capable of doing harm are wasting away while waiting for the destruction of their master, he should suppress them by means of silent punishment (*upāṃśudaṇḍa*).
He should settle either his own countrymen or those expelled by another king in places where they have been driven out.

And to one who is a member of that same family and capable of recovering what is owed, or to one born of noble lineage who is capable of harassing the enemy situated in the borderlands or forest regions, he should grant land of inferior quality.
Having fixed the payment of treasury and army as one-fourth of that which is possessed of qualities, he might, while providing assistance, provoke the citizens and the country-folk.
When they are provoked, he should have him killed by them.
He should remove one who is censured by his own kinsmen,
or settle him in a region that is subject to affliction.

Regarding one who has returned from exile: he should conceal the natural defect on account of which he was previously dismissed, and he should intensify the quality on account of which he has now returned—thus.
Regarding the paternal estate, one should conceal the father's faults and proclaim his virtues. Thus.

One should cause to be practiced a righteous conduct that has not been performed before, and one should cause others to continue what has already been performed by them. One should not cause unrighteous conduct to be practiced, nor should one allow what has been performed by others to continue if it is unrighteous.
(The Application of Means for Destroying Enemy Forces)
For the sake of protecting the four social orders, one should employ the secret (esoteric) methods against those who are most unrighteous.

The category of poisons, such as *kālakūṭa* and others, shall be introduced into the bodies of enemies by means of trustworthy persons disguised as those from various regions, with appropriate dress, skills, dialects, lineages, and backgrounds; these agents—

whether men or women of Mleccha origin— shall assume the forms of hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the deaf, the mentally dull, or the blind, and administer the poison during the use of another's body for food or other purposes.

In the king's pleasure gardens, armories, treasuries, and in the enjoyment of various articles, secret agents shall conceal weapons; and those who live by trade, night-walkers, and fire-tenders shall conceal fire.

The powder of *citra-bheka*, *kauṇḍinyaka*, *kṛkaṇa*, the five types of *kuṣṭha*, and the *śatapadī*; or the powder of *ucci-diṅga*, *kambalī*, *śatakanda* (or *kardama*), fuel-wood, and *kṛkalāsa*; or the powder of the house-lizard, the blind snake, the *kakrakaṇṭaka*, the putrid insect, and *gomārikā*—when combined with *bhallātaka* and *avalgu-jara*, these cause instantaneous death, as does the smoke produced from them.
Alternatively, a worm or any other [insect] heated with black serpents and priyaṅgu seeds will cause it to dry up;
this formulation is considered to take away life instantly.
The root of *dhāma*, *argava*, and *yātudhāna*, combined with the powder of *bhallātaka* flowers, produces results within half a month.
A powder made from the roots of the *vyāghātakī* plant mixed with the pollen of *bhallātaka* flowers is an insecticide that remains effective for one month.
The rations for men are one unit;
for donkeys and horses, they are double; and for elephants and camels, they are fourfold.

Smoke produced from *śata-kardama*, *uccidiṅga*, *kara-vīra*, bitter *tumbī*, and fish, combined with the chaff of *madana* and *kodrava*, or with the leaves of *hastikarṇa* and *palāśa*, when introduced into a windless place or downwind,
kills everyone within its range as it spreads.

The powder of *pūtikīṭa*, insects, fish, *kaṭutumbī*, *śatakardama*, fuel-wood, and *indrāgopa*— or the powder of *pūtikīṭa*, small *ārālā* insects, gold, and *vidārī*— mixed with the powder of goat horns and hooves,
is a smoke that causes blindness.

Smoke produced from the leaves of the *pūtikarañja*, yellow *tāla* leaves, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *guñjā* seeds, red cotton chaff, *anyāsphoṭa*, glass, and cow dung, ground together with liquid, causes blindness.
The slough of a snake, the dung of cows and horses, and the head of a blind snake constitute smoke that causes blindness.
The urine and excrement of pigeons, water-fowls, and carnivorous animals; of elephants, humans, and boars;

iron sulfate (*kāsīsa*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), barley husks, grain-particles, and rice; the seeds of cotton, *kuṭaja*, and *kośātaka*; cow-urine grass (*gomūtrikā*), the root of *bhāṇḍī*; the broken pieces of neem (*nimba*), drumstick tree (*śigru*), *phaṇirja*, *kākṣīva*, and *pīluka*; and the powder of snake-skin, fish-skin, elephant-claws, and horn.
Thus, this smoke, when produced from the chaff of *madana* and *kodrava*, or from the leaves of *hastikarṇapalāśa*, kills [the victim] as soon as it spreads, even in its individual parts.

Kālī, kuṣṭha, the root of naḍa and śatāvarī, or the powder of sarpa-pracalāka, kṛkaṇa, and the five types of kuṣṭha, when administered as smoke according to the previous method— either with fresh or dried palāla grass— produces blindness in all living beings when used during the onset of battle, in assaults, or in tumultuous crowds, provided that those who have applied cleansing water have treated their eyes beforehand.
The dung of the śārikā, the pigeon, the crane, and the balākā, ground with the juice of *arkākṣi*, *pīluka*, and *snuhi*, is an ointment that causes blindness and contaminates water.

A preparation of *yavaka*, the roots of *śāli* rice, *madana* fruit, and *jātī* leaves mixed with human urine; or a *madana* preparation combined with the roots of *plakṣa* and *vidārī*; or one combined with a decoction of *mūka-udumbara*, *madana*, and *kodrava*; or one combined with a decoction of *hastikarṇa* and *palāśa*.

The formulation of *śṛṅgī*, *gautamavṛka*, *kaṇṭaka*, *ara*, and *mayūrapadī*; the formulation of *guñjā*, *lāṅgalī*, *viṣamūlikā*, and *iṅgudī*; the formulation of *karañja*, *akṣī*, *pīluka*, *arka*, and *mṛgamāraṇī*; or the *madana* formulation combined with a decoction of *kodrava*, or combined with a decoction of *hastikarṇapalāśa*.
Or they may all together corrupt the fodder, fuel, and water.
The smoke of a lizard, a chameleon, a house-lizard, a blind snake, or a *dhūma* [serpent] causes blindness and madness.
The application of a house-lizard and a cricket causes leprosy.
That very [substance], when mixed with various entrails and honey, brings about urinary disorders (prameha);
when mixed with human blood, it causes consumption (śoṣa).
Dūṣīviṣa, the powder of madana and kodrava, and the application of apajihvikā constitute a poison-mixture.
The application of *mātṛvāhaka*, *añjalikāra*, *pracalāka*, *bhekākṣi*, and *pīluka* causes cholera.
A mixture of the five *kuṣṭha* drugs, *kauṇḍinya*, the flowers of the *karāja-vṛkṣa*, and honey causes fever.
A compound of *bhāsana*, *kulajihvā*, and *granthikā*, ground with the milk of a she-ass, causes muteness and deafness within a month or half a month.
KAZ14.1.26: That the men [in the army] receive only a sixteenth part [of the booty] is the same as previously stated.
The administration of medicines may be by means of decoctions of broken plant parts,
or as powders for living beings,
or by administering decoctions of all parts combined.
In this way, it becomes more vigorous.
Thus ends the perfection of yoga.

An arrow prepared with *śālmalī*, *vidārī*, and grain, combined with *mūlavatsanābha* and smeared with the blood of a muskrat (*cucchundarī*), pierces a man; once pierced, he bites ten other men, and those bitten bite ten others.

KAZ 14.1.30: A decoction made from the flowers of the *ballātaka*, *yātudhāna*, *anudhā*, *mārgava*, and *bāṇa* plants, combined with *elaka-akṣi*, *guggulu*, and *hālāhala*, mixed with the blood of a goat and a human, constitutes a poison for biting insects.

KAZ 14.1.31: Half a *dharaṇa* of this preparation, when introduced into water along with parched grain flour (*saktu*) and oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), vitiates a body of water extending for a distance of one hundred bows.
For by this, a succession of fish becomes poisoned when bitten or touched; and whoever drinks or touches this water [is likewise affected].

A lizard smeared with red and white mustard seeds and buried for three fortnights in the ground within a leather water-skin (*uṣṭrikā*), when dug up by one condemned to death, kills everyone whom it sees; or alternatively, a black cobra [acts in the same manner].

A charcoal or flame struck by lightning, or fire taken from wood struck by lightning and perfumed with incense, when offered as a sacrifice through a rite dedicated to Rudra under the asterisms of Kṛttikā or Bharaṇī and then consecrated,
burns irresistibly.
Having brought fire from a blacksmith, one should offer oblations separately with honey;
from a vintner, with liquor; and from a hunter, with clarified butter.
One should extinguish the fire of a woman with only one husband with a garland, the fire of an unchaste woman with mustard seeds,
the fire of a woman who has recently given birth with curd, and the fire of one who maintains the sacred fires with rice grains.
One should not enter the fire of a Caṇḍāla, nor a funeral pyre built with meat, nor one built with human remains.
All [these] together with goat fat, human fat, and *dhruva* [clarified butter].
One should offer oblations with the Agni-mantra using wood from the royal tree (śrīparṇī);
this fire is irresistible and bewilders the eyes of enemies.
Aditi, homage to you;
Anumati, homage to you;
Sarasvatī, homage to you.
O God Savitṛ, homage be to you!
To Agni, svāhā!
To Soma, svāhā!
Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā!

(Deception, therein the production of wonder) KAZ 14.2.01: A powder of *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, and *śamī* mixed with clarified butter constitutes a hunger-inducing preparation that lasts for half a month.
A gruel prepared with *kaśeruka*, lotus-root, sugarcane-root, lotus-fiber, dūrvā grass, milk, ghee, and the scum of boiled rice, is effective for one month.
Or, one may take the powder of *māṣa*, barley, *kulattha*, and the roots of *darbha* with milk and ghee;
or the juice of creepers, milk, and ghee prepared together; or, having drunk the paste of the roots of *sāla* and *pṛśniparṇī* with milk.
Or, having consumed that prepared milk together with honey and ghee, he fasts for a month.

Oil prepared with *Arka* seeds that have been soaked for seven nights in the urine of a white goat, and then kept for a month or half a month in a bitter gourd (*alābu*), causes deformity in four-footed and two-footed creatures.
For one who subsists on buttermilk and barley for seven nights or more, white donkey dung and barley cooked with white mustard oil produces disfigurement.
KAZ14.2.06: For either of these two, *siddhārthaka* oil processed with urine, excrement, and juice, with the addition of the powder of *arkatūla* and *pataṅga*, serves as a means for whitening.
The application of the dung of a white cock and a python is a means for whitening.

White mustard seeds soaked for seven nights in the urine of a white goat, along with buttermilk, the juice of *marka*, milk, salt, and grain, form a mixture that, when kept for a fortnight, causes whitening (*śvetī-karaṇa*).
When bitter gourds have become wrinkled, they should be kept for half a month; when ground with white mustard seeds, this mixture causes the hair to turn white.
The insect known as *alajunā* and the white house-lizard (*gṛhagolikā*):
when these are ground together and applied [to the hair], the hair becomes as white as a conch shell.
For one whose limbs have been rubbed with cow dung or a paste of *tinduka* and *ariṣṭa*, and then anointed with the juice of *bhallātaka*, there is a monthly remedy for leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Guñjā seeds that have remained for seven nights in the mouth of a black snake or in the mouth of a house-lizard constitute a preparation for leprosy.
An ointment consisting of parrot bile and egg-yolk is a formulation for leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
For leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), a decoction mixed with the paste of *priyāla* is the remedy.
One who consumes [a preparation] combined with the roots of *kukkuṭa*, *kośātakī*, and *śatāvarī* becomes fair-complexioned within a month.
Having bathed with a decoction of *vaṭa* and being smeared with a paste of *sahacara*, one becomes black.
Haritāla and manaḥśilā mixed with the oil of śakuna and kaṅgu produce blackening.
A powder of fireflies mixed with mustard oil burns at night.

KAZ 14.2.19: A powder of *kha-dyota* (firefly) and *gaṇḍū-pada* (earthworm), or a powder of marine organisms, or a powder of the flowers of *bhṛṅga*, *kapāla*, *khadira*, and *karṇikāra* mixed with the oil of *śakuna-kaṅgu* and the powder of *tejana* grass; KAZ 14.2.20: Soot from the bark of the *pāribhadraka* tree mixed with the fat of a frog causes the body to burst into flames when touched by fire.
A body smeared with a paste of *paribhadraka* bark and sesame seeds ignites when struck by fire.
A ball made of the soot from the bark of the *pīlu* tree blazes when held in the hand.
An object smeared with the fat of a frog ignites when touched by fire.
A limb smeared with that [substance], sprinkled with the oil of *kuśa*, mango, and fruit, or combined with the powder of *samudramaṇḍūkī*, *phenaka*, and *sarjarasa*, bursts into flames.
Oil prepared with an equal portion of the fat of frogs, crabs, and other such creatures, when used as an ointment for the limbs, causes the fire to blaze up.
A limb smeared with the roots of bamboo and *śaivala* moss, and anointed with the fat of a frog, ignites when struck by fire.

One whose feet are anointed with oil prepared from the paste of the roots of *pāribhadraka*, *prativiṣā*, *vañjula*, *vajra*, and *kadalī*, and processed with the fat of a frog, can walk upon glowing coals.
The *upodakā*, *pratibalā*, *vañjula*, and *pāribhadraka*—
with the root-paste of these, together with the fat of a frog.
One should prepare oil with this; having anointed the feet with it, they become stainless, such that one may walk upon a heap of glowing coals as if upon a bed of flowers.
A reed-lamp tied to the tails of swans, cranes, peacocks, or other large water-faring birds, serves as a beacon of fire at night.
Electrical fire is for the pacification of burns on the limbs.
Beans fed with the menstrual blood of a woman, mixed with the root of *vrajakulī* and the fat of a frog, causes them to cook in a glowing frying pan.
The remedy for the cleaning of the furnace is the following: KAZ14.2.33. Cleaning the furnace is the countermeasure.

A gem made of *pīlu* wood containing fire within, with a knot of *suvarcalā* root or a knot of thread wrapped in cotton, emits smoke from fire when placed in the mouth. Fire sprinkled with oil from *kuśa* and mango fruits blazes even in rain and wind.
Sea-foam mixed with oil floats upon the water and burns.
When fire is produced by friction using a spotted bamboo stick on the bones of those who are floating, it is not extinguished by water;
rather, it blazes up with water.

KAZ14.2.38: Fire produced by friction using a variegated bamboo stick and the left-side rib-bones of a man killed by a weapon or impaled on a stake; or fire produced by friction using a human rib-bone and the bones of a woman or a man—wherever such fire goes three times counter-clockwise, no other fire will burn there.
The *cuccundarī*, the *khañjarīṭa*, and the *khārakīṭa* are ground together and mixed with horse urine; this is the destroyer of fetters.
Or a magnet stone becomes double its size by being smeared with the fat of crabs, frogs, alkaline insects, and *vasā*.

A paste made from the marrow of the *kaṅka* crane, the *bhāsa* vulture, the ribs of a fish, blue lotus, and water-lily, ground with water, is a foot-salve for quadrupeds and bipeds that causes them to become like hell-beings (*nāraka*).
Having smeared sandals made of camel-skin with the fat of an owl and a vulture, and having covered them with banyan leaves, one travels fifty yojanas without fatigue.

The marrow or semen of the hawk, heron, crow, vulture, swan, curlew, and *vīcīralla* enables one to travel a hundred *yojanas*; likewise, the marrow or semen of the lion, tiger, leopard, crow, and owl [achieves the same].
Having boiled the fat of all castes from aborted fetuses or of stillborn infants in a camel-skin bag, that resulting fat is used for a range of one hundred *yojanas*.
One should cause agitation in the enemy by means of undesirable and miraculous portents.
The common saying is that this leads to the loss of his kingdom; thus, provocation is described as being similar [to deception].
(Pralambhana)

In that regard, the application of medicinal mantras (*bhaiṣajya-mantra-yoga*) is as follows: having taken the right and left eyes of one, two, or many of the following—cats, camels, wolves, boars, dogs, sheep, *dvāgulī*, *naptṛ*, crows, owls, or other nocturnal creatures; KAZ14.3.01. Having taken the right and left eyes of one, two, or many of the following—cats, camels, wolves, boars, dogs, sheep, *dvāgulī*, *naptṛ*, crows, owls, or other nocturnal creatures;
One should cause it to be made into powder in two ways.
Then, having rubbed the right [eye] with the left hand and the left [eye] with the right hand, one sees in the night and in the darkness.
Eka-āmlaka, varāhākṣī, khadyota, and kāla-śārivā:
one whose eyes are anointed with these sees forms at night.

Having fasted for three nights, one should, under the asterism of Puṣya, place barley grains in the earth within the skull of a man killed by a weapon or impaled on a stake, and sprinkle them with the milk of a ewe.
Then, having bound a garland of barley sprouts upon himself, he moves about with his shadow and form vanished.
Having fasted for three nights, one should have the right and left eyes of a dog, a cat, an owl, and a bat ground into two separate powders under the asterism Puṣya.
Then, having anointed his eyes accordingly, he moves about, his shadow and form having vanished.
Having fasted for three nights, one who has killed a man should, under the asterism Puṣya, have a probe and a collyrium-stick fashioned from *kāṇḍaka* wood.
Then, having had his eyes anointed with one or another of these eye-powders, he moves about with his shadow and form vanished.
Having fasted for three nights, one should have an ointment-box and an applicator-stick made of iron under the asterism Puṣya.
Then, having filled the skull of any one of the nocturnal creatures with collyrium and having inserted it into the vagina of a dead woman, one should burn it.
Having extracted that ointment under the asterism Puṣya, one should place it in that same ointment-box.
With his eyes anointed by that [ointment], he moves about with his shadow and form vanished.
